en: The *Bhāradvāja Śrautasūtra*, First Praśna: We shall now explain the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). 1. One who is about to sacrifice with the oblation of the new moon (*āmāvāsya*) causes [the cow] to yield milk for the curdling agent (*havirātañcana*) on the previous day, either from one or two cows. 2. Or alternatively, having caused the milk to be yielded in secret two or three days beforehand, he curdles it with that secret curd. 3. They milk continuously and without interruption until the day of the fast (*upavasatha*). 4. On the day when the moon is full, one should observe the fast for that full moon (*paurṇamāsī*). 5. Or rather, when [one knows] "tomorrow it will be full. 6. That day on which [the moon] is not visible is the new moon (*amāvāsyā*).

7. Or [he may think], "It will not rise tomorrow. 8. In this regard, this is the absolute rule: whatever ritual details (*dharma*) are prescribed without specific reference to either the full moon or the new moon day, they are to be performed on both occasions. 9. In rites for the gods (*daiva*), one should remain wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītin*). 10. In rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*), one should wear it over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītin*). 11. One should perform the rites for the gods moving either eastward or northward, keeping them to the right (*pradakṣiṇa*). 12. For the rites for the ancestors, the opposite direction applies. 13. One should not turn away from the sacrificial fire-altar (*vihāra*). 14. One should not circumambulate oneself or another using any part of the sacrificial apparatus.

15. Or, the monastery (vihāra) has its ritual service on the north side. 16. Whenever it is enjoined that "one offers," the Adhvaryu alone should offer with the *juhū* ladle and clarified butter into the Āhavanīya fire. 17. When no specific performer is designated, one should understand the Adhvaryu to be the performer; the Āgnīdhra is the second. 18. Whenever it is enjoined that "one worships" or "one consecrates with a mantra," the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) alone should perform that. 19. Ritual acts have a single mantra each. 20. The mantras are those prescribed at the beginning [of the section]. 1.1.11.1.1.10–21.

The end of the preceding [formula] is joined with the beginning of the following one (1). One should join the commencement of the ritual acts with the ends of the mantras (2). Now, where a mantra may be short and the ritual act long, one should mutter the mantra at the beginning of the act (3). Now, where it is enjoined that "one offers with two" or "one offers with five," one should offer the oblations with each individual mantra (4). Now, where one repeats a ritual act within a constituent part of the sacrifice, the mantra should not be repeated (5). One should offer all the oblations while the fire is indeed blazing (6). He who is about to enter upon a vow goes to fetch a branch.

7. [He takes] a branch of *palāśa* or a branch of *śamī*. 8. That which is turned toward the east and north, or toward the east or north, having many leaves, many branches, with tips that are not dried up and which is not hollow—that he cuts with the formula: "For food (*iṣ*), thee! 9. With "For strength (*ūrj*), thee! he bends it or strokes it. 10. Then he brings it back with the verse: "This food and strength, prepared for me, turned toward the east and north—with its many leaves and undried tips—I bring as a protector of cattle."

Thus [he says]. 11. With that [branch], he drives away six calves, beginning with the youngest, saying: "Ye are for Vāyu; ye are for Upāyu. 12. As many cows as one might fill with milk in a single pot, so great should be the measure of the others. 13. He touches one [cow] with the branch. 14. With that same [branch] he sends forth the cows, saying: "May the god Savitṛ impel you for the most excellent work; swell, O inviolable ones, for Indra who is the portion of the gods. 15. Or, "for Mahendra," if he is a sacrificer to Mahendra. 16. He touches one [cow] with the branch. 17. He consecrates them with a mantra once they have set out.
Drinking pure waters at a good watering-place, yielding [milk] for Indra for a hundred autumns—
may the weapon of Rudra pass you by.

"Thus [are the verses] for Mahendra," or "If he is a sacrificer to Mahendra. 19. 1.2 "May there be many steady cows with this lord of cattle"—with these words, he turns toward the house of the sacrificer. 1. He hides a branch behind the axle of the cart standing nearest the fire, or within the fire-hall, pointing westward, with the formula: "Protect the cattle of the sacrificer. 2. According to some, [he hides it] pointing eastward from behind. 3. "He who knows the house of the Adhvaryu becomes a possessor of a house. From the fourth ritual act onward, he should look forward, thinking: 'I shall do this; I shall do that. These indeed are the houses of the Adhvaryu."

It is known from scripture: "He who knows this thus becomes a householder. 4. Taking a horse's rib, an ox's rib, or a knife, he addresses the Gārhapatya fire with the mantra: "Thou art the announcer of the sacrifice. 5. With the words, "The Rakṣas is burnt away; the enemies are burnt away," he heats the sickle over the Āhavanīya fire. 6. Having stepped forward toward the east or the north with the words, "This prayer has gone forth toward the sacrificial grass," he fetches sacrificial grass made of Darbha from wherever it may be found. 7. The first [blade] he takes with the words, "Thou art Viṣṇu’s tuft."

He releases the stalk; he binds the second one with the formula: "Thou art the binding of the gods; thou art increased by rain. He releases two or three of its joints, for the remainder is the portion of the cows. He takes hold of the stalk with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take hold of the sacrificial grass, the seat of the gods. He cuts it at a joint with the formula: "O divine sacrificial grass, may I not cut thee along the length nor across; may I succeed at thy joint; may I, as thy cutter, suffer no harm. [He cuts] including the nail.

With the words, "O divine sacrificial grass, grow with a hundred shoots," he touches the grass that has been cut. With the words, "May we grow with a thousand shoots," he touches himself. Then he gathers it together with the formula, "Guard against contact with the earth; well-gathered, I gather thee. From this very same sacrificial grass, he makes a cord (*śulba*) consisting of three or five strands. He winds the cord around with the formula, "An unwearied womb art thou. He fastens it with the formula, "Thou art the girdle of Aditi. In this regard, this is the general rule for all cords whatsoever.

Those [ends] that do not meet should be wound around from left to right (pradakṣiṇa). Now, those that do meet, having wound a cord (guṇa) around them from right to left (prasavya), one should join them together from left to right. Having laid down a cord with its tip pointing north, he places sacrificial grass (barhis) upon it with its tips pointing east. At the final knot, saying, "Unharmed is the womb," he places the prastara-bunch upon it. Then he binds it, saying, "The binding for Indrāṇī. He makes a knot, saying, "May Pūṣan tie the knot for you. May it not come loose for you.
Thus he covers it from behind toward the front; according to some, from the front toward the back. Then he takes hold of it [with the mantra]:
"The Waters have smoothed you, the Aśvins have smoothed you, the seven Ṛṣis have smoothed you.
I take hold of the sacrificial grass (barhis), the banner of the dawns, with the rays of the Sun."

15. Thus he lifts it up with the formula: "I lift thee up with the two arms of Indra. 16. He places it upon his head with the formula: "I carry thee by the head of Bṛhaspati. 17. He brings it forward with the formula: "Follow along the wide atmosphere. 18. To the west of the Āhavanīya fire, at the place where the enclosing sticks (paridhis) are laid, he sets it down within the altar (antarvedi), not on the ground, with the formula: "I set thee down in the lap of Aditi. 19. He consecrates the one that has been set down with the formula: "Thou art going to the gods. 20. He places it as if above, in a well-known spot. 1.4.
Of those herbs which were born for the gods in the three ages of old, may I succeed in their joint when I bring the sacrificial strew (paristara).
May the essence of the waters, worthy of sacrifice, belonging to the gods, and auspicious, be mine. May I, your cutter, not come to harm; may I live for a hundred autumns.
I gird myself against the immeasurable with measured means for the sake of good action. May I not fall into any sin whatsoever; rising again, may [my merits] become abundant.

Thus, for the *paristaraṇa* grasses, these are prescribed: the *adhinidhānī*, the *āchedanī*, and the *saṃnahanī*. 1. He prepares a fuel-wood (*idhma*) of twenty-one pieces, made of *pālāśa* or *khādira* wood. 2. According to some, he binds together a fuel-wood of eighteen pieces. 3. There are fifteen pieces of wood for the *sāmidhenī* verses. 4. There are three enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*). 5. They are made of *pālāśa* or *kārṣmarya* wood; they may be dry or fresh, and must have their bark intact. 6. Alternatively, they may be made of *khādira*, *bilva*, *audumbara*, *vaikaṅkata*, or *rauhitaka* wood.

It is known: the largest is the middle one; the southern half is smaller and longer; the northern half is smallest and shortest. (7) There are two *āghāra*-fuel-sticks. (8) The *anūyāja*-fuel-stick is the twenty-first. (9) He prepares the cord (*śulba*) from *darbha* grass—either with roots or without roots—in an odd number of strands, in that same manner. (10) Upon it he collects the fuel-wood (*idhma*).
(11) "Since you, having assumed a black form, entered the trees, therefore I collect you in twenty-one parts, well-collected. (12)
I gather well-prepared the three enclosing-sticks, the three fuel-sticks that follow the life of the sacrifice, the supporting-ladle, the stirring-stick, and the fire-brand.
Thus he girds himself: "Thou art black, dwelling in the mountain ranges."

"O God, come forward; may I attain you," saying this, he conceals the knot from the front toward the back. 14. Then, having placed it so that it does not lie flat, he sets down the well-known wood-chippers. 15. 1.5.

On the following day, having prepared the sacrificial fuel (*idhma*) and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), and having observed the vow, he should perform the full-moon sacrifice on the day of the full moon (1); or he may do so on the previous day for the new-moon sacrifice (2). Furthermore, it is another view that one may act according to his desire regarding the full-moon sacrifice (3). He makes the *veda* grass-bundle out of *darbha* grass, saying: "Thou art the *veda*; as thou, O divine one, becamest the *veda* for the gods, so mayest thou become the *veda* for me" (4). [The *veda*] should have its end shaped like a calf’s knee for one desiring cattle, be made of *mūlaka* grass for one desiring food, and be threefold (*trivṛt*) for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).

They say that the Trivṛt is its head. Some recite the two preceding ritual options as being permanent. Then he cuts off a span’s length from this [branch]. According to some, it is a span’s length from the cord. Having set aside the recognizable tips of the Veda-grass, he causes a portion of Palāśa leaves to be cut from the branch with which he separates the calves, within the sacrificial altar. Having cut the branch from its base, he makes it into the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick), [reciting]: "Thou art the *upaveṣa*; they have held thee as a serving-vessel for the sacrifice."

"Preparing the oblation for Indra, may you be auspicious and effective for us. (10) Then he makes for it a strainer (*pavitra*) made of *darbha* grass, a span in length, consisting of three folds and circular: "You are the strainer of the Vasus, with a hundred streams; you are the strainer of the Vasus, with a thousand streams. (11) He attaches the root to the root and the tip to the tip; he does not make a knot. (12) While it is being made, the sacrificer consecrates it with the mantra:
"The triple-folded *darbha* blade from the *palāśa* tree, measuring a span, May this most excellent purifier in the sacrifice make my milk and oblation pure. (13)

Thus (13) they sweep the fire-houses and smear the sacrificial sites (14); as far as there is gravel, the two *sāṃnāyya* pots are smeared with cow-dung (15); the sacrificer and his wife adorn themselves (16). 1.6.16.1–6.

On the new moon day, when the sun is behind the trees, they perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. Having strewn Darbha grass with tips pointing south and east around the Anvāhāryapacana fire, he washes each of the vessels for the Piṇḍapitṛyajña and sets them out: the wooden sword (sphya), the offering-spoon (sruva), the butter-pot (ājyasthālī), the stirring-ladle (mekṣaṇa), the black antelope skin (kṛṣṇājina), the mortar (ulūkhala), the pestle (musala), the winnowing-basket (śūrpa), and whatever else may be required. The Adhvaryu, wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), pours the grain from the cart onto a pot placed upon a single strainer to the south. Having filled it, he wipes it clean.

Having placed a black antelope skin upon the mortar, the wife stands facing south-east and threshes the grain until it is separated from the husks; she winnows it once and cleans it once. Having cooked it over the Dakṣiṇāgni fire like rice grains still containing their husks, she sprinkles it with clarified butter that has been strained, or with unstrained ghee. To the south-east or north-west of the Anvāhāryapacana fire, having dug up a Vedi altar shaped like a single wooden sword (sphya) facing south-east, and having sprinkled it with water, he strews it with sacrificial grass cut in a single stroke, reciting:
"I bring this sacrificial grass, cut in a single stroke, soft as wool and pleasant, for the sake of the Pitṛs."
May my fathers, worthy of Soma, sit here, along with my grandfathers and great-grandfathers and their followers.
Thus (8). Having placed this *sthālīpāka* on it, and having set down to the south a seat-cushion (*kaśipu*), a pillow (*upabarhaṇa*), collyrium, and ointment, one by one (9). 1.7.9.1.7.

The Adhvaryu, wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), having bent his right knee, takes a portion from the *sthālīpāka* with the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), pours clarified butter over it, and offers the first oblation, saying: "To Soma, drunk by the ancestors, svadhā! Adoration! (1). He offers the second oblation, saying: "To Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the ancestors, svadhā! Adoration! (2). He offers the third oblation with whatever grains remain on the stirring-spoon, saying: "To Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt, svadhā! Adoration! (3). He places the stirring-spoon silently into the fire (4). He draws out a single burning brand from the Dakṣiṇa fire, [saying]: "Those who... (ye rūpāṇi).

"Releasing themselves, being *asuras*, they move by means of the *svadhā* offering; may Agni drive away from this world those who carry off the *parāpur*s and the *nipur*s. (5) The sacrificer, having bent his left knee and wearing the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), pours three handfuls of water onto the single wooden sword (*ekasphya*), saying: "O [Name], pour down for your father! "O [Name], pour down for your grandfather! "O [Name], pour down for your great-grandfather! (6) Right there, mentioning their names, with his hands turned downward and ending toward the south, he places three rice-balls (*piṇḍas*).

Now, if the name of the relative is not known, he should offer the first *piṇḍa* with the formula: "Svadhā to the fathers dwelling on earth! the second with: "Svadhā to the fathers dwelling in the intermediate space! and the third with: "Svadhā to the fathers dwelling in heaven! Having silently placed the fourth *piṇḍa*, and having said, "O fathers, rejoice here according to your respective portions," he turns away. He waits until the heat has subsided; once the heat has subsided, he turns back toward the *piṇḍas*, or he may turn back before the heat has subsided.

"O Soma-loving ancestors, you have rejoiced," [he says]. (4) Having turned around, he smells what remains in the vessel, [saying], "Bestow a hero upon us, O ancestors. (5) It is known from tradition that it should be eaten by one who is ill, eaten by one who desires food, and eaten by one who, though capable of eating, does not eat; by such a person it should be eaten. (6) In the same manner, having poured out handfuls of water, he gives ointment and oil for anointing, [saying], "Anoint yourself, so-and-so!"

"Anoint this," he says three times over each ball of rice (7). Having cut off a lock of hair or a fringe of the garment, he offers it [to the ancestors] with the verse: "These, O fathers, are your garments; depart from us, O fathers, do not cling to us" (8). One should have his hair cut during the latter part of his life (9). Having cut it, he worships with the *namaskāra* formulas, beginning with "Homage to you, O fathers, for the sake of sap" and ending with "May I be the most excellent among them" (10). Then he causes the fathers to rise with the verse: "Arise, O fathers, go forth, O heroes, follow the path of Yama."

"May he bestow upon us wealth and that which is auspicious; may he announce us as sharers among the deities"—with this [verse] (RV 10.15.4), he causes the ancestors to depart. He dismisses them with the verse, "Depart, O Soma-loving ancestors" (RV 7.35.11). He worships [the fire] with the three verses beginning with "Manasvatī," namely, "We invoke the mind hither" (RV 10.58.1–3). 1.9.11–13.

He throws back the firebrand with the verse: "Jātavedas has been our messenger for the oblation; having made the offerings fragrant, he has carried them away. He has given them to the fathers, and they have eaten them with the *svadhā* call. Knowing the way, O Agni, come back again to the gods. (1) He returns with the verse addressed to Prajāpati: "O Prajāpati... (2) With the *paṅkti* verse, "That which is in the intermediate space, on earth, and in heaven," he worships the Gārhapatya fire. (3) Having cast the once-cut grass-bundle into the fire and sprinkled it with water, he places the vessels used in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña in pairs.

He offers a counter-example: 4. One should cast the rice-balls into water, or feed a Brāhmaṇa, or throw them into the fire. 5. With the mantra, "Those ancestors who are equal and of one mind in the realm of Yama—for them let there be a world, *svadhā*, obeisance; may the sacrifice be prepared among the gods," he throws the first rice-ball. 6. "Those kinsmen who are equal and of one mind, living among the living, who belong to me..."

"May their prosperity be ordained for me in this world for a hundred years"—with these words, he offers the other two [piṇḍas]. (7) Or the wife eats the middle piṇḍa. (8) "A male child is indeed born," so it is known. (9) "O Fathers, bestow a fetus, a boy wearing a lotus-wreath."

"Just as here in the world of the fathers, may you live a long life" is the formula prescribed for the consumption [of the remnants]. (10) The Piṇḍapitṛyajña is thus concluded. (11) This rite is ordained in exactly this manner even for one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), with the exception of the worship of the Gārhapatya fire. (12) One view is that he should bring another fire to take the place of the Gārhapatya. (13) Another view is that he should worship whichever fire he offers the oblation into. (14) In that case, the word "Gārhapatya" would be omitted because its consecration (*saṃskāra*) is prohibited. (15) 1.10

Then he gives the command: "Strew around [the fires]! Enclose the fire! May the enclosed fire protect the sacrificer. May these gold neck-ornaments, the essence of the waters and the plants, be for the sacrificer as wish-granting cows in yonder world, in that place. 2. Then he strews around the fires with *darbha* grass, both the front ones and the back ones, with their tips pointing eastward. 3. Or rather, those at the rear and the front have their tips pointing northward. 4. On the southern wing, the tips are upward; on the northern wing, they are downward. 5. To the south of the *Āhavanīya* fire...

He prepares the seats for the Brahman and the sacrificer: the eastern one for the Brahman and the western one for the sacrificer. On the day of the full moon, the sacrificer himself performs the Agnihotra. On that night of the new moon, not even his children drink milk. Having performed the Agnihotra with barley-gruel on this night, he sets aside the remnants of the Agnihotra as the curdling agent for the oblation. Having washed the Sāṃnāyya vessels, he places them in pairs: the cooking pot and the milking vessel to the north of the Gārhapatya fire.

The branch-strainer (*śākhāpavitra*), the fire-stirring stick (*upaveṣa*), the rope for the sacrificial post (*abhidhānī*), the two cords for the post (*nidāne*), and whatever else he may require. 11. Having poured water into the *agnihotra*-ladle across the strainer, he purifies it three times with the tips pointing northward, using the *gāyatrī* verse "May the god Savitṛ purify you" (*devo vaḥ savitotpunātu*) line by line. 12. Then he consecrates them, beginning with "O divine waters, you who purify first" (*āpo devīr agrepuvaḥ*) and ending with "You are sprinkled" (*prokṣitā stha*). 13. He sprinkles the vessels for the *sāṃnāyya* offering after turning them face upward. 14. 1.11.

"Be purified for the divine rite, for the sacrifice to the gods," he says three times. (1) Then he heats these [implements]: "The Rakṣas is burned away; the evildoer is burned away. (2) Then he awaits the cows as they approach: "These come hither, yielding honey, possessing offspring, glorious, and of every form; becoming many as they are born again—may Indra cause you, O cows, to rest here. (3) Having taken the halter with the words, "Thou art the girdle of Aditi," he fastens it on the calf with the words, "Thou art Pūṣan."

"Ye are Pūṣan," he says, or rather [he says] "all of you. Then he says, "Announce to me when she has been approached. He consecrates her when she has been approached with: "Free from disease, I unite you with offspring; becoming abundant, may you increase through the nourishment of wealth. He consecrates her as she sits down with: "Swell with strength, milk, and ghee; living, may I sit beside you who are living. Then he issues the command: "Do not pass between the separation and the cow that has been approached. They do not pass between while she is being milked.

9. And if he should pass by the sacrificial hall, he should say, "May the *sāṃnāyya* offering not be spoiled. 10. Having taken up the fire-stirring stick (*upaveṣa*) with the formula, "Thou art the bold one; grant us spiritual power (*brahman*)," he draws out embers from the *gārhapatya* fire towards the north with the formula, "The danger from enemies has been driven away. 11. Upon them he places the cooking pot (*kumbhī*) with the formula, "Thou art the heat (*gharma*) of Mātariśvan. 12. Then he surrounds it with embers from the right (clockwise) with the formula, "Be heated by the austerity of the Bhṛgus and the Aṅgirases. 13. Then he places the branch-strainer (*śākhāpavitra*) upon it with its tip pointing eastward.

"You are the purifier of the Vasus, with a hundred streams; you are the purifier of the Vasus, with a thousand streams. (14) 1.12. Having taken hold of the pot together with the two strainers, he restrains his speech. 1. He remains seated, maintaining [the flow]. 2. He consecrates the sound of the stream with the mantra: "They milk the fountain, the four-holed jar, the divine Iḍā, honey-sweet and finder of heaven."

"O Indra and Agni, quicken that which is full of truth; may that establish the sacrificer in immortality. (3) While the milk is being milked, he consecrates the drops with: "The drop is offered, the speck is offered. (4) Having finished milking, he carries [the vessel] away. (5) He asks him: "What have you milked? Tell us, O Indra-like one, the sacrificial food that provides power. (6) Or, "For Mahendra," if he is a sacrificer to Mahendra. (7) He pronounces the name [of the cow]: "That one in whom the milk of gods and men is deposited. (8) He consecrates her with: "She is all-life. (9)

He pours [the milk] through the strainer into the pot with the formula: “May the god Savitṛ purify you with the strainer of Vasu, which has a hundred streams and is well-purifying. (10) While it is being poured, he consecrates the drops with the formula: “The drop is offered, the speck is offered. (11) He causes the other two cows to be milked in exactly the same manner. (12) He consecrates the second cow with: “She is all-encompassing”; the third with: “She is the maker of all. (13) When the three have been milked, he releases his speech with the formula: “May she yield much; may Indra swell again the oblation for the gods.”
"May it be fit for the calves, for men, and for milking again. He utters this three times. Or he says, "O Mahendra," if he is a sacrificer to Mahendra. 1.13.14–15.

Having uttered the formula and without touching [the cow], he causes the other [cows] to be milked silently; he pours the rinsing water into the pot with the words, "Be united, O you who are rich in nectar! (1). Having cooked it, he removes it from the fire toward the north, as if dragging it, with the words, "May the cows be firm, may the lord of the cows be firm; let not your sacrificer be harmed! (2). According to some, [he removes it] toward the east; according to others, toward the northeast. (3) Having made the bottom cool, he mixes it with curds, saying, "With Soma I mix thee, for Indra, the curds! (4). Or, "for Mahendra," if he is a sacrificer to Mahendra. (5)

He brings the remnant of the *agnihotra* [with the formula]: "Thou art the continuity of the sacrifice; I continue thee along with the continuity of the sacrifice. (6) Having brought the remnant of the *agnihotra*, one should bring curd—so says Āśmarathya. Having brought curd, one should bring the remnant of the *agnihotra*—so says Ālekhana. (7) If he should not find the remnant of the *agnihotra*, he should cause it to coagulate with rice grains. If he should not find rice grains, he should cause it to coagulate with herbs. (8) "O Waters, be watchful among the oblations, as you are watchful among the gods."

"Thus, be watchful for the sacrificer in this sacrifice"—with these words, having poured water into the lid, he covers [the vessel] with a wooden bowl or a metal bowl containing rice, saying: "Thou art unassailable; I cover thee for Viṣṇu, for the sacrifice, with water from a non-empty vessel—those waters which lie purified around. 9.1.14.

One should not cover [the vessel] with something made of clay. If one should cover it with something made of clay, one should place a blade of grass or a piece of wood in between before covering it. Having covered it, he sets it down so that it is not on the ground, saying: "O Viṣṇu, protect the sacrificial offering. In the same manner, at night, he drives away the calves for the morning milking. Or rather, he may drive away the calves for both milkings during the afternoon itself. Having placed the potsherds, he causes the morning milking to be performed as in the case of the evening milking. This much is the difference.

He places the strainer with its tip pointing upward. He does not anoint it. It is known from scripture: "One who has not performed the Soma sacrifice should not perform the *sāṃnāyya* offering. According to some, however, he should perform it. Some prescribe the *sāṃnāyya* for Indra; others prescribe it for Mahendra. Those who sacrifice to Mahendra are: one who has heard much [Vedic learning], a village leader, a nobleman, an Aurva, a Gautama, and a Bhāradvāja. They, having established their sacred fires (*agnīn*) from the very beginning, should sacrifice to Mahendra. Now, others are those who sacrifice to Indra. If one who sacrifices to Indra should desire to sacrifice to Mahendra...

On the following day, having strewn grass around the fires as before, and having washed his hands with the formula, "May I be able for you two, for the work, for the gods," and having rinsed the vessels, he arranges them in pairs—ten on the west and ten on the east: the wooden sword (sphya) and the potsherds; the Agnihotra-ladle and the winnowing basket; the black antelope skin and the yoke-pin; the mortar and the pestle; and the lower grinding stone and the upper grinding stone, to the north of the Gārhapatya fire. Then the dipping-spoon (sruva), the Juhū-ladle, the Upabhṛt-ladle, the Dhruvā-ladle, and the Prāśitra-vessel.

And the *ājyasthālī*, the *veda*, the *pātrī*, the *praṇītāpraṇayana*, and the *iḍāpātra*—these he places to the north of the *āhavanīya* fire. The remaining vessels, including those for the morning milking (*prātardoha*), are placed at the end according to their availability. The *sruva* ladle and the *sphya* are made of *khadira* wood; so too the *śamyā* and the *prāśitraharaṇa*. The *juhū* is made of *parṇa* wood; the *upabhṛt* is made of *aśvattha* wood.

The *dhruvā* and the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle are made of *vaikaṅkata* wood. (5) The *sruva* ladles are one span (*prādeśa*) long, or one cubit (*aratni*), or one forearm (*bāhu*) long; they have hollows for the skin, their handles are rooted [in the bowl], their spouts are shaped like an elephant’s trunk, or they have tails like a crow’s, or they have pouring-spouts at the top of the mouth. (6) Regarding those [materials] for which no specific tree has been prescribed, Āśmarathya says that they may be made from any tree fit for sacrifice. (7) 1.16

"Made of *vaikaṅkata* wood," says Ālekhana; "they should be made of *vāraṇa* wood for purposes other than the oblation," for it is known: "Therefore, a sacrificial error is made of *vāraṇa* wood; one must not, however, offer with it. Starting from the *gārhapatya* fire, he spreads a continuous line of *ulapa* grass blades pointing eastward as far as the *āhavanīya* fire, saying: "Thou art the continuity of the sacrifice; I spread thee for the continuity of the sacrifice; for the continuity of the sacrifice, I spread thee. At this point, the *brahmán* priest enters. Two *darbha* blades, a span in length, cut evenly at both ends from the sacrificial grass, serve as the *pavitra* strainers.

He recites: "You two are purifiers; you belong to Viṣṇu; may Vāyu purify you with his mind. (6) Having placed a blade of grass or a piece of wood between [the blades of grass], he cuts them, but not with his fingernail. (7) Then he wipes them with water, saying: "You two are purified by the mind of Viṣṇu; you two belong to Viṣṇu; you two are purified by Vāyu. (8) Then he consecrates them with the mantra: "These two are the out-breath and the in-breath, the limbs of the sacrifice in their entirety. (9)

"May they move about, swelling [the waters], the two purifiers that cleanse the oblation. (9) With the formula, "For service thee," he takes the *praṇītā* water-vessel and washes it with the formula, "Thou art made of wood; be purified for the gods. (10) It is known from tradition: "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should have the water led forth with a vessel of *kāmsya* metal; one desiring cattle, with a *godohana* vessel; and one desiring stability, with an earthen vessel. (11) 1.17.

Having sat down to the north of the Gārhapatya fire, he pours water into a vessel over which a strainer has been placed, saying: "Who takes you? Let him take you. While taking the water, he meditates upon this [earth] with his mind. Having filled the cup to the brim and purified it three times with two strainers whose tips point northward, he consecrates it as previously described. He addresses the Brahman priest, saying: "O Brahman, I shall lead forward the waters; O Sacrificer, restrain your speech. While leading forward the *praṇītā* waters, he restrains his speech until the call for the *haviṣkṛt*.

Born together with Brahman, sustaining the vital breaths and not spilling [the water], he takes it up with the wooden sword (sphyá) or without taking it up, saying: "Who leads you? May he lead you. O divine waters, I lead you forth; may they establish the sacrifice for us."

"Gladdening, dripping with ghee, flowing with water, descending upon the sacrificer for thousandfold prosperity"—with this, he mutters the mantra mentally. (6) To the north of the Āhavanīya fire, he places the *praṇītā* waters, saying: "Who yokes you? Let him yoke you. (8) Having covered them with *darbha* grass and taken up the two strainers (*pavitra*), he touches the vessels, saying: "May the divine hosts sit together; the vessels for the sacrifice to the gods. (9) "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee; thou art made of wood. (10)

Thus he takes up the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle with the formula, "For the impulse, thee" (10); the winnowing basket with, "For the impulse, thee" (11); and having stepped forward with, "Follow the wide atmosphere," he heats them over the *āhavanīya* fire with, "The Rakṣas is burnt away; the enemies are burnt away" (12). 1.18.12.

He addresses the sacrificer: "Sacrificer, I shall pour out the oblation. The sacrificer replies: "Om, pour it out. If the sacrificer should be away on a journey, he should say: "O Agni, I shall pour out the oblation. Having stationed a cart behind the Gārhapatya fire with its pole pointing eastward and having placed the grains for the sacrificial cakes upon it, he touches the right yoke-halter with the mantra: "Thou art the yoke; injure him who injures us. He does the same for the left one. Having touched the left pole with the mantra: "Thou art the most bountiful of the gods," [he proceeds].

He mutters: "May Viṣṇu step upon thee" (TS 1.2.13g). He places his right foot upon the northern wheel. He mounts [the cart] with: "Thou art the unshakable oblation-holder" (TS 1.2.13h). He gazes at the circumference with: "I gaze upon thee with the eye of Mitra" (TS 1.2.13i). Having uncovered [the space] with: "Wide open for the wind," he sits inside the cart, recites the *Daśahotṛ* formula, and, having poured handfuls of rice or barley into the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle with: "May the five restrain thee," he pours them out into the winnowing basket across the strainers with: "Of the god Savitṛ... (TS 1.1.4a).

‘At the impulse of the Aśvins, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I pour out what is pleasing to Agni’—with this *yajus* he pours out three handfuls, and the fourth silently. (10–11) When the portions have been poured out, he pours the remaining grains after them for the sake of providing a portion for the *bhakṣas*. (12) In the same way he pours out the subsequent sacrificial cake: ‘for Agni and Soma’ at the full moon sacrifice; ‘for Indra and Agni’ at the new moon sacrifice for one who does not offer the *saṃnayya*. (13) Now, if he should pour them out into a vessel, having placed the wooden sword (*sphya*) to the south, he should mutter all the formulas pertaining to the cart over that vessel. (14) 1.19

"This belongs to the gods," he says, touching the portions that have been set aside. "This [belongs] to us together," he says over that from which he has taken out [the portion]. Taking up the oblation with the words, "For prosperity, not for misfortune," he goes forth, saying, "Here do I release myself from the noose of Varuṇa. He gazes toward the sacrificial ground with the words, "May I behold the light of Vaiśvānara, the sun. He descends with the words, "May the dwellings of heaven and earth be made firm. He brings [the oblation] forward with the words, "Follow along the wide mid-region. He places it down behind the Āhavanīya fire.

"I set thee down in the lap of Aditi"—with these words he hands it over [saying], "O Agni, protect the oblation! O Agni and Soma, protect the oblation! O Indra and Agni, protect the oblation!"—according to the respective deity; or simply, "O Agni, protect the oblation. Having poured water through the strainer into the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle which contains the *śūka* grass, and having purified it three times with the two strainers whose tips point northward, he consecrates it as before. He addresses the Brahman priest, saying, "O Brahman, I shall sprinkle. Being thus authorized...

With the formula, "By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I sprinkle thee, acceptable to Agni," he sprinkles the oblation. With the words, "To Agni-Soma," he sprinkles according to the respective deity.

He sprinkles each [portion] three times. (11) While sprinkling the oblation, he sprinkles over the fire. (12) Having sprinkled the oblation, he sprinkles the vessels. (13) Having turned them face upwards, he should perform this three times with the formula, "Be purified for the divine rite, for the sacrifice to the gods. (14) Regarding the remainder of the sprinkling water, Āśmarathya says it should be used for the *prokṣaṇī* water; Ālekhana says one should sprinkle with all of it. (15) 1.20

Taking the black antelope skin with the *sāvitra* formula, he shakes it three times over the rubbish-heap with its neck pointing upward and its hair-side turned outward, saying: "The demon has been shaken off; the enemies have been shaken off. To the north of the sacrificial ground, he spreads it with the neck toward the west and the hair facing upward, saying: "Thou art the skin of Aditi. He aligns the hairy side toward himself, saying: "May the earth recognize thee. Without letting go of the black antelope skin, he places the mortar upon it, saying: "Thou art the wooden pressing-stone for the soma. Without letting go of the mortar...

He pours out the oblation with the formula three times: "Thou art the body of Agni, the release of speech; I take thee for the enjoyment of the gods. A fourth time he does so silently. Having taken up the pestle with the formula, "Thou art a stone, belonging to the forest-king," he calls out to the preparer of the oblation three times.

"O preparer of the oblation, come!"—thus for a Brāhmaṇa; "Come hither!"—thus for a Rājanya; "Come!"—thus for a Vaiśya. (6) While threshing, he recites: "Drive away the Rakṣas; may I slay the rival from heaven. (7) When the rice grains have appeared, he gives the command to the Āgnīdhra loudly: "Strike together! (8) Taking up either a stone or a wooden yoke-pin, the Āgnīdhra recites: "Thou art the crusher, honey-tongued," and with a verse addressed to Savitṛ, he strikes the lower and upper millstones loudly: "Utter food for us; utter strength for us. (9) He strikes twice on the lower millstone and once on the upper. Moving the pestle back and forth three times, he completes the process nine times. (10) 1.21

To the north, he brings forward a winnowing basket made of bamboo, reed, or *nalada* grass, with the formula: "Thou art increased by rain. (1) He pours out the sacrificial oblation with the formula: "May that which is increased by rain receive thee. (2) On the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), he winnows it away with the formula: "The *rakṣas*-demon is winnowed away; the enemies are winnowed away. (3) With the formula, "The *rakṣas*-demon is struck down," he strikes against the husks. (4) Having poured the husks onto the middle cake-pan, he scatters them beneath the black antelope skin with the formula: "Thou art the portion of the *rakṣas*-demons. (5) Having touched water, he separates [the grain] with the formula: "Vāyu [separates] you..."

"Separate them," [he says], and pours the rice grains into the vessel with the formula: "May the divine Savitṛ, the golden-handed, receive you. He touches the grains that have been poured out with: "Be purified for the gods. He gives the command to the preparer of the oblation: "Pound [the grain] three times. The sacrificer's wife comes forward and husks it, or another person does so. He makes the grains well-husked three times. Having set aside the husks in a known place, he pours the water used for washing the rice onto the rubbish-heap (utkara).

"Whatever husk remains when [the grains] are being thrice-pounded, let the waters carry that away from here as the portion of the Rakṣases. (12) In the same manner, having taken the black antelope skin, he shakes it. (13) 1.22

The spreading of the sacrificial grass has been explained. 1. Upon the black antelope skin, as if toward the neck, he places the *śamyā* peg behind [the skin] with its knob facing north, saying: "Thou art the support of heaven. 2. Upon the *śamyā* he places the lower grinding stone (*dṛṣad*), saying: "Thou art the bowl belonging to the mountain. Upon the lower grinding stone he places the upper grinding stone (*upalā*), saying: "Thou art the bowl belonging to the daughter of the mountain. 3. Upon the lower grinding stone he pours out the rice grains, saying: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I pour thee out, acceptable to Agni. [He adds: "To Agni and Soma," according to the respective deity.

He grinds three times with the *yajus* formula and silently a fourth time. He grinds continuously. With "For breath, thee," he pushes the lower millstone forward; with "For out-breath, thee," [he pushes] it backward; with "For diffused breath, thee," he places it in the middle position. With "Along the long extension for the sake of life," he finally pushes it forward. He causes the flour to fall onto the black antelope skin with "May the god Savitṛ, the golden-handed, receive you. He looks at what has fallen with "I behold you with unimpaired vision."

Thus, [the Adhvaryu] gives the call for the preparer of the oblation: "Without mixing [the grain], make it into fine flour. 1.23.10. Either the wife or a female slave grinds the grain. Having taken the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick) with the formula, "Thou art the bold one; grant us spiritual power," he draws out two glowing coals from the *gārhapatya* fire toward the west. He throws one of them away toward the north-western intermediate direction with the formula, "O Agni, drive away the fire that consumes raw flesh; expel the consumer of corpses. Having established the other coal [on the altar] with the formula, "Bring hither the gods to the sacrifice," he places a potsherd upon it with the formula, "Thou art firm; make the earth firm. Having placed his left hand over it, he takes hold of it with his finger.

He applies charcoal to the potsherd with the formula: "The Rakṣas is burnt away; the enemies are burnt away. He places each preceding potsherd with the formulas: "Thou art support," "Thou art foundation"; the southern one with "Thou art law"; the northern one with "Ye are piled"; the sixth with "Thou art the host of the Maruts"; and he places the remaining two with "Thou art piled" and "Thou art piled around."

He silently prepares eight [potsherds]. In the same manner, he places the subsequent set of potsherds. He prepares eleven, or twelve for that of Indra and Agni. In this way, from this point forward, the ritual actions are performed upon them in their proper sequence. Then he covers them with embers, saying: "Be heated by the heat of the Bhṛgus and the Aṅgirases. At this point, he places the boiling water (*madantī*) on the fire. When the vessel has been heated and fanned, he, restraining his speech, pours the flour through the strainer into the vessel, saying: "By the impulse of the god Savitṛ..."

"At the impulse of the Aśvins, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I strew [the grass] acceptable to Agni; [acceptable] to Agni and Soma," thus according to the respective deity. He does so three times with the sacrificial formula (*yajus*) and a fourth time silently. 1.24.11–12.

Then he purifies these [grains] with two strainers, verse by verse, with the *gāyatrī* mantra: "May the god Savitṛ purify you. (1) He mixes the sacrificial oblations (*haviṣ*) with the *praṇītā* waters. (2) Or, having purified them with another [mantra] using the *yajus*, (3) he takes [the water] from the *praṇītā* vessels with the *sruva* ladle, holds it up with the *veda* grass-bundle, and pours it in. (4) With the words, "The waters have united with the waters," (5) he pours it into the ground flour. (5) With the words, "You are born from the waters; be mixed with the waters," (6) he causes the mixture to overflow in a clockwise direction with the heated water. (6) Having mixed it together with the words, "I mix you for generation," (7) he completes the process. (7)

He divides [the rice] according to its portions, saying, "May you two separate," so that they shall not be brought together again. 7. Then he touches them: with "For Agni, thee! the southern ball; with "For Agni and Soma, thee! the northern one at the full moon sacrifice; for one who does not offer the *saṃnayya* (curd-mixture), at the new moon sacrifice, he uses "For Indra and Agni, thee! 8. With "Here I strike away the face of the attacking army," he strikes the embers out from the potsherds using the *veda*-grass-bundle. Then, with "Thou art the head of Makha," he takes the southern ball and places it in the south.

He places [the first] on the upper part of the potsherd with the formula, "Thou art the heat, the all-enlivening. (9) In the same way, taking the second lump, he places it on the upper part of the other potsherd. (10) From this point onward, the ritual acts are performed upon these [potsherds] in successive order. (11) Here he pours out clarified butter, or [he pours it] into the upper [vessel]. (12) 1.25

He spreads out all the potsherds with the formula: "Spread wide; may the lord of the sacrifice spread wide for thee. He makes them not too high, not like cakes, shaped like tortoises, and the size of a horse's hoof. Having poured water into a vessel, he strokes each one clockwise with the ointment, saying for each: "Take hold of the skin."

He does not let it drip excessively. Three times he carries fire around it [with the formula]: "The *rakṣas* is excluded; the enemies are excluded. Or [he may do so] with [the verse]: "The wise Lord of Victuals has gone around. He heats it with firebrands [with the formula]: "May the god Savitṛ bake you. He sets it ablaze with *darbha* grass [with the formula]: "May Agni not burn your body. Or he releases his speech [with the formula]: "Bake without burning. With the formula: "Be united with the *brahman*," he covers the cake with ash along with glowing coals using the *veda* grass-bundle. Then follows the washing of the fingers.

Having heated the washing-water from the vessel with a firebrand and having drawn three lines inside the altar, either eastward or northward, with a wooden sword (sphya), he pours out the water three times toward the west so that it flows together, reciting these mantras one by one: "To Ekatā, svāhā! [and so forth].
Thus ends the first section;
now begins the second section.

Taking up the wooden sword (*sphya*) with the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ... he sharpens it with a blade of grass, saying: "Thou art hundred-edged, made of wood, the slayer of the enemy; thou art thousand-edged, hundred-fold in brilliance, the wind, sharp-edged. To the west of the Āhavanīya fire is the altar (*vedi*), measured by the height of the sacrificer or of unlimited size, extending eastward. It is as wide as necessary so that the sacrificial oblations may fit upon it. With the *veda* (sweeper), they discerned the earth and the altar; that earth spread out over all earthly things.

"He bears the embryo within the worlds; from that, the sacrifice is born, the giver of all. With these words, he sweeps the altar three times with the *veda* grass-bundle, either before or after the *stambayajus* formula. From the eastern third of the front part of the altar, he carries away the *stambayajus*. Having placed a blade of *darbha* grass within the altar, either pointing eastward or northward, with the words, "Thou art the girdle of the earth," he strikes it with the wooden sword (*sphya*), saying, "O Earth, place of divine sacrifice, I have not harmed thy root with the sacrificial grass. "Araru is driven away."

Saying, "To the earth," he carries away the clods of earth together with the grass by means of the wooden sword (sphya) for the sake of Sūnapāt, saying, "Go to the fold, go to the cow-pen. 7. Saying, "May the sky rain for you," he looks toward the altar (vedi). 8. To the north, he scatters [the earth], saying: "Bind him, O God Savitṛ, in the furthest distance with a hundred fetters—he who hates us and whom we hate—do not release him from there."

Having silently carried [the earth] four times, he encloses the altar with the wooden sword (*sphya*), saying: "May the Vasus enclose thee with the Gāyatrī metre" on the south; "May the Rudras [enclose thee]" on the west; "May the Ādityas [enclose thee]" on the north. Indeed, every rite pertaining to the altar is performed with the wooden sword. Thereupon he issues the command: "O men, come and prepare this altar, rich in Vasus, rich in Rudras, and rich in Ādityas, at the height of heaven and at the navel of the earth, so that this sacrificer may suffer no harm."

"May this [earth], beloved by the gods, [be placed] in the lap of Aditi. May all the gods delight in this; may the increases of wealth enter the sacrificer. (6) Then, having removed the outermost skin of it, he causes it to go to the rubbish-heap. (7) Then he digs it—two finger-breadths, three finger-breadths, or four finger-breadths deep; or as much as a furrow, or as much as a chariot-track, or as much as the white part of the heel; or [he digs] with the mantra: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, the wise perform their work. (8) He cuts the root. (9) Ā.

"One should construct an altar whose soil is brought from elsewhere for one desiring cattle; one whose soil is dug up from the site for one desiring progeny—so it is known. One view is that, having dug, one should always pour in other soil. Another view is that one should pour in other soil even in an altar that has not been dug. Wherever one digs, there one should mutter the mantra for digging. When the oblations have been placed on the fire, one should prepare the altar for the Full Moon sacrifice. For the New Moon sacrifice, one should do so on the previous day before the bringing of the sacrificial grass. Having performed whatever rites precede the northern tracing-out, one observes the fast. The rest is the same."

He addresses the Brahman priest: "O Brahman, I shall perform the northern tracing. (8) Urged by the Brahman, he traces the altar with the wooden sword (*sphya*): "Thou art the Truth" on the south; "Thou art the seat of Truth" on the west; "Thou art the glory of Truth" on the north. (9) Then he levels it towards the west with the wooden sword, [saying]: "Thou art support; thou art self-support; thou art the foundation. (10) Having fixed the wooden sword crosswise in the western third of the altar, he issues the call.

"Set down the *prokṣaṇī* waters; set down the fuel and the sacrificial grass; cleanse the *sruva* and the *sruk* ladles; gird the wife; bring the clarified butter"—thus says one [teacher], that the Āgnīdhra should perform these rites.

"Adhvaryu," is another [name]. 12. Having poured out the *prokṣaṇī* waters, he places the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) to the south of the *sphya*, without touching it, along the track of the *sphya*. 13. He should meditate upon whomsoever he hates. 14. On the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), he throws the *sphya* towards the east with its point facing westward, saying: "Thou art hundred-edged, made of wood, the slayer of those who hate. 15. He utters the name of him whom he hates. 16. Having washed his hands, he cleanses the *sphya*.

He does not fasten the cord at the top (17). Having prepared the altar, he should not strike the vessels until he has washed his hands (18). To the north of the *praṇītā* waters, he places the fuel and the sacrificial grass behind them with their tips pointing east (19). 2.3. The fuel is on the south and the sacrificial grass on the north (1). Taking the *sruva* spoon, the *sruk* ladles, and the *prāśitra-haraṇa* vessel, he heats them over either the *gārhapatya* or the *āhavanīya* fire, saying: "The *rakṣas* is burnt away; the enemies are burnt away" (2). Having divided them with the tips of the *veda* grass, he cleanses them.

Or, without dividing [the water], holding the *sruva* ladle with its bowl turned upward at the tip, he cleans it by moving from the front toward the inside, gathering the water from all sides into the cavity, and from the base toward the handle, thinking: "May I not wipe away the cow-pen. He cleans the *juhū* ladle while holding it turned upward, moving from the front toward the inside with the tips, eastward with the middle parts, westward with the middle parts on the outside, and from the base toward the handle, thinking: "May I not wipe away speech and breath. He cleans the *upabhṛt* ladle while holding it crosswise, moving from the front toward the inside with the tips...

[He cleanses] the western [side] with the middle [parts], the outer [side] with the middle [parts], and the eastern [side] with the roots [of the grass-blades], [saying]: "May I not wipe away my staff, my sight, or my hearing. (6) As with the *sruva* spoon, so [he cleanses] the *dhruvā* ladle, [saying]: "May I not wipe away offspring or the womb. (7) [He cleanses] the *prāśitraharaṇa* vessel, [saying]: "May I not wipe away form or color; O steed, I cleanse thee, the subduer of rivals. (8) One should not let the cleansed and the uncleaned touch each other. (9) If they should touch, one must heat them again over the fire and then cleanse them. (10) He heats the cleansed vessels [over the fire], [saying]: "With the most brilliant splendor of Agni, I heat thee. (11) 2.4
Then, having touched these brooms with water, he throws them into the fire on which he has finished cooking: "The craft of heaven is spread abroad; it rests upon the peak of the earth."

"By this [cord] with its thousand branches, we destroy our rival; svāhā! (1) He throws it onto the rubbish-heap. (2) He girds the wife—whether she is sitting with her knees raised, or standing, or he himself girds himself—with a girdle of muñja grass having a loop on one side, either inside or outside the garment, with the words: "Desiring favor... (3) Having made a loose knot above the navel, he winds it around to the right of the navel, saying: "O Agni, lord of the house, invite me [to the sacrifice]. (4)

He addresses the *gārhapatya* fire with the mantra: "O wives of the gods, invite me hither. He stands behind the *gārhapatya* facing the wives of the gods. He worships the place of the wife of the gods with the mantra: "O wife, this is your place; homage be to you; do not harm me. To the south of that spot, he sits down facing north, saying: "May I be like Indra, never widowed; may I be like Aditi, possessed of noble sons."

When that strainer has been placed [on the vessel], he pours out abundant clarified butter with the formula: "The milk of the great ones, the essence of the plants; of thee, as thou art inexhaustible, I pour out for the sacrifice to the gods. (1) He places it over the Dakṣiṇāgni fire with the verse: "Over this Viṣṇu strode. (2) Or, having melted it, he pours it out. (3) With the formula "For food, thee," he places it over the southern half of the Gārhapatya fire. (4) With the formula "For strength, thee," having taken it down and supported it with the Veda-grass-bundle, he causes the wife to support it. (5) She, closing her eyes and not breathing out, gazes at it.

"The milk of the great ones, the essence of the plants—with an unerring eye I gaze upon thee for the sake of good progeny. (6) "Thou art brilliance," [saying this] he places it over the northern half of the Gārhapatya fire. (7) "For brilliance thee! [saying this] he takes it down, holds it up with the Veda-grass-bundle, and brings it forward [saying], "Thou art brilliance; follow after brilliance. (8) He places it over the Āhavanīya fire [saying], "May Agni not take away thy brilliance. (9) To the north of the *prokṣaṇī* waters, he sets it down on the track of the wooden sword (*sphya*), [saying], "Thou art the tongue of Agni, the well-being of the gods; for every station, for the gods..."

"For each Yajus, become [the means of success]," he says ten times. (10) Then the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer, having closed their eyes and not breathing out, gaze at it, beginning with "Thou art the clarified butter" and ending with "may I partake of thee. (11) Then he purifies it three times by moving it back and forth through two strainers with their tips pointing north, using these mantras: "Thou art the bright," "Thou art the light," "Thou art the luster. (12) With two strainers soaked in clarified butter, he purifies the sprinkling waters (prokṣaṇīs) verse by verse with the Gāyatrī mantra: "May the god Savitṛ purify you. (13) 2.6

With the *sruva* spoon not withdrawn, he takes the clarified butter (*ājya*) within the altar (*antarvedi*), having placed the *sruca* ladles upon the *veda* grass-bundle. He takes four portions into the *juhū* ladle with these three mantras: "The bright one for the bright one; for every domain, for every deity, for every sacrificial formula, I take thee. He takes the fourth portion with the mantra: "For the five winds, thee. In this same manner, he takes [the butter] into the *upabhṛt* and the *dhruvā* ladles with the subsequent mantras. Eight portions are taken into the *upabhṛt*, and four portions into the *dhruvā*.

For one desiring cattle, there is a fivefold taking [of the clarified butter]. (4) With those very same formulas, the sacrificer recites the consecratory prayers (*anumantrayate*). (5) Or rather, the Adhvaryu priest may take [the butter] with the formulas belonging to the Adhvaryu; the sacrificer recites the consecratory prayers with the formulas belonging to the sacrificer. (6–7) He takes more [butter] into the *juhū* ladle, less into the *upabhṛt*, and most into the *dhruvā*. (8) Holding [the ladles] level with the edge [of the altar], he takes [butter] into the *juhū*; at the middle point, into the *upabhṛt*; and when the *dhruvā* is resting on the ground, [he takes it] into that. (9) One does not move back behind what has been taken within the altar (*antarvedi*). (10) There is no clarified butter on the rubbish-heap (*utkara*).

He places something down. Having consecrated the sprinkling waters with the mantra, "The divine waters, flowing forward," he addresses the Brahman priest, saying, "O Brahman, I shall sprinkle. Being permitted by the Brahman, he sprinkles the fuel with the mantra, "Thou art black, dwelling in the mountain; for Agni, svāhā! He sprinkles the altar with the mantra, "Thou art the altar," and the sacrificial grass with the mantra, "Thou art the sacrificial grass. He sprinkles each of these three times. Having placed the sacrificial grass with its knot toward the east within the altar, he sprinkles it: the tip with the mantra, "For heaven, thee!"

Together with the offering-spoon (*sruc*), he sprinkles the knot from the front toward the west, saying, "For prosperity, thee! (1) Whatever remains of the sprinkling-water (*prokṣaṇī*), he pours it out within the altar (*antarvedi*) with the words, "Svadhā to the fathers! (2) Starting from the southern hip of the altar, he causes a continuous stream to flow along to the northern hip. (3) With the words, "May Pūṣan untie your knot," he loosens the *barhis* grass. (4) He draws it upward, forward, hidden, and then back toward the west. (5) He takes up the *prastara* bundle from the front.

He does not stroke it, nor does he wipe it, nor does he shake it; drawing it out as it were, he takes it up with the formula, "Thou art the tuft of Viṣṇu. He inserts the two strainers into it with the formula, "May this Prāṇa and Apāna enter the sacrificer; for they have become the two purifiers (potṛ) in the sacrifice, the strainers that cleanse the oblation. Thereupon he issues the command: "Strew the sacrificial grass (barhis); enclose the altar; let not the kin be separated while lying there."

"Strew with green, golden *darbha* grass; these are the gold coins (*niṣka*) of the sacrificer at the center," [he says]. (8) He hands the *prastara* bundle to the *brahmán*, saying, "I make you one whose body is whole through out-breath and in-breath. (9) The *brahmán* hands it to the sacrificer, saying, "I place out-breath and in-breath in the sacrificer. (10) "In me, out-breath and in-breath," the sacrificer replies. (11) He spreads the cord, saying, "I spread thee, O wool-soft one," continuously from the southern hip up to the northern shoulder. (12) On the entire [altar].

On the altar, he spreads the sacrificial grass (*barhis*)—abundant, not too visible, soft as wool—with the formula: "I spread thee, soft as wool. He spreads it in three layers or five layers, ending toward the east or toward the west. He covers the roots with the tips [of the grass]. At each layer, he mutters the mantra. Here, some remove two firebrands for the sake of the after-offerings (*anūyāja*). Holding the *prastara* bundle, he lays down the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), touching them together behind the *āhavanīya* fire.

With the mantra, "Thou art the Gandharva Viśvāvasu, with thy top upward and middle [part]," he places the southern [kindling stick]; with "Thou art Indra’s arm," the southern; and with "Mitra and Varuṇa, thee," the northern. (3) The southern one is directed toward the Āhavanīya fire, and the northern one is directed downward. (4) From this point onward, the ritual acts are performed among these [sticks] in this very sequence. (5) Having consecrated the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra, "May Sūrya protect thee from the east," he places two kindling sticks for the *āghāra* libation upright in the middle of the fire. (6) With the mantra, "Thee, O Sage, the enjoyer of the oblation," he places the southern [stick]. (7) The northern [stick] is placed silently. (8)

Having made two *vidhṛti*s (separators) from the *barhis* grass, each containing a blade within it, he places them in the middle of the altar with their tips pointing north, saying: "You two are the restrainers of the people. (9) He places the *prastara* (grass-bundle) upon the two *vidhṛti*s, saying: "Sit on the seat of the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas. (10) Upon the *prastara*, he places the *juhū* ladle, saying: "Thou art the *juhū*, dripping with ghee. To the north of the *juhū*, he places the *upabhṛt* ladle, closer together and below the two *vidhṛti*s, saying: "Thou art the *upabhṛt*. (13) To the north of the *upabhṛt*, he places the *dhruvā* ladle, even closer together and above the two *vidhṛti*s.

"Thou art firm," [with these words] he places them without touching one another. To the south of the *juhū* or to the north of it, he places the *sruva*; to the north of that, the *dhruvā*. "Thou art the bull, belonging to the Śakvarī meters, the son of the *ghṛtācīs*; by thy dear name, sit in thy dear seat," [with this he places the *dhruvā*]. 2.9.16.

Then he consecrates them with the remainder of the section beginning, "These have settled. (1) He consecrates the clarified butter with [the formula]: "You are Viṣṇu-portions; you are the abodes of Viṣṇu; you are the abodes of Prajāpati. (2) Having taken the butter-pot together with the dipping-spoon, the Veda-grass-bundle, and the offering-ladle, and having sat down behind the Gārhapatya fire, he removes the ash along with the embers from the sacrificial cake using the Veda-grass-bundle while reciting: "Here I drive away the face of the attacking army," and then consecrates it with: "O Sun, shine forth as light for great sensory power and strength. (3)

He spreads a base in the vessel with the mantra: "I prepare for you a pleasant seat; I fashion it well-favored with a stream of ghee. Sit upon this, O immortal one; take your stand, being well-disposed, in the essence of rice. (4) He sprinkles it with clarified butter on the right side with the mantra: "May Agni, whose source is ghee, swell; may he approve the oblations. Anoint yourself; I sprinkle you, who are well-formed and a finder of wealth, with the luster of cattle, as one pleasing to Agni."

Silently he pours the *sāṃnāyya* over [the rice]. With the verse: "O Soma, that self of yours which has entered into the cattle, which has spread throughout the abode of the gods—becoming possessed of self and rich in ghee, go to the gods; find the light for me, the sacrificer. (5) He places it in the offering-ladle with the verse: "The moist one, expanding, the guardian of the world, the cooked one, the progenitor of thoughts, rises up. (6) He does not turn it around, nor does he break it. (7–8) 2.10

"May prosperity, the essence of the earth, not depart," with these words he anoints the potsherds. Then he anoints them completely, without leaving any part untouched, with the formula: "May the god Savitṛ anoint you with honey. He anoints from above and then anoints from below. Having made them well-anointed and free of spots like those of a tortoise, and having adorned the *sāṃnāyya* offerings, he should set down the oblations on the altar within the sacrificial ground using the *caturhotṛ* formula at the full moon sacrifice, and the *pañcahotṛ* formula at the new moon sacrifice. At the first full moon sacrifice, he uses the formula: "Bhūḥ bhuvaḥ suvaḥ. This is done once every year.

One should place them using these very same [formulas] throughout; Āśmarathya says this should be done in the first year alone, while Ālekhana says it should be done year after year. To the west of the ladles, he places the two *puroḍāśa* cakes. Having joined the two *sāṃnāyya* vessels in the middle of the altar, he places the boiled milk on the southern corner of the altar and the curd on the northern corner. Or rather, according to some, the boiled milk is placed first and the curd afterwards. In front of the *dhruvā* ladle, he places the *veda* grass-broom with the formula: "This *veda* found the earth hidden in the cave."

"May he find the world for the sacrificer in the thickets and deep caverns; may he of many deeds perform the flawless sacrifice. (11) Having strewn around the edges of the altar, he prepares the seat for the Hotṛ. (12) Behind the altar, it is strewn with Darbha grass whose tips point northward. (13) 2.11

Then he gives the command: "Recite for the fire being kindled! (1) Sitting down, he places a fuel-stick upon the fire at each *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*). (2) When he recognizes [the verse], "O Agni, kindled, you are invoked," then, leaving aside one *anūyāja* fuel-stick, he places the entire remainder of the fuel-wood onto the fire. (3) With the *veda* grass-bundle, he fans the *āhavanīya* fire three times. Taking clarified butter from the *dhruvā* vessel with the *sruva* ladle, covering it with the *veda*, and having drawn it along under the northern junction of the enclosing sticks, he sits facing southeast.

He pours the oblation continuously and straightly, meditating in his mind upon Prajāpati. Having taken ghee from the vessel for ghee with the *sruva* ladle, he replenishes the *dhruvā* [ladle] with the verse: "May the *dhruvā* swell with ghee. In this regard, there is this specific rule: wherever he takes ghee from the *dhruvā*, he replenishes it in that very same manner.

He makes a reverential salutation with joined palms toward the Āhavanīya fire, saying: "Thou art the world; expand! O Agni, O sacrificer, here is homage. (1) He takes up the *juhū* ladle, saying: "Come, O *juhū*! He takes up the *upabhṛt* ladle, saying: "Come, O *upabhṛt*! (2) He places the *juhū* upon the *upabhṛt*, saying: "May you two today be well-guided for me, dripping with ghee; may you be easy to turn and easy to handle. (3) In this regard, there is this specific rule: wherever he places the *juhū* upon the *upabhṛt*, he deposits it from above at the front [of the *upabhṛt*], and he withdraws it from the front. (4) And he does not let them clatter together, nor does he place them at the level of his navel.

He holds the two *sruva*-ladles; according to some, he holds them level with his breaths. Without letting the *prastara* [grass-bundle] become entangled, he steps over it in front of the *dhruvā* [spoon], saying: "O Agni and Viṣṇu, may I not step upon you. He stands to the south, saying: "Thou art the station of Viṣṇu. His right foot remains within the altar (*antarvedi*).

As if sniffing, having led [the ladle] along the southern junction of the enclosing sticks while standing upright, he pours the *āghāra* libation—continuous, straight, directed eastward and then northward—while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, saying, "The sacrifice has risen upward. (10) One desiring rain should pour it downward; one desiring heaven should pour it upward. (11) He offers this as the most abundant of all oblations. (12) Having offered, he breathes out. (13) Saying, "Hiṃ! O great light," he lifts up the ladle. (14) Without letting the two ladles touch each other, he steps back across. (15) 2.13

"Protect me, O Agni, from evil conduct; establish me in good conduct"—these two mantras are used for the stepping forward and the stepping back. Regarding this, there is this specific rule: those oblations which he offers on the north side, he offers after having moved along the northern junction of the enclosing sticks; those which are on the south side, he offers after having moved along the southern junction of the enclosing sticks. He steps across with his right foot toward the south, and with his left foot toward the north.

Or rather, having stepped back to the north with the left foot forward and the right foot following, he anoints the *dhruvā* with the *juhū* [spoon], saying: "Thou art the head of Makha; may light be united with light. Having taken clarified butter from the *dhruvā* with the *sruva* [ladle] while reciting "The raised one of wealth," he pours it over the *juhū* with "To the one rich in heroes, Svāhā! He anoints the *dhruvā* with the *juhū* while reciting "By sacrifice, sacrifice is continued. Having set down the two spoons, he takes a blade of grass from the edge of the altar and both stand facing east on the rubbish-heap (*utkara*) to the north for the *pravara* invocation.

"This one shall be the Adhvaryu; he indeed shall be the Adhvaryu. I stand in the place of Viṣṇu, the sacrifice of the sacrifice. Let speech perform the office of the priest; let mind perform the office of the priest. I take refuge in speech: Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ!"—thus says the former Adhvaryu. "Who here shall be the Agnīdh? He indeed shall be the Agnīdh. I stand in the place of Viṣṇu, the sacrifice of the sacrifice. Let speech perform the office of the priest; let mind perform the office of the priest. I take refuge in speech: Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ!"—thus [says the other]. (2.14)

The other [priest], the Āgnīdhra, takes hold of the wooden sword (sphyá) and the cords for binding the fuel (idhmasamnahánī). He addresses the Brahman priest, saying: "O Brahman, I shall cause the announcement for the Pravara. Being urged by the Brahman, he causes the announcement, saying either "Āśrāvaya" or "Ośrāvaya. The Āgnīdhra responds with "Astu śrauṣaṭ. In this regard, there is this general rule: wherever the Adhvaryu may cause the announcement, the Āgnīdhra must always stand to the west of the rubbish-heap (utkara), facing south, holding the wooden sword.

Holding the *sedhmasaṃnahana* cord upwards, he causes the response (*pratyāśrāvayati*). However, in the case of the Soma sacrifice, this takes place in the *āgnīdhra* shed. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he chooses the *pravara*: "May Agni, the divine Hotṛ, worship the gods—he who is wise and discerning, like Manu, like Bharata, like Adova, like Adova"—according to the lineage of the sacrificer. He chooses three ancestors from the seers (*ārṣeya*) who are the authors of the mantras, starting from the most recent. Or rather, he chooses simply as "like Manu. For a king, he chooses the ancestors of his domestic priest (*purohita*). [The Hotṛ continues: "May he speak with the power of Brahman; may he bring [the gods] hither."

Having said, "The Brāhmaṇas are the promoters of this sacrifice," he pronounces the name of the Hotṛ in a low voice, saying, "So-and-so"; [he pronounces] "the human one" loudly. Having thrown a blade of grass upon the altar (vedi), [he concludes]. 2.15.12–14.

"It is known that they proceed without uttering [the names of the deities]. When he recognizes [the moment], saying, "O Adhvaryu, hold up the ladle full of ghee," then, having taken up the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles and stepped forward, and having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Recite the offering-verse for the *samidhs*. At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the oblation. Having called for the *śrauṣaṭ* again and again, he gives the direction for the subsequent offerings, saying, "Recite! Recite! He offers the *prayāja* oblations moving eastward behind the point where the *āghāra* libations meet; or he may offer them at the same spot. Alternatively, he performs the sacrifice first to the *samidhs* and then to *tanūnapāt*.

The *iḍā* is to the south, the *barhis* grass to the west, the *svāhā*-utterance to the north, and the middle [portion] in the center. (7) One should offer all the oblations where the fire is most brightly kindled. (8) When about to offer the fourth [oblation], he pours half of the butter from the *aupabhṛta* ladle into the *juhū*. (9) Having performed the five *prayāja* offerings and returned [to his place], he sprinkles the sacrificial oblations with whatever ghee remains in the *juhū*: first the *dhruvā* ladle, then the *āgneya* cake, then the subsequent [cake], then the boiled milk (*śṛta*), then the curds (*dadhi*), and finally the *aupabhṛta* ladle. (10) Then, he places the two ladles in their proper places.

Having set it down, he takes it up again; thus he takes it up until the offering to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. Then he proceeds with the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*). Having issued the command, "Recite for Agni," and having taken four or five ladlings of clarified butter into the *juhū* spoon, he steps forward, causes the announcement to be made, and says, "Sacrifice to Agni. When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers it in the eastern part of the northern half [of the fire]. He does not offer this [oblation] to the north of another oblation. Having stepped back, [the ritual continues]. 2.16

He issues the command: "Recite the invitatory verse for Soma. Having taken the clarified butter as it was drawn, having stepped across and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "Sacrifice to Soma. At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he offers it in a straight line with the previous offering, in the eastern part of the southern half. He does not offer this [offering] to the south of another offering. Having stepped back, there is this specific rule: he cuts portions of the clarified butter and the milk with the *sruva* ladle, but he cuts the portion of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) with his hand. For the Jamadagnis alone, the portion is fivefold; for others, it is fourfold—even if he is not a Jamadagni.

Having addressed the son of Jamadagni, he should perform the five-fold cutting (pañcāvatta). Then he issues the command: "Recite for Agni. Having spread a base of ghee in the *juhū* ladle, he cuts a portion from the middle of the cake for Agni using his thumb and two fingers joined together; he then cuts a second portion from the eastern half and a third from the western half, if it is a five-fold cutting. [He says: "Do not fear, do not tremble; may I not harm you; may your splendor not depart. Support the offering, pour [the ghee] over it. I shall cut portions corresponding to your own portions."

"Salutation to you; do not harm me," [he says]. (10) Without breaking them, he cuts portions the size of a thumb-joint. (11) Having sprinkled the cut portions with clarified butter, he sprinkles the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) in return. With the mantra: "Whatever I have done contrary to the rule for myself while cutting your portions, I anoint that back again with clarified butter; may it swell for you once more. (12) Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to Agni. (13) When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers in the middle. (14) As if covering [the fire] and without pouring out the clarified butter, having offered the clarified butter, he offers the cake (*puroḍāśa*), and then the clarified butter again. (15) 2.17

He offers each preceding oblation with the formula *svāhā*, up until the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. Or rather, he may offer the *āghāra* libation from the ladle. Then he gives the direction for the *upāṃśuyāja*: "For Viṣṇu," he says in a low voice; "Recite the invitatory verse for the *upāṃśu*," he says loudly. Having taken the clarified butter as it was drawn, having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "For Viṣṇu," in a low voice; "Sacrifice," loudly. He offers when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered. Some prescribe a single *upāṃśuyāja* dedicated to Agni-Soma; others, one dedicated to Prajāpati. This [offering] occurs only on the full moon day.

7. As with the cake for Agni, so he proceeds with the final cake: "To Agni and Soma" at the full moon sacrifice; "To Indra and Agni" at the new moon sacrifice for one who does not offer the *saṃnayya* (curd-mixture). 8. Now, if he should offer the *saṃnayya*, he issues the command: "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra. 9. Or rather, "Recite the invitatory verse for Mahendra," if he is a sacrificer to Mahendra. 10. Having spread a base of clarified butter in the *juhū* ladle, he cuts off two portions of the cooked rice; twice from the curds; four portions if it is a fourfold cutting, three times if it is a fivefold cutting. 11. Having sprinkled clarified butter over it, having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "Sacrifice to Indra."

Thus [he offers], or "to Mahendra," he says; at the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering. Having stepped back, he performs the two *pārvaṇa* offerings with the *sruva*-ladle: "On the Full Moon day, we sacrifice to the bull, the vigorous one, the Pūrṇamāsa. May he milk for us excellent strength and thousandfold increase of wealth. To the Full Moon, the bountiful giver, to Prāṇa, *svāhā*!"—thus on the full moon day. "The New Moon, fortunate and very gracious, swelling again like a milch-cow. May she milk for us excellent strength and thousandfold increase of wealth. To the New Moon, the bountiful giver, to Apāna, *svāhā*!"—thus on the new moon day. (2.18)
In this rite, he offers the Nāriṣṭha oblations:
"O Sacrifice, these ten bodies of yours are worthy of sacrifice; may the sacrificer gratify them with clarified butter.
Praising the instruction of the two Nāriṣṭhas, the sacrificer has become immortal within the divine assembly of the gods—Svāhā!"
O you two of a hundred powers, that portion of strength which the gods have ordained for you—by that I gratify you;
by that may you both be satisfied. *Am̐hahau svāhā!*
I am in the world of the gods who perform good deeds; this sacrifice of mine shall not be in vain.
