I, the wise one, follow the two *nāriṣṭha* offerings, since Indra assigned them their share. *Svāhā!*
O divine Soma, be one who does not cause the wife to stray; O Maruts, be gracious to us at this sacrifice.
Let not hostile power find us, nor ill-spoken word; let not hateful forces find us—Svāhā!

Thus [having prepared the oblation], he then issues the command: "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. Having spread a base of ghee in the *juhū* ladle, he makes an offering from the northern half of each of the sacrificial portions (*havis*), taking four cuttings once each, or twice if there are five cuttings. These portions for the deities are the largest. Having poured ghee over them twice, he does not pour ghee back over the sacrificial substance itself. Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "Recite the offering verse for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers the oblation in the eastern part of the northern half, passing beyond the previous offerings.
Having stepped back, he places the two offering-spoons (srucau) in their respective places. At this point, some authorities prescribe the *prāśitra* portion; others prescribe it later.
Thus ends the second section.
Now begins the third section.

Having spread a base of clarified butter in the *iḍā*-vessel, he cuts off the first *iḍā*-portion from the southern half of the eastern side of the *puroḍāśa* dedicated to Agni, [reciting]: "The *iḍā* seen by Manu, whose foot is in ghee, impelled by Mitra and Varuṇa."

1. "Without piercing [the cake] from the southern half, I cut off the portion for the one-faced [deity]. 2. Having pierced the back, he cuts off the sacrificer’s portion from the eastern half, as thin as a hair and long. 3. From the point of the incision, he cuts off the second *iḍā* portion. 4. In this manner, he cuts off the *iḍā* portions from all the sacrificial oblations (*havis*). 5. These [portions] should be the thickest among those intended for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. 6. Having sprinkled [them with clarified butter], having carried the oblations between the vessels, he places the *iḍā* before the Hotṛ. 7. Or, the Hotṛ himself takes the *iḍā*. 8. In front...

The Adhvaryu steps across to the south of the Hotṛ without releasing his hold, as it were (8). With the *iḍā*, he encompasses the Adhvaryu (9). Having sat down behind him facing east, he anoints the two finger-joints of the Hotṛ with the *sruva* spoon (10). Having anointed the front one, he anoints the back one (11). Having returned by the same way he came, sitting in front facing west, he places the *iḍā* of the *iḍā* (the sacrificial food) [on the hand] (12). He spreads a base once for the Hotṛ’s portion held in the hand, places two portions upon it, and pours clarified butter over it once (13). Or, the Hotṛ himself takes the subsequent portion of the *iḍā* (14).

Then the Adhvaryu mutters this mantra: "Invoked, may I be possessed of cattle. (1) When he recognizes [the words], "This sacrificer is invoked," then the sacrificer mutters this very same mantra. (2) Once the Iḍā has been invoked, the Hotṛ eats the intermediate Iḍā, saying: "I eat thee, offered to Vācaspati; I eat thee, offered to Sadasaspati. (3) When the Iḍā has been invoked, the priests, with the sacrificer as the fifth, eat it, [saying]: "O Iḍā, enjoy our portion; quicken our cows, quicken our horses!"

"May we all, with our whole selves and all our attendants, be those who eat of it. Having consumed [the portion], he remains silent until the purification. Within the altar, they purify themselves over the *pavitra* [strainers] with the mantra: "May the mind, as light, enjoy [the offering]. Having split the *puroḍāśa* cake dedicated to Agni toward the east and having taken the *prāśitra-haraṇa* vessel, he cuts off the *prāśitra* portion [with the formula]: "Let this not be less than the size of a barley grain; let it be made ready from the piercing [of the cake]."

"May we not cause harm to the sacrifice; may this oblation be pure and well-offered. (7) Having thus [cut] from the subsequent [portions] without breaking them, (8) having pinched off a portion the size of a barley grain or a *pippala* fruit with the thumb and the ring finger, having placed it in the *prāśitra-haraṇa* vessel, having sprinkled it with clarified butter, and having taken hold of it with the *veda* grass-bundle, he carries it around to the Brahman priest in front of the Āhavanīya fire. (9) Having placed the sacrificer’s portion in front of the *dhruvā* ladle, (10) 3.2.

Having placed the *puroḍāśa* cake dedicated to Agni upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the sacrificer touches it; we shall explain that in the section concerning the duties of the sacrificer. Then, having divided it into four parts, he assigns them: "This for the Brahman; this for the Hotṛ; this for the Adhvaryu."

"This for the Āgnīdhra," [he says]. "This for the sacrificer," [saying this] the Adhvaryu sets aside the sacrificer's portion. These portions are larger than the portions cut from the *iḍā*. Having assigned [the portions] to the Āgnīdhra, he places the sixfold portion (*ṣaḍavatta*) before him. Having spread an underlayer of ghee, having cut the portion, and having poured ghee over it, he again spreads an underlayer, cuts the portion, and pours ghee over it; thus he completes the sixfold portion. The Āgnīdhra eats it, [reciting]: "Invoked is Dyaus Pitar; may Dyaus Pitar invoke me."

"May Agni [lead] from the Āgnīdhra for life, for splendor, for living, for merit," [he says]. (7) With the *veda* grass-bundle, he distributes the portions for the Brahman and the sacrificer. (8) He gives one portion to the Hotṛ and another to the Adhvaryu. (9) "Thou art the portion of the Earth," [with these words] the Hotṛ eats; "Thou art the portion of the Atmosphere," [with these words] the Adhvaryu; "Thou art the portion of Heaven," [with these words] the Brahman, when the rite is concluded, eats. (10) Having cooked a large quantity of rice-porridge on the Anvāhāryapacana fire, having sprinkled it with clarified butter—or not having sprinkled it—and having removed it from the fire, the sacrificer touches the *anvāhārya* porridge placed within the altar. We shall explain that in the section concerning the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). (11) 3.3

"Let it be offered to the worthy recipients of the sacrificial fee," he issues the command. (1) He should say to those who are to the north of the officiating priests, "Come here to the south. (2) To them, as they sit to the south, he gives the *anvāhārya* rice as the sacrificial fee, saying, "O Brāhmaṇas, this is your boiled rice. (3) "Go around by the north," he says again. (4) Having carried out the remnants of the oblation and having thrown the firebrands back into the fire, he issues the command: "O Brahman, we shall set forth; O Āgnīdh, having placed a fuel-stick on the fire, cleanse the enclosing sticks and the fire once each. (5)

The Āgnīdhra, having been summoned by the Brahman, places the fuel-stick for the after-offerings (anūyāja) with the formula: "This is thy fuel-stick, O Agni; through it mayest thou increase and swell; and may the lord of the sacrifice increase and swell, Svāhā! (6) With the wooden sword and the cords used for binding the fuel, the Āgnīdhra wipes the enclosing sticks and the fire once each.

Silently [he places] the enclosing-sticks (paridhis). He cleanses the fire with the formula: "O Agni, winner of the prize, I cleanse thee who hast run for the prize, who hast won the prize, the vigorous one, the winner of the prize, for the sake of winning the prize; Agni, the eater of food, for the sake of eating food. Thus he cleanses the fire. Then, having touched these cleansing-brushes with water, he throws them into the Āhavanīya fire with the formula: "O Rudra, lord of beings, moving in the threads, the bull—do not harm our cattle! Let this be an oblation for thee, Svāhā! According to some teachers, he throws them onto the rubbish-heap (utkara). 3.4.8–10.

Having taken up the *juhū* and the *upabhṛt*, having poured the contents of the *upabhṛt* into the *juhū*, having stepped across and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Sacrifice to the gods. At the *vaṣaṭ*-call, he makes the offering. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa* again and again, he gives the direction for the two subsequent offerings with the words, "Sacrifice! Sacrifice! He performs the *anūyāja* offerings westward, in front of the junction of the *āghāra* libations. He places the final *anūyāja* facing eastward. With the final one, he joins the others together. Having stepped back and placed the two ladles in their proper place, he separates them with the two *vājavatī* verses, beginning with: "By the impulse of strength..."

With his right hand, palm upward, he lifts up the *juhū* ladle together with the *prastara* grass-bundle. Then, with his left hand, he holds down the *upabhṛt* ladle, saying: "By means of subjugation, Indra has made my rivals low. With the words, "And the uplifting," he lifts up the *juhū* ladle.

With the words, "And the support," he holds down the *upabhṛt* ladle. With the words, "The gods have increased the sacred power (*brahman*)," he pushes forward the *juhū* ladle toward the east. Then, with the words, "May Indra and Agni scatter my rivals in all directions," he throws the *upabhṛt* outside the altar toward the west. Having sprinkled the *upabhṛt* with water and lifted it up, he anoints the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) with the residue from the *juhū*.

With the formula "For the Vasus, thee," he sprinkles the middle [part]; with "For the Rudras, thee," the southern; with "For the Ādityas, thee," the northern. (12) He does not place the *juhū* on the *prastara*. Having smeared the *prastara* with the two *vidhṛtis*, and having thrown the *vidhṛtis* back onto the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he anoints the *prastara* in the ladles: with the formula "Licking that which is anointed," he anoints the tip in the *juhū*; with "May the birds depart," the middle in the *upabhṛt*; with "May I not wipe away offspring or the womb," the root in the *dhruvā*. (14) In this very same manner, he anoints the second [bundle].

He throws the *prastara* together with its branch into the *āhavanīya* fire, pointing eastward as if above, with these mantras: "May Agni cause thee to go to the deity by means of the red [horse]," and also with, "Ye are the spotted deer of the Maruts; go to heaven; from there, send rain upon us. (1) He does not let it fall back; (2) he should not throw it too far forward; (3) he should not cast it toward the east. (4) Having bent his hand somewhat crookedly, he finally deposits it downward. At the point where he recognizes [the formula], "This sacrificer, so-and-so, desires," that is [the place].

Having placed the *prastara* [grass-bundle] upon [the fire], he says, "O Āgnīdhra, cause it to go. (5) Three times the Āgnīdhra raises the *prastara* upward with his joined palms. (6) He should not separate it sideways. (7) Then he says to the Adhvaryu, "Throw it after [the fire]; perform the *saṃvāda* (call-and-response). (8) The Adhvaryu throws after [the fire] a blade of grass taken from the front, saying, "May there be well-being for the bodies. (9) He points downward with his finger three times, saying, "This very thing, this very thing. (10) He touches the seats of the vital breaths, saying, "May the breath be unimpaired. (11) He wipes his mouth, saying, "O Agni, you are the protector of life; protect my life. (12)

12. Having touched this [earth] with the formula, "Thou art firm," [the Adhvaryu says], "The Āgnīdhra has come. [The Āgnīdhra replies], "He has come. [The Adhvaryu says], "Make it heard! [The Āgnīdhra replies], "Śrauṣaṭ! 13. Grasping the middle enclosing-stick (paridhi), he issues the direction: "May there be a good path for the divine Hotṛs; may there be well-being for the human ones; pronounce the Śaṃyu-formula! 14. While the Śaṃyuvāka is being recited, he throws the enclosing-sticks into the fire: the middle one with the formula, "The enclosing-stick which you placed around," and the other two with, "May you be united at the path of the sacrifice! 15.

He pushes the northern half of the embers downward. (16) Having placed the mouth of the *upabhṛt* ladle into the *juhū*, he makes an offering over the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) with the remnants of the oblation, saying: "O great ones, you who have a share in the remnants! (17) At this point, the officiating priests consume the remains of the sacrificial offerings. (18) 3.6

The *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles have been cleansed; the Adhvaryu takes up the *veda*, the Hotṛ takes up the wooden sword (*sphya*), and the Āgnīdhra takes up the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*) and the water-jar (*udakamaṇḍalu*). (1) Intending to perform the offerings to the wives (*patnīsaṃyāja*), they walk around [the altar] facing westward. (2) The Adhvaryu proceeds to the south of the Gārhapatya fire, while the other two proceed to the north. (3) He places the two ladles on the two doorposts with the formula: "I place you in the seat of Agni Vāma, whose house is unassailable. (4) He pushes forward the two door-bolts with the formula: "O two door-bolts, protect the two doors. (5) If he were to pour out [the grain] into a vessel, he should do so using the wooden sword (*sphya*).

He should release [the ladle] with the other [hand]. Sitting with their knees raised toward the Gārhapatya fire, they perform the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings with a low sound. Having made the *upabhṛt* spoon the *veda*, he issues the direction: "Recite the invitatory prayer for Soma. Having taken the clarified butter exactly as it was drawn, and having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "Sacrifice to Soma. When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers it in the southern half [of the fire]. With the very same butter as it was drawn, they perform the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings. He issues the direction: "Recite the invitatory prayer for Tvaṣṭṛ. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "Sacrifice to Tvaṣṭṛ. When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered...

He offers in the northern half [of the ladle]. 14. According to some, he sacrifices to Soma on the north and to Tvaṣṭṛ on the south. 15. At this point, one desiring a son should sacrifice to Rākā; one desiring cattle, to Sinīvālī; one desiring prosperity, to Kuhū. 16. He issues the direction: "Recite the invitatory verse for Rākā. 17. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "Sacrifice to Rākā. 18. When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering. 19. He issues the direction: "Recite the invitatory verse for Sinīvālī. 20. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "Sacrifice to Sinīvālī. 21. When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering. 22. 3.7.1–22.

He issues the command: "Recite for Kuhū. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "Sacrifice to Kuhū. At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering. He sacrifices to the wives of the gods (*devānāṃ patnīḥ*) in an enclosed space, or not in an enclosed space. He issues the command: "Recite for the wives of the gods. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "Sacrifice to the wives of the gods. At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering. He issues the command: "Recite for Agni Gṛhapati. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "Sacrifice to Agni Gṛhapati. At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering. Having caused the wife to take hold [of the sacrificer],...

With the *sruva* ladle, he offers on the *gārhapatya* fire: "May the wife go together with her husband through their good deed; may they become the two yoke-horses of the sacrifice; being in harmony, may they cast away the enemies; may they grasp the undecaying light in heaven—*svāhā*! (11) With the *sruva* ladle, he anoints the joints of the fingers of the *hotṛ* priest. (12) Having anointed the lower [joint], he anoints the upper one. (13) He places four drops of clarified butter for the *hotṛ* as the *iḍā* portion, and six for the *āgnīdhra*. (14) The *adhvaryu* and the wife touch the *iḍā* while it is being invoked. (15) Once the *iḍā* has been invoked, he consumes it.

The Hotṛ eats; the Āgnīdhra [eats]: "May Mother Earth be invited; may Mother Earth invite me. May Agni from the Āgnīdhra's place [invite me] for long life, for splendor, for living, and for merit. (16) Having eaten, they both perform the ritual purification (mārjana). (17) It concludes with the Iḍā. (18) 3.8

Or [the offering] may be accompanied by the *śaṃyu* formula. If he should perform it with the *śaṃyu* formula, he should take a blade of grass from the *veda* and anoint its tip in the *juhū*, its middle in the *sruva*, and its base in the *ājyasthālī*. For that, the same procedure applies as for the *prastara*. Having placed the wood-chips from the faggot on the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, he performs the oblations of the flour-smearings and the husks. Having poured the husks into four ladlings of clarified butter, he offers them, beginning with "O Agni, of unimpaired life-force, of cool body... and ending with the *svāhā* call. With the clarified butter alone, he [offers] the flour-smearing.

He offers oblations with the mantra: "Whatever has adhered to the mortar, the pestle, and the winnowing basket; whatever on the grinding stone and the potsherd—those scattered drops and splashes I offer together. May all the gods enjoy this oblation! Whatever many drops remain in the sacrifice, I offer them all well-sacrificed and well-poured into the fire, Svāhā! (6) The Hotṛ throws the Veda-grass-bundle three times onto the lap of the wife with the mantra: "Thou art the Veda; thou art acquisition."

He [the sacrificer] should look with these mantras: "May I see... (7). The wife throws them out one by one toward the west, saying: "Drive away the hater; drive away the enemy" (8). Or the wife throws them out herself (9). It is known from tradition: "She becomes desirous of a male child" (10). At this point, some prescribe the untying of the Veda-bundle (11). The Hotṛ goes from the Āhavanīya fire while spreading the Veda-bundle, reciting the remainder of the section beginning: "The ghee-filled, nest-like... (12). At this point, some prescribe the two Pārvaṇa oblations (13). It is known from tradition that he offers all the expiatory oblations (*prāyaścitta*) with the *sruva* ladle (14).

Or, having taken [the oblation] with each offering: "Brahman is the support of the mind; Brahman is of speech, Brahman of sacrifices, and of oblations, of clarified butter. Whatever is redundant in the rite and whatever is deficient, may the sacrifice, making amends for the joints, proceed as it is ordained. May this offering, consecrated by Svāhā, go to the gods—Svāhā! Whatever has been called out for the *āśrāvaṇa*, or over-called for the *atyāśrāvaṇa*, the *vaṣaṭ* uttered, or the hymn recited in excess in the sacrifice; whatever is redundant in the rite and whatever is deficient, may the sacrifice, making amends for the joints, proceed as it is ordained.
May this offering, consecrated by Svāhā, go to the gods—Svāhā!"

O gods, whatever transgression we may have committed against you through speech, even if it was unintentional—an offense against the gods—may the Maruts avert that sin from us to some other place, away from us, for the enemy who seeks to harm us; svāhā!
That has been stretched out by me; that is being stretched out again. The sweetest prayer is recited for the hymn of praise.
This ocean is indeed the universal healer. May you both be fully satisfied by this which is consecrated with *svāhā*. *Svāhā!*

Up from the darkness we [have risen]. Up that one. The bright [sun]. This my [prayer], O Varuṇa. That I entreat of you. You, O Agni, for us. As such, you, O Agni, for us. You, O Agni, are the messenger. Prajāpati.
I set up this boundary for the living, so that no other may reach the midst of them. May they live a hundred long autumns; may they place death beyond them with this mountain—svāhā!

Svāhā to the desired; vaṣaṭ to the undesired, svāhā! Svāhā to the remedy for ill-sacrificed offerings; svāhā to expiation; svāhā to misfortune; svāhā to the divine bodies; svāhā to prosperity; svāhā to complete prosperity. 2.3.10

To that Sarasvatī who is the mistress of the household, to her, Svāhā! To that Sarasvatī who is the mistress of the dwelling, to her, Svāhā! O Indra, make our kinsmen well-disposed toward our food and our home, Svāhā! Whatever we have done, whatever we have not done, whatever we have passed over, whatever we have exceeded in our offerings, or whatever we have not exceeded—that, O Viṣṇu, establish as a sacrifice within the sacrifice, Svāhā! From whatever we fear, O Indra, from that grant us freedom from fear; O Maghavan, be gracious for our protection; slay our enemies and our oppressors, Svāhā!

Bestower of well-being, Lord of the people, slayer of Vṛtra, dispeller of enemies, the sovereign, the bull-like Indra—may he go before us, the giver of well-being and the creator of fearlessness; Svāhā!
O Lord of the Bay Steeds, increasing through these songs, swell us with whatever is lacking here;
when you burst open the great cow-pens for your praisers, may we then be those who receive the greatest portion. Svāhā!
Whatever is performed erroneously in the sacrifice, whether it be unknown or known—O Agni, make that right for him, for you know the truth exactly as it is; Svāhā!
The sacrifice is commensurate with the Person; the sacrifice is commensurate with the Person.
O Agni, fashion that for him, for you indeed know it as it truly is. Svāhā!

Whatever mortals, with simple minds and feeble skill, do not contemplate the sacrifice, may Agni—the Hotṛ who knows the rite, the discerning one, the best of sacrificers—worship the gods according to the seasons; Svāhā!
Whatever of this rite I have overdone, or whatever I have done here deficiently—
may Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the wise one, make all that well-offered for me.

"To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the well-offerer of oblations, the fulfiller of desires—Svāhā! (1) Having offered the final oblation to Prajāpati (2), standing upright within the altar-ground, he offers the Samiṣṭayajus with the Dhruvā ladle (1). Having offered the first oblation with "O gods who know the way," he throws the sacrificial grass (barhis) after it (2). With "Svāhā to Speech," he offers the second (3). With "Place [it] in the wind, Svāhā," he offers the third (4). From the Hotṛ's seat, he strews the altar-ground, saying: "Strew it; enclose the altar; do not harm your kin lying here."

"The Hotṛ’s seats are green and golden; these are the gold ornaments of the sacrificer, O radiant one! (With this verse), he places the Praṇītā waters within the altar. "Who has unyoked you? Let him release you," (with this verse) he then releases the wife. "I loosen this bond of Varuṇa," (with this verse) she takes the cord and holds it together with water. He pours the full vessel into her joined palms. As it is being poured, he mutters this formula: "May I be united with long life, united with offspring. Having wiped her face, she rises, saying, "Prosperous..."

"May I be rich in cattle, rich in offspring, and a mistress of the household. (11) Then he hides the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick) on the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), with its thick end pointing westward from the east, [reciting]: "The fire-stirring stick which the gods established among men—those who are ill-disposed toward us, turn them away from us here! O fire-stirring stick, protect our offspring, our prosperity, and also our wealth; make our bipeds and quadrupeds firm and never-failing. (12) "Let the pain that is in the fire-stirring stick reach him whom we hate"—with these words, he utters the name of the one whom he hates. (13) 3.12

Then, seizing his name, he strikes him: "Drive that rival away from his home who attacks us; with the *nirbādhyā* oblation, Indra has cast him down. "Go beyond the three distant realms; go beyond the five peoples; go beyond the three luminous spheres as far as the sun is in heaven. May Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, lead you to the furthest distance."

"Because you do not return for eternal years. (1) "He is slain; we have killed so-and-so"—thus he should say regarding whom he hates. (2) When the rite is completed, he releases the potsherds with the verse, "The potsherds which [were used] in the Gharma. (3) The sacrificer should likewise consecrate them with this same formula. (4) Having concluded the Full Moon sacrifice, he subsequently offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Vaimṛdha. (5) In that regard, one may proceed according to his desire.

On the following day, the sacrificer chooses the Brahman priest with the formula: "O Lord of the earth, O Lord of the world, O Lord of the great being, we choose you as the Brahman. Having been chosen, he mutters: "I am the lord of the earth, I am the lord of the world, I am the lord of the great being; impelled by the divine Savitṛ, I shall perform the office of the officiating priest. O divine Savitṛ, they choose you here as Bṛhaspati, the divine Brahman."

That I declare to the mind; the mind to the Gāyatrī; the Gāyatrī to the Triṣṭubh; the Triṣṭubh to the Jagatī; the Jagatī to the Anuṣṭubh; the Anuṣṭubh to the Paṅkti; the Paṅkti to Prajāpati; Prajāpati to the All-gods; the All-gods to Bṛhaspati; Bṛhaspati to the Brahman. The Brahman is Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Suvaḥ.

"Bṛhaspati is the Brahman of the gods; I am the Brahman of men. O Bṛhaspati, protect the sacrifice. Having said this, he steps past the rear of the Āhavanīya fire and, from the south of the Brahman’s seat, throws away a blade of grass with the formula: "Expelled is Parāvasu! Having touched water, he sits down on the Brahman’s seat facing the Āhavanīya with the formula: "Here I sit in the seat of Arvāgvasu; impelled by the god Savitṛ, I sit in the seat of Bṛhaspati."
That I declare to Agni; that to Vāyu; that to Sūrya; that to Pṛthivī. 3.14.3

In this regard, the following is the absolute rule: one must remain strictly silent during ritual acts accompanied by mantras, but may act as he desires during those performed silently (*tūṣṇīka*). 1. He restrains his speech while the *praṇītā* waters are being brought forward, or once they have been brought forward, until the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*). 2. It is known from tradition that "he restrains his speech at every joint of the sacrifice. 3. Now, according to some, once the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*) has been commenced, he should restrain his speech during the *sāmidhenī* verses, the *prayāja* offerings, the *anūyāja* offerings, and the *stotra* and *śastra* recitations. 4. According to others, whenever an act is performed with a Ṛg-verse, a Yajus-formula, or a Sāman-chant, he should restrain his speech.

5. Now, some perform the transmission of the sacrifice to one another among the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). To the extent that the office of the priest is performed by means of the *ṛc*, to that extent the sacrifice resides in the *hotṛ*s; to the extent that it is performed by means of the *yajus*, to that extent [it resides] in the *adhvaryu*s; to the extent that it is performed by means of the *sāman*, to that extent [it resides] in the *udgātṛ*s. Furthermore, wherever in the sacrifice a rule is prescribed, to that extent the sacrifice resides in the *brahman* priest alone.

Therefore, during this disappearance [of the fire], the Brahman priest should remain restrained in speech. If he should speak out of negligence, he should utter these very *vyāhṛtis*: "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," or else the verse addressed to Viṣṇu. For it is known: "Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; by means of the sacrifice itself, he continues the sacrifice. When someone addresses him, saying, "O Brahman, I shall lead forward the waters," he then gives the impulse:
"Him! Lead forward the sacrifice; cause the deities to prosper; may the sacrificer be upon the back of the firmament!"
Where the world of the seven seers who have performed good deeds is, there place this sacrifice and the sacrificer.
"Oṃ, Praṇaya. When he addresses the Brahman priest, saying, "O Brahman, I shall sprinkle," he then gives the impulse:
"Him! Sprinkle the sacrifice; cause the deities to increase. May the sacrificer be upon the back of the firmament.
Where the world of the seven seers who have performed good deeds is, there place this sacrifice and the sacrificer."
"Oṃ, sprinkle!"—saying this twice, when he addresses him with the words, "O Brahman, I shall perform the northern tracing of the altar," he then gives the impulse: "Him!
O Bṛhaspati, enclose the altar; may the gods go their own way to their seats. Upon it let the sacrificial grass be spread; may the divine Earth be auspicious within for us."
O deity, cause him to prosper; let the sacrificer be upon the back of the firmament.
Place this sacrifice and the sacrificer where the world of the seven seers who have performed good deeds is located.
"Oṃ, accept [this]," he says three times. When the Adhvaryu addresses him, saying, "O Brahman, I shall sprinkle," he gives the impulse with the formula: "Hiṃ! Sprinkle the sacrifice. 4.3.16.
When the Adhvaryu addresses him, saying, "O Brahman, I shall recite the Sāmidhenī verses," he gives the impulse:
"Hiṃ! O Prajāpati, recite; cause the sacrifice and the deities to prosper; may the sacrificer be upon the back of the firmament."
Where the world of the seven seers who have performed good deeds is, there place this sacrifice and the sacrificer.

"Recite [the invitatory verse]," [he says]. When he addresses him, saying, "O Brahman, I shall announce the *pravara*," then he gives the impulse: "Him! O Lord of Speech, cause this speech to be heard; cause it to be heard among the gods, and [announce] me among men."
O Deity, cause him to prosper; let the sacrificer be upon the back of the firmament.
Where the world of the seven seers who have performed good deeds is, there place this sacrifice and the sacrificer.

"Oṃ! Make it heard! (he says) twice. When they bring him the *prāśitra* portion, he looks at it [with the formula]: "I look at you with the eye of Sūrya. He addresses it as it is being brought: "Go along the path of Truth. Having touched water, he receives it [with the formula]: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I receive you. Having spread out blades of grass, he places the handle on the ground in front [of him] with [the formula]: "I set you down upon the navel of the Earth."

He gazes at it, saying: "I behold you with the eye of Suparṇa, the Garuḍa. (7) Then, taking it up with his thumb and ring finger, he swallows it without chewing, saying: "I consume you with the mouth of Agni, with the belly of the Brāhmaṇa, with the sacred word (*brahman*) of Bṛhaspati; I place you within the belly of Indra. (8) Having sipped water, he sips water again, saying: "May those deities who are within the waters pacify [me]. Go to the belly of Indra, consecrated by *svāhā*! *Svāhā*! (9) 3.17

He touches the region of the navel with the formula: "Do not touch my belly; sit above my navel; I seat you in the belly of Indra. (1) He touches the seats of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) with the formulas according to their respective forms: "Speech in my mouth; breath in my nostrils," and so forth. (2) Having washed a vessel with water and filled it, he pours it out toward the east with the formula: "Quicken the quarters. (3) Having filled another [vessel], he pours it out toward himself with the formula: "Quicken me. (4) Wherever they bring him the portion for the Brahman priest, he should not [leave it] there before...
One should eat from a vessel that has been repaired. Whatever earthenware vessel might break during the sacrifice, one should touch it with this mantra:
"The earth has gone to the earth; the mother has gone back to her mother.
May we abound in sons and cattle; may he who hates us be shattered."

Thus, he touches the *anvāhārya* rice that has been placed within the *antarvedi*: "O Brahman, you are the Brahman; for the sake of the Brahman, you have been invoked today; do not harm me; having been invoked, be auspicious to me. When they address him with the words, "O Brahman, we shall set forth," he then gives the impulse: "Him! O divine Savitṛ, this has been declared to you; impel it and sacrifice it. Bṛhaspati is the Brahman; may he protect the sacrifice, may he protect the lord of the sacrifice, may he protect me."

"Oṃ, be established!"—thus [he says] eight times. He remains right there until the conclusion of the sacrifice. When the sacrifice has concluded, having gone out in the same manner he entered, he places a fuel-stick on the Āhavanīya fire with the formula: "Homage to the performed rite; homage to the unperformed rite, Svāhā! Having placed it, he stands worshipping [the fire] with the verse:

"The undeceived Jātavedas, sitting down first within this [sacrifice], has sacrificed the sacrifice. Winning gain, release us with a good release; bestow upon us wealth, O Jātavedas, and whatever is auspicious."
Sacrifice for us toward greater prosperity; unite us with a benevolent mind rich in strength.
Thus, in this manner prescribed, his office as Brahman-priest is established for the *iṣṭi* and animal sacrifices; his office as Brahman-priest is established. 12. 3.18.
Thus ends the third book.
Now begins the fourth book.
We shall explain the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). 1. On the day of the *parvan*, the sacrificer has his hair and beard shaved. 2. Having offered the *agnihotra*, [he recites]:
"O gods who know the way, find the way for the sacrifice!
By the divine Lord of Mind, let the sacrifice be set in motion from the wind."

Having murmured this, the Adhvaryu adds fuel to the fires at dawn. (3) With the verse, "O Agni, may splendor be mine in the invocations," he takes hold of the eastern fire. (4) He takes the other two silently. (5) He takes hold of the Gārhapatya with the second verse and the Anvāhāryapacana with the third. (6) Or he may take hold of each one with all three verses. (7) But he should either murmur the final verse or add fuel to the Āhavanīya. (8) Some prescribe the adding of fuel to the fires with the *vyāhṛtis*. (9) Some prescribe it as part of the sacrificer's duties. (10) While the fires are being supplied with fuel, the sacrificer worships them, saying: "I take hold of Agni, the good chariot, who is the source of bliss, who ascends the rising sun for the sake of the day."
May Āditya, the supreme light among lights, rest for the sake of the sacrifice and the deities tomorrow.
The Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas, together with Indra and the deities—
I first encompass them within my own abode through my inspired wisdom.
I first embrace those gods who have entered this fifteenfold strength;
may Agni, the bearer of oblations, bring them here, and may this full-moon offering be theirs within me.
This oblation of the new moon belongs to them within me.

Thus, according to their respective characteristics, [he addresses] the Āhavanīya fire. 11.4.1: "The sacrificial animals have come from the assembly of the gods between the two fires; them I first enclose within my own abode with my wise thought."
Standing between the two fires, he mutters:
"May offspring of every form rejoice here, dwelling together with Agni the householder;
as the first, I encompass them within my own abode through my wisdom."
May the cattle of every form delight here, dwelling together around Agni the householder;
them I first enclose within my own abode with wise intent.
Thus [he addresses] the Gārhapatya fire:
"This is the fire of the ancestors; it has carried the oblations to the ancestors. I enclose it from the front; may it make our food free from poison."
Thus [ends the section on] the Anvāhāryapacana fire. 3.
O eternal one, may the hall-keepers kindle thee, the share of victory.
O Agni of the assembly-hall, mayest thou shine for me for a hundred autumns for the sake of conquest.
Thus, may the food belonging to the household be brought for a hundred autumns;
may Ahirbudhnya bestow prosperity and the sacred word upon the household.
Thus ends the section on the guest-offering (Āvasathīya).
Here, I announce the sacrifice to the Vasus, of whom Agni is the eldest.
O Indra, I proclaim this sacrifice to the eldest Rudras.
This sacrifice I announce to the Ādityas, with Varuṇa as their chief.

Thus [regarding] all [the rites], Āśmarathya says that one should take that very fire which was carried forward for the Agnihotra; Ālekhana says that one should carry forward a different fire. Some recite these in this sequence: eating, adding fuel to the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*), and undertaking the vow (*vratopāyana*); others [recite them as]: adding fuel to the fires, eating, and undertaking the vow.

Some say that the commencement of the vow consists of eating and adding fuel to the fires. Before the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is brought, the husband and wife should eat food mixed with clarified butter, provided it is other than beans and meat. According to another view, this should be done before the calves are driven away from their mothers. Then the sacrificer has his hair and beard shaved. Having stepped around behind the Āhavanīya fire and sat down to the south, facing north, he sips water while reciting the verse: "The plants are full of sap. Thereafter, he worships the Sun, saying: "Thou art the sovereign; thou art the protector of vows; thou art the lord of vows."

"I undertake the vow; I declare that to you; may I be able to do it; may I succeed through it. (7) If he should enter upon the vow when the sun has set, he worships the Āhavanīya fire with this very mantra. (8) "He enters upon the vow with sacrificial grass at the full moon, and with calves at the new moon"—so it is known. (9) 4.3

Standing to the south, he addresses the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra: "O Agni, Lord of Vows, I shall perform the vow. This [formula] should belong to the Brāhmaṇa alone, not to the other two castes. He worships Vāyu with "O Vāyu, Lord of Vows"; Āditya with "O Āditya, Lord of Vows"; and the Āhavanīya fire with "O Lord of Vows of vows. Finally, he worships the deities: "O gods, exert yourselves among the gods! May the first excel in the second, the second in the third; may the thrice-eleven [gods] protect me here!"

"May I be able to do this which I am doing; may the Self act for the Self. I shall perform this remedy; this is my universal remedy. O Aśvins, you two protect me! (3) Entering upon the vow (*vrata*), he meditates on the ocean with his mind. (4) He observes this vow: he does not eat meat, he does not approach a woman, he does not sit on elevated ground, and he avoids untruth. Having fasted that night, he either drinks water or eats forest food.

He lies down either in the chamber of the Āhavanīya fire or in the chamber of the Gārhapatya fire. On the following day, having passed behind the Āhavanīya fire and behind the seat of the Brahman priest, the sacrificer sits down facing the Āhavanīya fire. Sitting right there, he consecrates the rites as they are being performed. He consecrates the fires while they are being strewn around with the formula: "May both fires be strewn; may the deities dwell near me. I fast for the sake of the domestic animals; [I fast] for me, the lord of cattle, [to obtain] livestock. He strews grass around both fires. He consecrates the deities with the formula: "May the deities dwell near me. I fast for the sake of the domestic animals; [I fast] for me, the lord of cattle, [to obtain] livestock."
Thus, he consecrates the four *praṇītā* waters as they are being brought forward with the mantra: "Bhūśca, kaśca, vākca, arkaśca, gaurca, vaṭca, khaṃca, dhūśca, nūśca, pūśca."
The ten full virāj meters, consisting of single syllables, which have pervaded this entire world—
may those goddesses, acting in harmony through their power and possessing true knowledge, lead our sacrifice to well-being.
You are purified by Brahman. Who yokes you? Let him yoke you for all desires, for the sacrifice to the gods.

"Those which flow from the front, those from above, and those from all sides—with those rays as my strainers, I commence faith and the sacrifice. (5.4.5) He consecrates the oblation being set out with the mantra: "I invoke here Agni, the Hotṛ. (1) Having said that, he restrains his speech until the call for the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*). (2) He consecrates the entire sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) with the mantra: "Who yokes you? Let him yoke you. (3) He consecrates the altar (*vedi*) while it is being swept.
The four-tufted maiden, well-adorned, with a face of clarified butter, in the midst of the world;
being cleansed for great good fortune, grant desires to me, the sacrificer.
Thus, he consecrates the *stambayajus* as it is being carried away:

"O Gods, whoever hates me with the heart, with the mind, or with speech; whoever hates me with sacred knowledge, with ritual action, with what has been heard, or with the longing heart—Indra, with his thunderbolt, I cut off his head."
Thus, he addresses the *utkara* (mound of earth) as it is being taken up: "I prepare this dwelling for him among you, O gods, who practices the life of sacred study (*brahmacarya*).
Wise, with his mind fixed on austerity, he moves as an internal messenger among human beings."
Thus he consecrates both the western and the eastern enclosures: "By the measure, the over-measure, the counter-measure, and the up-measure of the sacrifice, I enclose thee."
O Bṛhaspati, encompass the altar; may the seats be well-disposed for you, O gods. Upon it let the sacrificial grass spread out effectively; may the divine Earth be gracious toward us within her womb.
he consecrates the skin as it is being torn away with the mantra: "If, while tearing [you] up, we have harmed the earth, the plants, or the waters..."
O Adhvaryus, you who have fashioned the wooden sword (sphyá), protect the atmosphere with the wooden sword; may he preserve us from that.

Whatever cruel thing we have done here while digging or preparing this altar with our minds, seeking the gods—may we not come to grief because of that; may the earth be auspicious to us along with all the worlds.
Having thus prepared it, he consecrates it with the mantra: "Becoming the earth, she nourished her greatness; therefore the goddess increases her milks.
The sacrificial ones go forth to the sacrifice, and here the herbs, the waters, and the Śakvarī verses bring auspiciousness."
Thus, he consecrates the *prokṣaṇī* waters as they are being set down:
"I, whose will is worthy of praise, address the divine Waters;
day and night they have flowed, the active ones."

Thus he consecrates the sacrificial grass (barhis) as it is being spread: "We have not harmed the sacrificial grass within the earth; may they cause the severed plants to sprout again. Those whose root you have struck with the wooden sword—may they be auspicious and well-disposed toward us."
Thus [he says] four times. He consecrates the clarified butter and the sprinkling waters while they are being purified:
"By means of the waters, purify the clarified butter; by means of the clarified butter, purify the waters thoroughly with the purifiers of Savitṛ.
O divine Śakvarīs, being in harmony, protect this sacrifice with the Śakvara [chant]."
Thus has the inspection of the clarified butter been explained; [now] the "butter-portions" (ājyagrahas). 4.7.
He recites the mantra over the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) being spread within the altar:
"May the plants and the waters here be well-disposed toward the sacrificer, O powerful ones."
May Parjanya, who rains upon the heavens, cause these to sprout forth—golden-hued, with a hundred shoots, and inviolable.
Thus he consecrates the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) as it is being spread:
"O sacrificial grass, soft as wool, being spread out, pleasant for the gods to sit upon—
place the sacrificer in the world of heaven, on the back of the firmament, in the highest sky."
Thus he addresses the altar as it is being strewn: "The four-tufted young woman, well-formed, with ghee for her face, clothes herself in sacred ordinances.
Being strewn for great good fortune, do thou milk desires for me, the sacrificer."

"Be auspicious and gracious to me; be pleasant and comfortable to me; be full of vigor and full of milk for me. Swell me with food and vigor; swell me with sacred knowledge and splendor; swell me with political power and strength; swell me with the common people and prosperity; swell me with long life and the eating of food; swell me with offspring and cattle; swell me with a [secure] world.
(3.4.8) He consecrates the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) as they are being laid down with these formulas, one by one: "Thou art firm; may I be firm among my kinsmen," and so forth.
In this sacrifice, I now place these enclosing-sticks (paridhis) around me for the sake of non-disturbance;
may Agni, the supporter, the sustainer, the most steadfast, drive away all enemies from here.
And with this verse he consecrates all [the fires], beginning with the Āhavanīya:
"I yoke thee with the divine prayer (*brahman*) so that thou, O Jātavedas, mayest carry this oblation.
Kindling thee, may we live long with good offspring and brave sons, offering tribute to thee."

O Agni, whatever of this sacrifice of mine may be harmed, or whatever of the clarified butter may be spilled, O Viṣṇu—with that I strike down the rival who is difficult to kill; I consign him to the lap of Destruction.
Most brilliant are thy burnings and thy lights, O Agni, which surround thy bodies;
with these do thou clothe thy armor on every side, so that the Piśācas who destroy the sacrifice may not harm thee.
Thus, as the two separating blades (*vidhṛtī*) are being placed down, he addresses them:
"With the two separating blades I cut off my rivals, those kinsmen already born and those yet to be born.
With the two restraining powers I drive away these [foes]; may I be the highest among my own people, O Gods!"
Driving away the enemy with the two press-stones, driving away all evil, lack of thought, and the short-lived demon;
sitting as goddesses in the world of the well-performed deed, bestow upon us progeny and wealth.

"You two are supports, you are separators, you are self-supporting; maintain the vital breaths in me, maintain offspring in me, maintain cattle in me. With these words, he consecrates the *prastara* as it is being laid down:

"This *prastara* is the supporter of both—the supporter of the *prayāja*s and also of the *anūyāja*s. It has supported the sacrificial fuel-sticks of every form; upon it I set down the offering-spoons."
he addresses the *sruk* ladles as they are being set down:
"Ascend the paths leading to the gods, O *juhū*, where the first-born seers of old abide."
O you with golden wings and a shining floor, whose limbs are well-formed, carry me to where the worlds of the righteous dwell.

You are the ladle, dripping with ghee; cherished by the sages through the Gāyatrī meters, remain unshakable and attend to the sacrifice. With your excellent guidance, lead the sacrifice toward the gods by means of the divine protection of Agni.
Thus [he says] regarding the *juhū* ladle:
"With the *upabhṛt* ladle as my weapon, I drive away my rivals—those kinsmen already born and those yet to be born.
May I milk the sacrifice like a cow that yields well; may I be superior, and my rivals be inferior."

O all-knowing one, you who are well-sustaining, the upholding ladle dripping with ghee, by means of the Triṣṭubh metre, remain unshakable and attend to the sacrifice; lead the sacrifice forward with good guidance unto the gods, through the divine protection of Indra.
Thus [he addresses] the *upabhṛt* ladle:

"O Agni, whoever, of evil intent, with speech or mind, has acted as an enemy or assailed me from afar—may his thought be cast down below the *dhruvā* ladle; may I be superior, and my rivals be inferior."

You are firm, the supporter, full of wealth; O all-knowing one, with the *jagatī* metre, being unshakable, attend to the sacrifice. With good guidance, lead the sacrifice to the gods through the divine protection of the Viśvedevas.
Thus [he places] the Dhruvā [ladle]. "Be gracious to me; sit on the earth, which is easy to sit upon, and spread me out with progeny and cattle in the world of heaven.
Sit in the sky, on the earth, and in the intermediate space! May I become superior, and may my rivals be inferior to me."
This *sruva*-ladle offers the oblations; with the hundred-syllabled *anuṣṭubh* metre, it anoints all the parts of the sacrifice by means of the divine protection belonging to Bṛhaspati.
Thus [he addresses] the *sruva* ladle:
"This vessel is full of ghee, an inexhaustible fountain with a hundred streams;
[may it be] by the divine protection of the Maruts."
Thus [having addressed] the vessel of clarified butter (ājyasthālī), he consecrates the two sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) being anointed with:
"Thou art satisfaction; the Gāyatrī is thy metre; satisfy me with splendor and with the luster of sacred knowledge."
You are satisfaction; you are the Triṣṭubh metre; satisfy me with vigor and heroic power.
You are satisfaction; you are the Jāgata metre; satisfy me with offspring and cattle.
Thus, he touches the oblations placed within the altar: "You are the sacrifice, resting on all sides; may the past and the future rest upon me from every side.
May there be for me a hundred blessings, and a thousand pleasant truths, rich in nourishment and abounding in cattle."
Thus [is the offering] for the cake dedicated to Agni:
"Thou art Prajāpati, resting on all sides; may the past and the future rest upon me from every side.
May there be for me a hundred blessings; may there be for me a thousand pleasant truths, full of nourishment and cattle."
Thus [ends] the offering to Agni and Soma:
"O Indra and Agni, whoever here desires what is less for me, the sacrificer at this sacrifice—drive him away from these worlds! May I obtain offspring rich in heroes."
Thus [is] the invocation to Indra.

This is the power of Indra, the immortal vigor; by this the cattle helped Indra. With that, O gods, protect me here! May I win food, nourishment, glory, force, and strength. May the cooked [oblation] take its place within me.
Thus it was cooked. That which entered the earth, whereby Prajāpati poured strength into Indra—
this is that bright, honeyed, vigorous draught, with which he subsequently strengthened Mahendra from above.
May curd satisfy me.
Thus, with the formula "O Agni, may splendor be mine in the invocations," he touches all [the substances] together with this entire section.
"May this sacrifice, rich in oblations, be established through the Ṛg, the Sāman, the Yajus, and the deities.
Through it, may we conquer the worlds possessed of the sun; may we attain the friendship of Indra and immortality."

And thus, while the *sāmidhenī* verses are being recited, he addresses them with the formula: "May the Aṅgirases favor me through the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*) of this sacrifice. Whatever blessing he desires, that he invokes. When he recognizes [the verse] beginning, "Kindled, O Agni, offered with oblations," then he addresses the Āhavanīya fire with:
"May Agni, kindled and offered with oblations, having been consecrated by *svāhā*, fulfill our needs. May this homage go well to the gods."

"Thus, O Agni Ucchuṣma, be for the sacrificer; be powerless against him who assails us. (6) While the *sruva*-ladle is being used to pour the *āghāra* libation, he consecrates it with: "Thou art the mind, belonging to Prajāpati. (8) [He consecrates] that which is in the *sruc* with: "Thou art speech, belonging to Indra, the destroyer of rivals. (9) 4.12

While the two *pravara* lineages are being invoked, he mutters: "O gods, O fathers; O fathers, O gods! Who I am, as such I sacrifice; him to whom I belong, I do not exclude. My own is the sacrifice, my own the gift, my own the pious work, my own the toil, my own the oblation. Of this mine, Agni is the witness, Vāyu the hearer, Āditya the proclaimer; Heaven is my father, Earth my mother, Prajāpati my kinsman."

"Whoever I am, as such I sacrifice; whoever I belong to, him I do not abandon"—with these words he consecrates each *prayāja* offering as it is offered, saying for each: "I gratify the spring among the seasons. "One is mine, one is his—who hates us and whom we hate."
May there be two for me and two for him who hates us and whom we hate.
Three for me, three for him—[whoever] hates us and whom we hate.
Four are mine, and four are his—those who hate us and those whom we hate.
Five [belong] to me; he who hates us and whom we hate possesses nothing at all.

"Through the sacrifice with Soma, may I become possessed of sight; through this sacrifice to the gods, may I become possessed of sight"—this is for the [oblation] to Soma (1). Some authorities prescribe a single combined consecration formula: "Through the sacrifice to Agni and Soma, may I become possessed of sight" (2). He consecrates the oblation-offering of the cake for Agni with: "Through the sacrifice to the god Agni, may I become an eater of food" (3). For the Upāṃśuyāja, he says: "Thou art a piercer; may I be unpierced; may I pierce so-and-so."

He pronounces the name of whomsoever he hates. 4. "By the sacrifice to the gods Agni and Soma, may I become a slayer of Vṛtra"—this for the offering to Agni and Soma. 5. "By the sacrifice to the gods Indra and Agni, may I become possessed of power and an eater of food"—this for the offering to Indra and Agni. 6. "By the sacrifice to the god Indra, may I become possessed of power"—this for the two *sāṃnāyya* offerings. 7. "By the sacrifice to the god Mahendra, may I attain victory and greatness"—this, if he is a sacrificer to Mahendra. 8. "Of Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, I..."

"Through the sacrifice to the gods, may I, long-lived, attain a firm foundation by means of this sacrifice"—this is for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering; and "May Agni protect me from ill-sacrificed [acts]"—this also [is for it]. 9. "Through the sacrifice to the god Vaimṛdha Indra, may I become free from rivals"—this is for the *vaimṛdha* offering. 10. 4.14.

He addresses the *iḍā* as it is being brought forward, beginning with "O thou of beautiful form and rain-like color, come! and ending with "Invited, may I partake of thy invitation. (1) During the low-toned invitation (*upāṃśūpahava*), he mutters the seven divine cows: "Come to abundance! Come to prosperity! Come to wealth! O *citti*, come! O *dadhiṣ*, come! O *iḍā*, come! O *sūnṛtā*, come! (2) During the loud-toned invitation (*uccairupahava*), [he addresses] the seven human cows: "Thou art consciousness; thou art thought; thou art wealthy; thou art delighting; thou art delight; thou art offspring; thou art noble. O goddesses, together with the gods, turn back toward me! Being pleasant, sprinkle me with pleasant ghee!"
This [speech] of mine has not been grasped by the seer, the Brahman, as it was given forth, like the surging oceans with the sacrificial ladle;
the speech of the sage stands at the forefront, pointing out [the way] with its ten horns.

And thus: 3. When the Hotṛ calls for the invitation to the *iḍā*, then the sacrificer, looking at the Hotṛ, should meditate on Vāyu in his mind, [saying]: "Vāyu is the calf of the *iḍā*; through Vāyu as my calf, may you milk for me faith, austerity, and the heavenly world. 4. While the *iḍā* is being invited, he mutters, beginning with "May that blessing of mine be true," and ending with "May I attain your favor. 5. He consecrates the *iḍā* once it has been invited, [saying]: "Through the sacrifice to the goddess *iḍā*, may I become prosperous and possessed of cattle.
6. He addresses the *iḍā* while it is being brought forward for consumption.
The cow Iḍā has come to us with her calf, milking out nourishment, swelling with milk;
may she come to us with food, with oblation, and with cattle—may Iḍā come to us.

Thus, the *mārjanī* has been explained (7.4.15). He touches the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) placed upon the sacred grass (*barhis*): "O radiant one (*bradhna*), swell! May there be no loss for me who gives; may there be no exhaustion for me who acts. You are the ordainer of the quarters. May my quarters be ordained; may my quarters—both divine and human—be ordained. May day and night be ordained for me. May the half-months be ordained for me. May the months be ordained for me. May the seasons be ordained for me. May the year be ordained for me. You are the ordainer; may it be ordained for me."
To you, the guardians of the quarters, the four immortal ones,
and to the overseers of all that has come into being, we offer this oblation with our sacrificial gift.

May the portioned one grant a portion to those who worship; O worshipper, may we not have a portionless portion. Cause the waters to swell; quicken the plants. Protect the two-footed; protect the four-footed. Send down rain from heaven.
This oblation belongs to the Brāhmaṇas, to those worthy of Soma, to the drinkers of Soma;
the non-Brāhmaṇa has been excluded from it, for here there is no place for a non-Brāhmaṇa.
Thus [he says]. He touches the Anvāhārya rice that has been placed within the altar:
"This vessel is full of immortality; it is a fountain with a thousand streams, never-failing.
It supports the earth, the mid-region, and the sky. By means of this cooked rice, may I overcome death."

Thus [he says]. With the remainder of the *anuvāka*, "Thou art the portion of Prajāpati," he touches the *brahman* priest with this very [formula]. 4.16 He consecrates the *anūyāja* fuel-stick as it is being placed [on the fire] with: "This is thy fuel-stick, O Agni; through it mayest thou grow and swell. May the lord of the sacrifice grow and swell. May we grow and may we swell. When it has been placed, [he addresses] the Āhavanīya fire:
"That which I cut off from thee, O Agni, or that which I, moving about, have cast away..."
O gods, cut down his progeny and his very root.
O Agni, whoever seeks to harm us— whether he be an equal or a stranger—
let nothing of him remain, just as nothing is left of a log that has been consumed by fire.
O Jātavedas, whoever hates me, and whoever I hate,
and whoever hates me— burn them all together, O Agni, both those whom I hate and those who hate me.
Thus [he says] twice; he then consecrates the faggot-binder with the formula:

"The altar, the sacrificial grass, the oblation placed upon it, the fuel, the enclosing sticks, the offering-ladles, the clarified butter, the sacrifice, the Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, the invitatory verses, and the Vaṣaṭ-calls."
May my unifications be bent together when the fuel and the binding are offered.

Thus, with these formulas, he consecrates each *anūyāja* offering as it is offered, respectively: "By the sacrifice to the gods through the *barhis*, may I become possessed of offspring," and so on for each mantra. (4) While the two ladles (*sruc*) are being separated, he consecrates them with the two *vājavatī* verses: "By the impulse of strength... and so forth. (5) He consecrates the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) while they are being anointed with the formulas: "I have gratified the Vasu gods with the sacrifice; I have gratified the Rudra gods with the sacrifice; I have gratified the Āditya gods with the sacrifice. (6) He consecrates the *prastara* bundle while it is being anointed.
Let the sacrificial grass be anointed with the oblation of clarified butter; let it be anointed with the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Maruts;
let it be anointed by Indra and all the gods. Let that which is offered go to the celestial sky, Svāhā!

1. When he recognizes [the deity] with the words, "Agni has enjoyed this oblation," he then consecrates each deity as it is invoked with these mantras according to the respective deity: "May I follow after the victory of Agni. 2. Whenever the Hotṛ pronounces the name of the sacrificer, then he should say: "These blessings have come, desiring to yield milk. 3. He consecrates with the mantra, "The pillar of heaven, stretched out, has risen up from the earth;
by that thousand-branched one, we cause our enemy to burn," a blade of grass that was previously not taken up and is now being thrown into the fire.
O herb, let him who hates me grieve greatly; let not I grieve.

5. When the four enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) are being thrown into the fire, he addresses the Āhavanīya with the mantra: "I loosen thy cords, I loosen thy reins. 6. He addresses the *śaṃyuvāka* offering with the mantra: "Through the sacrifice to the god Viṣṇu, may I attain a firm foundation through this sacrifice for the sake of well-being (*śaṃyu*). 7. Having offered the portions of the *saṃsrāva*, he consecrates them with the mantra: "The sacrifice has been offered by the Bhṛgus; it is the giver of wealth by the Yatis; it is the giver of blessings by the Vasus; it is full of blessings by the Atharvans. The Aṅgirases have gladdened this sacrifice with their morning recitations (*prātaranuvāka*)."

"From that sacrifice of mine which has been offered and consumed, let there be the arrival of wealth here. May the sacrifice be wealthy; may the sacrifice be rich in riches. From that wealthy sacrifice, let wealth come to me; let that wealth come to me. He pronounces the name of whatever he desires. 7.4.18

Having placed the *veda* grass-bundle within the altar (*antarvedi*), he touches it with these mantras: "Thou art the *veda*; thou art acquisition; may I acquire. (1) Immediately after the words "may I acquire," he should utter the name of whatever he desires to take from his rival. (2) He consecrates each offering of the *patnīsaṃyāja* sacrifices as it is offered: for the first, with "By the sacrifice to the god Soma, may I [attain]... ; for the second, with "By the sacrifice to the god Tvaṣṭṛ, may I [attain]..."; and for Rākā, with "By the sacrifice to the goddess Rākā, may I become possessed of offspring. (3)

"Through the sacrifice to the goddess Sinīvālī, may I become possessed of cattle," [he says] regarding Sinīvālī. "Through the sacrifice to the goddess Kuhū, may I become possessed of nourishment and cattle," [he says] regarding Kuhū. He addresses these three wives with these very [formulas] and adapts the mantras accordingly. 4. He addresses the two final Patnīsaṃyāja offerings with the formula: "The wives of the gods, Agni the lord of the house—this is the couple of the sacrifice; through the sacrifice to these two deities, may I prosper by means of that couple. 5. He addresses the Ājyeḍā with the formula:
"May Iḍā clothe us with ghee, she in whose footprint those seeking the gods purify themselves."
The Vaiśvānarī Śakvarī, increasing in power, has approached the sacrifice; she belongs to the Viśvedevas.

"Thus, may we be devoted to that Sarasvatī who is most blessed. (6) When the offering of husks has been made and the mouth has been wiped, (7) and when the *samiṣṭayajus* oblation has been offered, he eats the sacrificer’s portion with the formula: "May the lord of the sacrifice prosper through his blessing. (8) If the sacrificer should be away on a journey, he should place the sacrificer’s portion in the *dhruvā* ladle with the formula: "In that world of Prajāpati named Vibhān, I place you together with the sacrificer," and then offer it along with the *samiṣṭayajus*. (9) 4.19

Formerly, from the *pūrṇapātra* vessel, he recites: "O Sacrifice, be auspicious for me; come near to me, O Sacrifice! Be well-established for me; be well-sacrificed for me; be free from harm for me. O Sacrifice, homage to you; O Sacrifice, homage to you, and again homage to you, O Sacrifice! Be established for me with auspiciousness; be established for me with comfort; be established for me with prosperity; be established for me with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). Be established in accordance with the success of the sacrifice."

"Veneration to you, veneration to you, veneration to you"—with these words, he touches the *praṇītā* waters placed within the altar. "Who has unyoked you? Let him release you. Then, from above, he pours out a continuous stream of water, saying, "In the assembly, may you be mine. Then he sprinkles them in every direction with the formulas according to their respective forms: "May the gods and the officiating priests purify themselves in the eastern quarter," and so on. He pours the remainder within the altar, saying: "I send you forth to the ocean; go back to your own source."
"May I be unbroken in offspring; may my milk not be spilled. Thus he wipes his mouth. "O Sarasvatī, that sweetness of yours which is in the waters, in the cows, and in the horses..."
With that, O Sarasvatī, who art rich in steeds, moisten my mouth.

Thus, at the southern edge of the altar, he strides the Viṣṇu-strides eastward with his right foot, using these three mantras beginning with "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu. Standing, he mutters the fourth [mantra]. Then he worships the Sun, beginning with "We have gone to heaven; we have gone to the light," and ending with "I have become united with the light.
"Rising today, O thou of sun-like splendor, destroy my rivals.
By day, strike them down with lightning; as thou settest, cast them below."
Rising today, grant us our share as a father does for his sons;
you are the master of long life, O Sūrya, so bestow that upon us.
Rising today, O Sūrya, you whose greatness is like that of Mitra, ascending to the highest heaven, destroy the jaundice and the yellowness within my heart.
We place my yellowness in the parrots, in the female parrots we deposit it;
and then, O turmeric plants, we place my yellowness within you.
This sun has risen together with all-pervading power;
may it subject my enemy to me, and may I not be subject to my enemies.
Whoever curses us when we do not curse, and whoever curses us when we do curse—
may both Dawn and Night sweep away all that evil from him.

And thus he turns clockwise: "I turn following the turning of Indra; may those fortunes be auspicious, and may those that are evil perish. (2) If he should practice sorcery, he should wrap [his foot] with the heel of his right foot, saying: "Here I enclose the breath of so-and-so, the son of such-and-such, with grief. (3) He consecrates the *Anvāhāryapacana* fire with the mantra: "O Agni, carrier of oblations, cook for us our food, sweet for our offspring; be auspicious and pleasant to our children and our bodies."

Thus [he says]. 4. Having turned around with the words "Thou art brilliance," he addresses the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra: "May I be united with offspring; may offspring be united with me. 5. Having added fuel with the words "Kindled, O Agni, shine for me; kindling thee, O Agni, may I shine," and having worshipped with the words "May the sacrifice be wealthy and may I become more wealthy," he addresses the Gārhapatya fire. Beginning with "O Agni, thou purifiest our lives," he continues until the end of the verse, "a hundred winters. 6. He pronounces his son's name, uttering this blessing: "I invoke for my lineage this blessing that is full of light."

Thus [is the procedure] for one who has not yet fathered a son. "I invoke this radiant blessing for him," says one who has fathered a son. (7) Now, if he should have many sons, he should utter the names of them all: "For light, for offspring, thee!

(8) 4.21 Seated within the altar-ground, he mutters the *atīmokṣa* formulas beginning with, "Those gods who are destroyers of the sacrifice. (1) He consecrates the entire sacrificial ground with the formula, "Who yokes you? May he release you. (2) Here, some prescribe the consumption of the sacrificer’s portion. (3) The Brahmin sacrificer may also consume a portion of the *sāṃnāyya* offerings.

May this oblation be generative for me—possessing ten heroes, with a complete retinue—for my well-being; may it be a winner of self, a winner of progeny, a winner of cattle, a winner of safety, a winner of the world, and a winner of rain.
May Agni make my progeny abundant; bestow upon us food, milk, and seed. May he maintain for us the increase of wealth, nourishment, and vigor.

Thus for the boiled milk. "I have celebrated Dadhikrāvan," [he says] for the curds. 4. Then he releases the vow. 5. Standing to the south, he addresses the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra: "O Agni, lord of vows, I have performed the vow. 6. This [formula] should belong to the Brāhmaṇa alone, not to the other two castes. 7. "O Vāyu, lord of vows," [with this he] stands facing Vāyu; "O Āditya, lord of vows," [with this] the Āditya.

With the words, "O Lord of Vows, of vows," he addresses the Āhavanīya fire (8). He mutters the *punarālambha* formula for the sacrifice: "The sacrifice has come into being; it has truly come into being" (9). Having stepped forward toward the east, he should recite this verse: "O Agni, rich in cattle... (10). As he goes out following the path [of the sacrifice], he says: "I wish to satisfy the Brāhmaṇas" (11). Regarding this, Āśmarathya says that these duties pertaining to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) do not apply to one who is away on a journey. Now, Ālekhana says: the duties of the sacrificer are indeed prescribed even for one who is away on a journey; there is only this difference.

The Adhvaryu should perform those ritual acts which are to be performed while touching [the objects]; the Sacrificer, facing that direction at the proper time, should mutter the mantras. However, facing eastward, he should take the Viṣṇu-steps and say "gomatīm," saying "gomatīm. 13. 4.22. Thus ends the fourth book. Now begins the fifth book.

One who is about to establish the sacred fires shall fetch two kindling sticks (*araṇī*) from an *aśvattha* tree that has grown within a *śamī* tree and whose roots have not touched the ground; according to some, they should be from one whose roots have not touched the ground at all. [He does so] with the verse, "The *aśvattha* which has grown within a *śamī*," or with the following verse. The ritual materials (*saṃbhāra*) are explained by the Brāhmaṇa: there are seven terrestrial and seven arboreal ones. He brings them with these mantras, according to their respective forms: "Thou art the form of Vaiśvānara on the earth, flowing around. With the verse, "Thee whom I have gathered together, O Jātavedas," he [places] the collected materials.

The sacrificer touches the collected materials. 6. A Brāhmaṇa who desires, "May I be preeminent and endowed with spiritual luster," should establish his fires under the Kṛttikās. 7. He who desires, "May I cause all my offspring to prosper," should establish his fires under Rohiṇī. 8. He who desires, "May I be glorious," should establish his fires under Mṛgaśīrṣa. 9. He who, having previously been prosperous, should become more wretched, should establish his fires under the two Punarvasūs. 10. He who desires, "May my offspring be inclined toward giving," should establish his fires under the two former Phalgunīs. 11. He who...

He who should desire, "May I be possessed of fortune," should establish his fires under the two following [nakṣatras]. 12. Some recite them in reverse order. 13. He who should desire, "May gifts be bestowed upon me," should establish his fires under Hasta. 14. He who has rivals should establish his fires under Citrā. 15. According to some, a Rājanya should establish his fires under Citrā. 16. It is known from tradition: one desiring offspring should establish his fires under Viśākhā; one desiring prosperity under Anurādhā; and one desiring firm standing under the Proṣṭhapadas. 17. According to some, it should be under the nakṣatra of the Sun (Sūrya) alone. 18. 5.1.

A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires in spring; a Rājanya in summer or winter; a Vaiśya in autumn; a Rathakāra in the rainy season; and the Śiśira season is common to all classes. Now, if he intends to sacrifice with Soma, he should not wait for the seasons nor the lunar mansions.

One may establish the sacred fires at any season whatsoever. Alternatively, one may establish them on the new moon day or the full moon day. One should not, however, establish them on the full moon day that falls between the two *phalgunī* constellations. There is one view that the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) is permitted for the fourth caste; there is another view that it is not permitted. There is one view that the establishment of the sacred fires is not permitted for one whose father is still living; there is another view that it is permitted. A householder (*śālīna*) who has moved away from his home should establish the sacred fires after departing.

A Yāyāvara should not take heed [of such things]. He settles upon a sacrificial ground sloping toward the east with the mantra, "Go away, depart! (VS 1.28). Having measured out the shed on that site facing north, he prepares the Gārhapatya hearth in front of the middle post. In front of the Gārhapatya hearth, he prepares the Āhavanīya hearth. A Brāhmaṇa should establish his sacred fires at a distance of eight steps; a Rājanya, at eleven steps.

It is known that a Vaiśya [should perform the rite] in twelve [years], and the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*) takes place in the twenty-fourth [year]. According to some, it is at an indefinite time; according to others, it is measured by the eye. To the south-east, in the third part [of the space] closer to the site of the *gārhapatya* fire than to the site of the *dakṣiṇāgni*, he prepares the site for the *dakṣiṇāgni*. In front of the site of the *āhavanīya*, he erects the *sabhya* fire-place; in front of the *sabhya*, the *āvasatha*. Then the sacrificer has his hair and beard shaved. Wearing linen garments, the husband and wife should establish the fires.

When the sun is behind the trees, having brought fire from the *aupāsana* hearth, he establishes the *brāhmaudana* fire to the west of the site of the *gārhapatya*. At night, he silently pours out four *śarāva*-measures of rice for the *brahmaudana* on a hide or a mat. Or else, he offers the first portion with: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I pour thee out, acceptable to Brahman and Prāṇa. The second with: "To Brahman and Apāna. The third with: "To Brahman and Vyāna. [The fourth] with: "To Brahman."

The fourth [offering]: having poured it out, he cooks it in milk (6), or in four water-vessels (7). According to some, he does not rinse it nor does he pour water over it (8). Having cooked it like rice with living grains and having removed it from the fire, he offers it with the verse, "To the wise seer... (9). Then, having divided it into four parts, sprinkled them with clarified butter, and as if without cutting through [the connection], he presents them to the four *ārṣeya* priests (10). To those who have eaten their portions, he gives a common gift (11). Having brought clarified butter to the remainder of the *brahmaudana*...

He places three fresh fuel-sticks of the variegated *aśvattha* tree—possessing shoots and leaves, covered with clusters of buds, and a span in length—into the *brahmaudana* after it has been stirred. (12) He offers them with *gāyatrī* verses for a Brāhmaṇa, with *triṣṭubh* verses for a Rājanya, and with *jagatī* verses for a Vaiśya, beginning with the verse, "Worship Agni with fuel. (13) He should observe this vow: (14) from the time of the establishment of the fires (*āgnyādheya*), he should not eat meat, nor should he approach a woman. (15) They should not carry his fire out of the house, nor should they bring it from elsewhere. (16) This fire should not go out; (17) nor...

He should set out; or, if he should go after [the fire], he should likewise set out. Having cooked the *brahmaudana* in this very manner and having placed the fuel-sticks in this very manner, he should complete the remainder of the *bharaṇa* and establish the fires. If he does not initiate him within a year, he should do exactly the same. He who is about to establish the fire on the morrow observes the vow during that night: he does not eat meat, he does not approach a woman, and he does not sit on high ground. He should avoid untruth. According to one view, only the *adhvaryu* should observe the vow; according to another, everyone. 5.3.18–23.

At the site of the *gārhapatya* fire, he binds a speckled goat with the verse, "O Agni, cause the offspring to dwell together. On this night, they keep the sacrificer awake with lutes and drums and with sacred songs. He should kindle the fire that night with wood-shavings, using the verse, "Kindling the fire with wood-shavings. At dawn, he should heat the two fire-drills over that fire with the two verses beginning, "O Jātavedas, the seed of the world... He causes this fire to go out. He hands the two fire-drills to the sacrificer; the fire wards off the demons.

6. Thus the sacrificer awaits [the arrival of the two wives] with the verse: "O great two, mistresses of the people, in the seat of the Ṛta. 7. Having received them with the verse, "Ascend the ten-fingered [loom]," he consecrates them with the following two verses. 8. Then he restrains his speech, saying: "I depart from untruth; I approach truth. 9. He remains silent until the churning of the fire. 10. Then both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer take the fire into themselves with the two verses beginning, "In me I first take Agni. 11. They dig up the sites for the fires with the verse: "The impurity that is in her, as she is being dug up... 12.

Having sprinkled [the ground] upwards, he sprinkles it with water while reciting the verse, “May the goddesses be for our aid” (RV 10.9.4). (13) He scatters the ritual materials upon the dry, windless spots. (14) Having divided them into two parts, he places half in the eastern [spots] and half in the western ones. (15) With the formulas, “Thou art the ash of Agni; thou art the soil of Agni,” he scatters sand in the place of the Gārhapatya fire. (16) In the same way in the place of the Anvāhāryapacana fire, in the same way in the place of the Āhavanīya fire, and likewise in the places of the Sabhya and Āvasathya fires. (17) In this manner, from this point forward, the subsequent rites are performed in these [places] in their proper sequence. (18) 5.4

He pours out the earth-clods one by one for each of the kings: (1) "Thou art consciousness, the bearer of desires," with these words he pours out the saline soil (ūṣa). (2) While pouring them out, he meditates mentally: "Whatever dark [spot] was there in the moon, may that be here. (3) "Come forth, O Agni!"—with this verse he pours out the mole-hill earth. (4) "Whatever immortality is in the earth"—with this verse he pours out an ant-hill at the site of the Gārhapatya fire. (5) "Whatever immortality is in the atmosphere"—with this verse he pours it out at the site of the Anvāhāryapacana fire. (6) "Whatever immortality is in heaven"—with this verse he pours it out at the sites of the others. (7) "Up from the ocean"—with this verse he pours out the cooking-pot earth (sūda). (8) "So much [in extent] thou wast at first"—with this verse...

9. "This was struck by the Boar," O Goddess—thus [he addresses] the pebbles. 10. While scattering the pebbles, he should meditate upon whomsoever he hates. 11. To the north of the ritual materials, he throws down pieces of gold made of refined gold with the verse: "Those auspicious bodies of yours, O Jātavedas... 12. Having placed them one by one, he hands over silver to his enemy. 13. If he cannot find an enemy, he should throw it away. 14. Having thus combined [the materials], he scatters the wooden items: the lotus leaf, the *aśvattha*, the *udumbara*, the *palāśa*, and the *śamī*.
