Having removed the ashes from the *brāhmaudana* vessel and placed the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) together with the *daśahotṛ* formula, he stands by [the fire] and churns the fire on the horse with the mantra: "O Agni, be born together with Agni. While it is being churned, he causes the sacrificer to recite the *caturhotṛ* formulas. When [the fire] has been produced, he gives a choice gift (*vara*). He breathes upon the newborn [fire] with the mantra: "With the breath of Prajāpati, I breathe upon you. Then he grasps it with both hands with the mantra: "Mortals have generated the immortal. Thereafter, having lifted it toward the east before sunrise, [he establishes it] in the *rathantara* [sāman].

While being sung, he sits upon the ritual materials and establishes the *gārhapatya* fire. With the formula, "O Lord of Vows, I establish you with the vow of the Bhṛgus," he should establish it for one of the Bhṛgu lineage. With the formula, "O Lord of Vows, I establish you with the vow of the Aṅgirases," [he should do so] for a Brāhmaṇa who belongs to the Aṅgiras lineage. With the formula, "O Lord of Vows, I establish you with the vow of the Ādityas, the gods," [he should do so] for other Brāhmaṇa lineages. With the formula, "O Lord of Vows, I establish you with the vow of King Varuṇa," [he should do so] for a king.

"By the power of Indra, O Lord of Vows, I establish you with the vow," [he says] for a Kṣatriya; "By the power of Manu, the leader of the people, O Lord of Vows, I establish you with the vow," [he says] for a Vaiśya; "By the power of the Ṛbhus, the gods, O Lord of Vows, I establish you with the vow," [he says] for a Rathakāra. 7. He establishes all the fires within the very materials (saṃbhāras). 8. 5.6.

Having established the fire by means of the *ṛṣi-ādhāna*, he establishes it with the *vyāhṛtis*: "Bhūḥ! Bhuvaḥ! (1). Then, with the two *Sarparājñī* verses and with the second verse, "The earth with its abundance... (2). With these very [verses], the sacrificer pays homage to the fire once it has been established (3). Then, with the *Gharmaśiras* verse, "The Gharma is the head... (4). With this very [verse], the sacrificer pays homage to the fire once it has been established (5). Then, finally, he establishes the fire with these [verses]: "I spread the *ṛta*-clay... (6).

With these two verses, "Thou art a good householder" and "I am thine," the sacrificer worships the fire that has been established. Then, into the right ear of the horse, he causes the sacrificer to recite the formulas concerning the forms of Agni:
"O powerful one, bring hither that form of Agni which is purifying and dear among cattle."
O powerful one, bring hither that beloved form of Agni which is purifying and dwells within the waters.
O vigorous one, bring hither that bright and beloved body of Agni which is in the sun.

Thus, having kindled the fuel for the *gārhapatya* fire, he lifts up the *āhavanīya* fire with the formula: "I lift thee up for vigor and strength" (10). While it is being lifted, he sings the *vāmadevya* chant (11). He should lift the fire upwards as he carries it out (12), but he should not carry it higher than the height of his mouth (13). They hold the lifted fuel ready (14). Then, having brought [the fire] from the *anvāhāryapacana* or from anywhere else, he places it down while bending his knees (15), or by churning it with the two *araṇis* (16). Having established it according to the *ṛṣi*-based method of installation, he establishes it with the *vyāhṛti* "Bhuvaḥ" (17). Then...

With these two verses beginning with "The earth by the two queens of the serpents" and the third verse beginning with "The earth by its abundance," the sacrificer worships the fire that has been established. Then, with the verse beginning with "The wind, the breath, the head of the Gharma," the sacrificer worships the fire that has been established. 5.7.18–21.

Then, preceded by the horse, they proceed toward the east with the verse, "Go forward along the eastern quarter, O wise one," and with these four verses beginning, "From heaven, from earth, from the intermediate space. (1) First he carries [the fire] at knee-height, then at navel-height, then at mouth-height. (2) He should not allow the fire and the sun to pass each other. (3) He carries the fire in front and follows behind it. (4) To the south, the Brahman priest causes the chariot to turn, or the chariot-wheel, with the verse, "O Bṛhaspati, fly around with the chariot. (5) This [verse].

According to some, the Brahman priest mutters a verse of the *Apratiratha* hymn; likewise, he causes the chariot to roll until the wheel has turned three times. For one who has rivals or enemies, he should cause the wheel to turn three times again. At the halfway point, he gives a boon. Having placed gold at the halfway point, he steps across it with the formula: "Thou art the vault of heaven, O sun, the crossing-place, the support of the sacrificer. To the north of the ritual materials, he makes the horse step eastward with its right foot.

11. Having stepped forward with the verse beginning "He has stepped forth," he turns to the right on that very spot and makes [the horse] step westward with the following verse. 12. He should make it step from the side so that the embers of the fire already established fall upon its footprint. 13. If there should be no horse, an ox may perform this rite. 14. It is known from tradition that it should be placed in the footprint of a goat. 15. According to some, it should be placed in the footprint of a water-pot. 16. Having taken hold of the horse, standing facing west in front of it while the *Bṛhat* Sāman is being sung, he offers the oblation. 17. 5.8.17.

When the sun has half-risen, he establishes the Āhavanīya fire. (1) For one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), he should establish it when the sun has fully risen. (2) Having established it according to the procedure for the *ṛṣi*-fire-establishment, he establishes it with the *vyāhṛtis*: "Bhūḥ! Bhuvaḥ! Svaḥ! (3) Then [he establishes it] with the two *Sarparājñī* verses and with the fourth verse, "The earth by its abundance... (4). With these very [verses], the sacrificer pays homage to the fire once it has been established. (5) Then [he establishes it] with the "Gharma-head" verse: "The sun is the eye... (6). With this very [verse], the sacrificer pays homage to the fire once it has been established. (7) And [he establishes it] with: "I establish you, the breath, in immortality. (8)

With two verses [beginning] "He has attained, he has pervaded," he stands by [the fire] after finally placing it down. When the two [fires] have been established, he sings the Vāravantīya. One should not touch a fire that has been established but not yet offered into; it is known from tradition that it must be appeased with clarified butter and herbs.
"O Agni, that body of yours which is purifying among cattle, which is on the earth, which is in the fire, which is in the Rathantara, and which is in the Gāyatra metre—this, I secure for you."
To her, to you, svāhā!

O Agni, that purifying form of yours which is in the waters, which is in the intermediate space, which is in the wind, which is in the Vāmadevya [Sāman], and which is in the Triṣṭubh metre— this [offering] secures it for you. To that form of yours, Svāhā!

"O Agni, that pure and dear body of yours which is in the sun, which is in heaven, which is in the Āditya, which is in the Bṛhatī, which is in the Jāgata meter—this [body] of yours I here obtain. To that body of yours, svāhā! (12.5.9)

Having pacified [the fires] with clarified butter and medicinal herbs, he establishes the *sabhya* and *āvasathya* fires from the *āhavanīya* fire by means of the *ṛṣi*-based laying ritual (1); or alternatively, having churned them out from two kindling woods (2)—the *sabhya* fire in the assembly hall and the *āvasathya* fire in the dwelling (3). It is known [from tradition] that these two are located in the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire (4). One view is that one should sing the *yajñāyajñīya* chant.

"In all [sacrifices]," so it is further stated; "one should sing the Sāmans at the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya)," thus it is known. According to some, one should not sing the Sāmans at the establishment of the sacred fires. With the three verses addressed to Agni Pavamāna, he places three fuel-sticks of *aśvattha* wood, namely with these three: "O Agni, you purify our lives" (*agna āyūṃṣi pavase*). He places three fuel-sticks of *śamī* wood, anointed with clarified butter, with these three: "The wave of the ocean" (*samudrād ūrmiḥ*). With the verse "Kindled, O Agni, shine before us" (*preddho agne dīdihi puro naḥ*), he places a fuel-stick of *udumbara* wood.

"May we worship thee in thy highest birth, O Agni"—with this verse he offers a stick of *vaikaṅkata* wood; "That brilliant [splendor] of Savitṛ, the most excellent"—with this verse he offers a stick of *śamī* wood. (10) He offers one of each kind at all [the offerings]. (11) At dawn, he performs the *agnihotra* offering silently according to the procedure for the morning *agnihotra*. (12) In the forest, the sacrificer worships the *āhavanīya* fire with the "wild" (*ghora*) verses and the "wild" bodily forms: "O Agni, those wild bodies of thine—with them go to so-and-so," he should say, naming the one whom he hates. (13) 5.10

Having poured out the clarified butter across the strainer and purified it, and having heated and wiped the *sruva* and *juhū* ladles, he fills the *sruk* with four portions or twelve portions of butter and offers the *pūrṇāhuti* (full-oblation).

Having recited this verse, "Seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven your tongues," he offers with the utterance *svāhā*. (1) When the full-offering (*pūrṇāhuti*) has been offered, he gives a choice gift (*vara*). (2) In the same manner from this point forward in *darvihoma* offerings, he pours out the grain, purifies it, heats it over the fire, cleanses [the ladle], and finally places the *svāhā* utterance. (3) Those offerings for which one offers while reciting specific formulas are *darvihomas*; and those for which one should offer when [the text] enjoins "he offers. (4) Thereafter, the sacrificer worships the Āhavanīya fire with the verses: "O Agni, those two auspicious bodies of yours, the Virāj and..."

He commences the ritual procedure for the offering to Agni. (1) It is the same up to the pouring out [of the grain]. (2) He pours out the oblation for Agni on eight potsherds. (3) When the poured-out oblation has been set down but not yet sprinkled, he then digs up the gambling-ground between the *sabhyā* and *āvasathya* fires, sprinkles it, scatters the dice, places gold upon the dice, and having spread them out and gathered them together, he offers with the verse: "He has sat down, firm in his vow... (4) While handing over a hundred dice to the sacrificer, he says: "Play for cows against rice; being honest, play for the joints! (ahiṃ santaḥ parvāṇi).

"Kill them!"—with these words, the sacrificer rises after having won the contest. On that day, they should gamble with his cow in the assembly hall. They must not harm its joints. He should present it to the members of the assembly. Whatever he may win with it, having prepared both kinds of food, he should feed the Brāhmaṇas. Having placed gold in the middle of the assembly hall, he makes an offering over it with the verse, "Now indeed, Brahmaṇaspati... Then the sacrificer worships the fires with the formula, "May they be fit..."

[He gives] to Heaven and Earth. With the two verses beginning "The fires which are of one mind," [he performs the rites]. (12) It is the same [procedure] up to the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). (13) It is known from tradition that the sacrificial fee should be increasing. (14) He first gives a cushion made of all-wool to the *agnīdh* priest. (15) A goat and a horse to the *brahman* priest. (16) A milch-cow to the *hotṛ* priest. (17) An ox to the *adhvaryu* priest. (18) To all [the priests], he gives a pair of cattle, a garment, and a chariot. (19) At the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), there are six, twelve, or twenty-four sacrificial fees. (20) One view is that one should calculate [the total] together with the prescribed sacrificial fees. (21) 5.12

"Except for those [sacrifices] where a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) has been specifically prescribed"—this is another [rule]. (1) If one who is not wealthy should establish the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), he should give even a single cow as the sacrificial fee. (2) The sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) concludes in the established manner. (3) Being about to offer the evening *agnihotra*, he recites the *Daśahotṛ* formula mentally and offers the oblation along with the cup (*sagraha*) into the *āhavanīya* fire. (4) For twelve days, while the fires are kept continuously burning (*ajasra*), he performs the *agnihotra*. (5) He observes the vow (*vrata*). (6) For twelve nights, he should either perform the offering himself or have someone else do so. (7) He must not go away on a journey. (8) He should wear an unwashed garment. (9) He himself [performs] the thirteenth [night].

One should offer ten [oblations]. The cow which they first milk for the Agnihotra is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the Agnihotra. One should set down the Agnihotra with these Vyahṛtis: "Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Suvaḥ. When the year has elapsed, one should set it down with these very same [Vyahṛtis]. Āśmarathya says it should be at the very first year; Ālekhana says every year. After twelve dawns have passed, he offers the Tanū-havis oblations: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Pavamāna.

The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of thirty-six *mānas* of gold. (16) The sacrifice is completed as a successful rite (*siddha-iṣṭi*). (17) Then, for Agni Pāvaka and Agni Śuci, the sacrificial fees consist of thirty *mānas* and forty *mānas* of gold respectively. (18) The sacrifice is completed as a successful rite. (19) On the following day, one may optionally offer the *tanūhavir* oblations. (20) One may do so optionally after half a month, a month, a season, or a year; according to some teachers, immediately (*sadyas*). (21) Or, they may have the same ritual procedure (*samāna-tantra*) as the [offering] to Agni. (22) It is known from scripture: "One who is about to perform the Soma sacrifice [should not perform these]. (23) 5.13

Before a year has passed, one should offer the *tanūhavis* oblations. Or alternatively, having offered clarified butter oblations to Agni Pavamāna, Agni Pāvaka, and Agni Śuci, one may offer them to the deities associated with Soma. After the *tanūhavis* oblations, one subsequently offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Soma, a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra-Agni, and a pap cooked in ghee to Aditi. The offering to Agni-Soma should be for a Brāhmaṇa alone, not for the other two castes. [The procedure] is the same up to the husking of the grain. Regarding the husked rice grains...

He removes the rice for the sacrificial porridge with the *vibhāga* formula; he grinds the other grains together. It is the same up to the placing of the potsherds. Having placed the potsherds for the offering to Indra and Agni, he places the vessel for the porridge with the first *kapāla* formula. He modifies the mantra to "Thou art firm."

With the formula, "Thou art firm," he pours out the rice-grains for the flour-mixture and purifies them (Sūtra 10). He purifies the clarified butter with a *yajus* formula and pours it into the pot for the *caru* (Sūtra 11). He adapts the mantra according to the specific vessel (Sūtra 12). He pours the grains for the *caru* into the fire with the mantra used for placing the oblation on the fire (Sūtra 13). He places the *caru* in that very same pot (Sūtra 14). From this point forward, this is the ritual procedure for the *carus*, except for the taking of the clarified butter (Sūtra 15). There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses (Sūtra 16). The procedure is the same up until the offering of the oblations (Sūtra 17). 5.14.18.

He consecrates the oblation offered to Āditya with the formula: "Through the sacrifice to the god Āditya, may I attain firm standing by means of this sacrifice. In this very same manner, he consecrates all the [other] Ādityas. At the time of the fourfold division of the remnants, he hands over the entire remnant of the offering to Āditya to the Brahman priest. Four officiating priests who are descendants of seers (*ārṣeya*) consume it. To those who have consumed it, he gives a cow as a choice gift. According to some, the *iṣṭis* pertaining to the establishment of the fires (*āgnīdhreya*) have Upāṃśu as their deity. The *iṣṭi* is thus completed.

It concludes. 7. One who is about to begin the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) should offer two oblations to Sarasvatī beforehand: one full [oblation] first, and one after [the main sacrifice]. He offers these with the two verses beginning, "That which the gods bestowed upon you. 8. He performs the *anvārambhaṇīyā* (inaugural) offering. 9. [The offerings are: a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni-Viṣṇu, a pap (*caru*) for Sarasvatī, and a cake on twelve potsherds for Sarasvant. 10. One desiring fortune (*bhaga*) should offer as the fourth [offering] a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Bhagin. 11. [The procedure] is the same up to the presentation of the oblations. 12. [The offering] to Sarasvatī...

He consecrates the oblation with the formula: "By the sacrifice to the goddess Sarasvatī, may I prosper in speech and in the food that sustains us. (13) In this very same manner, he consecrates all the offerings whose deity is Sarasvatī. (14) Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he performs the *jaya* oblations with the twelve formulas beginning, "Thought and thinking... (15). He should offer the thirteenth oblation with the formula: "Prajāpati gave the *jayas* to Indra, the bull... (16) 5.15.

The fourteenth [offering] with the verse "O Agni, giver of strength" is for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). His splendor becomes manifold among the people; however, his own self becomes as if variegated. A pair of cattle is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). The sacrifice is completed in the established manner. One who is about to begin the New and Full Moon sacrifices, having mentally recited the *caturhotṛ* formula, offers it along with the *graha* cup into the *āhavanīya* fire. He begins the New and Full Moon sacrifices. The Full Moon sacrifice comes first. This remains unchanged for one establishing the fires on the day of the New Moon; however, on the Full Moon day—

On the preceding full-moon day, having performed the *iṣṭi* sacrifice together with the *anvārambhaṇīyā*, he concludes it immediately. On the following day, he sacrifices with the *Paurṇamāsa*. Now, these are the observances for one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*): (11) He shall not speak untruth; (12) no Brāhmaṇa shall stay in his house without having eaten; (13) he shall not turn away a guest who arrives at sunrise from staying overnight; (14) he shall not eat in the evening until the *agnihotra* has been offered; (15) nor in the morning until the *agnihotra* has been offered; (16) he shall not give other food at night; (17) when giving food at night, he shall not eat himself. (18)

19. One should not eat food cooked on a fire made from the dregs of grain. 20. One should not place wet wood [on the fire]. 21. There are waters within navigable rivers; one should not drink of them. 22. One should not dwell in a salt-flat created by oneself. 23. One should not place silver upon the sacrificial grass (barhis). 24. Having uttered the sound "hiṃ" silently, one may approach a woman. 5.16.

We shall now explain the re-establishment of the sacred fires (*punarādheya*). Its ritual procedure (*kalpa*) has been explained by [the rules for] the initial establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*). We shall enumerate its modifications (*vikāra*). It is known from tradition that he who does not prosper through the initial establishment of the fires should perform the re-establishment. According to some, when one who has established the fires suffers a loss of a limb due to old age or the death of a son, he should then establish them again. It is known from tradition: "One desiring offspring should re-establish the fires; one desiring cattle should re-establish the fires; one desiring food should re-establish the fires; one desiring a firm foundation should re-establish the fires."

Āśmarathya says that for one who must re-establish the fires (*punarādheya*), the time limit does not expire as long as one lives; Ālekhana says it is one year. (7) One who intends to extinguish the sacred fire (*agnim udvāsayiṣyan*) should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni and a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara. (8) Prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering of that sacrifice, he offers these oblations: "O Agni, that dear body of yours which dwells in the animals while being purified—enter the earth together with that, along with the *Rathantara* Sāman and the Gāyatrī metre! Svāhā! (9) 5.17

O Agni, that purifying and beloved body of yours which dwells within the waters—with that, enter the intermediate space together with the Vāmadevya Sāman and the Triṣṭubh metre. From that, bestow upon us food and vigor, and increase our domestic prosperity; Svāhā!
O Agni, that pure and beloved body of yours which dwells in the sun—enter heaven together with it, by means of the Bṛhat Sāman and the Jāgata metre. From there, protect us with rain; Svāhā!
Those portions of yours, O Agni, which Indra brought as a boar—sit upon those flames, upon the ash of Vaiśvānara; Svāhā!
O Agni, those portions of yours which are like wish-fulfilling cows, collected together—by means of them, milk for us here our desires: offspring, prosperity, and also wealth; Svāhā!
O Agni, those materials of the forest trees which have been gathered together with you—go with them to the forest trees, to your own womb, each according to its proper place; Svāhā!
Agni has come as light; he has settled in his own dwelling.
Free from the sin of slaying, I have approached the gods with my mind; svāhā!

Thus, on the full moon day, he extinguishes the burning fires. One view is that he should have the fires suspended for a year; another view is that it should be for an unlimited time. Now, these are the lunar mansions for the re-establishment of the fires: Rohiṇī, the two Punarvasūs, and Anurādhā. He should establish them in the rainy season or in autumn. It is known from tradition that they should be established at midday. One view is that one should establish all of them at midday.

"The Āhavanīya, the Sabhya, and the Āvasathya"—this is another [view]. 4. It is the same up to the laying of the Gārhapatya fire. 5. He lays the Gārhapatya with all the Sarparājñī verses. 6. It is the same up to the lifting of the Āhavanīya fire. 7. The Darbha grass is from the *upolava* plant, cut at the joints, and blown upon for a year.

Having kindled the fuel-sticks for them, he lifts up the *āhavanīya* fire with [the verse]: "When thou, being angry, didst cast me away... (VS 2.27). He establishes the *anvāhāryapacana* fire with [the verse]: "That which was cast away by thy wrath... (VS 2.28). He establishes the *āhavanīya* fire with [the verse]: "That which was cast away by thy anger... (VS 2.29). With [the formula] "May the mind, the light, enjoy [it]" (VS 2.29), he worships each fire as it has been established. This is the same up to the silent *agnihotra*. He offers the silent *agnihotra* with [the verse]: "Seven are thy fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven thy tongues... (VS 2.29). This is the same up to the pouring out [of the oblation]. He pours out [the grain] for a cake on five potsherds dedicated to Agni. He...

This [offering] takes the place of the eight-potsherd [oblation]. (16) There are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses, or seventeen. (17) They proceed with the *upāṃśu* [muttered] offering prior to the final *anūyāja*, except for the *sviṣṭakṛt*. (18) [The ritual] is the same up to the *prayāja* offerings. (19) In four of the *prayāja* offerings, he inserts four case-forms (*vibhakti*). (20) 5.19

"O Agni, O Agni; in Agni, O Agni; with Agni, O Agni; Agni, O Agni"—thus [one should recite]. One view is that one should place this after the *yeyajāmaha* formula; another is that it should be placed before the word to be addressed. For one whom he desires to cause to perish, he should place the case-endings (*vibhakti*) for him after the *prayāja* offerings and before the *vaṣaṭ*-call. The final *prayāja* is self-perfected. It is the same up to the two *ājyabhāga* offerings. The *ājyabhāga* for Agni contains the word "awakening" (*budhanvat*), as in: "Awaken Agni with a hymn. The *ājyabhāga* for Soma contains the word "purifying" (*pavamānavat*).

"O Agni, thou purifiest our lives," [he says]. "May Agni Pavamāna, being pleased, accept the clarified butter as an oblation"—with these words he performs the sacrifice. One who desires offspring or cattle should perform the verse "Agni is the head" in the place of the Soma offering. "O Agni, him today..."—these are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses in the *paṅkti* meter. There are two for the principal oblation and two for the *sviṣṭakṛt*. "Return with vigor... [he says].

Accompanied by wealth, he, being afraid, offers the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) as two oblations (*āhuti*). 11. This remains the same up to the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). 12. He gives both kinds of fees: those pertaining to the establishment of the fires (*āgnyādheya*) and those pertaining to the re-establishment of the fires (*paunarādheya*). 13. These are the fees for the re-establishment of the fires. 14. 5.20.

"A repaired chariot, a mended garment, a bull set at liberty again, and gold weighing a hundred mānas"—thus [he says]. 1. It is the same up to the *anūyāja* offerings. 2. In two of the *anūyāja* offerings, he employs two case-forms (*vibhakti*), namely: "in the divine Agni" and "the divine Agni. 3. The section on the case-forms has been explained. 4. The final *anūyāja* is naturally accomplished. 5. The sacrifice is completed in the established manner. 6. He subsequently offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Varuṇa. 7. This very offering takes the place of the *agnīṣomīya*. 8. Of all [the offerings]...

The re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*) concludes with the offerings to those [deities] to be extinguished. (9) He who establishes the fire after the re-establishment should offer these oblations: *lekaḥ*, *salekaḥ*, *sulekaḥ*. (11) These take the place of the *darvihoma* offerings belonging to the establishment of the fires (*āgnyādheya*). (12) If the fire, having been mounted upon the two kindling woods (*araṇi*), should be lost, one should perform the re-establishment; so says Āśmarathya. One should perform the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*) [anew]; so says Ālekhana. (13) If both fires should go out when the sun rises or when it sets, one should indeed perform the re-establishment. (14) Thus ends the fifth book. (5.21)

Now begins the sixth question: we shall explain the worship of the fires (*agnyupasthāna*). 1. At the time of the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*), both the wife and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) observe the vow (*vrata*) until the oblation (*homa*) is offered. 2. While the oblation is being ladled out, the sacrificer follows behind it until the oblation is offered. 3. Some say that one should remain standing while the oblation is being ladled out. 4. When about to offer the oblation, he should touch water, saying: "Thou art lightning; strike away my evil. From the immortal I go unto the true; faith is in me. 5. After having offered, he says: "Thou art rain; strike away my evil. I have gone unto the true from the immortal; faith is in the waters. 6. In this very same manner at all [subsequent offerings].

One who is about to sacrifice at the *yajña-kratavaḥ* sacrifices and, having sacrificed, touches water. 7. Having risen after the final oblation, he worships the Āhavanīya fire by approaching it somewhat obliquely with these six verses beginning, "Going forward to the sacrifice... (RV 10.176.1–6). 8. And with these four verses beginning, "O Agni, may splendor be mine in the invocations... (RV 10.128.1–4), he worships during the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*). 9. Then, during the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*), having worshipped with this verse, "Both of you, Indra and Agni, I invoke... (RV 7.93.1), and having performed the worship with the others, he finally worships with this verse, "Mātariśvan brought another from heaven... (RV 10.148.1). 10.

Every year, he worships the Gārhapatya fire with the Āgnipāvamānī verses. With these six verses beginning with "O Agni, you purify our lives" (*agna āyūm̐ṣi pavase*), he worships the Āhavanīya fire. 6.1.11–12.

Having begun with, "O Agni, you are the giver of life; give me life," he worships at evening with, "O Citrāvasu, may I reach your end in safety. At dawn, he worships with, "O Arvāgvasu, may I reach your end in safety," using the *prātar-avana* formula. He worships three times with the *citrāvasu* formula and three times with the *arvāgvasu* formula. He places fuel-sticks on the Āhavanīya fire: the first with, "You are the fuel of Agni; protect me from malice"; the second with, "You are the fuel of Soma; be my protector from enemies."

"Thou art the fuel of Yama; protect me from death," with these words he offers the third [fuel-stick]. Having placed the fourth with "May we kindle thee for a hundred winters," he worships with the remainder of the section beginning, "O Agni, thou hast united with the splendor of Sūrya. He wipes his mouth with the verse:
"O Soma, we who bear our minds within our bodies under thy law, may we, possessing offspring, attain long life."

He stands by the cow-pen, beginning with "With vigor I look upon you; with vigor look upon me," and continuing until the end of "May your riches rest in me. (1) According to some, he touches the calf. (2) He stands by the Āhavanīya fire, beginning with "That desirable [splendor] of Savitṛ," and continuing until the end of "the breaker of the crooked one. (3) He stands by the Gārhapatya fire, beginning with "O Agni, lord of the house," and continuing until the end of "a hundred winters. (4) He utters his son's name. (5) This has been explained.

[The father] is as if he has a son born, and as if he has no son born. Then he says: "May the divine thread not be cut; may a human not cut it. May I not be cut off from the divine abode, nor from the human. (6) Having kindled the fires, he sits down between the two fires with the formula: "For light, for the thread, thee. (8) In this very same way, he worships [the fires] in the evening by means of the *agnyupasthāna* rite. (9) In the morning, he does so by means of the *prātar-avana* rite. (10) When the oblation has been placed on the fire, or while it is being ladled out, he should wash his hands with those verses that are designated as *avanejana*. (11)

With the remaining verses he worships the Āhavanīya fire. (12) He should recite the four subsequent verses of the *vihavya* hymn preceding the *agnīṣomīya* offering, and two *yājyā-anuvākyā* verses for the *āgneya* offering. (13) Some prescribe the worship of the fire with the *vyāhṛtis*. (14) 6.3 "May I be able to support you," say some. (1) "May I be able to support you; may my faith not depart from me," say others. (2) [The worship] with the *vātsapra* hymn, say some. (3) With the *māhitra* triplet, say others:
"Great let be the protection of the three—of Dyukṣa Mitra, of Aryaman, and of Varuṇa—the invincible. (4)
For not even for a moment, nor in the paths or at the obstacles, does that evil-doing enemy have power over them.
For those sons of Aditi bestow eternal protection and grant desirable boons to the donor.

Thus, this is the very procedure for the worship of the fires (agnyupasthāna) performed by one who is traveling abroad. 5. Only this much is different: the Adhvaryu should perform those rites which involve physical contact. 6. At the proper time, the sacrificer (yajamāna), facing that direction, should mutter the mantras. 7. When about to depart on his journey, he says, "Tend the fires. 8. He worships them with the *bhāsvat* verses and the *virājakrama* formulas, as in the ritual of establishing the sacred fires (agnyādheya). 9. He places a fuel-stick (samidh) on the Āhavanīya fire with the verse: "O Jātavedas, my name was first [given]... 10. Standing between the two fires, he mutters: "O Mitra and Varuṇa, protect these houses of mine for me."
"May Pūṣan protect these [cows], undestroyed and unharmed, until our return. Thus [he says]. 11.
6.4 Restraining his speech, he proceeds, saying: "May we, O Indra, who possess the Soma, not stray from the path, nor from the sacrifice."
May no hostile powers remain within us.
Lead us upward, O Agni, toward the higher regions, you who are invoked with clarified butter;
unite us with the increase of wealth and make us abundant in progeny.

Thus: (1) he restrains his speech in the presence of the fires and releases it when they are not present; (2) he goes on a journey while observing the vow; (3) he pays reverence to the fires according to the season; (4) if he should go on a journey while the fires have not been paid reverence, he should pay reverence to them right there, thinking: "Remaining here, I support you, O Agnis, who are there, with my breath, my speech, and my mind;
may life not abandon me while I am away."
With the light of Vaiśvānara, I worship you.
Having thus prepared five pieces of fuel, he approaches the fires with the verse: "Bringing [offerings] at all times with an unafflicted mind,
O Agni, may we, as your neighbors, not come to harm."
Homage be to you, the bountiful one; homage to you, O Agni, who dwells at the Upasad rites. Adorn your own bodies and endow me with wealth.

Thus, he restrains his speech when away from the fires and releases it when in their presence. Having returned from a journey, he says, "Tend the fires. He worships them with the *bhāsvat* verses in the *virāj-krama* meter, as at the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*). He modifies the mantra to "Thou hast guarded [them]. (6.5) "O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two have guarded these houses of mine;
may Pūṣan protect them uninjured and undisturbed until our return."

Thus, he places three fuel-sticks on the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "Thou art the fuel of Agni" (TS 1.5.10.1). Having placed them, he stands worshipping with these four verses beginning, "My name and thine, O Jātavedas" (TS 1.5.10.2–5). He offers an oblation for one who has been away from home with the verse, "May the mind, the light, enjoy [the offering]" (TS 1.5.10.3). One should not offer before the tenth day. Now, when he has stayed for at least nine nights and is about to set out from home, he should gather everything together so that all other carts are yoked. Then, [he proceeds] to the cart standing nearest the fire.

The right [fire] is yoked; the left is unyoked. 7. Then he offers the oblation to Vāstoṣpati. 8. Having recited this verse, "O Vāstoṣpati, recognize us," he offers with the following one. 9. He does not place [the fire] back once it has been offered. 10. Having thoroughly cleansed the embers, he deposits the fires onto separate kindling woods—each fire that is habitually maintained—with the verse, "This is thy seasonal womb," for each one. 11. Or rather, he deposits them within himself with the verse, "O Agni, whatever body of thine is worthy of sacrifice, come and ascend to it. 12. When about to churn [the fire], he mutters [the following].

We shall explain the *agnihotra*. In the evening, the sacrificer issues the command: "Carry forth the *āhavanīya* fire. In the morning, he says: "Carry forth the *āhavanīya* fire. Having taken up the *upaveṣa* with the formula, "Thou art the fire-stirrer; grant us spiritual power (*brahman*)," the *adhvaryu*, a religious student (*brahmacārī*), or the *kṣīrahotṛ* addresses the *gārhapatya* fire with this verse: "O good *gārhapatya*... Then he awakens it with: "Awake, O Agni! Be watchful for him. Unite this man with his sacrifices and pious works. In this higher common dwelling-place, may all the gods and the sacrificer sit together."

4. Thus, before the shadows overlap, he draws out the blazing Āhavanīya fire from the Gārhapatya with the formula: "With speech as the Hotṛ, with breath as the Udgātṛ, with sight as the Adhvaryu, with mind as the Brahman, and with hearing as the Agnīdh—by means of these five divine officiating priests (ṛtvij), I draw you forth. 5. While it is being drawn forth, the sacrificer mutters: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! Om! Being drawn forth, draw me up from evil—that which I have done unknowingly and that which I have done knowingly;
whatever sin has been committed by day, from all that, once drawn up, release me!"
"Thus at evening. "Whatever sin has been committed against the night, release me from all that; release me from it! Thus at dawn. He establishes the fire in the place of the Āhavanīya.
I offer the oblation of immortality into the immortal; I offer the fire upon the earth for the conquest of immortality.
Through that, may I win infinite desire, which Prajāpati first won. *Agnim agnau svāhā*.
Thus in the evening; "To Sūrya in Agni, svāhā!"—thus in the morning. (7) 6.7.

The sacrificer himself, having brought fuel-wood, places large logs upon the fires with these five verses, one for each mantra, beginning with "O Agni, whatever [faults]... (1). The largest log is placed on the Āhavanīya fire (2). The Gārhapatya fire is maintained as a constant (3). They should carry forward the Āhavanīya fire every evening and morning (4); or rather, once it has been carried forward in the evening, it may remain until the morning Agnihotra (5). For one who has attained prosperity, the Āhavanīya fire is maintained as a constant (6), or for one desiring long life (7). Day by day, they should either fetch the Anvāhāryapacana fire or churn it out.

8. Or, [the fires] are maintained perpetually. 9. The *sabhya* and *āvasathya* fires are perpetual. 10. He sweeps around the fires with the formulas: "O Agni, Sovereign, be purified! for the *āhavanīya*; "O Agni, Carrier, be purified! for the *anvāhāryapacana*; "O Agni, Lord of the House, be purified! for the *gārhapatya*. 11. Having offered in this very same manner, he sweeps around them. 12. He strews grass around the fires: first the *gārhapatya*, then the *anvāhāryapacana*, then the *āhavanīya*. 13. Having washed the *agnihotra* vessels, he places them in pairs to the north of the *gārhapatya*.

The *sruva* ladle is made of *khadira* wood; the *agnihotrahavaṇī* offering-ladle, the *upaveṣa* fire-stirring stick, and the *agnihotra-sthālī* milk-pot are made of *vikaṅkata* wood; the pot has its lid facing upwards and is not turned on a lathe. (14) After sunset, having tethered [the cow], he lets the calf of the *agnihotrī* cow loose to the south. (15) Then, having turned it toward the east or the north, they milk her using both the pot and the milking vessel. (16) "A Śūdra must not milk," says one tradition. "If one so desires, a Śūdra may indeed milk," says another. (17) However, a Śūdra must certainly not milk the *agnihotra* [cow]; for it is known that this [milk] is pure and does not pass beyond [the bounds of purity]. (18) 6.8

One should milk the two front [cows] for the eldest son of the eldest wife, or for one who desires the office of domestic priest, or for one whose prosperity has reached its height. One should milk the two rear [cows] for the youngest son of the youngest wife, or for one who wishes to thrive, or for one who is inferior to his younger brothers. One should first milk the two front [cows] for the eldest son of the eldest wife.

Some say that one should first milk the two others for the youngest son or the grandson of the youngest; however, regarding the regular rule for milking, one may act according to one's desire. One does not touch [the vessel] during the milking. Having milked, one brings the milk. Having passed to the south of the Āhavanīya fire, the sacrificer sits down in his own place; the wife sits in the wife’s place. Then, when the sun has set, having seen the stars or at the onset of night, he performs the evening *agnihotra* offering. At dawn or at daybreak, he performs the morning *agnihotra*, either before sunrise, after sunrise, or exactly at the moment of sunrise.

"Some say that one should offer when speech begins to speak. When he offers at sunrise, by that he wins the Agniṣṭoma; when at midday, by that the Ukthya; when in the afternoon, by that the Ṣoḍaśin. When he offers in the first watch of the night, by that he attains the first round of the night; when at midnight, by that the middle; when in the last watch of the night, by that he attains the final round of the night—so it is known. One should not think, however, that the offering must be made at all these times."
In times of distress, one should understand that the sacrifice has been offered. He sprinkles water around the fires: first the *gārhapatya*, then the *ānvāhāryapacana*, and then the *āhavanīya*.

"O *ṛta*, I sprinkle you with *satya*," he says in the evening. "O *satya*, I sprinkle you with *ṛta*," he says in the morning. Now, according to some, he says in the evening: "O you who are *ṛta* and *satya*, I sprinkle you."

"By truth and by reality, I sprinkle you," he says in the morning; having offered in this very same manner, he sprinkles. Having stepped forth from the *gārhapatya* fire, he pours out a continuous stream of water toward the east as far as the *āhavanīya*, saying: "You are the continuity of the sacrifice; I lead you for the continuity of the sacrifice; for the continuity of the sacrifice, [I take] you. Taking the *upaveṣa* with the formula, "You are the bold one; grant us spiritual power (*brahman*)," he draws out embers from the *gārhapatya* toward the north, saying: "You are the makers of beings; drive away the danger from our people. Having made them separate, he places the *agnihotra* milk upon them.
The footprint of Iḍā is rich in ghee; O Jātavedas, enjoy this oblation of the moving and the unmoving.
May there be delight here for those seven domestic animals of every form.

6. Then, while kindling it with a blade of grass, he looks at it, saying: "You are the source; may I become pre-eminent through offspring, cattle, and sensory power. 7. When it has reached a state of complete combustion, or when it has been placed on the fire, he then causes it to be born again by sprinkling water with the *sruva* ladle, saying: "May I not lose your heat. 8. It should not be sprinkled with water by one who desires brilliance, one who desires sacred luster (*brahmavarcasa*), one who is performing a malevolent rite, or one who intends to cross over [an obstacle]; likewise for one who desires, "May a hero be born to me. 9. Having kindled it in the same manner with a blade of grass, he [sprinkles] three times.

He performs the *paryagni* (carrying fire around) with the formula: "The *rakṣas* is excluded; the enemies are excluded. (10) Having cooked it, he removes it toward the north as if drawing it out, with the formula: "Thou art the Gharma, the bestower of increase of wealth; establish vigor here. (11) With the formula: "Ye are makers of prosperity; the danger from the enemy is repelled," he mixes the embers into the *Gārhapatya* fire. Then, taking the *sruva* spoon and the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle with a verse to Savitṛ, he heats them over the *Gārhapatya* fire with the formula: "Burnt away is the *rakṣas*; burnt away are the enemies. (12) Having heated them, he touches them with the formula: "May the sacrificer and his wife be unharmed. (13) 6.10

He addresses the sacrificer: "Om, I shall draw up the oblation for the gods from the sacrificer’s evil," at evening; "Om, I draw up the oblation for the gods from the sacrificer’s evil," in the morning. Having whispered, "Thou art the oblation of the gods; may there be safety for me from death, may there be well-being for me, may there be freedom from fear for me," the sacrificer responds loudly, "Om, draw up the oblation for the gods from my evil. If the sacrificer does not respond, the Adhvaryu himself should respond.

He draws up four ladles full, either in succession or not. He draws up the first ladle with: "I draw you up for Agni and for the Earth. He draws up the second with: "And I draw you up for the Waters and for the Plants. He draws up the third with: "And I draw you up for Vāta and for the Atmosphere."

With the words, "And for Sūrya and for Heaven I lift you up," he lifts it up for the fourth time. (4) He should not close his eyes until the *hotṛ* has finished his recitation. (5) Having offered the oblation, he should look toward the Great One (the sky). (6) Having touched the lifted *agnihotra* with the *daśahotṛ* formula, he touches both the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) and the vessel (*sthālī*), saying at evening: "In harmony with the gods who come in the evening, may the gods who come in the evening lead me safely across. At evening.

"As if carrying upwards, traverse the wide atmosphere; go! (1) With "Svāhā to Agni Vaiśvānara," he deposits it in the middle region. (2) Having lifted it with "For Vāta thee," he places it upon the sacrificial grass behind the Āhavanīya fire with "Grant me life. (3) In the center of the fire, he places a fuel-stick: "This is thy fuel-stick, O Agni; through it, grow and swell."

"May your lord of sacrifice increase and may he swell; svāhā! (4) He offers the oblation on a kindled fuel-stick with "Agni is light, light is Agni; svāhā! in the evening; and with "Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya; svāhā! in the morning. (5) Or alternatively, [he offers] in the evening with "Agni is light, light is Sūrya; svāhā! and in the morning with "Sūrya is light, light is Agni; svāhā! (6) With "For food, thee! he wipes off the residue downward in the evening.

He leaves over more for eating: "O Rudra, be gracious; O Arbham, be gracious; O Dhūrta, homage be to you; do not harm me. Thus he wipes the fire three times with the ladle. He points toward the north. Having wiped off the smearings in the same manner, and having set them down with the words, "Grant me offspring," wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), he smears the smearings on the sacrificial mound to the south with the words, "For the fathers, thee; gladden the fathers. Having touched water, he eats twice with his finger, making no sound, first with the words, "Thou art Pūṣan. Having sipped water...

With the formula, "From the embryos thee, quicken the embryos," he makes the second [offering]. He causes it to go to the teeth. Having touched [the offering] with the *barhis* grass and having turned around toward the north, he sips water with a ladle whose handle points either eastward or northward, saying at evening: "May there be for me Agni-like seed, productive."

"May there be solar seed and procreation for me"—thus [he says] at dawn. (8) Having gone out and purified the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle, he wipes the residue onto the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). (9) Having filled the ladle with water, he pours it out toward the east: first, "For the serpents, thee! Quicken the serpents! second, "Quicken the serpents and the ants!"

"Quicken the serpents and other people"—with these words he makes the third circumambulation to the right (10). He does not throw the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) into the Āhavanīya fire (11). He heats the Agnihotra-ladle over the fire with the formula, "The Rakṣas is burnt up; the enemies are burnt up" (12). He places his hand upon it (13), or having warmed his hand, he points it toward the north over the Agnihotra-ladle with the formula, "For the Seven Seers thee; quicken the Seven Seers" (14–15). 6.13

Having filled the *sruva*-ladle with water, he pours it out to the west of the *āhavanīya* fire with the formula: "I offer you as immortality into the earth, into Agni Vaiśvānara; *svāhā*! (1) In the same manner, he pours it out to the west of the *gārhapatya* fire. (2) He also pours some into the joined palms of his wife with the formula: "From the houses, I pour you into the houses; quicken them," pouring first in smaller amounts and then more. (3) If the wife does not attend, he should pour it twice upon the earth itself. (4) From this very remainder of the *agnihotra*, he offers two or four oblations into the *gārhapatya* with the *sruva*-ladle, [reciting]: "O Agni, Lord of the House... (5)

"Having reached [the end], enjoy [it], svāhā! (5). "O Lord of food, give us food," [he says] at the Anvāhāryapacana fire (6). According to another [tradition], no oblation is performed in the two latter fires (7). Having offered, he adds fuel with the verses: "Shine forth! You have shone; you have shone," [reciting] one verse for each [fire] (8). The sweeping around and the sprinkling around have been explained (9). One desiring cattle should offer the Agnihotra with milk from two [cows] (10). He should place the first [milk] on the fire and then bring the second (11). One desiring splendor should offer with clarified butter; one desiring cattle, with milk (12). Some say that milk should be used as the regular [offering].

They prescribe: with curd for one desiring sense-power; with barley-gruel for one desiring a village; with rice for one desiring vigor; with meat for one desiring fame; with *soma* for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). One desiring spiritual luster should offer with ghee for twelve nights. This same procedure applies to one offering with clarified butter (*ājya*); there is only this much difference.

At the time of pouring back the water, he should pour it back using two young *darbha* blades. (16) Now, if he should offer with curds, rice grains, or Soma, everything from the placing on the fire until the pouring back [of the ashes] is performed. (17) One should offer this prescribed *agnihotra* as long as one lives; one should offer it as long as one lives. (18) 6.14

We shall explain the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice. 1. One sacrifices with the first-fruits of rice. 2. There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses. 3. The ritual procedure (*tantra*) is that of the New Moon sacrifice. 4. In this regard, there is this general rule: in all *iṣṭis* and animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*), the ritual duties (*dharma*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices follow along. 5. They are set aside by three means: by accomplishment, by prohibition, and by substitution. 6. Therefore, wherever a modified (*vaikṛta*) element is prescribed in place of an archetypal (*prākṛta*) sacrificial constituent, it shall take on the ritual duties of that [archetype].

Just as *śaramaya* [grass] is for the *barhis*, *śyāmāka* for the *barhis*, rice for the pot, the *caru* for the potsherd, and the *puroḍāśa* for the sacrificial cake—therein, modification (*ūha*) occurs according to the purpose. A modification arises from similarity, as when a single deity replaces one belonging to Agni; likewise, a double deity or a multiple deity replaces that of Agni-Soma or Indra-Agni, except in cases involving the deities of the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Just as in the case of "the *puroḍāśa* for Indra" and "the *caru* for Soma," the original [archetypal] forms should be understood by their own positions. Now, wherever another oblation (*havis*) is added to an archetypal deity—such as the *puroḍāśa* oblation for Viṣṇu—that very oblation shall be considered to possess its own specific ritual duty (*svadharma*). Whether one sacrifices with an *iṣṭi*, or with an animal sacrifice, or with *soma*, one should sacrifice either on the new-moon day or on the full-moon day. In that regard, two festival days (*parvan*) are established. Having concluded the first festival day, one should perform the *iṣṭi* on the subsequent one.

Then, having concluded with a single joint (*ekaparvan*), he performs the *sadyaskālā* sacrifice at that very joint; or rather, both may be performed within the same ritual framework (*samānatantre*). The modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) and the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) [are now discussed]. When there is a coincidence between the New and Full Moon sacrifices and a modified sacrifice, the New and Full Moon sacrifices are stronger. However, those elements of the *iṣṭi* and animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*) which are explicitly prescribed by direct scriptural revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) are stronger in those cases. He prepares a fuel-stick (*idhma*) consisting of twenty-three pieces of wood. Regarding this, there is the following specific instruction.

If the *sāmidhenī* verses are increased, the fuel-sticks (*kāṣṭha*) should be increased; if they are decreased, it is according to the original model. Up to the employment of the vessels, the procedure is the same. He employs three winnowing-baskets (*śūrpa*). He prepares three mortars (*ulūkhala*) and two grinding-stones (*dṛṣad*). Up to the taking up of the winnowing-basket, the procedure is the same. With the words, "For service, for you," he takes up the winnowing-baskets. Up to the pouring out of the grain, the procedure is the same. Having poured out the cake on eight potsherds for Agni made from old grain, he pours out the cake on eleven potsherds for Indra-Agni made from new grain.

A cake on twelve potsherds for Agni and Indra, or [for Indra alone]; a pap for the Viśvedevas, which is cooked in milk; a pap of *śyāmāka* grain for Soma; and a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth—or alternatively, he may offer these with new grain.

The *nāgneya* [offering] is the sixteenth; the mantra for the touching [of the grains] follows. Having set aside the *āgrayaṇa* [grain], he offers these oblations with the five verses beginning, "To him who has a hundred weapons, who has a hundred powers. This is the same up to the spreading of the black antelope skin. Upon a single black antelope skin, he places three mortars and two grinding stones. This is the same up to the pouring [of the grain]. Having poured out all the sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*), he calls the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*). Having pounded all [the grains], he strikes them together on the grinding stone and the millstone. All the sacrificial offerings [are prepared] in successive order.

He sows, winnows, and separates [the grain]. (24) Or rather, he may thresh the earlier and later portions in a single mortar. (25) In that case, the mantras beginning with the sowing and ending with the separation should be repeated for each individual seed. (26) 6.16

1. From the very beginning, he invokes the *haviṣkṛt* (the preparer of the oblation). 2. Having pounded all [the grains], he releases his speech. 3. At the end of all [the grains], he pours out the husks. 4. Until the state of being a continuous stream [is reached], he should discard each seed individually. 5. Or rather, he may follow them with those of the same kind. 6. This indeed is the procedure for various seeds from this point forward. 7. It is the same up to the removal of the sacrificial portions (*havir-udvāsana*). 8. Having removed the cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*), he fills it with clarified butter. 9. Its procedure is explained by that of the cake on one potsherd belonging to the *vaiśvadeva* [offering]. There is only this much difference.

He does not turn the back of the boat over, nor does he offer oblations with the names of the months. (Sūtra 10) It is the same up to the offering of the oblations. (Sūtra 11) He follows the Vaiśvadeva oblation with the mantra: "Through the sacrifice to the Viśve Devas, may I attain union with the vital breaths. (Sūtra 12) He follows the Dyāvāpṛthivī oblation with the mantra: "Through the sacrifice to Heaven and Earth, may I attain abundance and a firm foundation. (Sūtra 13) In this very manner, he follows all the Vaiśvadeva and Dyāvāpṛthivī offerings. (Sūtra 14) It is the same up to...

After the consumption [of the remainder], he eats of the rice with the verse: "O Gods, may you lead us toward what is better than our prosperity. Then: "May Agni eat first, for he knows how the oblation is;
may he, who dwells among all people, make the plants auspicious for us."

Thus regarding the *śyāmāka* grains: (17) "All should consume [the portion] with the mantra"—this is one view; "The sacrificer alone [should consume] the sacrificer's portion"—this is another. (18) He gives as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) the first-born of those calves that are born before the *ekāṣṭakā*. (19) The sacrifice is concluded in the established manner. (20) 6.17

Now, if one should perform the Śyāmāka sacrifice as a separate rite (*nānātantra*), when the Śyāmāka grains have been cooked, he should offer a *caru* of Śyāmāka for Soma. Its ritual procedure (*kalpa*) is exactly the same; there is only this difference: he gives a garment as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). The sacrifice is completed in the established manner. He performs the offering of the first-fruits of barley. The ritual procedure for these is explained by that of the rice (*vrīhi*). There is only this difference:
"That famous barley, mixed with honey, they ploughed up on the banks of the Sarasvatī.
Indra, the lord of the hundred rites, was the master of the plough; the Maruts, the bounteous givers, were the ploughmen."

Thus he eats barley. (7) He gives as the sacrificial fee the first-born of those calves that are born after the Ekāṣṭakā. (8) The sacrifice is concluded in the established manner. (9) He should perform either the New Moon or the Full Moon sacrifice with new grain. (10) Or he should offer the Agnihotra with new grain. (11) Or, having caused the Agnihotra cow to eat new grain, he should offer the evening and morning oblations with her milk. (12) Or else, having cooked four śarāva-measures of rice on the Gārhapatya fire and offered it to the deities of the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, with Sviṣṭakṛt as the fourth, [he completes the rite].

One should feed Brāhmaṇas. (13) Regarding green barley, *śamī* seeds, and vegetables, even if they are not desired, one may eat them according to one's inclination. (14) Roots and leafy vegetables are [suitable] for the production of gifts. (15) Having sacrificed with rice, one should sacrifice again with rice, and not with barley. Having sacrificed with barley, one should sacrifice again with barley, and not with rice. Or rather, one should sacrifice with rice alone. (16) In this very manner, one sacrifices crop after crop throughout one's life; one sacrifices throughout one's life. (17) 6.18 Thus ends the sixth book. Now begins the seventh book.

One who is about to perform the animal sacrifice (paśubandha), having mentally recited the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ formula, offers an oblation with the *sruva* ladle together with the *graha* cup into the Āhavanīya fire. With the verse, "O Viṣṇu, stride out widely," he offers the oblation for the sacrificial post (*yūpāhuti*) using the *sruva*. Then the Adhvaryu takes both the clarified butter remaining in the pot and the *sruva* ladle.

That which is the axe for hewing is the axe itself. They go in that direction toward which they intend to carry the sacrificial post (yūpa). These trees suitable for the sacrificial post are the *palāśa*, the *khadira*, and the *rauhītaka*. One who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should make it of *bilva* wood. That [desire] is constant. He should cut it so as not to obstruct the axle. For one whom he should desire, "May he be without a firm foundation," he should cut a tree that has grown upward. For one whom he should desire, "May he be without cattle," he should cut one that is leafless and has a withered top.

If one should desire, "May he be possessed of cattle," for him he should cut [the branch] with many leaves and many twigs. It is known from tradition: "One desiring stability should cut it so that it remains firmly rooted. One should not cut that which has turned toward the south, nor that which has turned toward the north, nor that which is crooked. He should cut that which is straight, whose bark-shavings point upward, and which, being straight, has its tip slightly bent downward.

Then he causes it to be carried forward, either eastward or northward, with the formula: "May it not scratch the sky with its top; may it not injure the mid-air. (1) He offers an oblation on the stump with the verse: "O Lord of the Forest, grow up with a hundred branches! (2) He touches himself with the formula: "May we grow up with a thousand branches! (3) He fashions the fingers according to the tips [of the wood] with the verse: "The adze, sharpening itself, [has fashioned] thee... (4) With this same [verse], he first shaves off [the hair] from the front. (5) The measurements begin at one *aratni* and extend up to three *trihasta*.

The sacrificial post (yūpa) is made of six cubits, or indeed of three or four cubits; it may be made of *pālāśa* wood for one who has performed the *nirūḍhapaśubandha* sacrifice, while according to some, other woods may be used for the *saumya-adhvara*. Then he fashions it so that it is neither too thick nor too thin at the top, making it tapered toward the end and having eight corners. It is smoothed down from the base. At the top, there is a *caṣāla* (wooden ring) eight-cornered and a span in width, which is curved in the middle. He extends the post above the *caṣāla* by as much as the thickness of the uppermost finger-joint.

According to some, it is two finger-breadths; according to others, three finger-breadths. (11) Having made a *svaru* from the shavings, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu. (12) There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses. (13) The sacrifice is completed in the established manner. (14) This [offering] takes the place of the adding of fuel to the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*). (15) Another view is that one should not take up the fire for the animal sacrifice (*paśviṣṭi*). (16) When that [offering] has been completed, having brought a branch, he prepares the altar in front of the *āhavanīya* fire. (17) It extends as far as the pole of a chariot toward the east.

It is a yoke-length in front and an axle-length behind. (18) Having performed that which is prior to the northern boundary-line, he measures out the high altar (uttaravedi) to the west of the location for the sacrificial post-hole with a wooden pin (śamyā).

(19) 7.2 Having placed the pin with its knob pointing northward in front, he draws a line toward the north inside [the pin] with the wooden sword (sphya), saying: "Thou art my path to wealth. Likewise to the south, [he draws a line] toward the east, saying: "Thou art my path to refreshment. Likewise to the rear, [he draws a line] toward the north, saying: "Protect me from distress."

In the same way from the north, [he measures] toward the east with the formula, "Do not cause me distress. Having stepped out one step toward the north from the northern edge of the altar, he likewise silently measures around the *cātvāla* pit with the wooden pin (*śamyā*). Taking the spade (*abhri*) with the verse addressed to Savitṛ, he draws the outline with the formula, "The *rakṣas* is enclosed; the enemies are enclosed. Having dug it knee-deep, or three spans deep, he carries away the loose earth with the formula, "May Agni know [you]. He pours it onto the high altar (*uttaravedi*) with the formula, "Thou art a boundary-mark; thou art a mighty queen. In this very same manner...

In the same way he takes up the second; in the same way the third. He takes up the second with the formula, "He who is in the second [layer]," and the third with, "He who is in the third. Having silently taken up the fourth, he spreads it out to the measure of a yoke-pin with the formula, "Spread wide! May the lord of the sacrifice spread wide for thee! Having struck it together with the formula, "Thou art firm," he sprinkles it with water with the formula, "Be purified for the gods! Whatever remains of the sprinkling-water, he should pour it out toward the south on the northern altar over a single wooden sword (sphya), saying, "The waters [wash away] the impurity."
"Carry it away"—with these words, he should meditate upon whomsoever he hates. He scatters sand, saying: "Be auspicious for the gods! He fashions the edges of the high altar (uttaravedi), [reciting]:
"Radiant and great, let him drink the Soma-mead; may he bestow unimpaired life upon the lord of the sacrifice.
Impelled by the wind, may he protect [us] himself; he nourishes all creatures and shines forth manifoldly."

Thus, having made the northern navel (*uttaranābhi*) of the middle *uttaravedi* four-cornered and a span (*prādeśa*) in measure, he touches both the altar (*vedi*) and the *uttaravedi* with the verse: "O two young maidens with four tufts of hair, with ghee for your face, in the midst of the world..."

"May the gods, dwelling together upon them, rejoice here on the highest firmament. (1) Then he sprinkles it, moving around it in each direction with these mantras according to their respective forms: "May Indra Ghoṣa protect you from the east with the Vasus," and so forth. (2) "May Tvaṣṭṛ protect you from above with his forms"—thus from above. (3) "Whatever remains of the sprinkling waters," etc., is the same as before. (4) "One should lead forward the fire on the previous day"—this is one view; "one should wait until the end of the sprinkling"—this is another. (5) Having kindled the fuel on the Āhavanīya fire, he issues the command: "Recite for the fire being led forward! (6) When [the verse] has been recited three times...
Having taken a fuel-stick at the first [oblation] and having made sand the supporting vessel, he offers the *udyata-homa* with the verse:

"Whatever sin we have committed against you, O Purifier, whether previously existing or what we may do later—strengthen your bodies with ghee; do not harm me who have approached you from the front, Svāhā!"

Having thus offered the *śeṣa* oblation, they proceed toward the east. While the fire is being held above, he pours the fivefold-drawn clarified butter across the northern altar (*uttaravedi*), placing gold in between, with the formulas: "Thou art *simhī*, the subduer of rivals, svāhā! on the southern shoulder; "Thou art *simhī*, the winner of good progeny, svāhā! on the northern hip; "Thou art *simhī*, the winner of abundance of wealth, svāhā! on the northern shoulder; "Thou art *simhī*, the winner of the Ādityas, svāhā! on the southern hip.

"Bring the gods for the god-loving sacrificer, Svāhā!"—thus he says in the middle (9.7.4). Having lifted up the offering-spoon with the words, "For the beings, thee," he lays down the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) made of *pūtudru* wood around the northern altar: the middle one with "Thou art all-living"; the southern one with "Thou art dwelling in the firm"; and the northern one with "Thou art dwelling in the unshakable. He pours the ritual materials (*saṃbhāra*) onto the navel [of the altar]: bdellium, fragrant resin, and a white tuft of wool from between the horns of a white ram that has not lost its tuft; according to some, it need not be from one that has not lost its tuft. [He places them with: "Thou art the ash of Agni."

"Thou art the soil of Agni," with these words he pours out the *upayamanī* (supporting) earth to the north. When he recognizes [the verse], "Sit down, O Hotṛ, in thine own world," he establishes the fire upon the *saṃbhāra* materials:
"O Sacrifice, be established; may riches enter thee manifoldly in a benevolent and most gracious manner.
Granting long life to the sacrificer, do thou, through the immortal, gladden the singer."

Having thus deposited [the fire], he kindles it with the verse: "The sacrifice has been established. Like Manu, we deposit thee; like Manu, we kindle thee. O Agni Aṅgiras, like Manu, sacrifice to the gods for the one who seeks the gods. (5) Having here offered a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the *saptavatī* verse, he offers the *atimukti* oblations:
"May Agni, knowing, lead the sacrifice; may those who destroy the sacrifice not find it. Proclaim the sacrifice to the gods; further prolong the life of the lord of the sacrifice. Svāhā! (6)

May Vāyu, Āditya, and the sacrifice, knowing the way, lead the sacrifice; may those who destroy the sacrifice not find it. Proclaim the sacrifice to the gods; further extend the lord of the sacrifice—svāhā!

Thus [ends the section]. Here, some prescribe the *pūrṇāhuti* (full-offering). 7.5. Here the ritual beginning with the *barhis* grass is commenced, provided that he has carried forward the fire on the previous day. But if it should remain overnight until the sprinkling [of water], then the ritual beginning with the *barhis* is commenced at that very time. 1. He ties two stalks of sugarcane as separators (*vidhṛtī*) and a broom of *aśvavāla* grass as the *prastara* onto the *barhis*. 2. He places the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) made of *kārṣmarya* wood upon the fuel-wood (*idhma*). 3. He prepares the fuel-wood consisting of twenty-three pieces of wood. 4. [The procedure] is the same up to the employment of the sacrificial vessels. 5. He employs a second *juhū* ladle as the *vasāhomahavanī* (the vessel for offering the fat).

A second *upabhṛt* as a vessel for the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), two vessels for clarified butter, a pot for cooking the animal victim, two omentum-roasting spits made of *kārṣmarya* wood—one with two prongs and one with a single prong—a heart-spit, a *svaru* chip, a wooden knife, two cords, a branch of *plakṣa* wood, a staff of *udumbara* wood for the Maitrāvaruṇa priest, and whatever else may be required. (6) In this regard, whatever ritual properties belong to the *upabhṛt* and those belonging to the *dhruvā*, these should also be performed for the vessel of speckled butter. (7) Whatever [properties] belong to the *ukhā* used for the *sāṃnāyya* [milk-offering], those should be performed for the pot for cooking the animal victim.

The rites for the *vapāśrapaṇī* (the two omentum-spits), the heart-spike (*hṛdayaśūla*), and the *plakṣa* branch should be performed [as prescribed]. (8) The duties of the *sruva* spoon apply to the *svadhiti* knife; the duties regarding milk apply to the animal victim. (9) He does not carry forward the *praṇītā* waters. (10) Having strewn grass around the fires, having washed his hands, having set out the vessels, having spread the *ulaparājī* grass, and having prepared the two strainers (*pavitra*), he issues the command: "O Sacrificer, restrain your speech! (11) With speech restrained, he touches the vessels. (12) Having prepared the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling-waters according to the established procedure, having addressed the *brahmán*, and having sprinkled the vessels.

Having released his speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviskṛt*), he then performs the subsequent tracing of the altar (*parigrāha*). This is the same up to the formal summons (*saṃpraiṣa*). 7.6.13–14.

"Clean the *sruva* and the *svadhiti*, and the *sruks*; gird the wife; bring the clarified butter and the curds"—with these concluding directions he bows. (1) It is the same up to the pouring out of the clarified butter. (2) Having poured out the clarified butter, he pours out the curds into the second *ājyasthālī*. (3) Its ritual procedure is explained by that of the clarified butter, except for the placing on the fire. (4) It is the same up to the taking of the portions of clarified butter. (5) He takes four portions in the *juhū* and four in the *upabhṛt*. (6) The speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) is taken five times.

Having mixed curds with clarified butter with these mantras, "Thou art the milk of the great ones," etc., he takes [the butter] in the *dhruvā* ladle according to the original procedure. Up to the placing of the ladles, the ritual is the same. Having placed the ladles and having placed the *veda* grass-bundle in front of the *dhruvā*, he takes the spade with the *sāvitra* formula and traces around the pit for the sacrificial post in front of the *āhavanīya* fire, half within the altar and half outside the altar, saying: "The *rakṣas* is traced out; the enemies are traced out. Having dug it to the depth of the upper part [of the post], he washes the sacrificial post with [the mantra]:
"Whatever a skillful carpenter has struck with his hand by means of the axe..."
May the pure, life-sustaining waters purify all that, being themselves pure, the pure one.

Then he gives the command: "Recite for the sacrificial post as it is being anointed. He anoints the top of the post with the formula, "May the divine Savitṛ anoint thee with honey. Having anointed the *caṣāla* (the wooden ring) on all sides with the formula, "Thou art Indra's," he fixes it on with the formula, "For the plants with good fruit—[fix thee] from there downwards. The sacrificer anoints the end [of the post] on all sides with a splinter of the post, rubbing it all around. At the place where the rope will be fastened, he rubs it three times. From the time of the anointing until the encircling with the rope, the sacrificer does not let go of the sacrificial post. Then...

He gives the command: "Recite for the post being raised. He raises it with the formula: "Support the sky; fill the mid-region. With the verse, "We desire to go to those abodes of yours," he places it in the hole. Then he adjusts it with two verses beginning, "Behold the deeds of Viṣṇu. He should make half of the post face toward the fire and the outer part sloped away from it. He fixes the lower part so that it is not visible. Having fixed the post facing the fire at the Agniṣṭhā point, he piles earth around it in a clockwise direction.

"Recite for [the post] as it is being encircled. He encircles it three times from left to right at the height of the navel or at the middle part with a triple-stranded cord, saying: "Thou art encircled; may the divine subjects encircle thee. He makes each subsequent coil higher than the preceding one, the last being the highest. Having interlaced the cord at the ends near the edge, he winds the end around. Having made the two parts equal, he passes the thinner part through the thicker part, saying: "Thou art the son of heaven. Taking the *svaru*, he hides it in the middle coil of the cord, or in the uppermost, or in all of them.

"Into the lap of the intermediate space I hide you," [he says]. 6. Then they bathe this animal—a goat that is not lacking a limb, not lacking teeth, red, hornless, two-colored, and fat. 7. "For food, thee! [with these words] he takes two blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*). 8. "Thou art the one who approaches," [with these words] he takes a branch of the *plakṣa* tree. 9. One desiring cattle should dedicate the animal with a branch that has many leaves and many twigs. 10. In front of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), facing westward, he dedicates the animal with the branch, the two blades of grass, and the formula: "Born from Prajāpati... with two verses.

Having begun with "The divine subjects [approach] the gods" and ending with "O wealthy ones, rejoice! I dedicate you, acceptable to Indra and Agni," (11) he places the lower friction-wood block with the formula, "Thou art the birthplace of Agni. He places two eastward-pointed darbha-blades with "Ye two are the testicles. (12) With "Thou art Urvaśī," he takes the lower fire-drill; with "Purūravas," the upper fire-drill. (13) With "Anointed with ghee, produce the male," he anoints the cavities with the vessel of clarified butter. (14) Having placed the two fire-drills together with "Thou art life," he issues the command. (15) 7.9

"Recite for the fire being churned," [he says]. When the first verse has been recited three times, he churns the fire three times from left to right with these mantras: "Be born after the Gāyatrī metre. When it is born, he says, "Recite for the fire that has been born. When he is about to cast it [into the fire], he says, "Recite for the fire being cast. When he recognizes [the verse], "Forward the god for the feast of the gods," he casts it forward along the front of the northern enclosing stick, or at the junction, with the mantra: "May you two be of one mind toward us. Having taken clarified butter with the dipping-spoon (sruva), he makes an offering over it.

With the verse, "Fire moves, having entered into fire," he takes the rope with a formula addressed to Savitṛ and fastens the animal's right half of the head with its tether, saying, "O divine oblation, I seize you with the tether of Truth. Then he binds it to the sacrificial post from the front facing westward, saying, "Be bold; I bind you, acceptable to Indra and Agni, for the sake of men. Those animals which are sacrificed subsequent to the set of eleven that face this way, he binds to the north of the post; those of the set of eleven, to the south.

Then he sprinkles it from above with the formula: "I sprinkle thee, acceptable to the waters, the plants, and Indra and Agni. (10) He makes it drink with: "Thou art the drinker of waters. (11) He sprinkles it from below with: "O divine waters, season this well-prepared oblation for the gods. (12) 7.10 Thereupon he issues the command: "Recite for the fire being kindled! (1) It is the same [procedure] up to the anointing of the *dhruvā* ladle. (2) Before the anointing of the *dhruvā*, he anoints the animal: "May thy breath unite with the wind," on the head; "May the limbs unite with those worthy of sacrifice," on the two shoulders.

"May the lord of the sacrifice [be united] with his blessing"—thus [he says] over the two buttocks. (3) It is the same up to the *pravara*. (4) Having chosen the Hotṛ according to the standard procedure of choosing, and having called for the *āśrāvaṇa* again, he chooses the Maitrāvaruṇa, saying: "Mitra and Varuṇa are the two *praśāstṛ*s; [choose] from the *praśāstṛ*. (5) It is the same up to the *prayāja* offerings. (6) Taking the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* spoons, stepping forward, and having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "Prompt for the *samidh*s! (7) He makes the offering when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered. (8) Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa* each time, he issues the summons for the subsequent [offerings], saying: "Prompt! Prompt! (9) At every fourth [offering].

He pours the butter from the *aupabhṛta* ladle into the *juhū*. (10) He does this entirely at the eighth [fore-offering]. (11) Having performed ten *prayāja* offerings, he leaves over a portion of the clarified butter for the eleventh. (12) Having stepped back, he anoints the *svaru* and the *svadhiti* with the *juhū*. He anoints the *svaru* three times and one edge of the *svadhiti* once. (13) With those two, he anoints the animal, saying: "Anointed with ghee, may you two protect the animal. (14) He anoints the animal with that very edge which was anointed. (15) With that same [edge], he cuts off portions of the cooked sacrificial food (*havis*); with the other [edge], he dissects it. (16) As for the method of dissection, there is another view that it may be done according to one's preference. (17) 7.11

Again, he hides the *svaru* [in the earth]. Handing the axe to the *śamitṛ*, he says: "May this edge of yours be well-known. Then he issues the command: "Recite for the fire being carried around. Taking a firebrand from the *āhavanīya*, the *āgnīdhra* carries the fire around the animal, the place of the *śamitṛ*, the *catvāla* pit, the sacrificial post, and the *āhavanīya* fire. According to some, he carries the fire around the animal alone.
