While the fire is being carried around, he offers the *apāvya* oblations with the verse: "The ancestors, knowing [the rite], receive [the offering]..."

Having gone around three times [to the right], he sets down the firebrand; then, having set it down, he goes back around three times again. (7) Having released the animal from the sacrificial post, the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer both take hold of the two omentum-spits. (8) Having taken hold [of them] and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he issues the command: "O Hotṛ, give the impulse for the oblations to the gods. (9) When he recognizes [the Hotṛ's response] with the words, "Bring the fire to him," then the Āgnīdhra, taking a firebrand from the Āhavanīya fire, proceeds first. (10) They lead the animal northward between the *cātvāla* pit and the *utkara* mound.

"O Revatīs, enter the lord of the sacrifice with a pleasant abode," [he says]. (11) "The breath of the sacrificer is distinct from that of the animal," with these words the Adhvaryu addresses the sacrificer. (12) To the north, the Āgnīdhra rubs down a firebrand; this becomes the *śāmitra* fire. (13) He should bring it from the western *gārhapatya* fire, or he may produce it by friction. (14) Of the two bundles of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with which he dedicates the animal, he sets aside one for the purpose of spreading. (15–16) 7.12

With the verse, "Be united with thy body," he pushes one of the two [hearths] toward the south, near the *śāmitra* fire. Upon that [fire], they cause the animal to be quieted, facing westward with its feet turned northward. Having said, "Quiet it, making it free from groaning," the Adhvaryu turns away from the animal as it is being quieted. Both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer remain sitting, gazing at the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), [reciting]:
"May offspring of every form rejoice here; may the all-sustaining mothers [rejoice] in this sacrifice.
Dwelling together around Agni as their home, may they favor us with milk and clarified butter."
May those whose udders have four openings, filled with honey and ghee,
be full of milk for us in this cow-pen, increasing our vigor.

4. When it has been bound, he offers the *saṃjñapta-homa* with the verse: "That the victim has uttered a cry... (VS 6.18). 5. He releases the tether of the victim with the formula: "O slaughterers, come near! (VS 6.19). 6. Having pierced the tether with a single-pronged pin, he throws it away into the *catvāla* pit or onto the rubbish-heap (*utkara*) with the formula: "May Aditi release the tether! (VS 6.20). 7. If he should practice sorcery, he should drive a wooden stake or a clump of grass into the ground with the formula: "I make the one who acts as an enemy fall low! (VS 6.21). 8. The wife worships the sun with the formula: "Homage to you, O outstretched one! (VS 6.22). 9. Then he leads her toward the east with the formula: "Unassailable, go forward! (VS 6.23).
10. At the *cātvāla* pit, the wife touches the water with the mantra: "O divine waters, you who seek purity... 11.7.13.

Having stepped out together with their wives, they purify themselves at the *cātvāla* with the mantra: "Purified, we have served; may we be your servers. 1. The wife causes the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) of the animal victim to swell, and the Adhvaryu sprinkles [it]. 2. According to some, the Adhvaryu causes them to swell and the wife sprinkles [them]. 3. "May your speech swell!"

With these mantras, according to their respective forms—"May your breath swell"—he pours [the water] on the necks with the mantra, "The pain that has gone to your breaths. With the mantra, "That which is cruel in you, that which is solidified," he causes the entire animal to swell. With "May your navel swell," he [sprinkles] the navel; with "May your anus swell," he [sprinkles] the anus.

Having poured out the remaining water along the spine with the seven verses beginning "Pure and virtuous" (ŚB 3.2.1.7) and the [remaining] verses beginning "To those who are peaceful, to the peaceful plants" (ŚB 3.2.1.8), he places a blade of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with its tip pointing eastward to the south of the navel with the formula, "O plant, protect him! (ŚB 3.2.1.8). With the formula, "O axe, do not harm him! (ŚB 3.2.1.8), he strikes transversely across the sacrificial grass with the axe. Having pushed aside the tip of the sacrificial grass and having smeared the thick end with blood, he discards it with the formula, "Thou art the portion of the Rakṣases" (ŚB 3.2.1.8). Having touched water, he extracts the omentum (*vapā*) with the formula, "For food, thee! (ŚB 3.2.1.8).

"Be purified for the gods; be adorned for the gods," with these words he washes [the omentum]. "O Heaven and Earth, clothe yourselves in ghee," with these words he covers the two omentum-spits. "For strength, thee! with these words he pierces it with a single-pronged spit at its thickest part. "Uninterrupted may be wealth accompanied by brave sons."

"I cut you out, acceptable to Indra and Agni"—with these words he cuts around [the omentum]. (15) The *śamitṛ* stands holding the omentum-extractor with his fist until the offering of the omentum. (16) Both the *adhvaryu* and the sacrificer again take hold of the two omentum-spits. (17) Having stepped forward with the words, "Follow along the wide mid-region," (18) 7.14.

At the *śāmitra* fire, he heats the omentum (*vapā*) with the formula: "The *rakṣas* is burnt away; the enemies are burnt away. (1) Having taken up the fire-brand (*ulmuka*) once more, the *āgnīdhra* goes forward first. (2) In this same manner, the *adhvaryu* proceeds toward the *āhavanīya* fire. (3) In this same manner, he places the omentum upon the final ember. (4) The *āgnīdhra* throws the fire-brand back into the *āhavanīya*. (5) Having carried the omentum between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, and between the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the *āhavanīya*, the *pratiprasthātṛ*, seated facing north on the south side, [places it] upon the *āhavanīya*.

He cooks the omentum. 6. Beneath the omentum, he throws away the tip of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with the formula: "O Vāyu, partake of the drops. 7. Having taken clarified butter with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), he makes an offering over it with the formula: "Thee they have established as the bearer of oblations. 8. While making the offering, he issues the command: "Recite for the drops. 9. When it has become cooked and golden-brown, then, having sprinkled it with clarified butter as in the *Sāṃnāyya* rite and having removed it from the fire in the same manner, he places it upon the sacrificial grass on a branch of the *Plakṣa* tree with the formula: "Make the plants bear good fruit. 10. [He adds: "May our enemies be driven away."

Having released [the ladles] from the two omentum-spits and having recognized [them] with the formula, "The butter-bearing ones," he steps forward for the final *prayāja* offering, calls for the *śrauṣaṭ*, and says, "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for the *svāhākṛti*s. (11) When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering. (12) Having stepped back, if he is about to perform the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, he first bastes the *dhruvā* with the *juhū*, then the clotted butter (*pṛṣadājya*), and then the omentum; but not the *upabhṛt*. (13) Thereafter, he proceeds with the two *ājyabhāga* offerings if he performs them. (14) Then he offers the *parivapya* first with the formula, "Svāhā to the gods! (15) Thereafter, he issues the formal command. (16) 7.15

"Recite the invitatory verse for Indra and Agni for the omentum and the fat of the goat. (1) Having made an under-layer of clarified butter in the *juhū* ladle and having placed a piece of gold within it, he cuts off the entire omentum. (2) Having placed a piece of gold on top, he pours clarified butter over it. (3) That [offering] becomes fivefold-divided (*pañcāvattā*). (4) Even if the sacrificer is one who performs fourfold-divided offerings (*caturavattin*), the omentum remains fivefold-divided. (5) If there should be no gold, he should cut off [the portions] from the clarified butter. (6) Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "For Indra and Agni, of the omentum and the fat of the goat..."

"Go forth! he says. When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers with this verse: "O Jātavedas, go to the gods with the omentum. Then he offers the subsequent *parivapya* oblation with: "To the gods, svāhā! He throws away the two omentum-spits with: "Svāhā! Go ye to the Maruts, the upward-moving ones. The one with two prongs is thrown toward the east, and the one with a single prong toward the west. Then he sprinkles them with the residue of the offering. He pours clarified butter over the opening of the animal's body. Having stepped out together with the wives, they purify themselves at the *cātvāla* pit with the mantra: "O Waters, carry away this impurity and whatever filth there is."
Whatever falsehood I have uttered, and whatever harsh word I have spoken;
I release myself from curses, I release myself from Varuṇa, I release myself from the fetter of Yama, and from every sin against the gods as well as from sin against men.
O Waters, release me from that sin; may you deliver me from all distress.
Thus, when the omentum has been offered, he gives a boon: a decorated maiden, or a bull, or three heifers. 7.16.14–15.

Having washed the vessels used for the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa), he sets them down—those which were employed for the vegetable offerings. Having prepared the two strainers (pavitras), he issues the command: "O sacrificer, restrain your speech. Restraining his speech, he touches the vessels. He offers the animal-cake made of rice, belonging to the same deity as the animal, on eleven or twelve potsherds. Having released his speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation (haviṣkṛt), he causes the animal to be dissected [with these instructions]: "Do not tear out the rectum; do not tear out the large intestine (vaniṣṭhu)."

"Bring together the diaphragm, the lungs, the spleen, the mesentery, and the fat," he issues the command. 6 They cook the animal on a pot. 7 Having pierced the heart with a spit, he cooks the sacrificial cake with water purified by a *yajus* formula. 8 While the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is already spread, he pours out the remnants of the flour. 9 When the animal is cooked, he proceeds with the sacrificial cake. 10 "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra and Agni regarding the sacrificial cake."

"Prompt the offering for Indra and Agni with the cake," he issues the command. "Recite for Agni; prompt the offering for Agni"—this is for the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation. The priests, with the Maitrāvaruṇa as the sixth, eat the *iḍā* portion once it has been invoked. They perform the ritual purification (*mārjana*). At this point, he offers the oblations of the flour-smear and the husks from the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*). He releases the potsherds. Having dipped the *juhū* ladle into the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), he asks three times. 7.17

"The oblation is cooked, O Śamitṛ! (1) "It is cooked," the Śamitṛ replies three times. (2) When it has been moved out three times, he makes the heart the uppermost part. (3) Having gone around by the north, he bastes the heart with speckled butter with the formula: "May your mind unite with [my] mind; may your breath unite with [my] breath; [may this be] pleasing to the gods."

"To Indra and Agni, the oblation rich in ghee, Svāhā! (4). "Svāhā to the steam for its non-disturbance," with this he consecrates the rising steam. (5). If they should tear the animal apart, he should consecrate it in exactly this same manner. (6). Having sprinkled the animal with clarified butter like the *sāṃnāyya* offering, and having removed it from the fire in that same way, he brings it between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, between the sacrificial post and the *āhavanīya* fire; having brought it forward, he places it on the southern shoulder of the altar with the *pañcahotṛ* formula. (7). A branch of the *plakṣa* tree serves as the upper covering. (8). Of that...

He cuts portions from the middle parts [of the limbs]. (9) He spreads an underlayer [of ghee] in four vessels: in the *juhū* and the *upabhṛt*, in the vessel for holding the collected portions (*samavattadhānī*), and in the ladle for the fat-oblation (*vasāhomahavanī*). (10) Having placed two chips of gold in the *juhū* and the *upabhṛt*, he issues the call: "Recite for the *manotā* as the oblation is being cut. (11) First he cuts a portion of the heart; then of the tongue; then of the chest; then of the left foreleg; then of the two ribs; then of the liver; then of the two kidneys; then of the right hip; then of the rectum. (12) He cuts twice from each one. (13) 7.18

Alternatively, having cut portions from the three principal parts in their proper sequence, he cuts from the remaining parts as desired. (1) Having placed the fat into the broth, he covers the *juhū* with the fat. (2) Having placed a piece of gold above it, he pours clarified butter over it. (3) Having poured clarified butter over the three limbs, he cuts portions for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering into the *upabhṛt* once each from the three limbs: from the right foreleg, from the left buttock, and from the middle part of the rectum. (4) Having already divided the rectum into two parts beforehand, he sets aside the thicker part for the *upayaj* offerings.

He places [the portions]. 5. He divides the *aṇiman* (the smallest part) into three parts. 6. Having divided its middle portion into two, he places it in the *juhū*; having divided the largest portion into two, he places it in the *upabhṛt*; and having divided the smallest portion into two, he places it in the *iḍā*. 7. Having placed the fat (*medas*) in the broth, he covers the *upabhṛt* with the fat. 8. Having placed a piece of gold on top, he sprinkles [clarified butter] over it twice. 9. He cuts the *iḍā* together into the vessel from the heart, the tongue, the liver, the kidneys, the rectum, the large intestine, and the seventh, the small intestine. 10. Right here, he also [cuts] the right buttock and the omentum.

Having placed the liver, the spleen, the pericardium, and the fat underneath [the portions], he sprinkles them with broth and pours clarified butter over them. (11) He takes a portion of the broth for the fat-oblation. (12) With the knife, he causes the stream to flow. (13) This is done once for a fourfold cutting, and twice for a fivefold cutting. (14) Having poured butter over those parts that have been cut off and those that have not been cut off, both the cooked and the uncooked, and having brought the entire animal together, he touches it with the formula: "May Indra's breath settle in every limb. (15) 7.19

With the side [of the ladle], he mixes the fat-oblation (vasāhoma) with the formula: "Thou art glory; may Agni mix thee with glory. Then he covers it with that same side [of the ladle] with the formula: "Svāhā! For the non-disturbance of the steam. Thereupon he issues the command: "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra and Agni regarding the oblation of the goat. Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for Indra and Agni regarding the oblation of the goat. At the half-verse of the offering-formula (*yājyā*), the Pratiprasthātṛ offers the fat-oblation with the formula: "O drinkers of ghee, drink the ghee! Having offered it, he leaves a remnant.

When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers the oblation. 7. With the remnants of the *vasā-homa*, he performs the *pratiyāga* (counter-sacrifice) to the quarters with these [formulas], offering to each quarter respectively: "To the quarters, *svāhā!* To the intermediate quarters, *svāhā!*" 8. Finally, facing eastward, he makes an offering with: "To the quarters, *svāhā!* Homage to the quarters! 9. Having offered the *nāriṣṭha* oblations here, and having once taken up the *pṛṣadājya* (speckled butter) with the *juhū* ladle, he says: "Recite the invitatory verse for Vanaspati. 10. Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "Prompt the call for Vanaspati. 11. When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he makes the offering. 12. Without stepping back across again, he issues the command: "For Agni..."

"Recite for the Sviṣṭakṛt," [he says]. Having brought the Upabhṛt over to the Juhū and having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Prompt for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering. Having stepped back and placed the two ladles in their proper places, [the ritual concludes]. 7.20.13–16.

He places the fatty portion (*medasvatī*) for the *hotṛ* as the intermediate *iḍā*. He spreads it with fat, he places it with fat, and he sprinkles it with fat. When the *iḍā* has been invoked, he brings the *adhyuddhi* to the *hotṛ* and the *vaniṣṭhu* to the *agnīdh*. He prepares the sixfold portion (*ṣaḍavatta*). They consume it and perform the ritual purification (*mārjana*). Then he issues the command: "O *agnīdh*, bring the embers for the *upayaj* offerings! O *upayaṣṭṛ*, sit down!"

"O Brahman, we shall set forth"—this is the beginning of the formal command (*saṃpraiṣa*). (6) It is the same up to the after-offerings (*anūyāja*s). (7) Having taken the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles and having poured the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) into the *juhū*, he steps across, calls for the *śrauṣaṭ*, and says, "Prompt for the gods! (8) He offers when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered. (9) Calling for the *śrauṣaṭ* at each subsequent [offering], he issues the commands, "Prompt! Prompt! (10) Having brought embers from the *śāmitra* fire, the *āgnīdhra* scatters them on the northern corner of the altar. (11) The *pratiprasthātṛ*, having cut the eleven sections of the rectum crosswise, [places them].

Having placed the fat into the *vasāhomahavanī* ladle, he performs the after-offerings (*anūyāja*), making an offering for each *vaṣaṭ*-call with these formulas one by one: "Go to the ocean, svāhā! and so forth. (12) The Pratiprasthātṛ wipes the smearings on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with the formula: "To the waters, to the plants, [svāhā]. (13) He touches himself with the formula: "Grant me mind and heart. (14) 7.21

Having performed eleven after-offerings (anūyāja), having stepped back and anointed the *svaru* in the *juhū* ladle, he offers the *svaru* with the *juhū* while reciting: "May your smoke go to heaven, your flame to the intermediate space; fill the earth with ashes, Svāhā! (1) It is the same up to the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings. (2) With the two *vājavatī* verses, he separates all the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles. (3) He anoints the *prastara* grass-bundle in all the offering-ladles. (4) He issues the direction: "Prompt for the *sūktavāka*! (5) He causes all [the ladles] to flow together. (6) He places them all upon the two *kaṭa* posts.

7. He performs the *saṃyājana* offerings for the wives with the tail (*jāghanī*). 8. He sacrifices to Soma with clarified butter; he sacrifices to Tvaṣṭṛ with clarified butter. 9. From the tail held upward, he cuts portions for the wives of the gods; from the tail held downward, for Agni Gṛhapati. 10. There are four cuttings each time for that which has four cuttings, and five cuttings each time for that which has five cuttings. 11. In this case, there are no under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*) or over-sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) [of clarified butter]. 12. From the tail held upward, he cuts the *iḍā* portion; from the tail held downward, for the *agnīdh*. 13. He gives the remainder of the tail to the wife and to the *adhvaryu*. 14. The arm [he gives] to the *śamitṛ*.

He gives it to a Brāhmaṇa, provided he is not a non-Brāhmaṇa. (15) It is the same up to the *samiṣṭayajus* offering. (16) He offers three *samiṣṭayajus* oblations: "O Sacrifice, go to the Sacrifice! This is thy sacrifice, O Lord of Sacrifice! O gods who know the way! (17) Between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, (18) having gone out, they proceed with the heart-spike (*hṛdayaśūla*). (1) At the junction of the dry and the moist, he throws away the heart-spike, saying: "Thou art heat; burn him who hates us and whom we hate. (2) "From every station, O King... (3)

Having worshipped the Āditya with the two verses beginning "O Varuṇa, loosen the highest bond," they purify themselves at the *cātvāla* pit with the formula, "May the waters and plants be friendly to us. (3) Having prepared fuel-sticks, they go forward without looking back. (4) Having placed fuel-sticks on the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "Fuel art thou; may we prosper," they stand in worship with the formula, "I have followed the waters. (5) In the same way, the wife, having placed fuel-sticks on the Gārhapatya fire, stands in worship. (6) The sacrificer stands in worship before the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) with the verse, "Hoping for great heroic strength. (7) The animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) is thus concluded. (8)

In this very manner, one should sacrifice with an animal every six months or every year. (9) A year should not pass for one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) without having sacrificed with an animal. (10) If it should pass, he would be a "flesh-eater" (*māṃsakhāda*). (11) It is known from tradition: "The fires of one who has established the sacred fires become 'over-eaters' (*aty-aśitā*); they eat his flesh when he does not sacrifice with an animal for a year. (12) If he should consume [the meat], he should consume it with this [formula]:
"I send the food to the fires with my mind; let them consume it together with me through my speech."
Being heedful and vigilant, I move with a peaceful mind; eat [your fill].
Thus, 13. If commanded, he should eat; having recited this mantra, he should eat; having recited this mantra, he should eat. 14. 7.23.
Thus ends the seventh question.
Now begins the eighth question.

One who is about to perform the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, having mentally recited the Pañcahotṛ formula, offers the Sagraha oblation in the Āhavanīya fire. He offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara and a pap to Pārjanya. He gives gold as the sacrificial fee for the Vaiśvānara offering and a milch cow for the Pārjanya offering. The sacrifice is completed in the established manner. This [offering] takes the place of the Anvārambhaṇīyā. On the full moon day of Phālguna or Caitra, he performs the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice on ground sloping toward the east. One view is that the Āhavanīya fire should be the one used for the New and Full Moon sacrifices.

Another [view] is that it belongs to the Soma sacrifice (saumika). 7. Everything else is performed except for the strewing upon the high altar (uttaravedi). 8. The ritual procedure (tantra) is that of the New Moon sacrifice (āmāvāsya). 9. It is the same up to the driving away of the calves. 10. He sends forth the cows with the formula: "Swell up, O inviolable ones; you are the portion for all the gods. 11. It is the same up to the gathering of the sacrificial grass (barhis). 12. The sacrificial grass is fresh (prasūmaya). 13. Having tied it together in three parts, he ties it together again as one. 14. In this manner, he prepares the fuel (idhma) consisting of twenty-three pieces of wood. 15.

The procedure is the same up to the employment of the vessels (16). He employs a second *upabhṛt* as the *pṛṣadājya*-holder; two *ājya*-pots; three *caru*-pots; and a vessel of *vājina* made of *pālāśa* wood (17). The procedure is the same up to the pouring out of the oblations (18). He pours out an offering on eight potsherds for Agni, a *caru* for Soma, a cake on twelve potsherds for Savitṛ, a *caru* for Sarasvatī, a *caru* for Pūṣan, a cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts, *āmikṣā* for the Viśve Devas, and a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth (19). The procedure is the same up to...

20. From the husks [he prepares] the husked rice. 21. He sets aside portions of the husked rice for the sacrificial pap (caru) with the *vibhāga-mantra*. 22. He grinds the remainder together. 23. From the flour thus mixed together, he sets aside a portion for Pūṣan. 8.1.

It is the same up to the morning milking (1). When the evening milk has been brought to the heated morning milk and the *āmikṣā* has been prepared, he then drains it, makes it *vājina* (curdled whey), and having drawn out portions into two vessels, he moistens [the *āmikṣā*] with a portion of the *vājina*. He sets aside the remainder of the *vājina* in a known place (2). Having placed the sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) on the fire and poured water for the *āpyas*, he then performs the subsequent tracing of the altar (3). It is the same up to the formal call (4). He concludes the formal call with the words: "Prompt [the Agnīdh] with clarified butter and curds" (5).

It is the same up to the taking of the *ājya* portions; he takes the *ājya* for the animal sacrifice (6). This much is different (8): having taken the *ājya* with two of the formulas belonging to the *aupabhṛta* [portions] from the vessel containing speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), he takes curds twice with the formula, "Thou art the milk of the great ones" (9). With one of the *aupabhṛta* formulas, he finally takes the *ājya* (10). Thus indeed, if he should sacrifice on the full moon of Caitra (11); but if on that of Phālguna, he should take them already mixed together, as in the *paśubandha* sacrifice (12). It is the same up to the removal of the sacrificial oblations (13).

Having taken out the cake on one potsherd, he fills it with clarified butter (14). He makes its back exposed (15). With "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," he sets down the oblations (16). The whey is placed on the rubbish-heap (17). When a year has elapsed, he should set them down with these same formulas (18). Having set down the oblations, he proceeds with the fire churned according to the ritual procedure for churning (19). There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses (20). It is the same up to the *prayāja* offerings (21). He performs nine *prayāja* offerings (22). At each fourth offering, he pours together the butter from the *upabhṛt* ladle.

He consecrates the offering to Pūṣan with the formula: "Through the sacrifice to the god Pūṣan, may I become possessed of nourishment and cattle. (1) In this very same way, he consecrates all the offerings to Pūṣan. (2) Having proceeded with the *āmikṣā* and having placed the cake on one potsherd upon the sacrificial grass, he spreads a layer of clarified butter in the *juhū* ladle and cuts off the entire cake from the single potsherd. (3) Having poured the remains back into the vessel at that very spot and having sprinkled it over, he offers it while it rests in the ladle. (4) If the offered cake should turn over, he should take it back, sprinkle it over again, and offer it once more. (5) Having given a boon, [he proceeds] with the ladle.
"Some say that he does not fashion it with his hand. Then he makes offerings over it with the names of four months: "Svāhā to Madhu! Svāhā to Mādhava! Svāhā to Śukra!"

"To Śuci, Svāhā! (7). "I pray for the well-being of the year-long [sacrifice]," thus the sacrificer mutters during the blessings of the *iḍā* (8). A first-born calf is the sacrificial fee (9). He performs nine after-offerings (*anūyāja*) with speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) (10). "He prays for the well-being of the year-long [sacrifice]; he prays for the celestial abode," thus the Hotṛ pronounces the blessing in the *sūktavāka* (11). Having cast away the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), he issues the command: "Recite for the Vājins" (12). Having spread a base of ghee in the *juhū* or in the cup, he pours the *vājina* over the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) while sprinkling (13).

Without sprinkling [the butter] and having stepped across [the altar], and having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Recite the offering prayer for the *vājins*. At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering with the [sacrificial ladle] being emptied. At the subsequent *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, he makes a second offering. 8.3.14–16.

Sitting with his knees raised, the Hotṛ performs the sacrifice without pausing. (1) Having offered the *vājina*, he leaves a remnant. (2) With the remainder of the *vājina*, he offers to the quarters as in the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*). (3) Having invited one another for the consumption, they eat; first the Hotṛ, then the Adhvaryu, then the Brahman, then the Āgnīdhra, and then the sacrificer. (4) Or, having divided it into equal portions, (5) all of them should invite one another mutually by their ritual names. (6) "N.N., invite me! is the invitation; "I am invited" is the response. (7) "Whatever semen of mine is spilled, whatever is born from me again..."
Whatever of mine remains established, with that make me immortal; with that make me possessed of good offspring.

"Of that which has been drunk by the horse, which has been invoked, I, being invoked, partake"—this is the formula. 8. It is the same up to the *samiṣṭayajus* offering. 9. He offers the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations belonging to the animal sacrifice. 10. The sacrifice is completed in the established manner. 11. Having extracted [the hair] with a three-striped porcupine quill and having shaved the beard with a copper razor made of *udumbara* wood, he causes the hair on the sides of the head to be trimmed with the formula: "Truth indeed is the Supreme Lord; truth nothing whatsoever transgresses. 12. In this very same way, he causes it to be trimmed at each subsequent joint with each subsequent mantra. 13.

For four months he does not eat meat, does not approach a woman, does not sit on elevated ground, and he loathes untruth; he sleeps facing the east and eats honey. (14) “He should eat honey”—this is one view. “It is for the sake of seasoning”—this is another. (15) According to some, however, he may approach his wife during her season. (16) In this very same manner, he observes the vow throughout all the intervals between the Cāturmāsya sacrifices. (17) 8.4

Then, after four months, he performs the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices. Their ritual procedure is explained by that of the Vaiśvadeva; we shall now enumerate the modifications. It is the same up to the driving away of the calves. The Pratiprasthātṛ drives away the calves for the Āmikṣā dedicated to the Maruts, and the Adhvaryu does so for that dedicated to Varuṇa. In front of the Āhavanīya fire, they prepare two altars: the Adhvaryu prepares the northern one, and the Pratiprasthātṛ the southern one. They are level and oriented toward the east.

Either with a span or with a cubit, without separating [the altars], whatever the Adhvaryu does, that the Pratiprasthātṛ does. To the east or to the west of the northern altar, the Pratiprasthātṛ carries away the *stambayajus*. From this point onward, he moves about by this same path. The *utkara* (heap of rubbish) is common; the *āgnīdhra* shed is common; the Hotṛ is common; the Brahman is common. In this regard, this is the specific rule: those rites which the Adhvaryu performs on the northern altar, those the Pratiprasthātṛ performs on the southern one.

13. Then he joins them together. 14. Starting from the northern hip of the southern altar, he scrapes with the wooden sword toward the southern shoulder; [the formula is] "May the earth be won. 15. Having performed that which was prior to the northern enclosure-line, he pours out the high-altar (uttaravedi) on the northern altar, not on the southern one. 16. The pouring out of the ritual materials takes place at both [altars]. 17. 8.5.

"On the previous day they lead forward the fires"—this is one view. "Having placed the oblations on the fire"—this is another. [The procedure] is the same up to the bringing of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). They bring two bundles of grass and prepare two fuel-sticks. [The procedure] is the same up to the employment of the vessels. Both employ the vessels. The offering-spoons (*sruva*) belong to the *śamī* wood, or they may be made of gold for the southern sacrificial area (*vihāra*). [The procedure] is the same up to the pouring out of the grains. Having poured out the five constant and moving offerings, beginning with "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni," he pours out [the grain] for the cake on eleven potsherds for Indra-Agni.

He pours out [the grain] silently for the *karambha* vessels; having poured out the barley for the two ram-effigies, they pour out the barley with the mantra. The Pratiprasthātṛ pours it out for the Maruts, and the Adhvaryu for Varuṇa. He pours out the cake on one potsherd for Ka. It is the same [procedure] up to the husking. He sets aside all the husks for the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*). With the mantra, they place two potsherds for roasting the barley upon the two ram-effigies. They prepare the parched grains (*dhānā*) so that they are slightly scorched.

While pouring [the grain], they both mutter the mantra for placing [the vessel] on the fire (16); while removing it from the fire, they both mutter the mantra for taking it down (17). Having fried the grains and sprinkled them with clarified butter, they take them down (18). At the proper time, they both adorn themselves (19). Wherever one might roast sacrificial grains, one should act in this very manner (20). The grains are pounded according to the procedure for flour (21). They prepare the two curd-mixtures (*āmikṣā*) according to the procedure for *āmikṣā* (22). He sets aside the scrapings of the oblation to Varuṇa in a known place (23). 8.6

Having placed upon the fire the oblations beginning with those for Indra and Agni, the wives prepare, for each person, vessels of *karambha* (barley-meal) from barley that has not been ground or from barley that has been slightly parched; there is one extra vessel for as many sons and grandsons as the sacrificer has. (1) She also prepares one for each woman. (2) They make two figures of rams: (3) the Adhvaryu makes the ram and the Pratiprasthātṛ makes the ewe. (4) For the woman, he makes female characteristics, and for the man, male characteristics. (5) Then, they make these two hairy with wool from the neck.

6. If they cannot find wool from a sheep that has not given birth, they should instead attach wool from *kuśa* grass. 7. Or the two [fires] may be prepared by baking in a pot (*kumbhīpākya*). 8. Having placed the single-pan sacrificial cake (*ekakapāla*) on the *kāya* fire, having poured out the oblation-materials for the *āpya* deities, and having kindled the fuel on the *āhavanīya*, he issues the command: "Recite for the two fires being led forward! 9. Whatever common commands there are, the Adhvaryu alone should utter them. 10. They lead the two fires together; they carry the *praṇītā* waters together. 11. The *praṇītā* waters are placed on the northern fire alone.

As they proceed, 12. At the northern [altar], he releases the vow. 13. Thereafter, they perform the two subsequent enclosures (parigrāha). 14. This is the same up to the formal command (saṃpraiṣa). 15. The command conforms to the specific ritual context. 16. It is the same up to the taking of the clarified butter (ājya) portions. 17. 8.7.

Both take up the *pāśuka* portions of clarified butter (*ājya*). This much is different. Having taken up the clarified butter with one of the formulas for the *aupabhṛta* portions from the two vessels of speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*)—using [the formula] "Thou art the milk of the great ones"—they both take up curds twice [with the formula] "Thou art the milk of the great ones. With two of the *aupabhṛta* formulas, they finally take up the clarified butter. This is indeed the case if he should sacrifice on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa. But if he sacrifices on the full moon of Āṣāḍha, they should take them mixed together, as in the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*). It is the same up to the removal of the sacrificial oblations (*havir-udvāsana*). The oblations end with that for Indra-Agni.

They place the two ram-figures upon the two portions of *āmikṣā* curd-mixture: 7. He places the ram upon the portion for the Maruts and the ewe upon the portion for Varuṇa. 8. Into these two, they scatter more than a hundred or more than a thousand leaves of *śamī* wood and shoots of *karīra*. 9. They pour them into the vessels of *karambha* porridge. 10. Having removed the cake baked on one potsherd according to the procedure for the one-potsherd offering, he places the oblations for the Maruts upon the northern altar. 11. On the southern altar, he places the portion for Varuṇa and the *karambha* vessels. 12. They exchange the ram-figures between the two portions of *āmikṣā*. 13. [The ram-figure] upon the portion for the Maruts...

He places a ewe on the northern fire and a ram on the southern fire. (14) Both perform the ritual with fires produced by friction; this is one view. The Adhvaryu alone performs it; this is another view. (15) 8.8 Then he issues the command: "Recite for the two fires being kindled. (1) In the same manner, during the wiping, he modifies the call to include two fires. (2) The northern fire has been wiped, while the southern fire remains unwiped. (3) Then the Pratiprasthātṛ asks the wife: "How many lovers do you have? (4) If she were not to disclose a lover who exists, she would obstruct a dear kinsman. She should point him out, saying: "So-and-so is my lover. (5)

It is known from the sacred tradition that by merely pointing him out, one causes him to be seized by the noose of Varuṇa. Having said, "May Varuṇa seize as many as he names," he leads his wife forward with the verse, "We invoke the Praghāsya gods. Having spread an under-layer of ghee in a winnowing basket made of *aiṣīka* grass, having poured the *karambha* vessels into it, having sprinkled them with ghee, and having placed them upon her head, the sacrificer, standing in front facing west together with his wife, offers the *karambha* vessels in the southern fire. The sacrificer recites the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*): "O Indra, do not indeed [seize] us... Both [the sacrificer and his wife] [participate].

The Pratiprasthātṛ ceases [his work]. (1) The Adhvaryu offers the oblations. (2) Having performed the rite with the offering to Indra and Agni, the Adhvaryu ceases. (3) The Pratiprasthātṛ proceeds with the offering to the Maruts. (4) With the first portion, he cuts off the ewe together; with the second, he cuts it off together with the *śamī* leaves and *karīra* fruits. (5) Having performed the rite with the offering to the Maruts, the Pratiprasthātṛ ceases. (6) The Adhvaryu proceeds with the offering to Varuṇa. (7) With the first portion, he cuts off the ram together; with the second, he cuts it off together with the *śamī* leaves and *karīra* fruits. (8)

Having offered the cake on one potsherd according to its ritual procedure, he makes offerings with the four subsequent names of the months: "To Nabhas, svāhā! To Nabhasya, svāhā! To Iṣa, svāhā! To Ūrja, svāhā! Then they both offer separately to the Sviṣṭakṛt.

10. "I pray for the well-being of these [cows] that have endured a full year," thus the sacrificer mutters during the blessings of the *iḍā*. 11. A bull with a prominent hump is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). 12. He performs nine after-offerings (*anūyāja*) with speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*). 13. "He prays for the well-being of those who have endured a full year; he prays for the celestial abode," thus the Hotṛ prays in the *sūktavāka*. 14. Both [the Adhvaryu and the Hotṛ] proceed with the *vājina* (curd-mixture). 15. "May the drops enter thee! O *valga*, fill my essence with the essence of the vessels.
Of that which has been made into food by the *vājins* and invoked, I, being invoked, partake. 16. 8.10.

They consume the sacrificial whey (vājina). May the consumption of the whey protect us; may the strength (vāja) protect us. May the seed that has been poured, the nectar for the sake of power, bestow upon us sensory vigor and wealth. May we not come to harm while consuming the sacrificial whey.

When he has been invited, [the other] says, "I eat, being invited," as the response. (2) Both place the two ladles on the pillar-stand. (3) The Adhvaryu alone performs the *saṃyājya* offerings for the wives. (4) Both offer the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations pertaining to the animal sacrifice. (5) The sacrifice is completed in the established manner. (6) They perform the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) with the husks and the scrapings of the offering to Varuṇa. (7) Therein, the entire purificatory rite is performed, except for that which pertains to the Sāman chant, the Adhvaryu’s formulas, and the eating of the *ṛjīṣa*. (8) The husks take the place of the *ṛjīṣa*. (9)

10. There is the scrapings of the cake on one potsherd. 11. Or rather, he should offer a cake on one potsherd to Varuṇa. 12. Having taken portions from it together with the scrapings, he should proceed with the ritual. 13. Or rather, there is no purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) belonging to the Soma sacrifice. 14. He should silently throw the chaff and the scrapings into the water. 15. Then, having put on other two garments, he should emerge. 16. These two garments may be given at will to whomever they desire. 17. Having returned, he performs the turning back. 18. The procedure for the turning back and likewise the observance of the vow have been explained. 8.11.

Then, after four months, he performs the Sākamedha sacrifices for two days. 1. He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Anīkavant at sunrise. 2. According to some, [he offers] "together with the rays as they spread forth. 3. The sacrifice is completed in the established manner. 4. At midday, he offers a pap to the Maruts Sāṃtapanas. 5. The sacrifice is completed in the established manner. 6. He commences the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the Gṛhamedhīya [offering]. 7. It is the same up to the driving away of the calves. 8. [He proceeds] with the Gṛhamedhīya without a sacrificial formula (*ayajuṣka*).

He drives away all the calves. (9) Having prepared the *veda*, he prepares the altar (*vedi*). (10) Here there is no sacrificial fuel (*idhma*) nor sacrificial grass (*barhis*). He does not lead forward the *praṇītā* waters. (11) Having strewn around the fires, having washed his hands, having set out the vessels, having spread the *ulaparājī* grass, and having prepared the two strainers (*pavitre*), he issues the command: "O sacrificer, restrain your speech! (12) With speech restrained, he touches the vessels. (13) For the Maruts Gṛhamedhins, he prepares a pap (*caru*) in the evening with the milk of all the cows. (14) Having caused all the cows to be milked into the strainers while they are not yet strained...

Having not strained the milk-curd (*payasyā*), he pours in the rice-grains (15). On either the *gārhapatya* or the *ānvāhāryapacana* fire, he cooks the neighboring-rice (*prativeśa-odana*) (16). Then he performs the subsequent tracing of the altar (17). It is the same up to the formal summons (*saṃpraiṣa*) (18). Here he does not urge forward the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*idhmā-barhis*) (19). It is the same up to the taking of the clarified butter portions (20). He takes [the butter] only in the *dhruvā* ladle (21). Having consecrated the sprinkling waters, having addressed the *brahmán*, having sprinkled the altar, having poured out the remainder of the sprinkling waters, and having consecrated the fire, [he places] the *dhruvā* within the altar.

Having set down the *sruva*-ladle, he sets it down [on the altar] while adapting the mantra: "She has sat down. 22 He consecrates the clarified butter (*ājya*) with the formula: "Thou art Viṣṇu’s; thou art Vaiṣṇava; thou art the abode of Prajāpati. 23 He does not throw a *prastara* grass-bundle for that sacrifice. According to some teachers, they proceed with the *Gṛhamedhīya* offering on the very same sacrificial grass (*barhis*) that was spread for the *Sāṃtapana* rite. 24 8.12

Then, having removed this *caru* and set aside its known *śara* grass, he draws out three portions of boiled rice (*odana*). He sets down the pot (*kumbhī*) without removing it from the fire, and the stirring-spoon (*darvī*) without wiping it. Having drawn out the portions of rice, he purifies them with a *gāyatrī* verse for each foot (*pāda*), decorates them, and places them down. At night they perform the *Gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice. There are no *sāmidhenī* verses here, nor the two *āghāra* libations, nor the *prayāja* offerings. Having thrown the *vedā* grass-bundle toward the *āhavanīya* fire, he issues the command: "O *agnīdh*, cleanse the fire thrice!"

The Āgnīdhra priest sweeps the fire-altar three times. Having performed the *pravara* invocation and having offered the two *ājyabhāga* portions, he issues the call: "Recite the invitatory verse for the Maruts, the Gṛhamedhins! (8) Having spread a base of clarified butter in the *juhū* ladle, he takes two portions from each of all the rice-messes for the four-fold portioning, or three portions from each for the five-fold portioning. (9) Having sprinkled clarified butter over them, stepped across, and caused the announcement (*āśrāvaṇa*) to be made, he says: "Recite the offering verse for the Maruts, the Gṛhamedhins! (10) He makes the offering when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered. (11) For the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he takes one portion from each of all the rice-messes. (12)

Having invoked the *iḍā* for all, the officiating priests consume that *iḍā*. (13) They present portions of boiled rice to the attendants (*umātayaḥ*), as many as there are who are entitled to eat the remnants of the sacrificial offerings (*havirucchiṣṭa*). (14) Others also may eat from it if there is plenty of rice. (15) The wife eats from the neighbor's house or from the *gṛhamedhīya* offering. (16) The *gṛhamedhīya* rite concludes with the *iḍā*. (17) They anoint themselves and smear themselves with unguents. (18) They let the calves stay with their mothers. (19) Well-fed and satisfied, they spend this night without returning home, their faces turned away from turning back. (20) The neighbors also cook food. (21) They drive the cows together. (22) 8.13

He commences the ritual procedure of Kraiḍina. 1. On the latter part of the night, they tie up the two calves of the Agnihotra cow and the Abhivānyā cow. 2. Before the morning Agnihotra, they perform the rite with the full ladle (pūrṇadarvya). 3. Having spread a base of ghee in the ladle and filled the ladle with the scrapings from the potsherds, he places the handle of the ladle upon it without wiping it. 4. Having sprinkled it with ghee, he offers it in the Gārhapatya fire. 5. Having recited the verse, "Full, O ladle, fly away," he makes the offering with the following verse. 6. Having summoned a bull, he makes the offering while the bull is bellowing.

He offers the oblation. (7) If the bull does not bellow, the Brahman priest should say, "Offer! (8) He offers when it bellows; he gives that bull to the Brahman. (9) He prepares a cake on seven potsherds for the sportive Maruts at the time when the sun has risen. (10) According to some, [he offers] with the formula, "Moving together with the rays. (11) The sacrifice is completed in the established manner. (12) When the sun has risen, having caused the cow *abhivānyā* to be milked, he prepares a cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts who possess their own strength (*svatavadbhyas*). (13)

The sacrifice is completed with success. 14. He commences the ritual procedure for the Mahāhavis offerings. 15. For these, the ritual rule is explained as being the same as that for the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings, except for the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha). 16. 8.14.

The sacrificial fee consists of *āmikṣā* from the southern fire-hall; this is the same up to the pouring out [of the oblation]. Having poured out the five regular *saṃcara* offerings—namely, the cake on eight potsherds for Agni, the cake on eleven potsherds for Indra-Agni, the pap for Indra, and the cake on one potsherd for Viśvakarman—the procedure is the same up to the taking up of the ladle. "O Agni, perform the office of the Hotṛ; perform the office of the messenger. Standing upright, you have attended to the sacrifice. May Heaven and Earth protect you at this sacrifice; may you protect Heaven and Earth at this sacrifice."

"O Sviṣṭakṛt, be for Indra and for the gods! Receiving this oblation, partake of the clarified butter; Svāhā! With these words, he pours the Āghāra libation from the ladle. Having offered the cake on one potsherd according to its ritual procedure, he makes offerings with the four subsequent names of the months: "To Sahas, Svāhā! To Sahasya, Svāhā! To Tapas, Svāhā!"

"To austerity, svāhā! (6). "I invoke the well-being of the full year," with these words the sacrificer mutters during the blessings of the *iḍā* (7). A first-born calf is the sacrificial fee (8). "He invokes the well-being of the full year; he invokes the celestial abode"—with these words the Hotṛ invokes in the *sūktavāka* (9). The sacrifice is completed as established (10). 8.15.

He commences the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*). 1. To the southeast of the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, he prepares a four-cornered altar (*vedi*) of the size of the sacrificer. 2. Its corners are in the cardinal directions, and its middles are in the intermediate directions. 3. Then, having enclosed it on all sides, he makes a door facing the northern corner. 4. Having performed [the rites] up to the digging out [of the hearth], he brings fire from the *anvāhāryapacana* and establishes it in the middle. 5. This [fire] serves as the *āhavanīya* in this ritual procedure. 6. Therein, those which...

The mantras addressed to the gods and those addressed to both [gods and ancestors] should be combined; [he recites]: "Thou art strewn for the gods and the ancestors; may I be able for the sake of the rite for the gods and the ancestors. Alternatively, they may proceed according to the original model. Up to the bringing of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the procedure is the same. He throws out the sacrificial grass together with its roots, or near the roots. The fuel-stick (*idhma*) is longer than the [usual] fuel, and the sacrificial grass is longer than the sacrificial grass [of the model sacrifice]. Up to the pouring out of the oblation, the procedure is the same. Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), he pours out [the grain] to the south of the cart, and to the north...

Or, wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), he offers a cake on six potsherds to Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs; parched grains (dhānās) to the Pitṛs seated on the sacrificial grass (barhiṣad); and a stirred drink (mantha) made with the milk of a cow that has borne a calf for the first time (abhivānyā) to the Pitṛs consumed by fire (agniṣvātta). (14) These oblations consist of barley. (15) Having moistened the barley with the water remaining from the sprinkling-vessels, he threshes it. (16) The procedure is the same up to the husking. (17) 8.16

Having divided the husked rice-grains into three parts, he places a pan on the Anvāhāryapacana fire for the purpose of roasting; upon it, they roast one-third of the rice-grains as parched grains (*dhānā*). 1. The preparation has been explained. 2. They grind the parched grains according to the procedure for ground flour (*piṣṭa*). 3. [The ritual] is the same up to the placing of the potsherds. 4. Having placed six potsherds in the southern half of the Gārhapatya fire, he places a pan on the Anvāhāryapacana fire for the sake of the parched grains. 5. He pours out the sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) into separate vessels. 6. He purifies [the butter].

7. Having poured water into the ground flour, he pours into it the stirred drink (mantha) from the milk of a cow that suckles another’s calf. 8. He makes a half-cup. 9. Having mixed the flours together, he stirs the stirred drink with a stalk of sugarcane, moving clockwise while facing south and not touching [the vessel]. 10. He makes it rest upon the stalk. 11. Having placed the sacrificial cake on the fire, they roast the parched grains (dhānāḥ) on the Anvāhāryapacana fire. 12. These remain there roasting until the removal of the oblations. 13. After that, he performs the subsequent tracing of the altar (parigrāha). 14.

The procedure up to the taking of the *ājya* (clarified butter) is the same. (15) He takes the *ājya* portions on the southern half of the *gārhapatya* fire. (16) All of them are taken four times (*caturgṛhīta*). (17) They remain right there until the placing of the sacrificial oblations (*havir*). (18) The procedure up to the spreading of the *barhis* (sacrificial grass) is the same. (19) Having first taken a blade of *barhis*, he goes around the fire three times to the left (*prasavyam*), spreading the grass as he goes. (20) He goes back around three times without spreading grass, holding [the bundle] upwards with the verse: "By this station, generating heroic deeds... (RV 3.8.4). (21) That becomes the *prastara*. (22) 8.17

He lays down two enclosing-sticks (paridhi), namely the middle one and the southern one; there are no separating-blades (vidhṛti) here. He silently places the prastara-bunch. They set down the clarified butter and the sacrificial oblations (havir) one by one. First they carry the fire, then the water-jar, then the clarified butters, and then the oblations. Or, he decorates each one individually.

"According to some, this is their serving of food. To the south, having placed one by one a cushion, a pillow, collyrium, and ointment, and having loosened [their garments], they turn their *prācīnāvīta* into *yajñopavīta*. Then he gives the direction: "Recite for Agni, for the gods, and for the Pitṛs as he is being kindled. He recites three times this *sāmidhenī* verse, "Desiring you, we invoke you. He places the fuel on the fire once, or having divided it into three parts. Having poured the *āghāra* libation with the *sruva*-ladle, he gives the direction: "O Āgnīdh!"

"Cleanse the enclosing sticks and the fire three times each. (11) This is the same up to the *pravara* invocation. (12) Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Sit down, O Hotṛ! (13) Such is the extent of the *pravara*. (14) He does not choose an *ārṣeya* lineage, nor does he choose a Hotṛ. (15) He performs four *prayāja* offerings, omitting the *barhis*. (16) Having proceeded with the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, they untie their sacrificial cords (*yajñopavīta*) and make them into the *prācīnāvīta* fashion. (17) At this point, some prescribe the encircling of the altar. (18) They transpose the *ājya* portions; they transpose the oblations (*havīṃṣi*).

The officiating priests move around. To the south of the *juhū* he places the *upabhṛt*; to the south of the *upabhṛt*, the *dhruvā*. To the south of the *puroḍāśa* he places the parched grains (*dhānās*); to the south of the parched grains, the stirred drink (*mantha*). The *juhū* remains in the same place; the *puroḍāśa* remains in the same place; and the Brahman priest and the sacrificer remain in the same place. 8.18.20–21.

Then he gives the command: "Recite for Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs, Svadhā! Having spread a base of clarified butter in the *juhū* ladle, he recites two invitatory verses (*puronuvākyā*) for each of all the oblations together with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, both containing the *praṇava*. For those who offer five-fold portions (*pañcāvattin*), he cuts six-fold portions; for those who offer four-fold portions (*caturavattin*), he cuts five-fold portions. From each of the principal oblations, he cuts twice from the six-fold portion. Having cut from the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), he cuts from the parched grains (*dhānā*). In the same way, he cuts from the stirred drink (*mantha*). Having sprinkled [clarified butter] over them and stepped across toward the north, [he says]: "Svadhā."

Thus he causes [the Āgnīdhra] to announce. "Let there be *svadhā*," [the Āgnīdhra] responds. "To Soma accompanied by the Fathers, *svadhā*!"—thus he issues the direction. "Those who [desire] *svadhā* for us"—this is the *āgūḥ*. "Svadhā! Homage!"—with these words he utters the *vaṣaṭ*. Then he issues the direction: "Recite the *svadhā* for the Fathers seated on the sacrificial grass (*barhiṣad*). Having spread a base of clarified butter in the *juhū* ladle, having taken a portion of the parched grains (*dhānā*), he takes a portion of the stirred drink (*mantha*). In the same way, he does so for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). Having sprinkled [the portions] with clarified butter and stepped across toward the north, he causes [the Āgnīdhra] to announce: "Svadhā!"

"Let there be *svadhā*," he responds. 14. "To the *barhiṣad* ancestors, *svadhā*!"—thus he gives the direction. 15. "We who [offer] *svadhā*,"—this is the *āgūr* formula. 16. "Svadhā! Adoration!"—with these words he utters the *vaṣaṭ* call. 17. Then he gives the direction: "After [the offering] to the *agniṣvātta* ancestors, *svadhā*! 18. Having spread a base of ghee in the *juhū* ladle and having taken a portion from the stirred mixture (*mantha*), he takes a portion from the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). 19. In the same manner, he takes portions from the parched grains (*dhānā*). 20. Having sprinkled [the portions] with ghee and stepped across toward the north, he causes the announcement to be made: "Svadhā!"

"Let there be *svadhā*," he responds. 21. He gives the direction: "To the *Agniṣvātta* Pitṛs, *svadhā*! 22. "We invoke *svadhā*," is the *āgūḥ*. 23. "Svadhā! Homage!"—with these words he utters the *vaṣaṭ*. 24. 8.19.

Some authorities prescribe performing the ritual without bringing the portions together. Then he issues the call: "Recite for Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt, Svadhā! Having spread a base of ghee in the *juhū* ladle, he cuts a single portion from the southern half of each of the sacrificial oblations—four portions if they are of four-fold cutting, and two portions each if they are of five-fold cutting. Having sprinkled them with ghee and stepped across toward the north, he causes the announcement to be made: "Svadhā!"

"Let there be *svadhā*," he responds. 4. He gives the direction: "To Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt, *svadhā*! 5. "We invoke *svadhā*," is the *āgūr*. 6. He utters the *vaṣaṭ* call: "*Svadhā! Namaḥ*! 7. From the top of the *mantha*, he should cut off the *iḍā* portion; from the other two [oblations], he cuts them off [afterwards]. According to some, he cuts off the *iḍā* from the *mantha* first. 8. When the *iḍā* has been invoked, they consume it by smelling, beginning with the Hotṛ, then the Adhvaryu, then the Brahman, then the Āgnīdhra, and finally the sacrificer. 9. Taking a water-pot, he goes around the fire three times toward the left, sprinkling water while saying, "May the fathers be purified."

Sprinkling water three times, he goes around [the fire] in the opposite direction with the verse, "By this power, generating great deeds... (RV X.72.6). Having mixed the remnants of the oblation and formed them into three balls, he places them on the three corners—on the one at the back, the one on the south, and the one on the east. Or rather, it may be the reverse of this. He offers them with these mantras, "This for thee, O father, and those who follow thee," etc., just as in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. 8.20.10–13.

Having wiped the smearings on the northern corner [of the altar] with the formula, "O Fathers, enjoy yourselves here according to your portions," they go out toward the north and stand by the Āhavanīya fire until the stars appear. (1) Having touched one another, they mutter: "O Maghavan, may we gladden thee who art fair to behold. (2) They stand by the Gārhapatya fire with the verse, "They have eaten, they have rejoiced. (3) With the words, "The Soma-loving Fathers have rejoiced," they walk away. (4) With the words, "Go forth, O Soma-loving Fathers," they return again. (5) [They throw] the fringe silently.

Having cut off a lock of hair from the fringe of their garments and offered it, they present [the cloth], saying: "This, O fathers, is your clothing; do not seek anything else from us, O fathers. (6) The ritual action, beginning with the application of collyrium and ending with the worship of the Gārhapatya fire, is performed as in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. (7) Here, some prescribe the sprinkling of water around the altar. (8) Having loosened their Prācīnāvīta garments, they put on the Yajñopavīta. (9) They transpose the offering-spoons; the officiating priests move around in reverse order. (10) Having covered the enclosure, he issues the command: "O Brahman!"

"We shall set forth," [he says]. (11) He performs two after-offerings (*anūyāja*) without the *barhis* grass. (12) He issues the call for the first after-offering with "Sacrifice to the two gods! and for the latter with "Sacrifice! (13) At the *sūktavāka*, the Hotṛ unties his head-band. (14) Here the wife does not sit beside the altar; they do not perform the *saṃyāja* offerings; he does not offer the *samiṣṭayajus*. (15) The sacrifice is completed in the established manner. (16) According to some, it ends with the *śaṃyu-formula*. (17) 8.21

He prepares one *kapāla* (potsherd) for each person, just as he does for the *karambha* vessels. Having placed the potsherds on the northern half of the *gārhapatya* fire, he bakes them. Then, having either sprinkled them with clarified butter or not, he removes them from the fire and places them in a bag.

Either in two bags or in bags [filled with earth], according to some teachers, they carry [the sacrificial vessels] covered with a sheath. From the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire, he carries a single fire-brand, emitting smoke, toward the west. Having gone to the intermediate direction between north and east, he scatters one [of the potsherds] upon a mole-hill, saying: "For as many as we are who belong to the household, for them I have performed this service. At a crossroads, having kindled a single fire-brand and strewn grass around it, he spreads an underlayer on a middle palāśa leaf—or on the last leaf of all—and taking portions from each of the one-potsherd cakes once each, he pours clarified butter over them and offers them. This...

"O Rudra, that which is your portion, together with your sister Ambikā—enjoy that, svāhā! (7) With these two verses beginning "A remedy for the cow," the sacrificer consecrates the oblation that has been offered. (8) Taking up the cakes on single potsherds, one for each person, they walk three times clockwise around the crossroads while reciting the verse: "We worship Tryambaka... (9) If she should be desirous of a husband, she too should walk around, reciting:
"We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the bringer of a husband.
Like a cucumber from its stem, may I be released from here, but not from my husband."

Thus, having thrown them upward ten times, they recover them. (8.22) "O you who are fortune, may I obtain a share of you"—having gone around and around, they pour them together for the sacrificer. They should pour them together for one who desires a husband; this is one view. Another view is that it should be for the sacrificer. Having placed them in a cloth and hung them on a tree outside the cow-pen, they stand in worship, [reciting]: "This is your portion, O Rudra; enjoy it. With this favor, pass beyond the Mūjavat mountains. With bow unstrung, with Pināka staff in hand, clad in a skin."

They descend three times; having sprinkled [the water] around, they purify themselves with the formula: "May the waters and plants be friendly to us. (6) Having prepared fuel-sticks, they return without looking back. (7) Having placed fuel-sticks on the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "Thou art fuel; may we prosper," they stand in worship with the formula, "I have moved along the waters. (8) In the same way, the wife, having placed [fuel-sticks] on the Gārhapatya fire, stands in worship. (9) Having returned, she offers a pap of rice cooked in ghee to Aditi. (10) Its ritual procedure is explained by that of the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*), except for the granting of a boon. (11) Some [offer] a white horse.

They prescribe: "These sacrifices are to be performed on the same day, except for the Anīkavat and the Kraiḍina. Thereafter, he turns back; the turning back has been explained, as well as the practice of the vow. 8.23.12–15.

Then, after four months, he performs the Śunāsīrya sacrifice—either monthly, or every half-month, or at intervals of four days, three days, two days, or even one day. Its ritual procedure is explained by that of the Vaiśvadeva; we shall now enumerate its specific modifications. It is the same up to the pouring out of the oblations. Having poured out the five constant *saṃcara* offerings—namely, the cake on eight potsherds for Agni and so forth—he offers a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra-Agni, a pap for the Viśvedevas, a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra-Śunāsīra, and milk for Vāyu.

"The cake for Sūrya on one potsherd"—thus the ritual procedure for the milk from the morning milking is explained. Having offered the cake on one potsherd according to its specific ritual sequence, he makes an additional offering with the name of the current month: "To the Serpent, to this [month] belonging to Bṛhaspati, svāhā! At the benedictions of the *iḍā*, the sacrificer mutters: "I invoke the well-being of the revolving year. A plow drawn by twelve oxen, or six oxen, or two oxen, or even a single ox [is given]. In the *sūktavāka*, the Hotṛ invokes: "He invokes the well-being of the revolving year; he invokes the celestial abode."

10. He offers one *samiṣṭayajus* oblation. 11. The sacrifice is completed successfully. 12. In that same manner he turns back. 13. The procedure for turning back has been explained. 14. The Cāturmāsya sacrifices are concluded. 15. 8.24.

We shall now explain the optional Cāturmāsya sacrifices. (1) One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva [parvan]. (2) He should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva at whatever season of the year his milk supply is greatest, or else when his milk supply is greatest in the spring; then he should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva. (3) One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva alone, and not with the other parvans, until he has obtained a thousand cattle. (4) Having obtained a thousand cattle, he should sacrifice with the other parvans according to their respective seasons. (5) One desiring a village should sacrifice with the Śunāsīrīya [parvan]. (6)

It is known from tradition: "One desiring rain should settle near water; one desiring offspring should sacrifice with this very [rite]; one desiring cattle should sacrifice; one desiring food should sacrifice; one desiring firm standing should sacrifice. (7) We shall now explain the five-year cycles. (8) Having commenced on the full moon of Phālguna and having sacrificed for three seasons and three years, one should cease for one month. (9) Having commenced on the full moon of Caitra and having sacrificed for two seasons and two years, one should cease. (10) The Vaiśvānara-Pārjanya [offering] and the Pañcahotṛ [offering] constitute the common framework (*tantra*). (11) After having sacrificed with the Cāturmāsya [offerings], one sacrifices with Soma.

"One should sacrifice. It is known from scripture: "The Cāturmāsya sacrifices are indeed the form of Soma. If one is unable to perform the Soma sacrifice, one should sacrifice with an animal. If one is unable to sacrifice with an animal, there is the repeated performance of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices. It is known from scripture: "In every three years, one should omit one month. [This is repeated. Thus ends the eighth book (praśna). Now begins the ninth book.

An expiation characterized by Vedic revelation is prescribed for a transgression of the rule. (1) When multiple expiations are heard for a single fault, they should be combined because they serve distinct purposes. (2) These consist of recitation (*japa*), burnt offerings (*homa*), and sacrifices (*ijyā*). (3) They exist for the purpose of destroying the fault. (4) They are to be performed immediately after the fault occurs. (5) Once the fault has been removed, the entire ritual action is to be performed again. (6) There is no re-performance of that [specific act] unless there is a scriptural injunction to that effect. (7) If one who has maintained the sacred fires should depart on a journey, he should offer an oblation into the *gārhapatya* fire with the verse: "To you, O best of the Aṅgiras... (8).

Having consigned the fires into separate fire-drills, he departs. Wherever he halts, there he completes this sacrifice. If the Āhavanīya fire of one who has carried forward the fires should go out, he should lead forward another fire with the verse, "Agni has looked toward the forefront of the dawns," and having worshipped it with "Bhūḥ," he offers a full ladle of clarified butter with the verse:
"To him who, possessing oblations, seeks to win Agni for the feast of the gods—to him, O Purifier, be gracious! Svāhā!"

Thus (11). Then he offers this oblation with the verse, "Viṣṇu strode through this" (12). He should mentally mutter the Yajus formula for entering upon the vow (13). Should anyone follow him, he should perform the same rite, excluding the leading forward of the fire (14). He should churn the Gārhapatya fire (15), and the Anvāhāryapacana fire according to the original model (16). If the fire of one who has established the sacred fires should go out before the distance of a yoke-pin's throw, he should collect it with the verse:
"This is one [place] for thee, and that beyond is another; unite with the third light!
Be pleasant to the body as it enters, dear to the gods in the highest birthplace. (17)

Thus [ends section] 17.9.1. If he should depart further away, he should go after him and stay there. Then he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt (the maker of the way). He should fetch sacrificial grass from near the road. An ox is the sacrificial fee. The sacrifice is completed in the established manner. If, after the calves have been separated for the sake of the oblation, they should suckle [their mothers], he should offer a barley gruel to Vāyu. That [gruel] should take the place of the milking, whichever [cow] they might suckle after being separated. Then, having separated the calves for the subsequent oblation, he should fast. If the evening milk—

If there should be an affliction of the sacrificial oblation (*havir-ārti*), one should set aside rice for Indra and fast. (9) Whatever [milk] may be available in the morning, that he should cook. (10) Then, there should be another *puroḍāśa* cake for Indra. (11) Having taken portions from it together with the morning milk (*prātardoha*), he should proceed with the offering. (12) Then, having driven away the calves for the subsequent oblation, he should fast. (13) This very same expiation applies when the morning milk is afflicted. (14) The difference is only this much.

Having brought together [the milk] here with the evening milking, he should proceed. (15) If both milkings should meet with misfortune, he should offer a five-śarāva measure of cooked rice for Indra. (16) Regarding this, Āśmarathya says that he should sacrifice to both deities, Agni and Indra. Now, Ālekhana says that he should sacrifice to Indra alone. (17) The cake on eight potsherds for Agni is obligatory. (18) Then, having driven away the calves for the subsequent oblation, he should fast. (19) If his wife should be in her courses on the day of the vow, he should exclude her and sacrifice. (20) He should spread out a cord toward the north. (21) 9.2 Having sacrificed to her, he should invite her [to eat].
I am he, you are she; I am the sky, you are the earth; I am the Sāman, you are the Ṛc.
Come, let us two unite; let us deposit seed for a male son who shall know [the truth], for the increase of wealth, for good progeny, and for heroic vigor.

Thus: (1) If the *sāṃnāyya* or the *agnihotra* should spill, one should pour it into an anthill with a verse addressed to Prajāpati and worship it with the word "bhūḥ. (2) Then, having milked another [cow], one should offer again if it was the *agnihotra*. (3) But if it was the *sāṃnāyya*, one should drive away the calves for the subsequent oblation and fast. (4) If an insect should fall into the *sāṃnāyya* or the *agnihotra*, one should pour it out between the enclosing sticks with the middle leaf of a *parṇa* tree, using the verse addressed to Heaven and Earth. (5) Then, having milked another [cow], one should offer again.
If it rains on the Agnihotra, or if it rains on the Sāṃnāyya after one has driven away the calves for the subsequent oblation and is fasting, [one should recite]:
"Mitra, knowing, ordains men; Mitra has supported the earth and the sky.
Mitra gazes upon the people with unblinking eyes; for the sake of Truth, he offers the oblation rich in ghee."

Thus he should sacrifice. (8) Then, having milked another [cow], he should sacrifice again. (9) If, after the first oblation has been offered, the subsequent oblation should spill over, or if the first [should spill] because of the subsequent one, he should offer it again with the subsequent [verse]:
"O Vanaspati, wherever you know the secret names of the gods, there lead the offerings."

Having placed a fuel-stick with the verse addressed to the trees (*vānaspatyārcā*), he should offer again silently (10). Then, having milked another [cow], he should offer again (11). If the Āhavanīya fire should go out after the first oblation has been offered, he should place gold on the final wood-shard and offer over it, saying: "Agni has gone to the wood, the wood has gone to Agni; svāhā! (12). 9.3.
If a coal should fall outside the enclosing-sticks before the fore-offerings (*prayāja*s), he should press it down with the back of the *sruva* ladle, saying:
"May darkness not overcome me, may the sacrifice not be extinguished, may the sacrificer not be extinguished."
Homage be to you as you approach; homage, O Rudra, to you as you depart; homage to you wherever you sit.

"Do not harm the Adhvaryu; do not harm the sacrificer," if [he is] from the east; "Do not harm the Brahman; do not harm the sacrificer," if from the south; "Do not harm the Hotṛ; do not harm the wife; do not harm the sacrificer," if from the west; "Do not harm the Āgnīdhra; do not harm the cattle; do not harm the sacrificer," if from the north. Then he throws it after [the firebrand] with the verse: "The thousand-horned bull, Jātavedas, whose back is the Stoma, rich in ghee, of beautiful countenance."
May it not fail us; may we not abandon you like a stray cow. Grant us prosperity in cattle and prosperity in heroes.

"Thus, having struck [the fire-drill], one should offer an oblation," so say some (3). One should strike with that by which [the fire] might leap out (4). If the fire of one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) is not produced while being churned from the two fire-sticks (*araṇi*), [he should recite]:
"The men, with their thoughts and the movement of their hands, have generated from the two fire-sticks the praiseworthy fire—the far-seeing, the lord of the house, the active one. (5)

Having consecrated [the mixture] with this mantra, he should take [some of it] from wherever else he may see [it], mix it, and offer it as an oblation (5). Then, without hurrying, he should churn it again (6). If he cannot find anything else, he should offer it into the right ear of a goat (7); however, he must not eat of that goat thereafter (8). If he cannot find a goat, he should offer it into the right hand of a Brāhmaṇa (9); but he must not deprive that Brāhmaṇa of his lodging for the night (10). If he cannot find a Brāhmaṇa, he should offer it into a clump of Darbha grass (11); however, he must not sit upon those Darbha blades (12). 9.4.9–12.

If he should not find *darbha* grass, he should offer [the oblation] into water. Regarding this, Āśmarathya says: "One should not distinguish between these waters as 'fit for drinking' or 'unfit for drinking'; rather, one should regard even unfit water as fit for this year-long vow. Ālekhana says: "Even if it is unfit for drinking, one should indeed take up this water for the duration of the year. According to some teachers, however, one should not wash one's feet with water. At the end of the year, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) to Agni Vratapati. The sacrifice concludes in the established manner. If the fires of one who has established the sacred fires should become mixed with other fires...

Alternatively, one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vivici; then [one] to Vratapati. The sacrifice concludes successfully. (6–8) If the fire of one who has established the sacred fires should burn his house, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kṣāmavat; then [one] to Vratapati. The sacrifice concludes successfully. (9–11) Now, if they should become mixed with what is being consumed by fire, having offered to Vivici, he should offer to Śuci; then [one] to Vratapati. The sacrifice concludes successfully. (12–14)

Now, if they should be joined with lightning, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Apsumat; then [an offering] to Vratapati. The sacrifice is completed as established. Now, if they should be joined with a funeral fire or a birth-fire, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Saṃkusuka; then [an offering] to Vratapati. The sacrifice is completed as established. Now, if all [these fires] should come together, he should perform the Kṣāmavatī offering at the end. If the Agnihotra-pot should leak, he should consecrate it with a mantra.
The embryo that is leaking, Agni has made it a remedy; Indra, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Bṛhaspati have caused it to drip away upon the earth. It does not reach the navel; Nirṛti is driven far away.

Thus [it is said]. 22. One should cause what has been spilled to be carried into the water. 23. 9.5. If it should be unheated, one should consecrate it with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu. If the moon rises over the sacrificial oblation that has already been set out, one should divide the rice grains into three parts. Those which are of medium size, he should make into a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Dātṛ (the Giver). Those which are the largest, he should make into a pap of boiled milk for Indra Pradātṛ (the Bestower). Those which are the smallest, he should make into a pap of boiled milk for Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa. If the moon rises while the oblation has not yet been set out, for which deities should one set it out?

"From the natural ones," says Āśmarathya; "from the modified ones," says Ālekhana. This [offering] is not for one who does not maintain the sacred fires, according to one view; it is for such a person, according to the other. One who, being a regular performer of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, should let either the Amāvāsyā or the Paurṇamāsī pass by, should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt. He should fetch sacrificial grass from near a path. An ox is the sacrificial fee. The sacrifice concludes in the established manner. Now, according to some, it is known: "The sacrifice of him whose [sacrifices] are interrupted is indeed torn asunder."

When the sacrifice has been commenced, he offers this intermediate oblation. That very cake on eight potsherds for Agni which is offered at the full moon and that which is offered at the new moon—of that, he should make one for Agni Pathikṛt (the Maker of the Path).

By that very path he returns again; he does not interrupt the sacrifice.
