(9) He who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) should, if while away on a journey he should eat meat or approach a woman on a festival day (*parvan*), offer a cake on eight potsherds (*puroḍāśam aṣṭākapālam*) to Agni Vratapati. (10) Some authorities prescribe the *Vratabhṛt* offering for this occasion. (11) He who has established the sacred fires should offer this same oblation if he should shed tears. (12) Āśmarathya says that whatever [transgression] he might commit, it must simply be expiated by this rite. Ālekhana says that he should perform only the *Ārtijam* offering. (13) 9.6 If the cow intended for the Agnihotra should sit down after being let loose, he should make her stand up.
The goddess Aditi, of universal form, has risen; she has bestowed long life upon the lord of the sacrifice, providing a portion for Indra, Mitra, and Varuṇa.

Thus (1). Having milked it, he should give it to a Brāhmaṇa whose food he would not otherwise eat (2). Now, if it should quiver, he should milk another (3). If the milk should spill while being milked, he should consecrate it with this mantra: "Whatever milk today has clung to the earth, whatever has flowed into the plants, and whatever into the waters..."

"May there be milk in the houses, milk in the cows, milk in the calves, and may there be milk in me! (4) Then he pours water into it with the verse: "I send you forth to the ocean... (5) Having offered that [milk] exactly as it is, however it may be, he should then milk another cow and offer again. (6) If the milk spills, or if it has been placed on the fire, or if it overflows, one should milk [another cow] and offer; so says Āśmarathya.

Having offered that very [milk] in whatever state it may be, one should then milk another cow and offer again; so says Ālekhana. (7) If the [milk] being ladled out spills, or if it has already been ladled out, or if it has been carried forward for the sake of the offering, one should milk another [cow] and offer; so says Āśmarathya. Having offered that very [milk] in whatever state it may be, one should then milk another cow and offer again; so says Ālekhana. (8) If [the milk] of one who has run forward should spill, one should sit down where it has spilled and take it up again.
Having offered that very [milk] in whatever state it may be, one should then milk another cow and offer again. (9) 9.7

"If it should spill once, or twice, or thrice, one should not pay heed to it"—so it is known. Āśmarathya stated that this refers to all *agnihotra* offerings; Ālekhana stated that it refers only to the offering with the *sruva* ladle. If it should spill a fourth time, having poured the remainder back into the pot and having taken four spoonfuls from there, he should offer it. Or else, having recited a verse addressed to Varuṇa over the clarified butter (*ājya*), he should offer it with that Varuṇa verse. Now, according to some teachers:

If [the milk] being milked should break, one should wash another [vessel] and milk it; if the milked [milk], one should milk another; if [the milk] placed on the fire, one should milk another; if it should spill, one should milk another; if it is being ladled out, one should milk another; if it has been ladled out, one should pour it back again and milk another. If it is being carried toward the east, he should touch it with: "O Prajāpati, you are the body offered in the Viśvabhṛt; svāhā!"

Having recited the verse dedicated to Varuṇa over the clarified butter, he should offer it with that same verse dedicated to Varuṇa. (6) If [the milk] should turn red or become discolored in any other way, having enclosed the Anvāhāryapacana fire, he should offer it with the formula: "To Agni accompanied by Rudra, svāhā! (7) If it should crackle like *śili-śili*, he should say, "May it burn up so-and-so," naming the one whom he hates. (8) If the evening oblation should spill, he shall not eat until the morning oblation; if the morning oblation should spill, he shall not eat until the evening oblation. (9) 9.8

If, while the *āgnihotra* oblation has been placed on the fire, a dog should run between the two fires, one should take ashes from the *gārhapatya* fire and, reciting the verse addressed to Viṣṇu, "Viṣṇu strode through this [world]," one should move upward from the *āhavanīya* fire and scatter the ashes over the dog's footprint. One should know that this same rite applies to the track of a boar or a *ekasṛka*. If the sun should set while the fire has not yet been carried forth, one should fasten gold with a blade of *darbha* grass and go forward first; a *brāhmaṇa* of noble lineage (*ārṣeya*) who knows much of the sacred lore should follow behind and carry forth the fire.

One should follow after the Agnihotra fire. Having established the fire and set out the Agnihotra oblation, one should remain seated without breathing until the sun sets; then, having offered the oblation and given the sacrificial fee, one should worship with the word "bhūḥ," according to Āśmarathya. One should worship with "bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ," according to Ālekhana. Without eating, he observes the fast for that night. On the following day, he offers a cake on ten potsherds to Varuṇa.

According to some, [the oblation] is cooked rice (caru). 8. The sacrifice concludes with the established [rite]. 9. If one should let the time for the evening *agnihotra* pass by, he should offer [an oblation] with the mantra: "To the Night, to Vastor, obeisance, Svāhā! 10. This very [offering], according to Āśmarathya, is the regular *agnihotra*. Now, according to Ālekhana: having offered the oblation with this mantra to bring about the [proper] time, he should then perform the regular *agnihotra*. 11. In that case, the procedure for the offering (*homakalpa*) is the same. 12. There is only this difference.

One should say "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ" before the Hotṛ recites. (13) If one should let the season of the morning Agnihotra pass by, one should offer with "prātarvastoḥ namaḥ svāhā. (14) Āśmarathya says that this alone is the regular Agnihotra; now, however, Ālekhana [says as follows].

Having performed the oblation with this mantra at the appropriate time, having set down the regular *agnihotra* fire, and having sat without breathing until the fire has gone out, he should give a gift, perform the oblation, and worship [the fire] with "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. (15) Having followed the fire to its end, he should establish another *āhavanīya* fire with the verse: "Agni has looked toward the forefront of the dawns. (16) Then he addresses it: "Be secure right here; do not abandon this one, the descendant of such-and-such. (17) 9.9

Then he should offer a *caru* oblation to Mitra and a cake on one potsherd to Sūrya. The sacrifice concludes in the established manner. When that sacrifice has been completed, the husband and wife, remaining silent and fasting for this day, sit while kindling the fire. He should perform the evening *agnihotra* with the milk of two cows. On the following day, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati. The sacrifice concludes in the established manner. If the sun should rise while his fire has not yet been carried forward, he should take clarified butter in four ladlings and, standing to the east...

One should proceed thus: A Brāhmaṇa who is an Ārṣeya and well-versed in the Vedas should, following the [proper] sequence, draw out the fire. Following the sequence, he should follow it with the Agnihotra. Having established the fire and set down the Agnihotra oblation, sitting down facing west in front of it, he should offer this clarified butter with [the verse]:
"May Uṣas, together with her banner, enjoy the sacrifice accompanied by the gods—the most honey-sweet for the gods! Svāhā!"

Thus [ends section 9]. Thereafter, one should constantly perform the Agnihotra (10). In that case, the procedure for the oblation is the same as before (11). That which was prescribed as an expiation for the morning [rite] when it has been allowed to pass its proper time applies here as well (12). This much is the difference: here one does not follow the Āhavanīya fire [into the earth] (13). One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Jyotiṣmat (14). The sacrifice is completed in the established manner (15). 9.10.

Now, according to some: if the sun should set or rise while someone’s fire has not been taken out, he should offer two portions of four ladlings each with the verses, "May the mind, the light, enjoy [the oblation]" and "The thirty-three threads. (1) If he should offer before sunset, then having offered again at sunset, he should stand in worship with the verse, "Be you both harmonious for us. (2) If he should offer in the dead of night, then having offered again at dawn, he should stand in worship as before. (3) If the sun should rise while the Agnihotra is still unoffered, though the intention was to offer it before sunrise.

If [the fire] should go out at the end, he should lift [the embers], carry them toward the east, or upward, and having placed them down, sit until they have gone out. When they have gone out, he should then offer with "bhūḥ svāhā. If the Gārhapatya should go out while the Āhavanīya has not gone out, he should follow the Āhavanīya [embers], place the ashes of the Gārhapatya together, and churn [the fire] with the verse, "From here Agni was first born. Then he consecrates it with: "Delight in food, in wealth, in power, in splendor, in vigor, and in offspring. [He then establishes] the Āhavanīya.

Having brought it forward, he kindles it with the formula: "May the two springs of Sarasvatī kindle thee; thou art the sovereign (samrāj), thou art the far-shining (virāj). Then he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tapasvat, Janadvat, and Pāvakavat. The sacrifice concludes in the established manner. This very same expiation applies when the Āhavanīya fire has gone out while the Gārhapatya fire is still maintained. The difference here is this: one does not cause the Gārhapatya fire to go out. One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Jyotiṣmat, but not to Agni Tapasvat. The sacrifice concludes in the established manner. 9.11

If, before the evening *agnihotra* has been offered, the eastern fire should go out, one should place the *agnihotra* milk on the fire, ladle it out, run out with the eastern fire, and follow after with the *agnihotra*. (1) A Brāhmaṇa who is well-versed in the Vedas should carry forth the fire. (2) One should give whatever wealth he had previously intended to give. (3) This same procedure applies in the morning. (4) If, before the morning *agnihotra* has been offered, the western fire should go out, one should cause the former fire to go out, churn the latter fire, and offer the oblation after carrying it forth, provided that one is not in haste. (5) But if one is in haste—

Having settled down by the former fire, he should then carry it forward to the east and offer the oblation. However, that would be a repetition (*jāmi*) if he were to make the other fire what was previously his own fire. Therefore, having settled down elsewhere, he should churn the fire, carry it forward, and offer the oblation.

Then he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tapasvat, Janadvat, and Pāvakavat. The sacrifice is completed in the established manner. If, while the evening *agnihotra* has not yet been offered, another fire should go out, he should settle down by the former fire, carry it forward from that very place to the east, and offer the oblation. Then he addresses it with a mantra.
From these very wombs was Agni Jātavedas first born;
knowing the way, may he carry our oblation to the gods by means of the Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, Jagatī, and Anuṣṭubh meters.

"Delight yourself for the sake of food, for wealth, for power, for splendor, for vigor, and for offspring"—thus he causes him to delight. "Thou art a sovereign; sit upon a good seat"—thus he makes him sit on a good seat. "May the two springs of Sarasvatī protect thee"—the two springs of Sarasvatī are indeed the *Ṛc* and the *Sāman*; by means of these two he protects him, and by means of these two he brings him to fulfillment. He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Jyotiṣmat and a pap of barley to Varuṇa. The sacrifice concludes in the established manner. Now, according to some...

If another fire should follow [the first] while the Agnihotra has not yet been offered, it should be churned from those very same embers. Now, if such embers are not available, one should rub the two kindling woods together with ashes and churn; "he thus generates him from his own womb," so it is known. Thereafter, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tapasvat, Janadvat, and Pāvakavat. The sacrifice concludes in the established manner. Now, according to some...

Whichever fire should go out, it must be churned from those very same pieces of wood. Alternatively, if there should be fuel of grass or fuel of wood-chips, one should touch the two churning sticks (*araṇī*) with ashes and then churn; for it is known [from scripture]: "One thus generates him from his own womb. Then, one should offer a cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) to Agni Tapasvat, Janadvat, and Pāvakavat. The sacrifice is completed as established. Or rather, one need not perform the *anugateṣṭi*; one should simply offer these oblations: "To Mitra, svāhā!"

“Svāhā to Varuṇa! Svāhā to Sūrya! Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Agni Vratapati! Svāhā to Agni Tapasvat, Janadvat, and Pāvakavat! Svāhā to Agni Śuci! Svāhā to Agni Jyotiṣmat! (13) He offers with the *vyāhṛtis* both individually and collectively. (14) 9.13

One whose *agnihotra* has been interrupted should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tantumat. One for whom they should perform a sacrifice in another's fires, or who should himself sacrifice in another's fires, should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu. One from whose fire they should take fire to another fire should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Anīkavat. One for whom, while the *agnihotra* is being placed on the fire or the oblation has been set out, a man, a dog, a horse, or a chariot passes between, should offer an oblation with the verse: "Thirty-three are the threads... (RV 10.53.6).

"It should pass between the two fires," so it is known. According to some, this applies when a cart or a chariot passes between the two fires. One does not fix a specific time for this. Then, having sprinkled water there, one should turn the cow back. One should erase the footprint with the verse, "Over this Vishnu strode. Having followed after [the fire], one should establish another Āhavanīya fire with the verse:
"O Agni, that footprint of yours which was first set forth has extended along the rays of the sun;
bring that wealth-abiding one back to us, and unite us with your favor that brings strength."
O Agni, you are far-extending, the beloved and most excellent Hotṛ;
through you, they extend the sacrifice.

Thus [ends section] 9. Then one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt (the path-maker). 10. One should fetch sacrificial grass from near a path. 11. An ox is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). 12. The sacrifice concludes in the established manner. 13. One should offer this very same sacrifice when the *stotra* has been confused. 14. This same [sacrifice] when the *śastra* has been confused. 15. This same [sacrifice] for one whose fires have become separated from the fires [of another]. 16. This same [sacrifice] for one who has died abroad. 17. It is known from tradition: "One should indeed perform it for one who has died abroad. 18. They should offer the *agnihotra* with the milk of a cow that suckles the calf of another until they have touched the bodies [of the deceased] with the fires. 9.14.

He strews the fires with *darbha* grass whose tips point toward the south and east. (1) Holding a fuel-stick beneath [the vessel], he steps forward. (2) He characterizes Soma accompanied by the ancestors (*pitṛmat*) as the first oblation, and Agni Kavyavāhana as the second. (3) They should pour out the water used for rinsing the vessels toward the south. (4) They should give the sacrificial implements to a Brāhmaṇa. (5) They should cast them into the water. (6) A son’s grindstone should be made of stone, and his mortar of iron. (7) If unstrained clarified butter should spill, one should give a living creature that has been cut up. (8)

If there is anything winnowed or any wonderful wealth in his house, he should give that. According to some, this is the reverse: [he gives] the wonderful [wealth] when it is not winnowed, and [the winnowed] when it is winnowed. Now, if the offering-spoon (sruva) should spill, wherever it spills, he should place a span-length of wood there facing east with the words, “To the Lord of the Earth, svāhā!”; facing south-east with “To the Lord of the World, svāhā!”; and facing west with “To the Lord of Beings, svāhā!”

"bhūtāya svāhā"—with this [formula], he pours [the remainder] toward the north (11). "Then he should pour it together," says Āśmarathya; "he should consecrate it with the verse 'I pour thee together' (*saṃ tvā siñcāmi*)," says Ālekhana (12). "He should consecrate what has been spilled with the formulas 'To the Lord of Beings, svāhā! To the Lord of the World, svāhā! To the Lord of Creatures, svāhā!'"—so say some (13). No one speaks concerning any sacrificial oblation whatsoever (14). "The sacrifice has gone to the gods; may its essence favor me"—with this he should consecrate it; so say some, and they speak of this as occurring immediately after the clarified butter (15), if...
If the consecrated waters should spill, one should take them up with the three verses beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ" and then offer an oblation with the verse "tataṃ ma āpaḥ. 16. 9.15.

If the potsherd should break, he should join it together with the formula: "With the Gāyatrī of a hundred syllables, I join thee. This indeed applies if it breaks before the placing [of the potsherds]. But if it breaks after they have been placed, it is by this very same [procedure].

One should place [the potsherds] with the mantra. If a potsherd should be lost, one should offer a cake on two potsherds to the Aśvins and a cake on one potsherd to Heaven and Earth. Bhāgava becomes the Hotṛ; it is known that "one gives a one-year-old calf as the sacrificial fee. Āśmarathya maintains that however it may be lost, there must simply be an expiation.

For those who have already performed the *vimoka*, there is no drawing [of the lines] beforehand. (9) If one should offer the potsherds while performing the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, he should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara. (10) The sacrifice is concluded in the established manner. (11) One should perform this very same offering after having omitted either the new-moon or the full-moon sacrifice. (12) This [offering] is for one who eats the new grain without having first performed the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice. (13) For whomsoever twin calves are born, or twin cattle, or twin humans, he should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara. (14) For that sacrifice, the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) and the offering verse (*yājyā*) are in the *triṣṭubh* meter.

Ālekhana says that if one should not have enough for the portions (avadāna), [one should do so]. It is known from scripture: "They consume the spoiled oblation with water. If the oblation intended for a deity should become spoiled before it has been offered, one should consume that with water and offer another oblation intended for that same deity. In that case, the mantras beginning with the taking up of the ladle (sruk) should be repeated. Now, if the portion intended for the deity has already been offered, one should complete the remainder with clarified butter (ājya).
"One should set it aside," is one view; "one should silently offer the oblation," is another.

(9.17) Now, if all the oblations should be lost or become defiled, one should count them out with clarified butter and perform that sacrifice using clarified butter as the oblation. Therefore, one should perform another sacrifice that is not defective; for it is known from scripture: "By means of a sacrifice they effect the expiation of a sacrifice. How does one know an oblation is defiled? That which is unfit to be eaten by noble men who know the Dharma and desire the Dharma—one should not sacrifice to the gods with such. An oblation that is poorly cooked belongs to Yama as its deity.

It is understood that it goes to Yama alone. Having set aside that sacrificial oblation, one should cook four *śarāva*-measures of boiled rice on the *anvāhāryapacana* fire and offer it to four Brahmins like rice with living grains. Among those who partake of it, one should be a descendant of Bhṛgu. If one should omit the prescribed sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), one should give land that is fertile, well-situated, and firmly established. A sacrifice performed without a sacrificial fee is a withered sacrifice.

The sacrificer would become non-noble (9). He should give away a fertile field with crops (10). If he should invoke a deity who has no share, he should sacrifice to that deity with clarified butter according to how it was invoked (11). He offers it with his joined palms, saying: "I offer thee into the mouth of Agni; let not the sacrificer suffer harm, nor the wife of the sacrifice, nor the sacrifice itself."

"Into this mouth I offer you," or rather, one should give the full vessel (pūrṇapātra) to whichever deity the offering has been made. If what has been taken for a deity should spill before it is offered, or if one should omit the deity [in the invocation], he should give whatever abundant wealth he has in his house. Becoming non-terrible and worthy of sacrifice, sit down in your own place."
Do not perish, sent by the gods; be strengthened with clarified butter and splendor. Do not harm us in any way; for the peace of our well-being and security, sit down upon this sacred grass.

To the north of the *pariśrita* enclosure, facing east, the sacrificer has his hair and beard shaved. 11. He moistens his right *godāna* (the area behind the ear) with the words: "May the waters moisten [you] for life. 12. Having extracted [the hair] with a three-striped porcupine quill, he places three tufts of *darbha* grass with their tips pointing upwards [into the hair] with the words: "O herb, protect him! 12. [He applies the razor] with the words: "O axe, do not harm him!"

He places [the hair] down with the razor, saying: "O divine hero, shave these. He shaves [the hair], saying: "May I attain prosperity in what follows. The sacrificer mutters this mantra. It is known from tradition: "He has his beard shaved first, then the armpits, and then the head-hair. He cleanses his teeth with a tooth-stick made of Udumbara wood, without causing blood to flow. Having rinsed his teeth, he has his nails trimmed. [The nails are trimmed] starting from the little finger of the left hand.

Some say he bathes in a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Having placed gold in a conch-shaped pool (*śaṅkhinī hrada*), he bathes with the mantra, "May the mothers, the waters, purify us," and then emerges from the water with, "I come forth from the waters, pure and purified. Having sipped water, he puts on a new linen garment as an undergarment with, "Thou art the body of Soma; protect my body. He arranges the knot of his garment with, "Thou art the girdle of Soma. He eats whatever food is pleasing to him, saying, "Thou art vigor"—[referring to] curds mixed with ghee and honey.

And he becomes one who has partaken of the sprinkling. 6. From that point on, he observes the vow in increasingly smaller amounts. 7. With the words, "Thou art the milk of the great ones," having mixed fresh butter with two bunches of *darbha* grass, he anoints himself three times from front to back with the words, "Thou art the bestower of luster; bestow luster upon me. 8. He first anoints his face, then the limbs in the direction of the hair. 9. He becomes well-anointed. 10. He applies collyrium made from Mount Trikakud. 11. If he does not find [collyrium] from Mount Trikakud, he should apply whatever collyrium he can obtain. 12. [He applies it] with a *śara*-reed stalk together with its tuft.

With a blade of *darbha* grass or a bunch of *darbha* grass, while not running, he first [anoints] the right eye with the formula: "Thou art the pupil of Vṛtra; thou art the protector of the eye; protect my eye. He does this three times for the right eye and twice for the left. 13.10.4.

Then he purifies him three times with twenty-one bunches of *darbha* grass, seven by seven, using these mantras: "May the Lord of Thought purify you; may the Lord of Speech purify you; may the divine Savitṛ purify you. To every one of these, he appends the mantra: "With a flawless filter. He wipes upwards above the navel twice and downwards once. While being purified, he mutters this section: "Pavamāna, the dweller in light," and also "Whatever offense against the gods, O gods..."

With the mantra, "O Lord of the Purifier, by means of thy purifier, may I be able to accomplish that for which I purify myself," he enters the *prāgvaṃśa* hall through the eastern door with the verse, "To you, O Gods, we come" (*ā vo devāsa īmahe*). Having entered and passed behind the *āhavanīya* fire, standing to the south, he addresses the *āhavanīya* with the remainder of the section beginning, "Indra and Agni, Heaven and Earth" (*indrāgnī dyāvāpṛthivī*). This same procedure applies to him until the *sutyā* day. At this point, some authorities prescribe the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering. Whatever [is prescribed] regarding the *dīkṣaṇīyā*...

Having set aside the clarified butter, he then offers four initiation oblations (*dīkṣā-āhuti*) with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), using these mantras: "To Ākūti, to Prayuj, to Agni, Svāhā! (and so on). (9) With the offering-ladle (*sruc*), he offers the fifth [oblation] with the mantra: "The divine waters, vast, all-beneficent... (10) Having filled the ladle either with four portions or twelve portions of butter, he offers the full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with this verse: "All [the gods] of the leader of the god... (11) According to some, he offers it after making an opening for the cavity. (12) He sews up the right fore-foot of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*). (13) Or two [feet].

Having ascended, he mutters this [verse]: "I have mounted this good ship... (RV 10.53.8). With the words, "Thou art the protection of Viṣṇu; thou art the protection of the sacrificer; grant me protection," he covers himself completely. With the words, "Protect me from the gaze of the stars," he wraps his head with a turban. Or rather, he covers his head as well as possible. He prepares a *kumbakurīra* on the head of the wife. They call a net a *kurīra*. It is known that it is made of black wool from living sheep. Then he [covers her] with a linen garment.

He causes him to put on a garment that reaches down to the feet. They announce that he has put on his upper garment. He girds the sacrificer at the waist from one side with a triple-stranded girdle made of muñja grass, which is broad and has loops on both ends, with the formula: "Thou art the strength of Aṅgiras. Having made a knot above the navel so that it is visible, he tucks the end around to the right of the navel. He girds the wife with a cord as in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, using the verse: "I gird thee... Then [he gives] him a three-fold or five-fold [cord].

He gives him a black antelope horn that curls to the right, [with the mantra]: "Thou art the womb of Indra; do not harm me. (13) He fastens it with this same mantra. (14) With it he digs up a clod of earth from the altar, [with the mantra]: "For the sake of cultivation, for good crops. (15) [With the mantra]: "For the sake of plants with good fruit," he scratches his head whenever he feels an itch. (16) [With the mantra]: "O horn, loosen this knot; whatever is knotted in his feet, whatever is knotted in his heart, whatever is knotted in his mind," he [scratches] his limbs. (17) Then, for him, an udumbara...

He hands over the initiation-staff (*dīkṣitadaṇḍa*), measured by the mouth, with the formula: "Thou art made of the wood of the forest, well-established; O resplendent one, bestow splendor upon the sacrificer. (18) According to some, it should be made from whatever tree is fit for sacrifice and bears fruit. (19) He receives it with the formula: "May the divine Lord of the Forest be well-disposed toward us today. (20) 10.6.18–20.

He consecrates the *camasa* vessel for the offering of the vow with the mantra: "Thou art wide-extending, the supporter of people; protect me, thy rival, until the conclusion of this sacrifice. Then he bends his fingers: "Svāhā! To the sacrifice with the mind!"—twice; "Svāhā! To Heaven and Earth!"—twice.

"O Heaven and Earth, from the intermediate space," these two [verses]; "Svāhā! I undertake the sacrifice from the wind," with this he closes his fists. Then he makes him recite the *saṃbhārayajus* formulas: "Agni with the *yajus*-formulas. Thereafter, he restrains his speech until the rising of the stars. If he should release his speech before the stars have risen, he should recite the verse to Viṣṇu, the one to Agni-Viṣṇu, the one to Sarasvatī, and the one to Bṛhaspati, and then restrain his speech once again. He should say, "Thou, O Agni, art the guardian of vows," if he has released either his fists or his speech.

He should release [the fast-food]. Then he announces him: "This Brāhmaṇa, named so-and-so, the son of such-a-one, the grandson of such-a-one, the great-grandson of such-a-one; the son of such-a-woman, the granddaughter of such-a-woman, the great-granddaughter of such-a-woman—has been initiated. He says this three times in a low voice and three times aloud. Whosoever may be initiated, he should announce him simply as a "Brāhmaṇa. He undergoes initiation in the afternoon. If one should desire of someone, "May he be an ascetic," he should initiate him in the morning. Having risen, he puts on the black antelope skin. He observes this vow.

He does not eat with me, nor does he approach a woman, nor does he sit above [me]; one should loathe falsehood. (13) He speaks human speech with a lisp; one should address a learned man as *canasita* or *vicakṣaṇa*. (14) It is understood that one should address a Brāhmaṇa as *canasita*, and a Rājanya or a Vaiśya as *vicakṣaṇa*. (15) One should converse only with a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya. (16) From among these alone should they employ him. (17) If a conversation with a Śūdra should occur, one should say to one of these [three]: "Look at this! (18) 10.7

1. He shall not uncover [his head] before the purchase of the Soma. 2. He shall not let go of the black antelope horn before leading away the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*). 3. He scratches himself with the black antelope horn. 4. He smiles while covering [his mouth]. 5. Upon seeing something impure, he mutters: "The mind is unbound, the eye is poor; the Sun is the best of lights; O Consecration, do not abandon me! 6. While being rained upon, he mutters: "O moistening waters, bestow strength, bestow vigor, bestow strength; do not destroy my consecration, do not destroy my ascetic heat. 7. [He does not step out] from the consecrated shed.

He should go abroad [only] after [the sacrifice is completed]; let the sun neither rise nor set while he is away from the *dīkṣitavimita* (the hut of the consecrated). He should lie down turning toward the *āhavanīya* fire from the south; he should not lie on his face nor on his back. He should not turn away from the fire. He may smile according to the season.

If he should sit elsewhere than on a black antelope skin, he should consecrate that place with the mantra: "The sacrifice has gone to the gods; may its nourishment favor me. He should not utter his name; he should not speak of him as evil; he should not address him directly.

Only one who has been initiated (dīkṣita) should speak [to others]; he should not eat food until the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma (āgnīṣomīya). At will, however, he may do so once the āgnīṣomīya is completed, or when the omentum (vapā) has been offered, or when the King Soma has been purchased. Or rather, having set aside [the food] for the sake of the sacrifice from the very beginning, he should undergo initiation; then they may eat from other sources. These aforementioned observances (vrata) commence after the initiatory offering (dīkṣaṇīyā). Now follow these applications of materials: namely, scratching with the black antelope horn (kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā), sitting on the black antelope skin (kṛṣṇājina), and carrying the staff (daṇḍa). The wife observes the milk-vow (payovrata).

She remains a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacāriṇī*). 9. With the words, "You two are impellers," she releases four fingers. 10. When the milk has been offered as a vow-food (*vrata*) and the stars have been seen, she releases her speech with the words, "Prepare the vow-food. 11. She keeps watch during this night. 12. Barley-gruel is the vow-food for a Kṣatriya, curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) for a Vaiśya, and milk for a Brāhmaṇa. 13. These are the vow-fasts pertaining to the consecration (*daikṣa*). 14. However, for all [classes], there is a distribution of the udders during the Upasad days. 15. 9.

He cooks the sacrificer’s fast-food on the *gārhapatya* fire; [he cooks] that of the wife on the *dakṣiṇāgni*. Whatever expiation there is for spilled *agnihotra* milk, that is the expiation for the fast-food. Now, some indeed consume only milk as their fast-food; one should not do so.

Having cooked the gruel with milk, he should consume it as his fast-food. (4) If there should be too little, having milked another cow and cooked it, he should consume it as his fast-food. (5) If no milk should be available, having cooked it in water itself, he should consume it as his fast-food. (6) If there should be curds, they should prepare this very thing for him as curds. (7) If he should desire solid food, they should add parched grains for him; they should add flour for him; they should bring clarified butter for him.

It is known from tradition that, at the very least, one should consume fruits as the *vrata* for the sake of not interrupting the *agnihotra*. 8. Having brought the *vrata*-food around behind the *āhavanīya* fire, he hands it to him. 9. Then he says to him: "O *vratin*, perform the *vrata*; enter upon the *vrata*. 10. Those who are not initiated do not look upon the initiated one while he is performing the *vrata*. 11. With the words, "We meditate upon the divine thought," he washes his hands. 12. With the words, "The gods who are born of mind, joined with mind," he consumes the *vrata* at midnight. 13. Having consumed the *vrata*, he sips water, saying: "May you waters become auspicious when drunk; may you be very kind within our womb, our belly."
O you who possess healing waters, free from disease and sinless, be auspicious to us so that we may live.

He worships the rising sun with the formula: "Those words which were first in the bull among cattle, those [words] the bright Sun was first among; those words I send forth for you according to their respective portions; may they come back to us again as auspicious words. (1) When the sun has risen and the *vrata* milk has been milked, he releases his speech with the words: "Prepare the *vrata*. (2) He consumes the *vrata* food in the same manner at midday. (3) When the sun is above the trees, the one who provides the *vrata* restrains his speech, saying: "Make the fires radiant; O consecrated one, restrain your speech; O wife, restrain your speech."

Thus (4). Likewise from this point forward (5), he consumes the fast-food at midnight and at midday (6). Likewise near sunrise (7). When the sun is above the trees, the giver of the fast-food restrains his speech (8). "The fast-food is not prescribed on the day of the Soma-pressing"—this is one view.

"Let it be known," [he says]. 9. When about to sleep, he addresses the Āhavanīya fire with: "O Agni, do thou keep watch; may we rejoice. 10. Having awakened, he mutters, beginning with "Thou, O Agni, art the guardian of vows," and continuing until the end of "All the gods have turned toward me. 11. Whether he is about to sleep, or has already slept and awakened, or if he should speak words unfit for one who is consecrated, he should say: "Thou, O Agni, art the guardian of vows. 12. From this point forward, this is the rule for going to sleep and waking up.
13. "May Pūṣan [protect us] with gain, Soma with wealth. 14. 10.11.

He instructs those who bring gifts; whatever they obtain, he accepts it with the mantra: "May the divine Savitṛ, the giver of wealth, grant us this much; O Soma, bring more! May I, bestowing gifts, not fail in my fulfillment; may I not fail in my lifespan."

With these mantras, "O Moon, be for my enjoyment," he accepts [the gift] according to its form; with the Sāvitra mantra, he accepts another. For twelve days he begs for the sake of the sacrificial fee. With "For Vāyu, thee," he points out one that has been lost. With "For Varuṇa, thee," one submerged in water. With "For Nirṛti, thee," one that has collapsed. With "For Rudra, thee," one killed by Mahādeva. With "For Indra, thee," one killed by a ram, or one that has become shattered. With "For the Maruts, thee," one struck by lightning. With "For Indra, thee..."

11. With the formula, "O victorious one," he should take whichever army he may encounter that is not fleeing. 12. With the formula, "For Yama thee," [he should take] when [the army] is unknown. 13. If he should come upon one that has not been assigned, he should not let it graze among the cattle. 14. Now, if he should wish to set out, having consigned the fires into the separate kindling woods (*araṇi*), he should depart by means of a chariot. 15. If a chariot is not available, he should depart taking a part of a chariot with him. 16. With the formula, "May the auspicious ones look upon me; go toward what is better," he consecrates the *āhavanīya* fire. 17. With the formula, "O divine waters, O son of the waters," he plunges into the water. 18. [He recites: "The unbroken thread..."

He covers [the ground] while crushing a clod of earth with the formula, "In accordance with the likeness of the earth. (18) He places sand or a clod of earth in the middle and at the edge with the formula, "Be united with the earth. (19) Now, if he cannot cross by boat, he should cross taking both the kindling woods and the chariot. (20) If no chariot is available, he should cross taking a part of the chariot. (21) 10.12

Having requested a Kṣatriya, he settles upon a place for the sacrifice to the gods near water that slopes toward the north-east, saying: "We have come to this sacrificial ground of the earth. Or rather, one should not request a sacrificial ground; instead, one should worship the Sun with this mantra: "Look at this, O Dispenser! Look at this! Look at this, O Nāka! It is the most delightful, the highest Truth, which they call immortal. The Sun shines most widely with his rays."

"Following the two, Heaven and Earth, the sons of the gods"—thus [he recites]. (3) The sacrificial ground for the gods should not extend beyond [the altar] by even a *devayajana*-measure. (4) Some authorities prescribe the formal selection of the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) at the very beginning. (5) "One should cause [the sacrificer] to sacrifice on a sacrificial ground where oblations are offered first"; these optional sacrificial grounds are explained in the Brāhmaṇa. (6) It is known from tradition: "One should purchase the Soma from a descendant of Kutsa. (7) According to some, [one may buy it] from a Śūdra. (8) Or, at the place of the *uparava* holes on the high altar (*uttaravedi*), there is a red bull-hide.

Having spread out a skin with the neck toward the east and the hair upward, he places the King (Soma) upon it; having placed a water-pot to the north, he issues the command: "O Soma-seller, purify the Soma! 9. Within an enclosure, the Soma-seller sorts the King (Soma). 10. There are no observers of him while he is sorting it. 11. 10.13.

He commences the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the *prāyaṇīyā* offering. At that point, these [rites] are not performed: the adding of fuel to the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*), the taking up of the vow (*vratopāyana*), the girding of the wife (*patnīsaṃnahana*), and the *anvāhārya* rice-offering. Whatever *iṣṭis*, animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*), or Soma sacrifices there may be—in all of them these are not performed. At the *udayanīyā* and the *anūbandhyā* offerings, the taking up of the vow and the girding of the wife are performed. All [these rites] are performed at the *udavasānīyā* offering, with the exception of the *anvāhārya*. In this regard, there is this specific instruction.

Whatever oblation comes forward in the extended ritual procedure (*tantra*), those [acts] which have already been performed are not performed again—just as, for example, the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings in the animal-cake sacrifice (*paśupuroḍāśa*) and other such rites. 6 He offers the introductory oblation (*prāyaṇīya*) as a pap (*caru*) to Aditi. 7 It is cooked in milk. 8 [The procedure] is the same up to the placing [of the oblation]. 9 Having taken out the pap, he places it down with the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula. 10 In this very vessel, he sets aside the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*) and the scrapings (*niṣkāsa*) in a well-known place. 11 There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses.

There are twelve [deities], equal to the two Ājyabhāga offerings. He sacrifices four Ājyabhāgas: Pathyā Svasti in the east, Agni in the south, Soma in the west, and Savitṛ in the north; Aditi in the middle of the oblation. The Prāyaṇīyā offering concludes with the Śaṃyu-formula. At this point, some prescribe the pouring out of the King (Soma). Having taken four portions of the clarified butter from the Dhruvā vessel into the Juhū ladle for the Prāyaṇīyā, he ties a piece of gold with a knot on a Darbha blade and places it [in the ladle] with the formula: "This is thine..."

"O Śukra, this body is splendor"—this is the *somakrayaṇī* (the cow for purchasing Soma). It should be one that is not crooked, without deformed ears, not one-eyed, not lame, not with seven hooves, not ruddy, not tawny-eyed, and either one year old or two years old. It is known from tradition: "With a cow that has a hump, long hair, and ears like the *lodhra* tree, he purchases the Soma of the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice. 10.14.19–20.

Gazing at her, he offers the oblation with the mantra: "Thou art swift; thou art held by the mind. (1) Having taken another portion of four ladlings, he draws out the gold from the clarified butter with the mantra: "Thou art bright; thou art immortal. (2) He consecrates the clarified butter with the mantra: "The oblation for the Viśvedevas. (3) Releasing the gold, he worships the sun with the mantra: "I have mounted the eye of Sūrya. (4) He consecrates the cow for the purchase of Soma, beginning with "Thou art consciousness; thou art thought," and ending with "O Indra, [come] for the sake of Soma. (5) Then, with her right foot, he [marks] the southern [spots].

He steps along six footprints with the mantras, "Thou art Vasvi," and "Thou art Rudrā" (6). He takes hold of the seventh footprint with the mantra, "May Bṛhaspati gladden thee in happiness" (7). Having placed gold upon that footprint, he offers this fourfold-drawn oblation with the mantra: "I sprinkle thee on the head of the earth, on the place of sacrifice, in the station of Iḍā, rich in ghee; Svāhā! (8). As far as the ghee has spread, so far he traces around [the footprint] with the wooden sword, saying: "The Rakṣas is traced around; the enemies are traced around" (9).

In this very manner, he traces around [the footprint] with the black antelope horn. 10 He pours as much [grain] as fits into the vessel, saying, "To us, riches! 11 Saying, "Thine, O Indra, be the riches," the Adhvaryu hands it to the sacrificer. 12 Saying, "Thine, O Agni, be the riches," the sacrificer hands it to his wife. 13 While the footprint is being given to the wife, the Adhvaryu consecrates it with the formula, "May I not be separated from the abundance of wealth. 14 He makes the wife look at the Soma-purchase cow with the formula, "O Goddess, look together with the goddess Urvaśī. 15 [The footprint.]

He pours out a vessel of water with the verse, "Make the earth swell" (VS 11.50). Having washed both hands together with gold on the footprint, he scatters one-third of it into the cold ashes of the Gārhapatya fire. In the same way, he scatters a third portion into the Āhavanīya fire. He leaves a third portion for smearing the axle. The wife places that in her house. With his hand containing gold, he worships the sun. 10.15.16–21.

"O King, we shall buy Soma; we announce it to you. Prepare the seasons; prepare the sacrificial fees according to the season and according to the deity. 1. Here some prescribe the pouring out of the King (Soma). 2. They go to the presence of the King by means of a cart, [reciting] "We have indeed gone upon the path. 3. The front plank has been removed. 4. Having unyoked on both sides of the King and having set him down facing forward, he consecrates him with the mantra: "May this [Soma], O King, be joined with thy [Soma]. 5. To the north of the King, upon a skin...

Having spread out a double-folded linen cloth with its fringes pointing eastward or northward, he measures the King (Soma) upon it with his hand containing gold, [reciting] "Toward that god Savitṛ... (RV 7.45.1). He measures with one [finger-breadth] at a time, making a pause after each. On all [fingers], he places the thumb underneath. He does not use the same finger for the fifth measurement as he did for the first; he uses that very same finger for the last. He measures five times with the sacrificial formula (*yajus*) and five times silently. Having gathered the remainder with the words "For the subjects, thee" (*prajābhyas tvā*), and having tucked in the ends of the cloth, he binds it with a linen turban with the words "For the breath, thee" (*prāṇāya tvā*).

With the words, "For the *vyāna* breath, thee," he unties [the cloth]. Having loosened it, he gazes at it with the formula: "Do thou breathe after the offspring; let the offspring breathe after thee. The sacrificer addresses the King Soma that has been handed over by the Soma-seller with these mantras: "This is thy portion belonging to the *gāyatrī*; thus announce to Soma for me. Then he says: "O Soma-seller, is the Soma yours for sale? The Soma-seller replies: "It is for sale. He purchases it with the formula: "I purchase from thee the Soma, full of vigor and full of milk."

"The vigorous one, the overcomer of enemies—for you I shall buy [Soma] with a cow," [he says]. 16. This has been explained. 17. "Soma the King deserves even more than this," says the Soma-seller. 18. "Soma the King deserves even more than this," says the Adhvaryu. 19. 10.16.

He buys [Soma] with gold, saying: "I buy your bright [essence] with the bright. The Soma-seller says: "King Soma is worth even more than this. The Adhvaryu says: "King Soma is worth even more than this. He buys [Soma] with a goat, saying: "You are the body of austerity. The Soma-seller says: "King Soma is worth even more than this. The Adhvaryu says: "King Soma is worth even more than this. He buys [Soma] with a cow; he buys [Soma] with a bull; he buys [Soma] with an ox; he buys [Soma] with a pair [of animals].

He purchases [the Soma] with a garment; he completes the transaction with ten [cows], or with an indefinite number. It is known from tradition that "he purchases with three. Some authorities prescribe four: "with a cow, gold, a goat, and a garment. Furthermore, one may purchase the Soma for a sacrifice where the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of twenty-one items with a single [cow] alone—provided it is not crooked-horned, has no ear-tick, is not one-eyed, is not lame, does not have seven hooves, is not reddish-brown, is not tawny-eyed, and is one year old.

Some authorities prescribe that there should be a "cow of excellence" (kalyāṇagavī). It is known from tradition that one should purchase Soma for a sacrifice with a thousand-fold dakṣiṇā for thirty thousand, for a Vājapeya with a hundred, for a Rājasūya with two, and for an Aśvamedha with a thousand. Having taken gold from the Soma-seller, he gives a tuft of white wool to the sacrificer, saying, "In us be light. At the proper time, the sacrificer makes that [wool] the center of the *daśāpavitra* strainer. The strainer must be made from white wool.

It is understood that the *amotā* (unsewn) cord is to be used. 16. He ties on a black [cord] with the formula: "Here I tie the necks of the biting serpents. 17. With that [cord], he strikes the seller of Soma, saying: "O seller of Soma, darkness! 18. He points out the articles for the purchase of Soma with the remainder of the section beginning: "Svāna, Bhrāja... 19. 10.17.

[The Adhvaryu] takes the King [Soma] from the Soma-seller with the formula: "Thou art self-born; thou art self-existent; born for this rite, I take thee by the *ṛta*; protect us by the *ṛta*. (1) When the Soma has been purchased, he uncovers it. (2) The sacrificer hands the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa. (3) According to some, he hands the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa on the day of the pressing (*sutyā*). (4) As the King [Soma] is being brought forward, the sacrificer addresses him with the formula: "As Mitra, come to us, bestowing good friendship. (5) He places [the Soma] upon the right thigh of the sacrificer with the word "Indra."

"Enter the right thigh, O Syūma, desiring him who desires thee; may thou be pleasant to him who is pleasant," [he says]. (6) The sacrificer asks the Adhvaryu, "Adhvaryu, have you been able? (7) "I have been able," replies the Adhvaryu. (8) "How have you been able? asks the sacrificer. (9) "We have made Viṣṇu our hymn, the Bṛhatī our metre, and we have joined the Yajus-formulas; the mountains have yielded, and I have entered the well-flowing waters," [with these words] the Adhvaryu gives his assent. (10) The sacrificer turns the Soma-purchase cow around with the formula, "May Rudra turn thee back."

With the remainder of this *anuvāka*, he ransoms that [cow] with another cow and releases her into the sacrificer’s cow-pen. They cause the Soma-seller to disappear by means of a spotted leather thong; according to some, they strike him with clods of earth, according to others, with sticks. 10.18.11–14.

Taking up the King (Soma), the Adhvaryu rises with the formula: "With life, with good life... (TS 3.2.4.1). He carries him forward with: "Go along the wide atmosphere" (TS 3.2.4.1). In the interior of the cart, he spreads a black antelope skin with its neck toward the east and the hairy side upward, with: "Thou art the seat of Aditi" (TS 3.2.4.1). Upon it, he places the King with: "Sit upon the seat of Aditi" (TS 3.2.4.1). Then he wraps him around with a cloth with: "In the forests he has stretched out the atmosphere" (TS 3.2.4.1). With the verse addressed to Sūrya, "Up that Jātavedas... (RV 1.50.1), he fastens the black antelope skin over him. [He recites: "O two bulls, come hither... (TS 3.2.4.1).

He drives forward the two oxen with the formula, "O bearers of the yoke. (7) He touches the two yokes as in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. (8) With the formula, "Thou art belonging to Varuṇa," he draws the cart forward. (9) With the formula, "May Varuṇa support thee," he props it up. (10) With the formula, "Thou art belonging to Varuṇa," he passes the noose of the yoke-thong around. (11) With the formula, "Thou art the prop of Varuṇa," he fixes the wedge. (12) With the formula, "The noose of Varuṇa is cast off," he fastens the bull. (13) In the same manner, he yokes the second ox on the left side. (14) [He takes] two green Palāśa branches.

Or, carrying a branch of the *śamī* tree, the *subrahmaṇya* priest creeps between the two carts. Then he issues the command: "Recite for King Soma as he is being carried away after purchase! O Brahman, restrain your speech! O *subrahmaṇya*, invoke the *subrahmaṇyā*! When the first [verse] has been recited three times, [the sacrifice proceeds]. 10.19.15–17.

Having stepped forward with the mantra, "He advances; move forward, O Lord of the Earth," and continuing until the end of "Thou art the bringer of well-being to the sacrificer" (TS 1.7.8.1), they proceed toward the east and then turn to the right. With the mantra, "We have indeed reached the path," the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer pass by the north of the King Soma. The sacrificer awaits the King Soma being carried away on the Agnīṣomīya cart, which has been seized by the ears, with the mantra, "Homage to the eye of Mitra and Varuṇa. They kindle the fires at the Āhavanīya.

They place the great [fire-pan] upon it. 6. The Adhvaryus lift up the throne-seat (āsandī). 7. It has a head-piece one cubit (aratni) long, side-rails reaching to the neck, and feet reaching to the navel; it is made of Udumbara wood with a girdle of Muñja grass. 8. Regarding this, there is this specific rule: wherever he may command many performers, the Adhvaryus alone shall perform that.

Where there are two Pratiprasthātṛs, there there should be a second [one]. 9. With the formula, "Thou art belonging to Varuṇa," he pulls the cart forward from the front of the *prāgvam̐śa* shed. 10. He stops it with its pole facing north. 11. With the formula, "May Varuṇa prop thee up," he props it up. 12. With the formula, "Thou art belonging to Varuṇa," he unties the noose of the yoke-thong. 13. With the formula, "Thou art the support of Varuṇa," he lifts out the *śamyā* pin. 14. With the formula, "The noose of Varuṇa is released," he unlooses the halter. 15. With the formula, "Thou art the seat of the truth of Varuṇa."
To the south of the Āhavanīya fire, he establishes the seat. 16. The ox on the right side is unyoked, while the one on the left remains unyoked. 17. 10.20.

Then he proceeds with the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the Guest-offering (*ātithyā*). He takes two stalks of sugarcane as separators (*vidhṛti*), and ties the *āśvavāla* grass-bundle as the *prastara* onto the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). He places the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) made of *kārṣmarya* wood into the fuel-wood (*idhma*). He prepares the fuel-wood consisting of one hundred and twenty pieces of wood. The procedure is the same up to the pouring of the oblation-materials. While the wife maintains contact [with him], he pours out the material for the Guest-offering; or [he may do so] with the hand of the wife. He takes [the material] five times with these mantras: "Thou art the guest-offering of Agni; for Viṣṇu, thee! In all [the portions], [he recites] the *sāvitra* formula: "That which is acceptable."

"One should attach [the formula]" is one view; "only in the three [verses]" is another. (8) There is a cake on nine potsherds for Viṣṇu. (9) From this point onward, the ritual invocations (*nigama*) belong exclusively to Viṣṇu. (10) Having released his speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*), he unyokes the northern ox in the same manner. (11) With the words, "Thou art Varuṇa’s," he takes away the garment of the King (Soma). (12) With the words, "Thou art Varuṇa, whose vow is firm," [he addresses] the King. (13) "O thou of flawless wings, descend upon the subjects who desire thee, desiring them; be pleasant to those who are pleasant."

"O King Soma, descend upon all thy subjects; let all thy subjects descend upon thee. Having thus brought him down, they carry him forward with the words, "Go through the wide atmosphere! (14) He causes him to enter by the eastern door toward the east with the verse, "Those abodes of thine which they worship with oblation. (15) 10.21

Having stepped past the Āhavanīya fire from the other side, he spreads a black antelope skin on the throne-seat with its neck pointing eastward and the hairy side upward, saying: "Thou art the seat of Aditi. Upon it, he places the King (Soma), saying: "Sit upon the seat of Aditi. Then he encloses it with a cloth, saying: "Thou art Varuṇa, whose vow is firm. Then he attends to it with a verse addressed to Varuṇa:
"Thus praise the great Varuṇa; pay homage to the wise guardian of immortality.
May he grant us a triple-layered shelter; do you [O gods] protect us always with blessings."

Thus [he says]. 4. Then he gives the command: "Do not go between the King (Soma) and the Fire. 5. [The procedure] is the same up to the taking of the clarified butter portions. 6. He takes four portions of clarified butter each time. 7. Having placed the *Atithya* oblation after the *Caturhotṛ* formula and having explained the *Saṃbhāra-yajus* formulas, he proceeds with the fire churned according to the ritual of churning (*nirmanthya*). 8. There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses. 9. [The procedure] is the same up to the *prayāja* offerings. 10. At the fourth [offering], he pours the entire portion from the *aupabhṛta* ladle into the *juhū*. 11. Here he does not pour clarified butter over the *aupabhṛta* ladle. 12.

The *iḍā* and the guest-offering (*ātithyā*) are concluded. Regarding this, one view is that one should invoke the *iḍā* over the entire sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*); another view is that one should cut off portions from it. Thus ends the tenth chapter.
Now begins the eleventh chapter.

When about to collect the materials for the *pravargya* rite, during the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, on the full moon or the new moon day, he silently places a fuel-stick of *kaṇṭakī* wood upon the fire and, whether he has not yet been initiated or if he is already initiated, he offers four ladlefuls with the verse, "They yoke the mind. If he is already initiated, he should place that very *kaṇṭakī* fuel-stick with this [same] formula.

"He should not offer oblations; he should merely recite the Yajus formula"—this is another [view]. Then he takes up the spade (*abhri*), made of *khadira*, *udumbara*, *veṇu*, or *vikaṅkata* wood. Its dimensions are those of the fire-shovel (*āgnikī*). Having taken up the spade with the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ... (VS 1.28), he addresses the Brahman priest with, "Arise, O Brahmaṇaspati! (VS 1.29). The Brahman priest stands up. Both recite the second half-verse. They take up the black antelope skin. They lead after [the sacrificial animals]: a he-goat, a castrated goat, and a stallion.

With the verse, "May Brahmaṇaspati go forward," they proceed eastward with the horse at their head. Alternatively, these materials for him have been brought out into an enclosed space; the clay-digging pit is in front of the Āhavanīya fire.

Each preceding one is the other. (12) Having spread out the black antelope skin with its neck to the east and the hair upwards over the clay-digging pit by means of the northern [end], he addresses the two, Heaven and Earth: "May the divine Heaven and Earth conform to me; may they be favorable to me. (13) He strikes at the clay-digging pit with the spade, saying: "May I succeed today; [this is] the head of Makha. (14) He carries it away, saying: "For Makha thee! For the head of Makha thee! (15) He pours it silently onto the black antelope skin. (16) In this very same manner, he carries away the second [portion].
In this manner he does it a third time; the fourth time he remains silent, taking as much clay as he thinks will suffice for the Pravargya vessels. 11.1.18–19.

Then he consecrates the earth dug up by a boar with the formula: "So much [in extent] wast thou in the beginning" (1). From here onwards, it is the same (2). Then [he consecrates] the mound of an anthill with the formula: "O divine ants" (3). From here onwards, it is the same (4). Then [he consecrates] the *pūtīka* plants with the formula: "Thou art Indra’s vigor" (5). From here onwards, it is the same (6). Having mixed together the hair of a black antelope skin and the hair of a goat, [he consecrates them] with the formula: "Thou art born of fire; thou art the seed of Prajāpati" (7). From here onwards, it is the same (8). Then he causes a horse to smell these [substances] with the formula: "Bestow life; bestow breath" (9).

Then he milks them over with [the formula], "May honey make thee sweet. (10) Some authorities prescribe the milking over before the smelling. (11) Many Āryas carry them away, holding them together. (12) They place them to the north of the sacrificial ground on a spot that has been dug up, sprinkled with water, strewn with sand, and enclosed. (13) Then he pours warm water over them with [the formula], "May honey make thee sweet. (14) Whatever materials there are for mixing the cauldrons, and whatever else he considers necessary for strengthening, [he places there]. (15)

In this regard, this is the absolute rule: whatever water-related rite is performed during the Pravargya, it is done with the *madantī* waters alone. A woman does not look at it, nor does a Śūdra. One should not breathe over it while performing the rite. Having held his breath, he performs the action with a bamboo tube without breathing over it. One should not pass between the Pravargya vessel and the sun. Wherever the Pravargya may be moved away from, if the sun should set, one should desist right where it has been brought to its conclusion.

On the following day, he should complete the remainder. (21) Having kneaded the clay, he forms a lump with the formula, "Thou art the head of Makha. (22) With the formula, "Ye two are the feet of the sacrifice," he grasps [the clay] with his two thumbs and fashions the *mahāvīra* vessel, either one span high or of unlimited height, shaped like a bird of prey (*vāyavyākṛti*), with three elevations or five elevations. (23) With the formula, "I fashion thee with the *gāyatrī* metre," he makes the first [elevation]; with "with the *triṣṭubh* metre," the second.

He leads it back for the third time; he establishes it on the sands to the north with the formula: "May you be heated by the heat of Sūrya; you are a sacrifice" (makha). In the same way he establishes the second, and likewise the third. The others [the remaining vessels] are done silently. From this very clay he makes the *dogdhra* (milking vessel), having handles like an elephant's trunk and provided with spouts, just as a ladle has a handle. The Adhvaryu’s portion is larger, and the Pratiprasthātṛ’s is smaller. From this same clay he also makes the *ājyasthālī* (clarified butter pot) and the two circular *māruta-kapāla* (Māruta potsherds).

7. [He places] seven bricks of the *gharma* type, [with the formula] "The nest-like one" (*kulāyinī*), if there is a piling of the fire-altar (*agnicityā*). 8. Then they smooth them with smoothing agents: with unwashed *caṇḍātaka* cloths, *gavīdhuka* seeds, *klītaka* plants, bamboo joints, and clarified butter. 9. Then, at the time of fumigation, having kindled the dung of a stallion on the *gārhapatya* fire, he takes up the first-made *mahāvīra* vessel with two hooves and fumigates it with [the mantra]: "Thou art the secretion of the stallion. 10. In the same manner, he fumigates the second; in the same manner...

The third [is placed] with the formula; the others silently (12). From this point onward, he takes up the Mahāvīras by means of the two hooves (13). Having dug a pit in front of the Gārhapatya fire and having spread it with the red-heating materials, he brings down the first-made Mahāvīra there with the formula, "Thou art flame" (14); the second with, "Thou art light" (15); the third with, "Thou art radiance, thou art heat" (16). Having silently placed the others alongside and covered them with the red-heating materials, he kindles Muñja grass over the Gārhapatya fire and heats [the vessels].
"To radiance, thee!"—thus in the east; "To flame, thee!"—thus in the south; "To light, thee!"—thus in the west; "To heat, thee!"—thus in the north. 16.11.3.

Or rather, he attends to all [the Mahāvīras] from all sides while they are being baked, either with the verse "This [Mahāvīra], by its greatness, has reached the sky," or with the following one. All the attendances are accompanied by mantras. When they are baked, the Adhvaryu takes up the two fire-stirring sticks (*dhṛṣṭī*) with the words "For success, thee! and removes the first-made Mahāvīra with the formula, "May the god Savitṛ remove thee. He establishes it on the sand to the north with the formula, "Not falling upon the earth, fill the regions and the quarters. Then he gazes at it with the formula, "Thee, belonging to Sūrya..."

"I gaze upon you with my eye"—with these words he removes the second [fire] in this same manner, and likewise the third. The others are removed silently. Then he heaps sand around them from left to right, saying: "Here I enclose so-and-so, the son of such-and-such, with subjects, cattle, and Vedic splendor. For a Kṣatriya, he says "with subjects"; for a Vaiśya, "with cattle. Then he moistens them with abundant goat's milk, using these mantras: "I moisten thee with the Gāyatrī metre," and so forth.

Three by three, one for each; or else, one for each with all [the verses] together. Then he ties them up on a black antelope skin and fastens them with the formula: "O God who goes before, I have fastened thee. According to another view, this mantra is to be used at a later time. When they are about to proceed with the *pravargya* ceremony, they close the doors and enclose the area for the wife. The Hotṛ sits down to the west, the Adhvaryu to the east, and the Brahman, the Sacrificer, and the Prastotṛ to the south.

To the north, the Āgnīdhra and the Pratiprasthātṛ, having touched the *madantī* water and performed the peace-rite (*śānti*) with the first *anuvāka*, spread darbha grass around the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) with the following [text] and bring down these *mahāvīra* vessels there with the formula: "O God, leader, sit upon thee. According to another view, this mantra belongs to the subsequent time; at this very point, he brings down everything pertaining to the *gharma*. He brings down the *samrāḍ-āsandī* made of *udumbara* wood. Some authorities prescribe it as being larger than the *rāja-āsandī*.

It is woven with single-strand cords made of muñja grass. (9) There are four offering-spoons (*sruk*) made of udumbara wood. (10) Of these, two are not bound [with cords]. (11) Of the two that are bound, the larger one is the *upayamanī* (supporting spoon), and the smaller is the *prokṣaṇī-dhānī* (ladle for sprinkling). (12) There are two *sruva* spoons made of udumbara wood. There are two *śapha* (hoof-shaped) scrapers made of udumbara wood, equal in size to the *mahāvīra* vessel. There is a stirring-ladle (*dhṛṣṭi*) made of udumbara wood. There is a central post (*methī*) made of udumbara wood. There are three pegs (*mayūkha*) made of udumbara wood.

Six chips of *udumbara* wood (13), thirteen enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) of *vikaṅkata* wood, and a fuel-stick (*samidh*) from a branch (14). Abundant fuel for the *gharma* oblation, made of *khadira*, *udumbara*, *vikaṅkata*, or *kārṣmarya* wood (15). Three fans made of black antelope skin, the hairs of which are white and black (16). It is known that the handles are made of bamboo and are a cubit in length (17); alternatively, they may have handles of *udumbara* wood (18). There are two ornaments (*rukma*), one of silver and one of gold (19), each weighing a *śatamāna*.

20. Two cords made of *muñja* grass; of these two, one is pre-soaked. 21. A cord made of *muñja* grass for the naming-rite (*abhidhānī*). Two stalks of *muñja* grass as supports. Three loops of *muñja* grass for the *viśākha* crossbar. 22. Two fresh cuttings of *muñja* grass with unbroken tips. 23. Ground grains of rice that have not been hulled, for the two *rauhiṇa* cakes. 24. Sand from the donkey-tracks. 25. Two blades of *muñja* grass as strainers—this is one view. Two blades made of *darbha* grass—this is another view. 26. 11.5.

Having silently prepared the *prokṣaṇī* waters in the *prokṣaṇīdhānī* vessel, he addresses the *brahmán*: "O *brahmán*, we shall proceed with the *pravargya*. O *hotṛ*, recite the hymn for the *gharma*. O *agnīdh* and *pratiprasthātṛ*, place the two rice-cakes (*puroḍāśa*) on the fire. O *pratiprasthātṛ*, perform the ritual distribution (*vihara*)."

"O Prastotṛ, sing the Sāmans!"—thus the Brahman gives the impulse with the Yajus formula, "The sky is anointed by the Sāmans. Having uttered this in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), he says aloud, "Om! Proceed, accompanied by Indra! Or rather, he says "Proceed" aloud, while everything else is in a low voice. Being thus impelled by the Brahman, he sprinkles all the vessels belonging to the Gharma sacrifice with the formula, "For Yama, thee!"

With these mantras, "For Makha thee," he sprinkles [the materials] three times (5). He sprinkles them from front to back (6). "He causes the sprinkled items to be spread out," so it is known (7). Then, having carried this royal throne-seat (samrāḍāsandī) around the front of the Āhavanīya fire and having established it to the east of the King’s throne-seat (rājāsandī), he spreads upon it a black antelope skin with the neck toward the east and the hair upward; upon that, he brings down the two Mahāvīra vessels which are not to be used [in the sacrifice], with the mantra: "O God, you who go before, may I attain you" (8). This mantra is for the later occasion.

"Thus it becomes," so it is said. Then, taking this central post (*methī*), the pegs (*mayūkha*), and the ropes for the two-pronged yoke-pins (*viśākhadāmāni*), he goes out by the southern door, passing in front of the *hotṛ* and behind the *gārhapatya* fire, and drives the central post to the south of the southern door for the *hotṛ* to look at. To the south of the eastern door-post of that same door, he drives a peg for the calf. To the south of the western door-post of that same door, [he drives one] for the goat.

At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ consecrates the clarified butter in the *ājyasthālī* according to the procedure for a *darvihoma*. According to another view, no such consecration is required for this. The Āgnīdhra places the two *rauhiṇa* cakes on the fire; they have been prepared silently. Having grasped the *mahāvīra* with the two pincers, he sweeps away the ashes with the untrimmed *veda*-grass, saying: "O God, go forward; may I attain you. With the *sruva*-ladle, he offers seven or eleven *prāṇa*-oblations into the *āhavanīya* fire, beginning with: "To Prāṇa, svāhā!"

"Vyañāya svāhā!"—thus [he offers]. 5. Then he anoints it with clarified butter, saying: "May the god Savitṛ anoint thee with honey. 6. Having placed a silver plate on the western mound and established the Mahāvīra pot upon it with the formula, "Protect the earth from heat," or having handed the Mahāvīra to another, he takes two bundles of Muñja grass and kindles their tips over the Gārhapatya fire with the formula, "For the flame, thee! 7. With their tips he kindles the roots of the northern bundles with the formula, "For the radiance, thee! 8. With their roots he kindles the roots of the southern bundles.

"Jyotiṣe tvā" (For light, thee)—with these [formulas], he places the tips of the northern [reeds] upon their roots with "Tapase tvā" (For heat, thee). He places them crosswise upon the gold plate with "Arcir asi, śocir asi" (Thou art flame, thou art glow). It is known [from tradition]: "He makes the southern ones the uppermost. Upon them, he establishes the Mahāvīra vessel with "Saṃsīdasva, mahān asi" (Sit down; thou art great). Then he fills it with clarified butter with "Añjanti yaṃ prathayantaḥ" (They anoint him as they spread him out). Without touching the Mahāvīra, the sacrificer extends his span eastward over it.

Wearing [the garment], he mutters, according to the form of each mantra: "Invincible from the front," and so forth; with these mantras, he touches the earth to the north, saying, "Thou art the horse of Manu, mother of many sons. 15–16. 11.7.

Saying, "For success, thee," the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ take up the two *dhṛṣṭī* (fire-stirring sticks) and draw out embers from the Gārhapatya fire toward the north, with the mantra: "O Agni, burn up our enemies within. With those embers, they two pile them around it clockwise, saying: "You are piled; you are piled around. Then they enclose it with thirteen enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) made of *vaikaṅkata* wood. The Adhvaryu lays down two of them pointing eastward, saying: "Thou art the measure."

"Thou art the measure," says the Pratiprasthātṛ while placing [the enclosing sticks] facing north. In this very manner, they enclose [the fire] with each subsequent mantra; the Adhvaryu with each preceding one, and the Pratiprasthātṛ with each succeeding one. The Adhvaryu alone places the thirteenth stick on the south side, saying, "Thou art the internal support of the atmosphere. Then he covers it with a golden plate, saying, "Protect the sky from heat. Then it is consecrated with the three verses beginning, "With these songs. Thereafter, he takes up the fans.

With "Thou art the Gāyatra," he fans it upward for the first time; with "Thou art the Triṣṭubh," for the second; with "Thou art the Jāgata," for the third. With those [fans], he fans it upward three times, saying "Honey! Honey! He gives one of them to the Pratiprasthātṛ and one to the Āgnīdhra. Then, led by the Āgnīdhra, they walk around [the fire] three times to the right, fanning upward. Then they sit down around it: the Adhvaryu in the east, the Pratiprasthātṛ in the south, and the Āgnīdhra in the north.

Shaking off [impurities] without intermingling, they sit together, kindling [the fire], propitiating with *praṇavas*, and anointing [the vessels]. (13) It is known from tradition that when [the fire] has blazed up, he takes up the gold plate (*rukma*). (14) When he recognizes [the verse] "With those [rays] by which you released the swallowed quail," then the Adhvaryu addresses the Mahāvīra vessel with the section beginning, "Ten [rays] toward the east, ten thou shinest toward the south. (15) When he recognizes [the verse] "O Aśvins, make our speech effective," then the Adhvaryu, rising up, says, "The Gharma is radiant. (16)

Then, led by the Adhvaryu, they walk around [the Mahāvīra] three times without fanning it. (17) Having taken up the fans, he hands them to the Pratiprasthātṛ. (18) The Pratiprasthātṛ, having carried them around in front of the Āhavanīya fire, places them on the *samrāḍ-āsandi* throne. (19) Standing each in their respective place, all the officiating priests and the sacrificer, reciting the hymn, gaze upon the Mahāvīra, [chanting]: "I have seen the herdsman... (20) However, the Pratiprasthātṛ causes the wife to recite the remainder of the section within the enclosed space, [starting with]: "May I consort with thee who art accompanied by Tvaṣṭṛ... (21) 11.8.11.8.19–21.

Then he gives the command: "O Āgnīdhra, set down the two cakes for the Hotṛ and the Maitrāvaruṇa. He sets down the two cakes, which have been spread with a base of butter and sprinkled over with butter, upon the two unobstructed ladles; one [cake] along the southern junction of the enclosing sticks.

Having taken the rope with the *sāvitra* formula at the northern junction of the enclosing sticks, he goes out by the eastern door and calls the cow that yields the *gharma* three times in a low voice: "O Iḍā, come! O Aditi, come! O Sarasvatī, come! (4) Having returned, having taken the two supports for the milker, he goes out by the southern door and calls her three times aloud: "O So-and-so, come! O So-and-so, come! according to her name. (5) With the formula, "Thou art the turban of Aditi," he fastens the cow that yields the *gharma* with the rope.

"Vāyu is its kid," [with these words] he [addresses] the calf (6). "May Pūṣan let you loose," [with these words] he lets it loose (7). "That breast of yours which is inexhaustible," [with these words] he addresses the cow that yields the Gharma-milk (8). Having tied up the calf with the formula, "O Dawn, O Gharma, O Mishi," he sits down beside her with the formula, "May Bṛhaspati sit down beside you" (9). "You are the Dānavas, you are the Peravas," [with these words] he touches the udders (10). He milks the larger one for the milker with the formula, "Swell for the Aśvins; swell for Sarasvatī" (11). The Pratiprasthātṛ silently milks the smaller goat (12).
Having given two portions of milk to the Agnīdhra and having run forward as before, he takes up the two hoof-receptacles: "Thou art Gāyatra" for the first, and "Thou art Traiṣṭubha" for the second.

The Pratiprasthātṛ takes up the supporting ladle with the formula, "Thou art the world. When he recognizes [the verse], "Arise, O Brahmanaspati," then the Āgnīdhra rises. When he recognizes [the verse], "Come hither, O milker of the cow, with milk," then he brings the milk. He consecrates the milk as it is being brought with the formula, "Come to me together with thy portion of vigor. With the formula, "O Indra and Aśvins, [of] the honeyed essence of the bee," he pours the cow's milk into the Mahāvīra vessel. "Svāhā! I offer thee to the rain-desiring ray of the Sun."
With these words he consecrates the rising heat; "Thou art honey, the oblation," [he says] over the goat's milk. 19.11.9.18–19.

Some prescribe the bringing forward of goat’s milk first. Having grasped the *mahāvīra* with its two handles while reciting, “I enclose thee for Heaven and Earth,” the Pratiprasthātṛ wipes away the ashes with the fringed *vedāgra* and supports it with the supporting tray while reciting, “I support thee with the intermediate space. Having lifted it up while reciting, “May I be able to bear thee, authorized by the gods and the Pitṛs,” he carries it forth while reciting, “Thou art splendor; follow after splendor. Even as he goes, he should recite the five names of the wind without taking breath.

He explains [the verses]: "To thee, O ocean, Svāhā! and "To Vāta, Svāhā! (4). Having inhaled, he offers the next five oblations with: "To Agni accompanied by the Vasus, Svāhā! (5). At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers the southern Rauhiṇa cake, supported by the ladle, with: "May Day, the light, enjoy it with its banner; may the fair-lighted one [enjoy] the lights, Svāhā! (6). Stepping across to the south, the Adhvaryu looks at the Brahman with: "Sitting to the south, [may he go] to all regions. (7) [He looks] at the Hotṛ with: "He has sacrificed here to all the gods. (8) [This is for] the Gharma over which the Svāhā-call has been uttered.

Having thus consecrated the *gharma* and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, when the response has been given, he issues the command: "Recite the offering prayer for the *gharma*. (9) When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering with the words: "O Aśvins, drink the *gharma*! (10) When the second *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers a second time with "Svāhā! To Indra! Vaṭ! (11) Having offered, the sacrificer consecrates the oblation with the remainder of the section beginning: "The Aśvins have drunk the *gharma*. (12) Then, holding it over the *āhavanīya* fire, he fills it with boiled curds. (13) As it drips, he consecrates it with: "Swell for food; swell for strength! (14)

Then he causes it to flow out toward the quarters: with "For brilliance thee! to the east; with "For splendor thee! to the south; with "For power of Indra thee! to the west; with "For prosperity thee! to the north.
