Having stepped back and poured the remainder into the supporting vessel, having placed the supporting vessel within the altar (antarvedi), and having placed a silver plate on the eastern mound (khara), he establishes the Mahāvīra pot upon it. 16 11.10

"You are the Dharma, the good Dharma for me; maintain the *brahmans* for us"—thus [he says]. "Maintain the *kṣatras*"—thus for a *rājanya*. "Maintain the *viś*"—thus for a *vaiśya*. "May the wind not cause you to spill"—thus [he says]. If he should practice sorcery, he should say regarding the one whom he hates: "I set you down in the breath of so-and-so; go to ruin along with him. At this point, the *pratiprasthātṛ* offers the second *rauhiṇa* oblation as before. He places pieces of wood smeared with ointment into the supporting vessel (*upayamana*) with these [formulas]: "To Pūṣan, the sap, svāhā! and so forth.

6. After reciting each mantra over all the smearings, he throws away the sixth chip toward the north without looking at it, saying: "To the Rudras who belong to the Hotṛ, svāhā! 7. He touches water. 8. Some authorities prescribe that the chips should be thrown away before the Rauhiṇa oblations. 9. Having silently placed a fuel-stick of *kaṇṭakī* wood on the fire, he silently offers the Agnihotra. 10. Or [he may offer] with the words: "Bhūḥ svāhā! 11. Having invited one another, they all consume the remainder in the supporting vessel.

First the Hotṛ, then the Adhvaryu, then the Brahman, then the Pratiprasthātṛ, then the Āgnīdhra, and then the sacrificer (yajamāna). 12. All [partake] directly. Or rather, the sacrificer alone partakes directly, while the others [partake] by smelling. 13. Having consumed the oblation with the formula, "The oblation is honey, the oblation," he hands the supporting vessel (upayamana) to the Pratiprasthātṛ. 14. The Pratiprasthātṛ, having purified himself at the mound for the remnants (ucchiṣṭakhara), places the supporting vessel within the altar (antarvedi); upon it, he places two gold plates, one of silver and one of gold.

Having brought the boiling waters and performed the *śānti* rite with the final *anuvāka*, and having poured out the water, he places all the implements used for the *gharma* into the supporting vessel (*upayamana*). Then he issues the command:

"Recite for the *gharma* as it is being set down. Having recognized the verse beginning with "In whom the seven Vasus," he carries [the vessel] around the front of the *āhavanīya* fire and sets it down on the royal throne (*samrāḍāsandi*). In the morning, he says: "Svāhā! To thee, for the rays of the Sun!"

With the formula, "Svāhā! To you, for the constellations," he offers in the evening twice. When he recognizes [the verse], "Eat grass, O inviolable one, at all times," then he releases the cow. In this very same way, he proceeds with the *pravargya* rite both in the evening and in the morning. In a rite with three *upasad*s, he does so six times; in a rite with six *upasad*s, twelve times; and in a rite with twelve *upasad*s, twenty-four times. This much is the difference. With the subsequent mantra, he offers the *rauhiṇa* oblation in the evening. With the formula, "You have carried me across from day to night; protect me," he offers the *kāṇṭakī* wood in the evening.

He places fuel on the fire. In the morning, he offers the Agnihotra with the mantra: "Carry me across from night; protect me from day. In the evening, he offers the Agnihotra with the mantra: "Agni is light, light is Agni, Svāhā!"

"Sun is light, light is sun, svāhā!"—thus at dawn (9). Or [one performs] the *saṃsṛṣṭahoma* (10). One chooses [the fire] for the *agniṣṭoma* (11); one should not choose it for the *ukthya* (12). One chooses it for the *viśvajit* sacrifice when all the *pṛṣṭha-stotras* are performed (13); one should not choose it for one's first sacrifice (14), or rather, one may choose it (15). One should choose it for one who is learned in the Vedas (*anūcāna*) and a scholar (*śrotriya*) (16); one may choose it for a "bad Brāhmaṇa" (17); according to some, for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) (18). Having chosen that [fire], for a year he should not eat meat, nor...

One should approach women, but not one made of clay; one should not drink from it, nor should one drink the leavings of this [vessel]. It is known: "That [act] sharpens one's vital energy. 11.12.20–21.

Intending to remove the Pravargya vessels, he gives a goat to the Agnīdh, a four-year-old cow to the Brahman, a milch-cow to the Hotṛ, and two gold plates to the Adhvaryu. Having poured together [the contents], he pours them out upon the western mound (khara) from the eastern one. Then, having placed this royal throne (samrāḍ-āsandī) to the north of the Āhavanīya fire, he places all the implements belonging to the Gharma oblation upon it. Having taken four portions of clarified butter in a ladle made of Udumbara wood, he offers three oblations into the Āhavanīya with these mantras: "O Gharma, that which is thy light in heaven... and so forth.

Alternatively, the Pratiprasthātṛ takes three fistfuls of fire-sticks together with their tips, kindles one of them in the Āhavanīya fire, and holds it at the height of his mouth. The Adhvaryu makes an offering over it with the mantra: "O Gharma, that [light] of yours which is in heaven, O Śuk... He then kindles another stick, throws the first one into the Āhavanīya, and holds the second at the height of his navel.

The Adhvaryu makes an offering over it with the formula: "O Gharma, that which is your light in the intermediate space... (6). Having kindled another fire and cast the previous one into the Āhavanīya, he holds it at the height of the knees. The Adhvaryu makes an offering over it with the formula: "O Gharma, that which is your light on the earth... (7). He then throws it after [the fire] into the Āhavanīya itself. (8) At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ leads the wife into the enclosed space with the verse: "May Anumati favor us today... (9). They go out with the verse: "In truth, O Anumati, you... (10). They bring in the wooden post (methī).

They follow the rays [of light]. They take up the two stools. 11. He carries away the stool for the remnants to the south. 12. Then, having placed two feet of this royal throne (samrāḍāsandi) within the altar and two outside the altar, he issues the command: "O Prastotṛ, chant the Sāmans! 13. Together with the wife, they go toward the finale (nidhana) of the Sāman three times. 14. A second time at the halfway point; a third time in front of the high-altar (uttaravedi). 15. With the words, "For the protection from heaven," they proceed during the first [round].
"May Brahmā protect you from the beyond," he says at the second [pouring]. "May Prāṇa protect you from the beyond," he says at the third. 16.11.13

Then, having placed this royal throne-seat (samrāḍāsandī) to the north of the northern altar (uttaravedi), he issues the command: "O Prastotṛ, sing the Vārṣāhara Sāman; sing the Iṣṭāhotrīya Sāman. They reach the finale (nidhana) of the Iṣṭāhotrīya Sāman, but not that of the Vārṣāhara. If he were to sprinkle water above, there he should cause the Vārṣāhara to be chanted. Taking a water-pitcher, he goes around the northern altar three times, sprinkling it while keeping his right side toward it, with the mantra: "Thou art auspicious, O bringer of peace. He does this three times without sprinkling [the ground] below.

"Go around, speak what is auspicious, and speak all around. Having touched the *uttaravedi* with the mantra, "The navel of the *ṛta* has four corners," he piles up two *khara* mounds to the north of the northern *nābhi* and spreads [the earth] over them with the mantra, "The seat of all life. In the region of the *mārjālīya*, he pours out the *ucchiṣṭakhara* (the mound for the remains) with the mantra, "Away with hatred, away with crookedness. Having touched water and placed gold on the *khara* to the north of the northern *nābhi*, he brings down upon it the *mahāvīra* vessel used for the ritual performance, and brings down the other two vessels, one after the other, in front and behind.

Or [he may fill] the southern and northern [cups]. 8. Then he pours into this *pracaraṇī* cup the milk of a cow with the formula: "Thou art the milk of the great ones, ordained among the gods. 9. [He pours] honey with the formula: "Thou art the light-shining, the sap of the trees and the plants. 10. [He pours] curd with the formula: "Thee, the vigorous, we pour down as the vigorous. 11. In this very same way he fills the second [cup], and likewise the third. 12. Or rather, he may first pour clarified butter, honey in the second, and curd in the third. 13. [He pours] with curd mixed with honey, with the formula: "O Gharma, this is thy food, this is thy nourishment."
He fills those that are capable of being filled; he sprinkles the others so that they may not remain empty; he fashions the shape of the sun. 11.14.14–16.

Now, if he should wish to fashion the form of a man, having brought down the other implements right here, he makes the form of the head [with the following]: (1) a cord of muñja grass with its tip uncut above represents the form of the top-knot; (2) two pieces of gold and two ladles of clarified butter represent the form of the eyes; (3) two *sruva*-ladles represent the form of the nostrils; (4) two milking-pails represent the form of the ears; (5) the vessel for the sprinkling-water represents the form of the mouth; (6) the pot for the clarified butter represents the form of the neck; (7) the two stirring-sticks represent the form of the collarbones; (8) the two hoof-shaped vessels represent the form of the shoulders; (9) the two *rauhiṇa*-offering vessels represent the form of the arms.

The ten *audumbara* fuel-sticks are the form of the ten fingers (10). The eastern pillar is the form of the ribs (11). On both sides, the two fans are the form of the two flanks (12). In the middle, the third [fan] is the form of the chest (13). In the center, the supporting tray is the form of the belly (14). Upon it he places everything made of cord; this is the form of the entrails (15). Behind, the transverse hoe is the form of the two hips (16). On both sides, the two stakes are the form of the two thighs (17). In the middle, the third [stake] is the form of the penis (18).

The two *rauhiṇaka* potsherds are the form of the two heels (20). Ten fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood are the form of the fingers (21). He pours the residue of the *rauhiṇa* flour upon it; this is the form of the marrow (22). Having loosened the cord of muñja grass from above, he lays it down; this is the form of the sinews (23). He covers it with *avakā* plants and smoke-grass; this is the form of the flesh (24). He sprinkles it with curd mixed with honey; this is the form of the blood (25). He covers it with a black antelope skin, with the neck pointing eastward and the hair on the upper side; this is the form of the skin.

The form of the body hairs [is completed]. 26 Having loosened the imperial throne-seat (*samrāḍāsandī*) from above, he sets it down; he thus produces the form of sovereignty (*sāmrājya*). 27 11.15 One should remove [the fire] onto the high altar (*uttaravedi*) for one who desires splendor; onto the high altar for one who desires food. 1 Or one may remove it either in front or behind. 2 One should remove it on an island in a river. 3 If one removes it on an island in a river, one should not sprinkle water around it. 4 Against whomsoever he may have enmity, in whatever direction that person may be, there he should remove it onto a branch of *udumbara* wood, saying: "Here I burn away the breath of so-and-so, the son of so-and-so, with pain. 5 Verily, by means of pain, he burns away his breath.

"It suffers from a sudden affliction," so it is known. 6. Where the *darbha* grasses are covered with *upadīka* insects, there he should remove [the fire] for one who desires rain. 7. They prescribe the regular ritual procedure on the *uttaravedi*. 8. Once removed, they should not sit around it until the leading forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*). 9. Here some prescribe the sprinkling of water around [the fire]. 10. Then they pay reverence to it, beginning with: "Thou art Ranti by name, the divine Gandharva; together with offspring, together with the increase of wealth. 11. [This takes place] at the site of the *mārjālīya* shed, on the mound for the remains of food.

"May the waters and the plants be friendly to us," with these words they purify themselves. Having worshipped the sun with "We have risen above the darkness" (*ud vayaṃ tamasaḥ pari*) and with the two verses beginning "Upward that" (*ud u tyam*) and "The bright one" (*citram*), they offer oblations in the *gārhapatya* fire and worship it with "This very one, for us... (*imam ū ṣu tyam asmabhyam*). 12–13. 11.16.

If the *gharma* should spill, he should consecrate it with two verses: "The sky has flowed upon the earth. If lightning should strike while they are performing with the *gharma*, he should offer oblations according to the respective signs with the verses beginning, "The lightning that struck from the east. If it strikes from all sides, he should offer all of them. Then he offers these expiations for the *gharma*: "To Prāṇa, svāhā!"

With the two sections beginning with *pūṣṇe svāhā*, he places the *gharma*-brick; with the section beginning with *udasya śuṣmād bhānuḥ*, [he places] the *kulāyinī* brick; with the section beginning with *yāste agne ādrā ryonayaḥ*, [he places] the *kulāyinī* brick; he touches the piled fire-altar with the *aiḍikī* formula using the section beginning with *agnir asi vaiśvānaro 'si*; with the words *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, [he performs] all the expiations (*sarvaprāyaścitta*). If the *mahāvīra* vessel should fall, he should lift it up with the two verses beginning with *ūrdhva ū ṣu ṇa ūtaye*. If it should break, [he recites] *vidhuṃ dadrāṇam*.

Having joined [the pieces] with the word *ṇam*, he should smear him with those adhesives intended for strengthening, using the verse: "Whatever else besides beans and meat there is, and whatever else serves as a means of binding. (10) If it should become impossible to move, he should cover the opening for another [victim]. (11) Whether they have carried the *gharma* around or not, they should carry it around him again with these two verses: "Return with vigor, together with wealth. (12) 11.17

Then he offers these expiations when the *gharma* has been disturbed, with the eight verses beginning, "O *gharma*, do not disturb us; may you not cause us distress. If, while performing the *gharma* rite, the sun should set, he should tie a piece of gold to a blade of *darbha* grass at the western door, worship with the verse, "Upward from the darkness," and [recite] "Upward that one."

Having offered two oblations into the Gārhapatya fire with the verse "The variegated one" (RV 1.164.43) and having cast the remnants into the fire, on the following day he worships the Sun with the verse, "The birds, the well-winged ones" (RV 1.164.21). 2. They consume the *dadhigharma* with the Anuvāka beginning, "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ. 3. If the cow that yields the *gharma* does not arrive at the time of milking, he should have another cow milked, cast the remnants into the fire, and give her to a Brāhmaṇa at the Soma-pressing. 4. If there should be no milk in the *gharma*-yielding cow, he should make the fourth foot of the skin into a teat and cause it to flow. 5. If he should milk curds [for the *dadhigharma*].

May there be peace through the [oblation] to Bṛhaspati. If milk for the Aśvins should have its *udarka* (concluding portion) missing, or if blood, or anything discolored, should be milked, one should enclose the Anvāhāryapacana fire and offer with the formula: "To Agni accompanied by Rudra, svāhā! If he should sit down, he should offer with two verses of Dhātṛ. If he should sit upon something impure or unfit for sacrifice, he should offer with the verse addressed to Agni and Varuṇa.

Now, therefore, follows the heating [of the milk] for the Soma-pressing (sutyā). 1. If it should be reddish before dawn, then it is to be heated. 2. At the time when the light appears, at the break of dawn, at the moment when the sun has half-risen, at the time when the sun has just risen, or when it has fully risen; 3. or at the morning pressing-time (prātaḥ-savana), or at the Saṃgava period; 4. or at the midday pressing (mādhyaṃdina) once the Pavamāna-stotra has been chanted. 5. It is traditionally known that the heating is performed only once in the Āgnīdhra shed. 6. These various modes of heating may be optionally substituted for the heating rites belonging to the Upasads. 7. The "Terrible Bodies" (ghorāstanvaḥ) have been explained.

In the forest, the *anuvāka* [beginning with] "anu vākya" and the two subsequent *anuvākas* [are recited]. (8) If a one-eyed animal should rise up while he is performing the *gharma* oblation, he should address it with the verse: "O Indra, as you wander, look out for the cows. (9) Having kindled a firebrand at both ends, he should throw it toward him with the words: "O Agni, converse with Agni! (10) Then he addresses it with the remainder of the *anuvāka* beginning: "Once, O Agni, homage to thee! (11) If a vulture, a female jackal, a *bhayeḍaka*, a long-faced owl, a spirit-possessed bird, or any bird should utter a cry;

If the *gharmaduh* cow should become infested with worms, one should kill its worms with the section beginning, "O worm, I kill you with Atri. Or rather, this expiation (*prāyaścitta*) may be performed universally for all such cases. If one intends to practice malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) against someone, he should offer a portion of that person's blood as an oblation with the section beginning, "Bring [the portion], having cut off the cooked [flesh]. If one is about to utter [a curse] against someone, he should observe celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for at least three nights; then, having gone to him, he should utter it against him with the section beginning, "By means of the *Brahman*, I curse you. [He should do this] against whomever he hates.

Having gone to the cow-pen, he should bury his own *jamā* plant with the anuvāka beginning, "Prick her, O thou that art born of *śimi*. Or else, he should shake the southern door-post of the cow-pen itself. If the Udgātṛ should not sing the *puruṣasāman*, the Adhvaryu himself should sing it with the anuvāka beginning, "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. 11.20.7–8.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*). On a festival day during the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious constellation, in the afternoon, having shaved his hair and beard, and having gone out toward the east or the north, he establishes the fire on a barren spot where no roof is visible, spreads grass around it, performs the introductory rites as before, touches the *madantī* water, and having performed the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) with the first Anuvāka, he places four fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood, anointed with clarified butter, with these mantras beginning, "The earth is the fuel. 2.
Then he worships the deities, saying: "O Agni, lord of vows, I shall perform the vow. Then he causes him to recite the introductory verses of all the Anuvākas.

Or, having performed the *śānti* rite with either the first or the last *anuvāka*, he then closes [the eyes] and restrains his speech. Then, having wrapped his head with a new (*ahata*) cloth so that it faces forward, he causes him to enter the village after sunset. He remains for that night either standing or sitting, maintaining silence. On the following day, having kindled the fire on a cleared spot where no roof-covering is visible and having strewn grass around it, he shows him the "six-fold" [set]; some say the "seven-fold."

He shows him the fire, the sun, a water-pot, a stone, a calf, a girl who has not yet reached puberty, and gold as the seventh (8). Or rather, he shows him the first three; the others he shows as they happen to be available (9). Then he worships the sun with the verse, "The birds, the fair-winged ones... (10). At this point, having given this garment to the teacher (11), he [instructs him] regarding his studentship (brahmacarya) (12). It is constant (13). He should not eat at night (14). If he should eat, he should eat [only] when the food is glowing hot (15). He should not use an earthenware vessel (16). Nor...

He should not converse with a woman or a Śūdra (17). He should not mount anything with wheels (18). He should not wear shoes or carry an umbrella (19). He should not look at a crowd, nor at palaces, nor at his own body, nor at a corpse, nor at an outcaste (20). 11.21.

On the eighth day and on the festival days (parvan), he should fast and remain silent; he must not go to sleep [during that time]. He should observe this vow for one year. He should study during that very year. If he does not study during that year, he should observe this vow for as long as his study lasts. After the year has passed, having established the fire in a cleared spot where the roof is not visible, having strewn grass around it, and having dismissed [the fires] as before, he should place fuel sticks upon the fire with the mantras recited in reverse order, and worship the deities with the mantras recited in reverse order. Here, he should offer a choice gift to the teacher.

Having given [the gift], he has his hair and beard shaved. 6. Then he undertakes the private recitation (svādhyāya) of the Veda. 7. It is obligatory. 8. One should not study unless one has formally concluded the session; nor at night; nor at dawn; nor after having committed an act of unchastity; nor after eating meat; nor after having had his hair and beard shaved; nor after having had the hair of his body removed; nor after having trimmed his nails; nor after having washed his teeth. 9. One should not study when anointed with oil, nor when smeared with ointment, nor when wet, nor in damp weather, nor when it has not rained for some time; nor while looking at green barley. 10. One should not study in the vicinity of domestic animals, nor of wild animals, nor near water, nor in the clouds.

He should not study in the shade when the sun has turned away [from the zenith], nor after seeing raw meat, nor after seeing blood, nor houses, nor corpses, nor outcasts (antāvasāyin). Having kindled the fire on a cleared spot where no roof is visible and having strewn grass around it, he should sit on *darbha* grass to the west of the fire, holding *darbha* or *dūrvā* grass in his hand, and recite the Veda facing away from the fire. Or, having given a gift, he may recite at the domestic fire (*aupāsana*). One who is about to begin his studies should recite after performing a propitiatory rite (*śānti*) with the first section (*anuvāka*); and after finishing his studies, he should do so with the last section.

While studying, one should not speak other words. (17) Wherever one perceives that an act of impurity has been committed, one should study only after performing purification once again. (18) Having gone out for the Pravargya ceremony, one should not study anything else until returning; one should not study anything else until returning.
(19) 11.22 Thus ends the eleventh book.
Now begins the twelfth book.

When the clarified butter from the *dhruva* vessel for the *ātithyā* offering has been taken five times into a ladle or a cup, he portions out the *tānūnaptra* with these mantras: "I take thee for Āpati," and so forth. Then the seventeen priests, including the sacrificer, or the four great priests with the sacrificer as the fifth, touch it together, saying: "Thou art unassailable, unassailable by the gods, the vigor of the gods, protecting against imprecation, and not to be imprecated. The sacrificer touches it, saying: "May the Lord of Consecration approve my consecration. Then the sacrificer should smell it three times.

"I offer you into Prajāpati, into the mind," [he says]. Or rather, he should lead [the King Soma] back day by day into each individual vow. Then he issues the command: "O Āgnīdh, [bring] the gladdening waters! The Āgnīdhra responds: "The divine waters gladden, immortal, increasing the cosmic order. The Adhvaryu says: "Run hither with them! Having purified [the King Soma] with the gladdening waters and loosened him, they cause the King to swell with their hands holding gold, beginning with the words: "O divine Soma, may that which they touch when they handle the *tānūnaptra*—may that strength of yours swell," and concluding with "svasti" (well-being).

With the formula ending, "O divine Soma, may I attain the pressing," (9) they perform the *nihnuvana* at the southern edge of the altar on the *prastara* grass, placing their right hands palm-upward and their left hands downward, with the words, "Desired riches for the impulse, for fortune" (10). Thereupon he issues the direction: "O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā" (11). He issues this same direction for all subsequent Subrahmaṇyā invocations (12). During the Subrahmaṇyā invocation, he causes the sacrificer to recite: "Thou art the Subrahmaṇyā; of thee, the earth is one foot."

"You are Subrahmaṇyā; of you, the intermediate space is one foot. You are Subrahmaṇyā; of you, the sky is one foot. You are Subrahmaṇyā; of you, the quarters are one foot. That which is beyond the dust (the sun) is your fifth foot. As such, milk for us nourishment, vigor, brilliance, sensory power, Vedic luster, and food. 13. In this very manner, he causes the sacrificer to recite at all *subrahmaṇyā* invocations. 14. 12.1.

Then he undergoes the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*). Standing to the south, he addresses the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra: "O Agni, lord of vows, you are the lord of vows. He tightens his girdle more closely; he clenches his fist more tightly. He becomes one whose vow is heated. He purifies himself with the *madantī* waters. He undertakes the vow with the mantra: "That body of yours, O Agni, which is Rudra-like... The sacrificial grass used for the guest-offering (*ātithyā*) is also that of the Upasads and the offering to Agni-Soma.

That very [grass] is understood to be the *prastara* and the *paridhi*. Having performed the *pravargya*, he commences the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the *upasad*s; or rather, first the *upasad*. That *barhis* grass is already spread.

The enclosing sticks are those worn by him. He prepares a fuel-wood of ten pieces. Having made the *veda* grass-bundle and having strewn around the fires, having washed his hands, having set out the vessels, having spread the *ulaparājī* grass-mat, and having prepared the two strainers, he issues the command: "O Sacrificer, restrain your speech. Restraining his speech, he touches the vessels. Having prepared the sprinkling waters, having addressed the *brahman*, and having sprinkled the vessels, he releases his speech at the call for the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*). He then performs the *stambayajus* rite, taking up only the darbha-blades of the sacrificial grass. Having fixed the wooden sword (*sphya*) upright—

He issues the command: "Set down the *prokṣaṇī* waters; place the fuel (*idhma*) nearby; cleanse the *sruva* and the *sruca* ladles; bring the clarified butter (*ājya*)! (15) This is the same [procedure] up to the taking of the clarified butter (16). He takes [the butter] from the *dhruvā* vessel alone (17). Having consecrated the *prokṣaṇī* waters and addressed the *brahmán*, and having sprinkled the fuel and the altar, he pours out the remainder of the *prokṣaṇī* water. Having consecrated the fire and placed the first *āghāra*-fuel stick, he sets down the *dhruvā* within the altar and places the *sruva* ladle there.
He modifies the mantra to "this is not non-existent. 18. He consecrates the clarified butter with the mantra: "Thou art Viṣṇu's; thou art the abode of Viṣṇu; thou belongest to Prajāpati. 19. 12.2.

Having placed the *vedī* in front of the *dhruvā*, he issues the call for the *sāmidhenī* verses. (1) There are nine *sāmidhenī* verses. (2) Having offered the *srauva* *āghāra* libation, he issues the call: "O *agnīdh*, cleanse the enclosing sticks and the fire three times each. (3) [The ritual] is the same up to the *pravara*. (4) Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "Sit down, O Hotṛ! (5) This much constitutes the *pravara*. (6) When he recognizes [the formula]: "O Adhvaryu, place the butter-laden ladle," then he takes eight spoonfuls from the *dhruvā* into the *juhū*.

Taking four portions into the *upabhṛt* ladle, he issues the command: "Recite for Agni" (7). Having stepped across and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "Sacrifice to Agni" (8). When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers half [of the butter] with the *juhū* ladle (10). Without stepping back across again, he issues the command: "Recite for Soma" (11). Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "Sacrifice to Soma" (12). When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers the whole [remaining portion] (13). Standing right there, he issues the command: "Recite for Viṣṇu" (14). Having poured the contents of the *upabhṛt* into the *juhū* and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "Sacrifice to Viṣṇu" (15).

When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he makes the offering. Having stepped back, he offers the *upasad* with the *sruva*-ladle using the verse: "O Agni, that body of yours which is the devourer... (VS 5.3). It is known from tradition: if they should fight in front [of the fire], he should place iron in the first [offering], silver in the middle one, and gold in the last one. According to some teachers, this applies if they should fight in battle. Having offered the *upasad*, they cause the King Soma to swell in the same manner and perform the concealment (*nihnava*) in the same manner. Then they proceed with the *upasad* rites. Thereafter, he gives the call to the *agnīdh*.

"Explain the wives of the gods, O Subrahmaṇya; invoke the Subrahmaṇyā," [he says]. 22. Sitting down to the west of the Gārhapatya fire, the Āgnīdhra explains the wives of the gods by reciting this section beginning with "O Indra, [the wives] of Senā. 23. The Subrahmaṇya invokes the Subrahmaṇyā. 24. The Upasad rite is concluded. 25. 12.3. In the afternoon, they proceed with the afternoon Pravargya and Upasad rites. 1. He offers the oblation with the same verse as before. 2. Only this much is different: those which would be the *yājyās* in the morning, he should make them the *puronuvākyās* in the evening.

Those which are the *puronuvākyās* shall be the *yājyās*. 3. Having turned their left hands upward, they perform the *nihnavana* (concealment) with their right hands held downward. 4. At midnight, he consumes the fast-food (*vrata*) from four teats. 5. He remains awake during this night. 6. In the early forenoon, they proceed with the two *pravargya-upasad* rites of the forenoon. 7. He offers the *upasad* oblation called *rajāśayā* here. 8. When the *upasad* is concluded, he measures out the great altar (*mahāvedī*), [saying]:
"I measure thee, the milk-abounding one, the well-milking cow of the gods, who does not fail. May Indra drink the Soma; may there be security for us."

Thus, having stepped three steps eastward from the front of the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, he drives in a peg; this is the peg marking the rear limit of the *vedi*. Then, having stepped thirty-six steps eastward from that, he drives in a peg; this is the peg for the sacrificial post-hole (*yūpāvaṭya*). From the peg marking the rear limit, having stepped fifteen steps southward and fifteen steps northward, he drives in two pegs; these become the two hips (*śroṇī*). From the peg for the sacrificial post-hole, [he steps] twelve steps southward.

Having stepped out twelve steps from that [central] peg, he drives in another peg. (16) There are two such [peg-spans]. (17) Then, having measured it diagonally with the measuring-cord, he stretches it around with a cord. (18) He stretches the *pṛṣṭhyā* line along it. (19) Then they mark it out with a wooden sword (*sphya*), a hoe (*vighana*), a rib-bone (*parśu*), and an axe (*paraśu*). (20) 12.4.12.4.19–20.

Then he consecrates it with the consecration belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices, excluding that which follows the bending [of the grass]. Having performed that which precedes the second tracing out of the altar, he measures out the northern altar to the west of the place for the sacrificial post-hole, using a wooden pin (śamyā), measuring either one śamyā or one yoke (yuga) in length.

Or alternatively, [he measures] ten paces in every direction. Having stepped out one pace toward the north from the northern edge of the altar, he drives in a peg; that becomes the *cātvāla* pit. Twelve paces behind the *cātvāla*, at that same distance toward the north, is the rubbish-heap (*utkara*). Six paces behind the rubbish-heap is the *āgnīdhra* shed. Between the *cātvāla* and the rubbish-heap, there is a path for movement.

According to some, [the path] is between the *cātvāla* and the *āgnīdhra*. Whatever one intends to carry along the *vedī*, one should carry it by this very route. Having performed the rites for the *uttaravedī* according to its procedure, having kept it burning, and having performed the rites up to the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), he causes it to be covered with branches of the *udumbara* tree and encloses it. At midday, he consumes the fast-food (*vrata*) consisting of three teats. In the afternoon, they proceed with the two afternoon offerings. He offers only on the *rajāśayā* brick. At midnight, he consumes the fast-food consisting of two teats. In the early morning, [they proceed] with the two morning offerings.

They proceed with the Pravargya and Upasad rites. (14) He offers the Upasad oblation upon the Harāśayā [fire]. (15) At that very time, they proceed with the afternoon Pravargya and Upasad rites. (16) He offers [the oblation] upon the Harāśayā itself. (17) At midday, he consumes the one-teat [milk] as his fast-food. (18) The Upasads are concluded. (19) 12.5

Having removed the *pravargya* vessel, he leads forward the fire according to the procedure for the fire; then, for the sake of the *āmikṣā* and the *dadhigharma*, he drives away the calves. He should designate them for Mitra and Varuṇa in the case of the *āmikṣā*, and for Indra in the case of the *dadhigharma*. Then the Adhvaryus bring abundant sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the great altar, as in the New and Full Moon sacrifices. Thereafter, he performs the second tracing of the altar, as in the New and Full Moon sacrifices. They do not perform the ritual over the already traced ground until the sprinkling of water. He prepares the sprinkling waters according to the procedure for the *prokṣaṇīs*.

Having consecrated [the materials] and addressed Brahmā, he sprinkles the altar and the sacrificial grass three times, as in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. Then they spread this sacrificial grass over the entire Mahāvedi, as in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
"Those who kindle the fire and spread the sacrificial grass continuously, for whom Indra is a youthful friend."

Some recite this as the *staraṇī* (the spreading formula). Others turn the two *havirdhāna* carts around behind the altar, facing east, after they have been washed, their knots untied, their yokes fastened, and their poles placed upon them, and they are covered with roofs. Then, on the northern altar-ground (*auttaravedika*), he offers an oblation with the verse, “They yoke the mind. From this point onward, all the rites pertaining to the *āhavanīya* fire are performed on this very spot. The wife, with her right hand, three times touches the southern pole-yoke of the southern *havirdhāna* cart at its third part from the front.

"Recite for the two *havirdhāna* carts as they are being moved forward. When the first verse has been recited three times, they move them forward while lifting them up, with the words: "Go forward; prepare the sacrifice. If a cart should creak, he should consecrate it with the formula: "O God of fair speech, speak auspiciously for our dwellings. The Adhvaryu, having placed a piece of gold on the southern track of the southern *havirdhāna*, offers an oblation with the verse: "Viṣṇu strode through this [world]. In the same manner, the Pratiprasthātṛ does so on the northern track of the northern *havirdhāna*.

Having placed gold nearby, he offers with the verse: "O ye two, be full of nourishment and full of milch-cows. In this regard, there is this specific rule: whatever rites belong to the southern side, the Adhvaryu should perform them; those belonging to the northern side, the Pratiprasthātṛ should perform. At the third part [of the distance], the Hotṛ, mentally, drives away human fear with his foot, saying:
"Drive away human fear; turn back the wheels. Go to the house of Soma!"

Thus [it is said]. According to some, [the one who places the axle] is the *adhvaryu*; according to others, the *brahman*; according to others, the *yajamāna*. Behind the *uttaravedi*, at three *prakramas* or at an indefinite distance, they place the two [axles] on both sides of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line so that they are centered; [they do so] with the formula: "Rest here on the height of the earth. The space between the two *havirdhāna* carts should be as large as required. They prop them up with the formula: "Thou art Vaiṣṇava; may Viṣṇu prop thee up. They are elevated in front. The *adhvaryu* [stands] by the southern *havirdhāna*.

To the north, at the piercing of the northern ear, he drives in a post with the verse: "Now shall I proclaim the heroic deeds of Viṣṇu. (1) They fasten the two *havirdhāna* carts to those posts with the formula: "O Viṣṇu, you are the seam. (2) He makes a knot with the formula: "O Viṣṇu, you are the firm one. (3) The first knot that he ties should remain clearly visible. (4) They level the ground behind them. (5) Having pulled up the *śamyās* upright, they enclose the area from above. (6) Having driven two pillars in front of the *havirdhānas*, [he places] its tip pointing north upon them.

Having placed the *vaṃśa* (bamboo beam) upon that [post], he fixes the *rarāṭī* (forehead-piece) against it with the formula, "Thou art the forehead of Viṣṇu. (7) He sews the *rarāṭī* crosswise through the *vaṃśa* with the formula, "Thou art the needle of Viṣṇu. (8) With the formula, "Thou art the fixed point of Viṣṇu," he makes a knot. (9) The first knot which he ties shall remain known and lie loose. (10) With the formula, "Thou art the back of Viṣṇu," he places the middle roof-covering on top. (11) With the formula, "Thou art the two straps of Viṣṇu," he fastens the two ends of the *rarāṭī*. (12) The mats...

He places the *stejanī* (water-strainers) in the intermediate spaces; these they call the "interstitial" ones. With the verse, "O lover of songs, may our songs encompass thee," he encloses [the shed]. They leave two doors open.

The eastern and western *śālāmukhīya* fires for the *hotṛ* and the *auttaravedika* fire are the same in their appearance (*sāṃkāśina*). The Adhvaryu sews [the altar] at the southern door with the formula, "O Viṣṇu, you are the needle," and the Pratiprasthātṛ at the northern door. He makes a knot with the formula, "You are the firmness of Viṣṇu. The first knot he ties should remain clearly known and lie loose.
He touches the completed [altar] with the formula, "You belong to Viṣṇu; for Viṣṇu, you! From the completed [altar], he steps out toward the east, leading the sacrificer.
For that heroic deed, Viṣṇu is praised like a fearsome beast, roaming and dwelling in the mountains,
in whose three wide strides all the worlds abide.

Thus it is known: "He causes [the sacrificer] to step three times. According to some, he steps out. They erect the *havirdhāna* shed with its beams facing east. The *āgnīdhra* shed has its beams facing east, with its door to the south; half is within the altar and half is outside the altar. The *sadas* hall is laid out crosswise, extending toward the north. Regarding this, there is the following specific instruction.

The Adhvaryu should not pass between the two Havirdhāna sheds (7). If he should pass, he should walk along with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu or one addressed to Kṣetrapati (8). He should not pass behind the Sadas (9). If he should pass, it is known that he should walk along with a verse addressed to Indra (10). Having stepped three steps eastward from the western peg, he drives in a peg; that is the western limit of the Sadas (11). To the south of the Pṛṣṭhyā line, at a distance of one step, he fixes the Audumbarī post in the middle of the entire Sadas (12). It is known that the Sadas measures nine aratnis across and twenty-seven [aratnis] extending northward.

According to some, there are eighteen [officiants] (13). According to some, he constructs the *sadas* to whatever extent he deems sufficient for the *ṛtvij*s, the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths, and the *prasarpaka*s (14). Having taken up the spade with the *sāvitra* formula, he traces around the pit for the *audumbarī* post, saying: "The *rakṣas* is traced around; the enemies are traced around" (15). Having dug it, he sprinkles the *audumbarī* post with water containing barley-grains, [using the formulas]: "For heaven thee! over the top; "For the intermediate space thee! over the middle.

"Thou for the earth"—with these words [he addresses] the root [of the post]. 16. The pouring out of water, the scattering of barley, and the spreading of sacrificial grass have been explained in the section on the sacrificial post (yūpa). 17. 12.9. With the verse, "Support the sky, fill the mid-air," the Udgātṛ priest raises the post with its ear turned eastward. 1. With the formula, "May Dyutāna Māruta raise thee," he fixes it with its ear turned eastward. 2. The filling around, the firming, and the sprinkling around have been explained in the section on the sacrificial post. 3. Then, having placed gold between its two ears, he makes an offering over it with the formula, "O Heaven and Earth, be filled with ghee, svāhā!"

He pours [the water] down to the very end. The Audumbara post is as high as the sacrificer; they erect it so that it reaches to the top of the roof-beams. He constructs the Sadas shed to be as high as the sacrificer, or even lower. If he should desire, "May Parjanya be rainy," he should erect it lower. If he should desire, "May it be rainless," he should erect it higher.

"It is known from tradition that they fix [the posts] up to the level of the navel. (7) With the formula, "Thou art Indra’s," he places each of the middle roof-coverings on top. (8) With the formula, "Thou art Indra’s seat," he places the southern ones. (9) With the formula, "The shade of all people," he places the northern ones. (10) He places the southern ones to the north [of the central ones]. (11) They face toward the post made of Udumbara wood. (12) One should fix the Agniṣṭoma with nine coverings, the Ukthya with fifteen coverings, and the Atirātra with seventeen coverings.

The *ṣoḍaśin* [chariot] has either nine roofs or fifteen roofs. "One desiring splendor (*tejas*) should erect one with nine roofs"—thus the optional rules regarding the roofs, as explained in the Brāhmaṇa, have been stated. Covering the interior, enclosing, sewing together, tying knots, and touching—these are the differences. These mantras belong to Indra. 12.10 We shall now explain the *uparavas*. Below the southern *havirdhāna* cart, in front of the axle and in the intermediate directions, there are four [holes], each a span (*prādeśa*) in width and separated by a span.

[The altar] is unbroken at the top and hollowed out below. Having taken the spade with a verse addressed to Savitṛ, he draws a line around it, saying: "The Rakṣas is enclosed; the enemies are enclosed. First on the two southern [corners], then the western, then the northern, then the eastern. In this manner, from this point forward, the rites are performed upon these [altars] in successive order. Having dug them to the depth of an arm's length, he strikes with the spade, saying: "I dig the Rakṣas-slayers, the Valaga-slayers, belonging to Viṣṇu."

He mutters the mantra only once: "Thou art Virāj, the slayer of rivals. Having lowered his arm, he throws out the loose earth with the formula: "Here I throw out that hidden treasure which a kinsman or a stranger has buried against us. Having placed it into the pit of the *uparava* hole, he presses it down with the formula: "I make him lower than this, whoever—whether a kinsman or a stranger—acts as an enemy; by the Gāyatrī metre. In this very same manner, with each subsequent mantra, having lowered his arm over each successive [pit], he throws out the loose earth with each subsequent [formula].

He suppresses [the enemy] with the *chandas* meters: the *traiṣṭubha*, the *jāgata*, the *ānuṣṭubha*, and the *pāṅkta*; these are the ones prescribed. (9) With the words, "The secret spell (*valaga*) is cast out," he carries away the loose earth. (10) With the words, "The malicious one is suppressed," having piled it on the mound (*khara*), he suppresses it. (11–12) 12.11

Then the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer touch [the stones]. (1) That which is the southern one of the two front [stones] is touched by the sacrificer; that which is the northern one of the two rear [stones] is touched by the Adhvaryu. (2) They touch their hands together from below. (3) The sacrificer asks: "Adhvaryu, what is here? (4) "Auspicious," says the Adhvaryu. (5) "May that be ours together," says the sacrificer. (6) Then they move around. (7) That which is the northern one of the two front [stones] is touched by the sacrificer; that which is the southern one of the two rear [stones] is touched by the Adhvaryu. (8)

They touch their hands together from below. 9. The sacrificer asks: "Adhvaryu, what is here? 10. "Auspicious," says the Adhvaryu. 11. "May that be in me," says the sacrificer. 12. Then he touches them with these mantras: "Thou art Virāj, the slayer of rivals. 13. Then he sprinkles them with sprinkling-water containing barley-grains, saying: "I sprinkle the ones belonging to Viṣṇu, the slayers of Rakṣases, the destroyers of secret spells (valaga). 14. He pours water over them, saying: "I pour down the ones belonging to Viṣṇu, the slayers of Rakṣases, the destroyers of secret spells. 15. "Thou art barley."

"Drive away hatred from us," with these words he throws barley-grain. (16) He spreads the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with the formula: "I spread you, the Rakṣas-slayers, the spell-slayers, belonging to Viṣṇu. (17) He sprinkles it with clarified butter (*ājya*) with the formula: "I offer upon you, the Rakṣas-slayers, the spell-slayers, belonging to Viṣṇu. (18) Thus some recite the mantras for the *uparava* holes. (19) "I sprinkle you two, the Rakṣas-slayers, the spell-slayers, belonging to Viṣṇu," with these words he sprinkles the two pressing-boards (*adhiṣavaṇaphalaka*). They are made of Udumbara, Palāśa, or Kārṣmarya wood; they may be either unperforated or perforated. (20) 12.12

The two lower pressing-boards (*adhiṣavaṇaphalaka*) are joined together at the front, cut even, and behind them they are two fingers wide, or four fingers wide. They are narrower in front and wider behind. He places two on the south side and two on the north side with the formula: "I set down these two belonging to Viṣṇu, slayers of Rakṣases, destroyers of secret spells. He piles earth around them with the formula: "I pile earth around these two belonging to Viṣṇu, slayers of Rakṣases, destroyers of secret spells. He strews grass around them with the formula: "I strew grass around these two belonging to Viṣṇu, slayers of Rakṣases, destroyers of secret spells."

"Thou art Vaiṣṇavī," he addresses [the two pressing-boards]. "The two slayers of Rakṣases, the destroyers of secret spells, thou art Vaiṣṇavī," [he says]. "I sprinkle thee, the slayer of Rakṣases, the destroyer of secret spells, who art Vaiṣṇava," with these words he sprinkles the hide of a red bull over the two pressing-boards. He spreads the hide of a red bull over the two pressing-boards with the hair upwards and the neck towards the pouring-out, saying: "The slayer of Rakṣases, the destroyer of secret spells, I spread thee, who art Vaiṣṇava. Upon it he places four pressing-stones, with their upper surfaces even and their striking-edges facing outward—the one most forward in the middle.

The fifth [verse] is: "Thou art great, O great pressing-stone; utter for Indra the great voice"—reciting these one by one. From the loose earth of the Uparava holes, he makes a four-cornered mound (khara) in front of the support of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, as large as he deems sufficient to hold the vessels. 10 12.13.

From the *cātvāla* pit, he scatters the *dhishṇiya* hearths: 1. In the *āgnīdhra* shed, within the altar, he scatters the *āgnīdhrīya* hearth with the formula, "Thou art abundant, the carrier. 2. To this mantra, he everywhere appends the phrase, "With the fierce weapon. 3. To the west of the opening of the *sadas*, on the *pṛṣṭhyā* line, he scatters the *hotrīya* hearth with the formula, "Thou art the bearer, the carrier of oblations. 4. To the south of the *hotrīya*, he scatters the *praśāstrīya* hearth with the formula, "Thou art invigorating, the wise one. 5. To the north of the *hotrīya*, he scatters the others toward the north. 6. With the formula, "Thou art Tutha, the all-knowing," he scatters the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* hearth. 7.

"Thou art the eager one, the sage," [this is] for the Potṛ; 8. "Thou art the swift one, the supporter," [this is] for the Neṣṭṛ; 9. "Thou art the seeker of aid, the worshipper," [this is] for the Acchāvāka; 10. On the southern half of the Vedi, [he establishes] the Mārjālīya with the formula, "Thou art the pure one, the Mārjālīya," [measuring it] by the Prṣṭi-line from the Āgnīdhrīya fire; 11. 12.14.

Then he pays homage to the others: 1. "Thou art the sovereign, Kṛśānu," [he says] to the Āhavanīya fire. 2. "Thou art the one to be attended, the purifying one," [he says] to the place where they chant the Bahiṣpavamāna. 3. "Thou art the swift one, possessed of mist," [he says] to the Cātvāla pit. 4. "Thou art unpolished, the preparer of the oblation," [he says] to the Śāmitra site. 5. "Thou art the abode of Truth, the light of heaven," [he says] to the Audumbarī post. 6. "Thou art the light of Brahman, the abode of heaven," [he says] to the seat of the Brahman priest. 7. "Thou art the ocean, all-encompassing," [he says] to the Sadas hall. 8. "Thou art the goat, the one-footed," [he says] to the Śālāmukhīya fire.

9. With the words, "Thou art the serpent of the depths," [he addresses] the *prājahita* fire. 10. With the words, "Thou art the sage (*kavya*), the bearer of the sages," [he addresses] the *anvāhāryapacana* fire. 11. Here some prescribe the spreading of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). 12. Then he issues the command: "Spread the sacrificial grass; prepare the *vrata*-milk; summon those who share in the *vrata*. 13. They do not spread [grass] over the *khara* mound, nor over the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths. 14. At this point, he gives him the one-breast *vrata*-milk. 15. 12.15

He initiates the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma. He binds a branch of the *plakṣa* tree to the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) used for the guest-offering (*ātithyā*). He places the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) of the guest-offering onto the fuel-wood (*idhma*). He prepares a fuel-wood bundle consisting of thirty-three pieces of wood. This remains the same up until the taking of the clarified butter portions (*ājya*). He takes the clarified butter portions pertaining to the animal sacrifice at the *Śālāmukhīya* fire. From this point onward, all rites pertaining to the *Gārhapatya* fire are performed in that very place. They bring forward the Soma, the pressing-stones, the Vāyu-cups, and the wooden trough (*droṇakalaśa*); they lead the wife forward, and they cause the Anūna-spoons to be moved along.

7. They assign the duties of the *gārhapatya* fire to the *śālāmukhīya* fire. 8. The wife goes forward first toward the eastern fire with the verse, "Let the Brahman’s wife go forward. 9. With the words, "O Agni, lord of the house, call me hither," and so forth, they perform the rites at the *śālāmukhīya* fire until the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) of the *gārhapatya*. 10. In his lap, the *brahmā* priest places the King Soma. 11. They summon the kinsmen of the sacrificer. 12. The sacrificer takes hold of the *adhvaryu*; the wife takes hold of the sacrificer; and the other sons and brothers take hold of the wife. 13.

Having covered the attendants with new garments and having brought the end of a garment near to the handle of the offering-ladle, he offers the Vaisarjana oblations with the mantra: "O Soma, you [offer] for those who have harmed the body... (VS 3.50). Having offered the second oblation with "May the swift one, enjoying the clarified butter, accept it; Svāhā! (VS 3.51), [he proceeds]. 12.16.14–15.

Having kindled the fuel at the front of the hall, he issues the command: "Recite for Agni and Soma as they are being led forth. When the first verse has been recited three times, they proceed eastward with Agni leading the way. Then they carry after him the clarified butter, they carry after the fuel and the sacrificial grass, they pour after the sprinkling water, and [they lead] the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma. The Āgnīdhra, having set down this fuel, makes an offering over it with the verse containing the word "lead": "May this Agni create wide space for us. Right here [he places] the pressing-stones and the Vāyavya cups.

He causes the *nakalaśa* to remain overnight at the Āgnīdhra shed. With the formula, "O Viṣṇu, stride out widely," they proceed eastward, with Soma leading. Having offered an oblation in the Āhavanīya fire, he causes King Soma to enter the Havirdhāna shed by the western door with the verse, "Soma goes forth, finding the path."

When the King [Soma] is near, the sacrificer addresses him: "O divine Savitṛ, this is your Soma; protect it; let it not deceive you. O Soma, as a god, you have approached the gods. (1) He turns clockwise, saying: "Here I, a human, [approach] humans, together with offspring, together with the increase of wealth. (2) He makes a hollowed gesture (*añjali*) toward the east, saying: "Homage to the gods! (3) Toward the south, he says: "Svadhā to the ancestors! (4) He steps out, saying: "Here I [emerge] from the noose of Varuṇa. (5)

He gazes at the sacrificial hall with the mantra: "May I behold the excellent light; may Vaiśvānara shine forth as light. (6) Thereupon, he releases the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*). (7) Standing to the south, he addresses the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra: "O Agni, Lord of Vows, you are the lord of vows among all vows. (8) He tightens his girdle very firmly. (9) Then he releases his two fists with the following mantras: "Svāhā! To the sacrifice, through the mind"—two times; "Svāhā! To Heaven and Earth"—two times; "Svāhā! From the wide atmosphere"—two times.

"OṂ SVĀHĀ! I undertake the sacrifice from the wind"—with these two [formulas] (10). "OṂ SVĀHĀ! I release the wind into speech"—with this he releases his speech (11). The vow is concluded (12). On the day of the Soma-pressing, he consumes the remnants of the oblation, [reciting]: "The Somas, the remnants of the oblation" (13). Then he sprinkles the fuel and the sacrificial grass (barhis) as in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices (14). Now, one [teacher] says that he should spread this sacrificial grass over the entire Great Altar (mahāvedi) (15).

"To the north of the *uttaravedi*," [says another]. Whatever sacrificial grass (*barhis*) should come from that point upwards, one should spread it in this very manner. It is the same up to the placing of the offering-ladles (*sruk*). Having placed the ladles... 12.18.16–18.

He cuts the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). (1) He cuts the sacrificial post during the initiation rites (*dīkṣā*) or during the *upasad* days. (2) It is known from scripture: "If the sacrificial post of one who has been initiated should be broken, he should take the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) and the clarified butter (*ājya*), churn fire at the base of the post, and offer an oblation. (3) Furthermore, if the Soma has already been purchased, he should offer the oblation in the *āhavanīya* fire itself. (4) [The ritual] is the same up to the bringing forward of the animal victim (*paśūpākaraṇa*). (5) He brings forward the animal victim for Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya*). (6) [The ritual] is the same up to the choosing of the priests (*pravara*). (7) Having chosen the Hotṛ priest with the standard *pravara*, and having again called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says "Upām̐... [etc.].

Taking up the wooden sword (asphya) and uttering the names, he chooses the other officiating priests to the north: 8. "Indra as the Hotṛ—this man here [is] human," [he says], choosing the Hotṛ. 9. "Agni as the Āgnīdhra—this man here [is] human," [he says], choosing the Āgnīdhra. 10. "The Aśvins as the two Adhvaryus; I and this man here [are] human from the office of the Adhvaryu," [he says], choosing himself and the Pratiprasthātṛ. 11. "Mitra and Varuṇa as the two Praśāstṛs; this man here [is] human from the office of the Praśāstṛ," [he says], choosing the Maitrāvaruṇa. 12. "Indra as the Brahman; this man here [is] human from the office of the Brāhmaṇ," [he says], choosing the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin. 13. [He continues in the same manner for the others.]

"O Maruts, this man from the office of the *potr*," [with these words] he chooses the *potr*. 14. "O *gnās*, this man from the office of the *neṣṭṛ*," [with these words] he chooses the *neṣṭṛ*. 15. Then he chooses the sacrificer: "Agni is the leader of the divine clans; this one, pressing the Soma, is the leader of men. May the household duties of us two not be deficient; may we prosper for a hundred winters. May we two, though not mingling our bodies, be united in our wealth. 16. Some choose [the sacrificer] at the *savanīya* [offering]; there he should say, "this one, pressing the Soma... 17. At the *agnīṣomīya* [offering], when choosing, he says, "...this sacrificer is the leader of men. 18. 12.19.
At each turn, he offers two *pravṛta* oblations with these two [verses]: "May I be beloved of speech; with a Ṛg-verse, prosper the hymn. One view is that he should offer them at every turn.

The Adhvaryu alone should offer the oblation; this is another view. Up to the offering of the omentum (vapā), the procedure is the same. When the omentum has been offered, the Subrahmaṇya priest invokes the Subrahmaṇyā litany addressed to the father and son. In the afternoon, he takes up the Vasatīvarī waters from flowing streams while standing against the current. He brings a jar near with the formula, "These waters are rich in sacrificial food. He should not pass by the very last flowing stream. He takes the water at the junction of shade and sunlight.

In the shade of a tree or of oneself; or he should take it when the sun sets over something that has not been grasped, or he should grasp it by means of light, or having placed gold [within]; or he should take it from the pot of a Brahmin who performs many sacrifices; according to some, he should take it after giving a boon. Then he places it to the west of the Gārhapatya fire with the formula: "I place you in the seat of Agni, whose house is secure. The procedure up to the *iḍā*-portion is the same. He carries the *samavatta* (the collected portions) to the south of the two *havirdhāna* carts, or to the north. From there...

He gives the command: "O Āgnīdhra, bring the embers for the supplementary offerings (upayaja). Having brought the embers from either the Śāmitra or the Āgnīdhra fire, the Āgnīdhra pours them out upon the Hotṛ’s hearth. The Pratiprasthātṛ performs the supplementary offerings. At this point, he does not offer the Svaru splinter at the end of the after-offerings (anūyāja).

He offers [the oblation] only at the *anūbandhyā* animal sacrifice, not at the *savanīya*. (18) Having commenced it during the day, he concludes it at night. (19) It concludes with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings. (20) Having performed the rite with the heart-spike (*hṛdayaśūla*), he does not perform the ritual worship of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). (21) They do not perform the rite with the heart-spike at the *agnīṣomīya* nor at the *savanīya*; according to some, they perform it only at the *anūbandhyā*. (22) 12.20

At night, while the sacrificer and his wife are seated within the *antarvedi*, they carry the *vasatīvarī* waters around them. (1) They should not carry the *vasatīvarī* waters around one who has not been initiated. (2) Having taken the water-pot and placed it on his left shoulder, having gone out by the southern door, and having walked along the southern edge of the altar, he sets it down on the northern corner of the southern *uttaravedi* with the formula: "You are the portion of Indra and Agni. (3) Having taken the pot and placed it on his right shoulder, he returns by the same way he came and [proceeds] with the northern [corner].

Having gone out through the eastern door and having walked around along the northern edge of the altar, he places [the vessel] on the northern corner of the northern altar with the formula: "You are the portion of Mitra and Varuṇa. (4) Having taken the pitcher and placed it on his left shoulder, and having returned by the same way he came, having gone out through the eastern door, he places it in the Āgnīdhra fire-hall with the formula: "You are the portion of the Viśve Devas; be watchful at the sacrifice. (5) He causes these [vessels] to remain overnight. (6) The Subrahmaṇya priest calls the Subrahmaṇyā litany, that which belongs to the father and son. (7) Then...

Then he gives instructions: "Prepare the milk-mixture (*āśira*) from the cow that provides the milk for the sacrificer’s vow; [prepare] curds for the wife for the *dadhi-graha* offering; [prepare] curds for the *gharma* from the cow that provides the milk for the *gharma*; prepare the heated and unanointed [milk] for the Maitrāvaruṇa cup, and the boiled and anointed [milk] for the Āditya cup. 8. They perform these tasks as directed. 9. At this point, he causes the evening milking for the *āmikṣā* to be performed. 10. They keep the sacrificer awake in the *havirdhāna* shed, and the wife to the east of the *vamśa*. 11. The *agnīdh* and the officiating priests remain there.
"No one dwells in the sacrificial hall; it is known that the sacrificer himself protects the King [Soma] during this night. Thus ends the twelfth question. Now begins the thirteenth question.

They wake up at the deep of night. With a verse addressed to Agni, he should touch the Āgnīdhra shed; with one addressed to Viṣṇu, the Havirdhāna shed; with one addressed to Agni, the offering-spoons; with one addressed to Vāyu, the Vāyavya vessels; and with one addressed to Indra, the Sadas. Regarding this, there is one view that he should touch them right here [at the time of waking]. Another view is that they are subsidiary parts of the ritual performed at the commencement of the ritual acts. In the Āgnīdhra shed, he offers the "Body of the Sacrifice" oblations: *Prajāpati manasāndho 'cchetaḥ* and so forth—these are thirty-three in number. He also offers the oblation for the affliction of the sacrifice (*yajñārti*).

It is known from tradition: "Having recited the preceding [verse], one offers with the following. However, first [one offers] with a single [verse]. On the mound (khara), he arranges the vessels with these mantras according to their respective forms: "Agni is the deity; the Gāyatrī is the meter; you are the vessel for the Upāṃśu [cup]. On the southern shoulder, he arranges the two vessels for the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma [cups].

First, he places the Upāṃśu cup to the west of the Antaryāma cup; or alternatively, the southern [cup] to the west of the Upāṃśu and the northern [cup] to the west of the Antaryāma. Between these two, he sets down the Upāṃśusavana stone so that it touches them. The vessels for the dual-deity offerings face west: the Indra-Vāyu vessel has three corners, the Maitrāvaruṇa vessel is made of goat-skin, and the Aśvin vessel has two corners. Behind those are the two vessels for the Śukra and Manthin; the southern one is made of Bilva wood, serving as the Śukra and Manthin vessels.

He sets out three vessels for the *atigrāhya* cups: 1. In front of the support of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, he places the *āditya* bowl and the *āditya* cup; in front of the support of the northern cart, on ground not strewn with sand, he places the *dhruva* bowl. 2. On the northern shoulder [of the altar], he places the four-cornered *audumbara* vessel for the *dadhi-graha*. 3. In the middle, he places the *pariplava* ladle, which has a handle like a sacrificial spoon. 4. According to available space, he places the four-cornered *khadira* vessel for the *ṣoḍaśin*, if the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice is performed. 5. These [vessels] are a span in measure and have upward-facing rims.

Those in the middle are curved and provided with pouring-spouts for the Vāyavya cups (6). Regarding those whose wood has not been specified, Āśmarathya says they may be made from whatever tree is fit for sacrifice; Ālekhana says they must be made of *vaikaṅkata* wood (7). By this, the application of trees for the *camasa* cups is explained.

"Let them be made of *nyagrodha* wood," so says another [tradition]. (8) There are ten cups, either provided with handles (*tsaruman*) or without handles (*atsaruka*). (9) There are ten cup-attendants (*camasādhvaryu*). (10) These cups belong to these [officiants]: the Hotṛ, the Brahman, the Udgātṛ, the Sacrificer, the Maitrāvaruṇa, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, the Potṛ, the Neṣṭṛ, the Acchāvāka, and the Āgnīdhra.

He assigns them to the cart according to their respective places. (11) Beneath the southern *havirdhāna* cart, behind the axle, he assigns the *droṇakalaśa* together with the fringe and the filter, [saying]: "I yoke the earth for thee along with light. (12) In the interior of the northern cart, he assigns the *ādhavanīya* [vessel], [saying]: "I yoke Vāyu for thee along with the intermediate region. (13) On the *prauga* [cart], he assigns the *pūtabhṛt* [vessel], [saying]: "I yoke speech for thee along with Sūrya. (14) At this point, some prescribe the employment of the hide for pressing and the pressing-stones. (15) They stand facing one another at the rear. (16) 13.2

Then he touches them, saying: "Dwellings of the waters, embryos of the cosmic order (ṛta), guardians of the world, hawks, guests, peaks of the mountains—like those who hasten to drink, with your voice you call Indra; with your roar you drive away disease. You are yoked; carry [the sacrifice]."

"Carry the sacrificer to the heavenly world," [he says]. 1. He begins the procedure for the *savanīya* offering. 2. It is the same up to the taking of the *ājya* portions. 3. From the ordinary *ājya*, he first takes [the portion] with the *pracaraṇī* ladle. 4. Together with the fuel-wood, he sprinkles those pieces of wood which he intends to place on the fire that day. 5. Whatever else he may place upon those two *āghāra*-fuel-sticks, he should place it only after it has been sprinkled. 6. It is the same up to the setting down of the ladles. 7. Having set down the ladles, he touches them, saying: "I yoke the three separate ones; they belong to the Sun."

Thus [it is said]. Here, some recite the purpose of the vessel: "Protect me from the mantra of the mouth, from any curse. Having offered in the Āgnīdhra fire, he pours down the King (Soma) onto the pressing-stones between the two poles with the formula: "For the heart, thee!"

With the two verses, "O King Soma, come hither; descend," he offers the Pañcahotṛ oblation in the Āgnīdhra fire and gives the direction to the Hotṛ for the Prātaranuvāka: "Recite for the gods who travel at dawn; O Brahman, restrain your speech; O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā; O Pratiprasthātṛ, pour out the grains for the Savanīya offerings and milk the curd-mixture. If he should hate anyone, he should prepare [the offering] while that person's words are being uttered. The Subrahmaṇya priest invokes the Subrahmaṇyā formula, which contains the word "son" (pitāputrīyā). At this point...
"One view is that he should offer the *savanīya* oblation and cause the *āmikṣā* to be milked; another view is that it should be milked later. 14.13.3.

When he recognizes [the verse], "Dawn has appeared with her bright cattle," he offers [an oblation] with the *pracaraṇī* ladle, [reciting]: "May Agni hear my call along with the fuel-stick. Having taken another fourfold portion and having taken darbha grass, he goes out and issues the command: "Go for water, O Hotṛ! O Camasādhvaryus of the Maitrāvaruṇa, come hither! O Adhvaryus of the Ekadhana vessels, come hither! O Neṣṭṛ, lead up the wife! O Unnetṛ, wait at the *catvāla* pit with the Hotṛ’s cup and the *vasatīvarī* waters! There are at least three odd-numbered *ekadhana* vessels.

3. They perform as they have been instructed. 4. With the words, "Go forth! Come forth! the Neṣṭṛ leads the wife forward. 5. At the place where he can hear the Hotṛ reciting the morning litany (prātaranuvāka), there the Adhvaryu should take water; if he were not to hear it, he would become deaf.

If [the water] should be cut off from the stream, if it is far away, he should draw it up by means of a counter-slope and take it. While the waters are flowing, he throws a blade of grass into them and offers this fourfold-drawn portion with the mantra: "O divine waters, O Son of the Waters. If there is already grass there before, he offers into that very [grass]. Having caused the oblation to overflow with *darbha* blades while reciting "Thou art the plougher," he draws out the water for Mitra and Varuṇa from those [waters] smeared with ghee with the mantra: "For the imperishability of the ocean, I draw you out. In this very same manner, he draws out the *ekadhana* waters.

"Of you, the Soma from Mount Mūjavan, I take the essence," [he says]. 11. Thus the wife takes the *pannejani* (foot-washing) waters, saying: "For the Vasus, for the Rudras, for the Ādityas, for the Viśve Devas, I take you as *pannejani* waters; for the sacrifice, I take you as *pannejani* waters. 12. They bring the water. 13. "Go forth! Come up!"—thus the Neṣṭṛ leads the wife forward. 14. 13.4.

To the north of the Neṣṭṛ’s hearth, the wife sets down the washing waters (pannejanī) with the formula: "For the Vasus, for the Rudras, for the Ādityas, for the Viśve Devas, I set you down as washing waters; for the sacrifice, I set you down as washing waters. 1. Having touched together the Hotṛ’s cup and the Maitrāvaruṇa’s cup over the Cātvāla pit, the Adhvaryu pours the Vasatīvarī waters into them with the formula: "The waters have united with the waters; the plants with the plants; those who observe vows with their vows. 2. Having poured [the water] into the Hotṛ’s cup...

He fills the cup of Mitrāvaruṇa; from the cup of Mitrāvaruṇa [he fills] the cup of the Hotṛ; from the cup of the Hotṛ [he fills] the cup of Mitrāvaruṇa. Then he anoints them together with the *pracaraṇī* ladle:
"May Varuṇa anoint you together, may Indra [anoint you] together, may Bṛhaspati, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Viṣṇu, bestowing wealth upon the sacrificer through progeny, grant him riches."

"Thus may the yokes be joined with their respective yoke-pins," and "May they be fit," [he says]. 4. The Hotṛ asks the Adhvaryu, "O Adhvaryu, have you drunk? 5. "We have indeed drunk," he replies. 6. Thereupon, if it is an Agniṣṭoma, he offers the Kratu-karaṇa oblation with the verse, "O Agni, that mortal whom you... 7. If it is an Ukthya, having offered [the oblation], he wipes the residue on the enclosing sticks (paridhi). 8. If it is a Ṣoḍaśin, having offered [the oblation] and wiped the residue on the enclosing sticks, he touches either the Droṇakalaśa vessel or the forehead-piece (rarāṭī) of the cart. 9. [In other cases] he neither offers nor wipes.

He causes the waters to enter the *havirdhāna* shed either by the rear door or by the front door; however, the sacrificer enters by the front door. Beneath the northern *havirdhāna*, he deposits the *vasatīvarī* waters, the *ekadhana* waters, and those for the *maitrāvaruṇa* cup. Having deposited the *hotṛ* cup in front of the axle beneath the southern *havirdhāna*, he proceeds with the *dadhi-graha* (curd-offering). He takes the curd in a four-cornered vessel made of *udumbara* wood, [saying]: "Thou art taken with a support; for Prajāpati, thee!"

"Into the luminous one, I take the luminous one," [with these words] he draws [the cup]. 4. He carries it away with "O Indra, [ward off] the mind of the hater. 5. He offers it with the remainder of the section beginning "For breath thee. 6. One who desires splendor should take a draught of clarified butter; one who desires Vedic luster should take a draught of Soma.

One who desires cattle should take the *dadhigraha* (curd-offering). This same ritual procedure applies to the *ājyagraha* (ghee-offering). Intending to take the *somagraha* (Soma-offering), he pours out the King Soma upon the pressing-skin, as much as he deems sufficient for a single draught. Having placed the other [Soma] nearby and having filled the *hotṛcamasa* with the *vasatīvarī* waters, he causes the sacrificer to recite over the *nigrābhya* waters, beginning with "Ye are *nigrābhya*s, heard by the gods," and ending with "May my troops not thirst."

Having mixed [the soma] with the *vasatīvarī* waters and being about to press it, he consecrates it with the mantra: "I have increased you with my mind, O well-born ones. (11) Wherever he may press [the soma], he should consecrate it in this very same way. (12) Then he presses it upon the lower stone with the pressing-stone. (13) 13.6

"The gods, the seekers, have prepared three fuel-sticks for the mighty, circling immortal one. Of these, they have placed one as a benefit for mortals; two, being sisters, have gone to the world. (TS 6.2.8.6) Wherever one should press [the Soma], one should press with the lower pressing-stone. This is the mantra for the pressing of this very [Soma]. Whatever first shoot of the being-pressed [Soma] falls, one should consecrate it with: "May it fall upon me, together with offspring, together with the abundance of wealth. One should consecrate it at every pressing; such is one view.

"Whosoever is the very first"—this is another [formula]. He should consecrate the drops with the mantra, "The drop has fallen. One view is that he should consecrate them at every pressing. "Whosoever is the very last"—this is another [formula]. At this point, the sacrificer makes a handle for the *daśāpavitra* (the fringe-filter). Then, with his hand holding gold, he pours an unbroken stream across the filter and draws [the Soma] into the vessel for the *dadhighraha* (curd-offering).

"One should take it with the *vāyavya* [verse] alone"—this is another [view]. (9) Then he places it on the mound (*khara*) with the formula, "This is thy womb. (10) Then, facing eastward, he offers it with his hand containing gold. The mantras for that are explained by those of the *dadhi-graha*. (11) Or rather, it is not governed by the rules of the *soma*, because it is a modification of the *dadhi-graha*. (12) In this case, the pressing is for the purpose of taking [the substance], because of its connection with what follows; and the mantra for the pressing belongs to the *somakaraṇī*. (13) In this regard, there is this specific instruction. (14) 13.7

He takes all the Soma portions with his hand, which holds gold, and offers them; 1. He offers all the Soma oblations facing the east; 2. Having offered, he consumes the remainder in the *sadas*; 3. He washes the vessel at the *mārjālīya* fire-altar; 4. From this point onward, they consume the Soma portions only in the *sadas*.

In the Āgnīdhra shed, he consumes the sacrificial oblations; at the Mārjālīya, he washes the vessels containing the remnants. Then he draws the Adābhya cup. He plucks three shoots from the King [Soma] that has been bound, with these mantras: "May the Vasus pluck thee with the Gāyatrī metre," and so forth. Having poured out some of the Nigrābhya waters, curds, or milk into the cup, he shakes the shoots with these mantras: "O bright one, I shake thy bright [essence] into the gladdening waters," and so forth. According to some, he shakes it with three [mantras]; according to others, with five.

According to some, [he offers] with seven [verses]. (10) Then he draws [the cup] for him with the vessel for the *dadhighraha* [curd-offering], [reciting]: "I draw your bright [portion] with the bright; may Agni protect us at the morning pressing"—with these three verses. (11) He carries [it] forward with [the verse]: "In him the fierce ones have settled. (12) He offers [it] with [the verse]: "Soma is the leader of Soma. (13) Thereupon he mixes the shoots (*maṃśu*) and the swollen [portions] (*śūna*), reciting each time one of these formulas: "O divine Soma, you are a desirer (*uśik*) with the *gāyatrī* metre," and so on. (14) According to one view, he should mix them at each pressing.

At that very time, he should also release each one individually; this is another [view]. (15) He gives twelve six-year-old cows as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and a garment made of bark-fiber (*kṛttidhīvāsa*). (16) Then he takes the *maṁśu* stalk. (17) Upon the pressing-skin, he pours out the King [Soma] as much as he considers sufficient for a single cup-draught. (18) 13.8

Then, having pressed [the Soma] once without pausing, and causing an unbroken stream to flow across the filter, he takes [the Soma] into the Adābhya vessel once without pausing. It is known from tradition: "He takes it while mentally singing the Vāmadevya. According to some, he should take it with a verse of the Vāmadevya, namely, "With what [help], O wonderful one, will he come to us? It is known from tradition: "It is to be taken with the out-breath; it is to be taken with the in-breath; having breathed out and breathed in, it is to be taken with the inter-breath. Having taken it, he breathes over a piece of gold weighing a hundred mānas.

"May our breath come from afar," [he says]. (5) Having covered the cup with gold, he touches water, saying, "May Indra and Agni grant me luster. (6) Then he offers it once without drawing breath, saying, "When they have run... (7) If he is unable to offer or take it up without drawing breath, he should offer it after a boon has been granted. (8) Having offered it, he consumes the remainder in the Sadas hall as before. (9) He gives twelve four-year-old cows as the sacrificial fee, along with a garment woven with a fringe. (10) Thereafter follows the Upāṃśusavana pressing.

He takes up the pressing-stone, beginning with "In the impulse of the god Savitṛ" and ending with "the winner of rain. (11) Having taken it up, he restrains his speech until the Āgrayaṇa draught. (12) Then, with his hand holding gold, he measures out the King [Soma] upon the high back [of the skin], using these mantras: "O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra... (13) In this regard, the procedure for measuring is the same as that at the purchase [of Soma], except for the act of sweeping together. (14) Thereafter, he draws the Upāṃśu cup. (15) He pours the King [Soma] onto the pressing-skin, as much as he deems sufficient for a single draught. (16) 13.9
