Standing in front and facing west, he pours the *dhruva* vessel into the *hotṛ*-cup with the remainder of the section beginning, "The firm [vessel] with the firm... (1). According to some, sitting behind and facing east, he pours it in the direction of the hair (anuloma) (2). He causes a continuous stream to flow until the conclusion of the recitation (śastra) (3). Having responded to the recitation, the Adhvaryu takes up the cup.

The cup-attendants (camasādhvaryu) take up the cups. Having stepped across and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "O reciter of the *uktha*, sacrifice the Soma-cups! At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, they offer the oblations. The cup-holders consume [the Soma] from their respective cups. He modifies the consumption formula for the draught by saying, "Of that which has been drunk by Agni Vaiśvānara... Thereupon, he worships either the Āditya or the Āhavanīya fire, saying, "Thou art well-being, the best of rays; bestow life and power upon me; may that come to me."

"It is known that he takes the name of whichever [deity] he desires. (8) Indeed, this is the case if it is an Agniṣṭoma. (9) Now, if it is an Ukthya: having poured the entire King [Soma] into the cups and having wiped the two jars with the fringes of the cloth, he turns them upside down; thus this part of the formal command (*saṃpraiṣa*) is omitted. (10) While pouring out the Agniṣṭoma cups, he leaves over the King [Soma] for three groups of cups. (11) Thereafter, he draws the Ukthya portion just as at the morning pressing. (12) This much is different.

The taking up and setting down of the cup for Mitrā-Varuṇa are performed with the formula, "For Indra and Varuṇa, thee. For the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, it is, "For Indra and Bṛhaspati, thee. For the Achāvāka, it is, "For Indra and Viṣṇu, thee. In this very manner he recites these formulas for consuming the draughts. (13) This is indeed the case if there is an Ukthya sacrifice. (14) Now, if it is a Ṣoḍaśin sacrifice, while drawing out the cups for the Achāvāka, he leaves over the King Soma for one group of cups together with its cup.

When the sun has been consecrated by the *samaya* formula, he begins the *stotra* of the *ṣoḍaśin* with gold. 1. They hold before him a reddish-brown horse, or a dark one. 2. They chant the praise while handing over the gold. 3. The *stotra* contains the word "bay" (*hari*), the *śastra* contains the word "bay," and the *yājyā* verse contains the word "bay. 4. He worships the *ṣoḍaśin* with the verse: "He than whom there is no other born superior, who has entered into all beings—Prajāpati, in harmony with his offspring, he, the *ṣoḍaśin*, dwells with the three lights."
Thus (5), he responds to the recitation with the *pratigara* in reverse order: "Othā moda iva madā moda ivomathā. (6) Having responded to the recitation, the Adhvaryu takes up the cup;

the Camasādhvaryus take up their goblets. (7) Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "O reciter of the *uktha*, sacrifice the Soma-draughts! (8) When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, they offer. (9) He offers the *ṣoḍaśin* draught with the formula: "O Indra, sovereign lord! You are the sovereign lord of the gods; make me a sovereign lord among men, long-lived and full of splendor. (10) The participants drink from their respective goblets according to their cups.
Indra the sovereign and Varuṇa the king—those two first partook of this portion for you.
Of those two, I partake of the portion. May Speech, being pleased, be satisfied with the Soma.

Thus [ends the section]. 11. A reddish-brown horse, or a mule, is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). 12. This indeed is the case if there is a *ṣoḍaśin* [sacrifice]. 13. Now, if it is an *atirātra*, while drawing out the *ṣoḍaśin* cups, he leaves over for the King [Soma] what remains from thirteen groups of cups. 14. With the verse, "O Indra, for thee who art dark-red," he touches each principal cup. 15. He draws out the cups belonging to the Hotṛ. 16. The *stotra* and the *śastra* take place here. 17. Having responded to the *śastra*, the Adhvaryu takes up the cup.

The cup-attendants take up the cups. (18) Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "O reciter of the *uktha*, sacrifice the Soma-cups. (19) When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, they offer the oblations. (20) Each cup-bearer consumes [the Soma] from his own cup. (21) He modifies the consumption mantra as follows: "Of that which has been drunk by Indra, whose metre is the *anuṣṭubh*... (22) Thus ends the first group of cups. (23) 14.16

In this manner, three other groups of cups (camasa-gaṇa) are prescribed: the second group of cups has the cup of the Maitrāvaruṇa as its chief; the third has the cup of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin as its chief; and the fourth has the cup of the Achāvāka as its chief. By this, the sequence of the *śastra* recitations and the *yājyā* offerings is explained. Thus ends the first round (paryāya) of the night. Two further rounds are prescribed in the same manner. He draws the *saṃdhi*-cups, having the Hotṛ’s cup as their chief. The *stotra* consists of the *trivṛt* chant. The *śastra* belongs to the Aśvins.

It is known from tradition that he concludes [the ritual] after sunrise, when more than a thousand [stotriya verses] have been recited. He offers a cake on two potsherds to the Aśvins. He bakes the sacrificial cake with water purified by a *yajus*-formula. While the *barhis* grass is already strewn, he pours out the remnants of the flour. Having responded to the recitation of the *śastra* and having removed the cake from the fire, he issues the command: "Recite the invitatory verse for the Somas of the day-after-tomorrow belonging to the Aśvins. The Adhvaryu takes up the *graha* cup; the Camasādhvaryus take up the *camasa* cups.

The Pratiprasthātṛ takes up the *puroḍāśa* cake. Having stepped across and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "Prompt [the Hotṛ] regarding the Soma-pressings set forth for the Aśvins of the *tiroahniya* day. At the utterance of the *vaṣaṭ*, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers the *puroḍāśa* as a complete oblation together with the Soma. He modifies the *bhakṣa-mantra* thus: "Of that which has the *paṅkti* metre and has been drunk by the Aśvins. This is indeed the case if it is an *atirātra*. Now, if it is an *aptoryāma*, while drawing out the *saṃdhi-camasas*, he distributes the King Soma in excess over the four groups of cups.

In that [rite], four *stotras* and four *śastras* dedicated to the Aśvins, together with their respective *yājyās*, are prescribed. Their ritual procedure is explained by the same rules as those for the *saṃdhicamasas*. There is only this difference.

The first group of cups has the *hotṛ*’s cup as its chief; the second has the *maitrāvaruṇa*’s cup as its chief; the third has the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*’s cup as its chief; the fourth has the *achāvāka*’s cup as its chief. By this, the sequence of the *śastra* recitations and the *yājyā* offerings is explained. Having responded to the third pressing with the words, "The hymn has been spoken, O Indra," he modifies the *bhakṣa* mantra [for the soma] drunk by the Aśvins with the verse beginning, "Of that which is in the *aticchandas* meter. Then he issues the command: "O Āgnīdh, bring the embers for the supplementary offerings (*upayaja*). This is the same [as the preceding ritual].

8. From the throwing away of the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*): having thrown away the enclosing-sticks, the Unnetṛ draws the *Hāriyojana* cup. 9. Intending to draw the *Āgrayaṇa* with the *Droṇakalaśa*, he issues the command: "Recite for Indra accompanied by the bay horses (*harivat*) regarding the parched grains (*dhānā*) and the Soma-juices. 10. He draws [the cup] with the formula: "Thou art taken with a support; thou art the bay one, the *Hāriyojana*. 11. Having mixed it with many parched grains, having stepped across, and having called for the *Śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for the parched grains and the Soma-juices set forth for Indra accompanied by the bay horses. 12. When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, having placed [the cup] upon his head and having stepped apart.

They pour out [the water] undifferentiatedly upon the *uttaravedi* with the formula: "Ye are to be filled; fill me. (1) They throw three pieces of wood each into the fire with these mantras: "Thou art the expiation for sin committed against the gods," and so forth. (2) Having placed yellow *dūrvā* grass into the remnants of the *ekadhana* waters, having pressed them together and made them strong, they distribute them according to the cups; standing behind the *cātvāla*, they smell them while facing eastward with the formula: "O divine Soma, of thee who art washed in the waters... (3) He pours out the remainder within the altar, or into the *cātvāla* according to some, with the formula: "I send you to the ocean; go back to your own source."
May our heroes be unharmed; let them rise up for us, and may our own property not be poured away.
Having thus led [the calf] four times, he consecrates it with the mantra:

"O Maruts, may this song of praise reach you; may it reach Viṣṇu, the protector of the infused seed, with his aids. And for the sake of progeny, may he bestow vigor; do you protect us always with your blessings."

Thus, having entered the Āgnīdhrīya shed, they consume the curds and drops with this verse: "I have performed the service for Dadhikrāvan. Then those who touched the *tānūnaptra* mixture release their bonds of friendship with this verse:
"Both are young seers, true lords of the law;
O lord of the law of truth, we release our bonds of friendship."

Thus (7). Then they perform the *saṃyājana* of the wives (8). It is the same up to the *samiṣṭayajus* (9). Having taken nine portions of clarified butter into the *juhū* ladle, he offers nine *samiṣṭayajus* oblations: six verses and three formulas from this section beginning with "May Dhātṛ, Rāti, and Savitṛ enjoy this" (*dhātā rātiḥ savitedaṃ juṣantām*).

He commences the ritual procedure for the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath). Having prepared the *veda* grass-bundle, having strewn around the fires, having washed his hands, having set out the vessels, having spread the *ulaparājī* grass-mat, and having made the two strainers (*pavitras*), he issues the command: "O Sacrificer, restrain your speech! (2) Restraining his speech, he touches the vessels. (3) He pours out the oblation on one potsherd for Varuṇa. (4) He bakes the sacrificial cake with water purified by a *yajus*-formula. (5) While the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is still spread, he pours out the flour-smear. (6) Having propped up the wooden sword (*sphya*), he issues the command.

"Place the *prokṣaṇī* waters; cleanse the *sruva* ladle and the *sruk* spoons; bring the clarified butter. (7) This is the same up to the taking of the clarified butter. (8) On this very altar he takes all the portions of clarified butter, each consisting of four scoops. (9) Having removed the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), he offers it into the *āhavanīya* fire with the verse: "O Agni, giver of life, enjoying the oblation... (10) Having offered, they take up the *avabhṛtha* materials: the wooden sword (*sphya*) together with the *sruva* ladle, the vessel for clarified butter, the *veda* grass-bundle, the sacrificial cake, the clarified butters, the *ṛjīṣa*, the two pressing-boards, the *khara* mound, the *pām̐sū* earth, and whatever else has been smeared with Soma.
It remains [available] except for the four vessels from which the Soma has been drawn. The sacrificer digs up a post made of Udumbara wood, saying:
"Bestowing support upon his mother, the supporter sucking at his mother;
may he establish for us abundance of wealth, food, and vigor."

Thus, with the verse, "O King Soma, that which they have cut from you with the pressing-stone," he offers the residue of the curdled milk (dadhyarjīṣa) over [the fire]. According to some, he offers over it with three verses; according to others, with five; according to others, with seven. He throws a black antelope skin into the *cātvāla* pit with the verse, "O Varuṇa, let thy wrath depart through our prostrations. Or rather, he may cause it to float away together with the *avabhṛtha* (purificatory bath). Then he issues the command: "O Prastotṛ, sing the *sāmans*! Together with his wife, they perform the finale (*nidhana*) of the *sāman* three times.

The first [altar] is prepared in the Middle Country, the second at the edge of the water, and the third on the bank. With the verse, "For King Varuṇa has made wide space," they proceed toward the altars. They approach the stationary *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) from the east, or from the north; according to some, from both the east and the north; according to others, from the south.

"Facing west," so say some (8). "The direction in which they go is the eastern direction (prācī dik)," (9). "A hundred physicians are yours, O King, a thousand," with these words they speak while looking back at the water (10). "Varuṇa’s noose has been stepped upon," with this verse they step onto the edge of the water (11). At this point, some prescribe the removal of the heart-spit (hṛdayaśūla) (12). Having plunged forward and standing [in the water], they perform the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) rite (13). Having poured the *sruva*-ladle libation, he issues the command: "O Āgnīdhra, cleanse the waters thrice! (14). The Āgnīdhra cleanses the waters thrice.

He cleanses [the waters] with the formula: "O waters, winners of the prize, whether you are about to flow for the prize or are about to win the prize—ye mighty ones, winners of the prize—I cleanse you for the winning of the prize; ye waters, eaters of food, for the sake of eating food. Thus he cleanses the waters. (15) 14.21 He pours the *āghāra* libation from the ladle over a blade of grass with the verse: "The face of Agni has entered the waters. Or, if there is already a blade of grass there, he offers upon that very spot. (2) He offers all the oblations upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). (3) [The procedure] is the same up to the invitation (*pravara*). (4) Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "Stay, O Hotṛ! (5)

This much is the *pravara* (5). He does not choose an *ārṣeya* nor a *hotṛ* (6). He performs four *prayāja* offerings excluding the one for the *barhis* (7). Having proceeded with the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, he takes a portion of the *puroḍāśa* and sacrifices to Varuṇa (8). Having taken the entire *puroḍāśa*, he sacrifices to Agnīvaruṇa as the *sviṣṭakṛt* (9). Then he issues the command: "O *agnīdh*, cleanse the waters once" (10). The *agnīdh* cleanses the waters once.

"O waters, winners of the prize, I cleanse you for the winning of the prize—you who have flowed toward the prize, who have won the prize, the prize-winning ones, the winners of the prize—for the sake of winning the prize; O waters, eaters of food, for the sake of eating food. Thus he cleanses the waters. (11) He performs two after-offerings (*anuyāja*) without the *barhis* grass. (12) "Sacrifice to the two gods!"—thus he gives the preliminary command for the first after-offering.

"Yaja" (Sacrifice), he says as the response. (13) Having filled the ladle with the *ṛjīṣa* (soma-residue), he dips it into the water, saying: "In the ocean is thy heart, within the waters. (14) Wherever a drop might rise up, there he should consume it, saying: "O divine Soma, of thee who art washed in the waters. (15) According to some, one should merely touch it. (16) He scatters [the residue] into the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) with the formula: "O *avabhṛtha*, O *nicaṅkuṇa*. (17) Having stepped forward and rinsed their mouths together with their heads, the sacrificer and his wife bathe. (18) They run over each other's backs, saying: "May the waters and plants be friendly to us. (19) 14.22

They approach the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) with the mantra: "O divine waters, this is your embryo. The sacrificer unties his girdle (*mekhalā*) with the mantra: "The bond of Varuṇa is loosened. The wife unties the noose of the cord (*yoktra*) with the mantra: "I loosen this bond of Varuṇa. At this very point, they both cast away all the marks of consecration (*dīkṣita-vyañjana*). Wearing two unwashed garments, they emerge from the *avabhṛtha*. The sacrificer puts on the Soma-cloth (*somopanahata*), and the wife puts on the Soma-enclosing cloth (*somapariśrayaṇa*). These two are given to the Adhvaryu at the *udavasānīyā* (concluding offering). Then he gives the command to the Unnetṛ: "O Unnetṛ, I draw up [the water] for you more abundantly."
Exalted, most honey-sweet songs and hymns go forth—
conquering all, winning wealth, providing inexhaustible aid, like chariots seeking booty. Like the Kaṇvas, like the Bhr̥gus, like suns, they have attained everything that is to be attained.
Thus the Unnetṛ leads out [the cups] for those headed by the Hotṛ, or for those headed by the Sacrificer:
"Arise, bestowing progeny and splendor; they have sent you forth toward wealth and sacrifices.
Embrace the Gāyatrī metre; then [be] fragrant in this house."

Thus [saying], they cast [the stone] toward the edge of the water while stepping up with the verse: "The noose of Varuṇa is released. (9) Having prepared the fuel-sticks, they return without looking back, preceded by the Unnetṛ, muttering the Mahīyā verses: "We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal; whatever debts I owe, whether paid or unpaid, which I discharge as tribute to Yama—remaining right here, we pay them back; living, we deliver this to the living. (10)
May we be free from debt in this world, free from debt in the next, and free from debt in the third world;
may we traverse all paths—those leading to the gods and those leading to the ancestors—free from debt.

"Thus: 'O fuel, may we prosper through thee'—having placed fuel-sticks on the Āhavanīya fire, they stand in worship with the mantra, 'I have followed the waters. (11) "In the same way, the wife, having placed [fuel] on the Gārhapatya fire, stands in worship.

(12) 14.23 "He commences the ritual procedure for the Udayanīyā offering. That which was the Prāyaṇīyā is also the Udayanīyā. There is this much difference: having poured the remnants of the Prāyaṇīyā into the vessel for the Udayanīyā, he cooks it. (2)

4. Here he does not take out the sacrificial porridge (caru) and set it down, nor does he perform the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ formula; they proceed with the concluding oblation (udayanīya) at the Śālāmukhīya fire. 5. He makes those verses which were the invitatory formulas (puronuvākyā) of the introductory oblation (prāyaṇīya) the offering formulas (yājyā) of the concluding oblation. 6. He performs the sacrifice to Pathyā Svasti as the last of the butter-portions (ājyabhāga). 7. The sacrificer does not eat the sacrificial food. 8. The sacrifice is completed in the established manner. 9. He commences the ritual procedure for the Anūbandhyā cow. 10. It is the same up to the bringing forward of the victim. 11. He brings forward the barren cow (vaśā) dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa as the Anūbandhyā. 12. Some [teachers] say there are three [such cows].

They prescribe: a two-colored cow for Mitrā-Varuṇa, a many-colored cow for the Viśve Devas, and a ruddy cow for Bṛhaspati. According to some, he proceeds with the offering of the cow for the Viśve Devas from the middle [of the altar]. (12) It is the same up to the offering of the omentum. (13) When the omentum has been offered, the sacrificer has his hair and beard shaved within an enclosure on the southern corner of the altar. (14) He subsequently offers the animal-cake of the Anūbandhyā cow and the oblations for the Devikās; these include a cake on twelve potsherds for Dhātṛ. (15) This is the last [offering].

He makes [the sacrificer] the supporter (dhātṛ). 16. In those same vessels in which the Soma juices are, they cook these charus. 17. The animal cake (paśupuroḍāśa) is accompanied by the formal summons (praiṣa). He issues the directions to the others: "Recite the invitatory verse! and "Offer the oblation! 18. For all of them, including the animal cakes, the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is common and accompanied by the summons; the *iḍā* portion is also common. 19. The animal sacrifice is thus completed. 20. 14.24.

Alternatively, one desiring cattle should prepare the *āmikṣā* for Mitra and Varuṇa as an optional alternative to the *anūbandhyā* cow. Prior to this, he has his hair and beard shaved. Sitting in front of the *havirdhāna* cart-shed, the *hotṛ* performs the sacrifice. Having proceeded with the oblations of the *devikā* deities, he proceeds with the offering for the deity of the *āmikṣā*. The rite concludes with the *iḍā* portion, beginning from the offering of the oblation. The *sviṣṭakṛt* and *iḍā* offerings for both the *āmikṣā* and the *devikā* oblations share the same ritual framework (*tantra*). Having untied the knots previously tied at the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna*, [he acts] at the *havirdhāna*.

They cause [the fire] to move toward the north. He burns the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) from the *āhavanīya* fire with the verse: "Whatever debt remains unpaid within me... (VS 12.59). If he should act as if mixed up, he should offer groats with his joined palms into the forest fire with the formula: "O all-consuming one, I offer thee into the mouth of the all-devouring fire" (VS 12.60). Thereafter, he worships the deities: with the verse "This one before us with the cloud... (VS 12.61) he worships either the *āhavanīya* or the forest fire; with "Thou, O Lord of the Cloud... (VS 12.62) he worships Vāyu.

He offers the Udavasānīya sacrifice, consisting of a cake on five potsherds dedicated to Agni, or one on eight potsherds. If it is the eight-potsherd offering, there are two *ṛc*s in the *paṅkti* metre for the *yājyā* and *anu-vākyā*; if it is the five-potsherd offering, they are in the *gāyatrī* metre. An ox is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). The sacrifice concludes in the prescribed manner if he does not hurry. Now, if he should hurry, having taken four spoonfuls of clarified butter into the *juhū* ladle, he should offer it into the *āhavanīya* fire with the verse, "O Viṣṇu, stride out widely. Whatever he may be able to give there, that he should give. That sacrifice lasts as long as the night.

It concludes on that very night; he should offer the evening *agnihotra* at its proper time, and the morning *agnihotra* at its proper time. From the *udayanīyā* offering onwards, the remainder of the sacrifice (*yajñapuccha*) is performed. The pressing day (*sutyā*) concludes on the same day. Now, if the pressing were to extend beyond the time for the *agnihotra*, one should offer back the missed *agnihotra* oblations, beginning with the evening *agnihotra*.

Or rather, he should not offer the counter-oblations (pratijuhoti). 10. A king or one who holds royal power who sacrifices with Soma offers the oblations of the Devasū offerings. 11. For these, the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) has been explained in the Rājasūya, except for the seizing of the elephant, the announcement, and the wiping of the mouth. 12. Every spring, one should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. It is known that its sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are threefold. 13. The Jyotiṣṭoma is concluded; the Jyotiṣṭoma is concluded. 14. 14.26.
Thus ends the fourteenth book. Now begins the fifteenth book.

Some [teachers] say that the Brahman priest must be a descendant of Vasiṣṭha; however, it is known from the sacred tradition that one may also appoint someone who is not a descendant of Vasiṣṭha, provided he knows the portions belonging to himself. When the King [Soma] is being measured or purchased, [the Brahman] sits to the south. When he is being carried away, he goes to the south. When the Great Altar (mahāvedi) or the High Altar (uttaravedi) is being prepared, he sits to the south. When they are about to cleanse the Sadas and Havirdhāna sheds, he goes between the Cātvāla pit and the Utkara heap, passes around the northern edge of the altar, and enters by the eastern door.

Having first entered by the eastern door, passed beyond the Āhavanīya fire from the west, gone out by the eastern door, and walked around the southern edge of the altar, one should sit to the south of the Uttaravedi; so says Āśmarathya.

Ālekhana says that one should go between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, pass beyond the northern edge of the *uttaravedi*, and sit down to the south. He remains right there until the *vaisarjana* oblations are offered. When they are about to offer the *vaisarjana* oblations, Āśmarathya says that one should go around to the south of the two *havirdhāna* sheds, to the south of the *mārjālīya*, and to the south of the *sadas*; then, having entered by the eastern door toward the east, and having passed in front of the *śālāmukhīya*, one should sit down to the south.

Having crossed over the Uttaravedi with the *apra* formula, having gone around to the north of the two *havirdhāna* sheds, to the north of the *Āgnīdhrīya*, and to the north of the *Sadas*, and having entered the *Vamśa* through the eastern door and passed beyond the *Śālāmukhīya* fire, he should sit down to the south; so says Ālekhana. 8.15.1.

Brahman places the King [Soma] upon his lap. When the *vaisarjana* oblation has been offered, he proceeds behind the fire. Having reached the *āgnīdhrīya* shed and handed over the King to the *pratiprasthātṛ*, and having returned by the same way he came, he goes out by the eastern door, passes to the south of the *sadas* and to the south of the *mārjālīya*, and sits down to the south of the *āgnīdhrīya*; so says Āśmarathya.

"Having gone around this very fire from the north, one should sit down to the south," says Ālekhana. (3) The Brahman places the King [Soma] on his lap. (4) When the Vaisarjana oblation has been offered, he goes forward first. (5) Having reached the two Havirdhāna sheds and handed over the King to the Pratiprasthātṛ, having gone around the south of the Havirdhānas, one should sit down to the south of the Uttaravedi; so says Āśmarathya.

Ālekhana says that he should pass to the north of the two *havirdhāna* sheds and to the west of the *uttaravedi*, and then sit down to the south. He remains right there until the offering of the omentum (*vapā*) of the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma. When the omentum has been offered, he purifies himself at the place where they perform the purification. 15.2.8–9.

Where they are about to take up the Vasatīvarī waters, he goes to the south of that place; he remains to the south while the waters are being taken up. Where they wake for the Prātaranuvāka, he wakes there. His path of movement is the same as that of those who are about to cleanse the Sadas and Havirdhāna sheds. Once the Prātaranuvāka has been commenced, he restrains his speech until the concluding verse (paridhānīyā). Where they are about to take up the Savanīya waters, he goes to the south of that place; he remains to the south while the waters are being taken up, and [to the south] while they are being brought forward.

He goes to the south (8). When they are about to press the King [Soma], he enters the *havirdhāna* shed by the eastern door, passes in front of the *khara* mound, and sits down to the south (9). He remains seated to the south while the King is being measured and while the pressing is taking place (10). While the cups (*graha*) are being drawn, he restrains his speech until the *āgrayaṇa* cup (11). In this very same manner, at each pressing, he sits to the south while the King is being pressed and restrains his speech while the cups are being drawn (12), [until] the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant.
Having been touched by them, he creeps along. He sits down to the south of those who are about to chant the praise.

When they address him, saying, "O Praśāstṛ, we shall chant the praise as the Brahman," then he gives the impulse: "Him! O God Savitṛ, this has been declared to you; impel it and perform the sacrifice! Bṛhaspati is the Brahman. Do not depart from the long-lived Ṛc, nor from the body-protecting Sāman. May your blessings be true, may your intentions be true. Speak Ṛta and Satya. Praise at the impulse of the god Savitṛ!"

"You are a ray; for dwelling, I impel you, the dweller; may I be praised"—with these words he gives the impulse for each stotra in this very manner. In this way, he places each subsequent *stomabhāga* formula higher than the preceding one. There are twelve in the *agniṣṭoma*, thirteen in the *atyagniṣṭoma*, fifteen in the *ukthya*, sixteen in the *ṣoḍaśin*, seventeen in the *vājapeya*, and twenty-nine in the *atirātra*.

"It is known [from scripture] that there are thirty-three [stotras] in the Aptoryāma. 4. When the Bahiṣpavamāna has been chanted, he steps across behind the Uttaravedi and sits down to the south. He remains right there until the offering of the omentum (vapā) of the Savanīya animal. 5. When the omentum has been offered, he purifies himself at the place where they perform the purification (mārjana). 6. Where they proceed toward the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana), he goes to the south of the two Havirdhāna carts, to the south of the Mārjālīya fire, and to the south of the Sadas; having passed around by the rear door, he enters the Sadas from the west.

"One should pass by the seat of the *praśāstṛ* and sit down to the south," says Āśmarathya. "One should pass behind the *uttaravedi*, go north of the two *havirdhāna* sheds, circumambulate the *mārjālīya* fire-altar to the south, enter the *sadas* by the eastern door, pass in front of the seat of the *praśāstṛ*, and sit down to the south," says Ālekhana.
By this [method], it applies to the two subsequent pressings (*savana*).
Thus ends the fifteenth question.
